\n“许家三娘歌声婉转，一定能讨得天子与贵妃欢喜。”\n教坊使的赞美她从来不敢相:
"Xu Sanniang has a voice like silk. Surely she'll charm both the Emperor and the Noble Consort." 
Sanniang never dared believe the overseer's praise. 
"One wrong note, and His Majesty will hear it at once." The Masked Troupe existed by imperial will; in matters of music, no one surpassed the Emperor's ear. There was simply no room for mistakes. 
For first‑time performers entering the palace, lifting one's head was unthinkable. 
Sanniang trembled so hard she barely knew what to do with her hands and feet. 
"She's thirteen—still just a little one." 
The Noble Consort said, her voice warm and gentle, pitched with perfect grace. Sanniang risked a glance upward. She saw a soft, dimpled smile—like spring light spilling over a garden in bloom. 

The Emperor wished to present a new composition, a song he wanted the troupe to sing for the Consort. 
It was said to be based on a village tune collected by wandering song‑gatherers—a melody about a young man longing for the one he loves, sleepless and restless. 
A man who ruled the world, able to bestow treasures beyond imagining—yet here he was, imitating the shy earnestness of a common boy, offering his heart a little awkwardly. 

Sanniang sang with exquisite care. She knew she wasn't bad—but she wasn't truly good either. 
In the Music Bureau, "not perfect" meant "wrong." 
As she waited for judgment, the words came: "Child, come here." 
She nearly stepped on her hem as she stumbled forward. 
The Noble Consort let out a soft laugh and placed a bright red fruit into her palm, saying she was delighted. 

Whatever the Emperor said afterward faded into a blur. It almost sounded as though he was asking what reward she desired— 
his voice low, authoritative, yet tinged with something gentler, almost coaxing. 
Around her, performers bowed, accepted their rewards, and withdrew. Spring was left to the Emperor and his beloved alone. 

Born into a family of musicians, chosen and welcomed into the Imperial Music Bureau—everything had unfolded as naturally as water flowing downhill. 
And as she stepped through the palace gates once more, Sanniang realized, quietly and to her own surprise: Perhaps she truly did love to sing.

\n一曲惊舟湖上，不知归梦难留。玉京多情故人，弦上话说从头。\n\n像江逸这样弱:
The zither's music spreads across the lake in gentle waves, a quiet sigh for how fate—not we—decides our meetings and farewells. In the capital, old bonds run deep, and through each lingering note, the stories of the past are softly told anew. 

Jiang Yi, though barely twenty, is already a virtuoso on countless instruments. By all rights, he could be arrogant—but he's not. To him, music is simply another language. What words cannot fully express, melodies carry with graceful ease. So naturally, he spends his days immersed in music, only gradually realizing others regard him as a "musical prodigy." Yet this language he speaks is rare, a dialect known to few, and most days, Jiang Yi feels like a wanderer far from home. 
That's why, when Velvet Shade invited him to perform at Revelry Hall and enjoy a night of music, Jiang was genuinely delighted. He knew Velvet Shade was closely connected with Grace Pavilion—a place famed for its masterful musicians and exquisite instruments—and so he hurried over without a moment's delay. 

It was a perfect day. On the flower-laden boat approaching Revelry Hall, Jiang could hardly contain himself; he stood at the bow, and the moment they reached shore, he leapt off the boat. Guided inside Grace Pavilion, he hadn't even caught sight of anyone before the sound of a flute reached his ears. 
His senses sharpened, yet a weight settled in his chest. The flute's tone was crystal clear, the technique flawless, and its timbre brilliantly radiant. But beneath that shining clarity lingered a profound sorrow, a hidden ache. Jiang didn't know who the player was or what trials he had endured, but the sadness in that music touched him deeply. 
He stood quietly behind the flutist, watching in silence as the melody unfolded. The man was slender, yet the breath behind his flute filled the room with a power that seemed to pierce through the skies. When the flutist finally turned and caught sight of Jiang, he startled, asking softly who the newcomer was. 

He had meant only to say, "I'm Jiang Yi, invited to perform at Revelry Hall," but the words caught in his throat, swept away by a sudden surge of emotion—like the quiet thrill of a boat drawing close to shore. Instead, he rushed to a nearby zither and let his hands speak for him. As the melody unfurled, the quiet ache he had heard in that flute earlier wove itself naturally into his playing. When the final note faded, he finally raised his head. The flutist was already seated opposite him at the zither bench, asking, "Does this piece have a name?" 
Jiang found his voice. "I just played what came to me." 
"There's the delicate longing of someone returning home, the vast breath of mountains and seas; a touch of the beauty in the moonlit sea, and the freedom of life flowing on through countless generations. What do you think of calling it ‘Dream of Mountains and Seas'?" 
Jiang considered it and then nodded. "It's a beautiful name." 
The man suddenly added, "So, you are Jiang Yi." 
"I am. And you, sir?" 
He didn't answer. He only smiled. "I named your piece. Shouldn't you name mine?" 
"I'm not good at naming things. I'm not good with words at all. That's why I let the music speak." 
"Ah. And you speak it well." The flutist tapped lightly on the hand Jiang still rested on the strings. 
"Master, how can you tease an honored guest like that!" A lively young voice cut in. A girl, still with a touch of youthful innocence, stepped into the room. "Master Jiang, you disappeared in an instant—I see you found the pavilion master all on your own." 
Jiang suddenly realized, "So this is the master of Grace Pavilion—no wonder the flute sounded so captivating." 
The master smiled, "Do you think you're on equal footing with me, Master Jiang?" 
Jiang quickly cupped his hands respectfully, "Far from it, Master Han." 
"Please, no need for such formalities—just call me Han Wei. Yuming, has Master Jiang's lodging been arranged?" 
"All taken care of," replied Ling Yuming, raising an intrigued brow. "Earlier, I caught the sound of a zither downstairs—bold and free, quite unlike your usual style. So it was Master Jiang? Truly exquisite." 
Han chuckled, "Are you implying my playing is stingy?" 
Ling teased gently, "Not nearly as grand as Master Jiang's." 
Blushing, Jiang hurried to interrupt, "You flatter me too much. I simply happen to know more instruments... As the young master of Grace Pavilion, Master Han outperforms me by far." 
Ling sighed with a smile, "Listen to that—‘just happen to know more instruments.' Hearing geniuses speak so modestly can frustrate the rest of us." 
Jiang's eyes widened as he waved his hands nervously, "No, no, not at all! Miss, your fingers are long and graceful—perfect for playing. You could never be ordinary!" 
Han laughed heartily, "Master Jiang may master many instruments, but he sure is shy of his words!" 
Taking their teasing in stride, Jian smiled softly, "Still, it's your flute, Master Han, that truly speaks—the words music cannot express." 
Han fell silent, a thoughtful look crossing his face. 
A delicate floral fragrance drifted through the hall. Before Jiang's arrival, rain had swept through the capital. Now, under clear skies and a gentle breeze weaving between the tall buildings, the lingering echoes of music filled the air. At this moment, the promise of the legendary "Ten Ballads of Pearlglow Lake" had yet to be made; Han was not yet withdrawn from the world; Jiang had not yet retreated into seclusion; and Ling was far from the wistful Flower Messenger she would become. Those unmatched melodies were still nameless, spontaneous creations, and the shadows of inevitable loss and sorrow lay quietly in wait, claws yet concealed. 
It was, in truth, a perfect day.

\n与庸人共事二三法：\n\n昔谓世多庸人，任匠首统建墨守之心方知，然也。\n与:
A Few Principles for Working with the Mediocre:

They say the world is full of mediocre fools. I only truly realized this after becoming the head artisan overseeing the construction of the Changeless Heart. It is absolutely true.
When dealing with the mediocre: First, never be direct. Second, never argue. Third, never spare the details. Fourth, never hold out any expectations.
I must compile a manual and force everyone to memorize it thoroughly. Opening sluice gates, measuring water levels, erecting weirs. Why must they bother me with every single triviality?
\n世上有没有眼睛的人，有没有良心的人，你说心和眼睛哪个更重要，很多人都说，心最:
In this world, there are those without eyes, and those without conscience. Tell me, which matters more, the heart or the eyes? Most would say the heart.
 But those without conscience thrive, while those without eyes suffer.
 This isn't fair.
 Storybooks don't write it this way. They tell of heroes punishing villains, emperors loving their people, bad men getting their due, good souls reuniting.
 So Ran couldn't understand.

 She couldn't understand why Uncle Sun moved away, why shop signs were smashed one after another, why Grannie Liu's face was wet with tears, why the streets roared with chaos, why Ren Xiaoping sobbed into his mother's arms louder than ever, why her father had gone to buy lotus pastries and never returned...
 She doesn't like this ending. Nobody likes this ending. Why should an ending nobody likes exist?

 She couldn't understand why when she says these truths, people who used to laugh now stay silent. When she angrily asks, they always say: "Ran isn't wrong." But now they just stayed silent.
 Can right things be mocked? Or must they go unanswered?
 She couldn't understand why people once laughed at her Gold Leaf Swordsman stories, but after her father vanished, they'd listen in silence.
 Did her father's disappearance make them stop loving this story?

 These are things the storybooks never wrote about.
 This wasn't how it should be. Uncle Sun shouldn't have left. The shop should always teem with hot meals. The kitchen fire should never die. Grannie Liu's cheeks shouldn't glisten with tears. Ren Xiaoping, for all his mischief, shouldn't wail like his heart was breaking. The river by her door should flow forever, and her father should have never walked away.

I write to express my deep gratitude for the "Militia Training Manual" you presented to me days ago, and to share a few findings regarding this text.

You recovered this volume from the water, and though many of its pages suffered severe damage that will require time to restore, its contents are simply astounding. Even upon a brief reading, I was struck by its unprecedented foresight. It is truly a gem of military theory.

The various strategies and ingenious methods detailed within are of the highest caliber, well worth a thorough and formal study by everyone here in Mohist City.

Furthermore, the book mentions bizarre yet fascinating mechanisms such as "flying vessels" and "fire-spitting tubes." These concepts are entirely unexpected and remarkably imaginative. I am profoundly intrigued and cannot help but wonder: who is the true author of this book? To possess such transcendent wisdom!

When you have the time, I urge you to keep a close watch near the site where this book was discovered. Please continue searching for any clues regarding its owner's origins.

\n夜深了，天工阁内仍灯火通明。\n“邹师兄，还不走啊，早点休息啊。”路过的师弟:
The night had deepened, yet Divinecraft Pavilion remained brightly lit. 
"Senior Brother Zou, still here? You should get some rest," a passing junior called out with concern. 
"He's still revising his paper—let's not disturb him," another whispered softly. 
"Senior Brother Zou, I'm heading off. I left the key where I always do. Don't forget to lock up." 
Zou smiled warmly in reply. 
Zou isn't the head disciple of the Mohist Hill. In fact, he's not even a core disciple, just an ordinary outer one. Still, whenever his name comes up, everyone from the elders to Buster speaks highly of him. 
The reason was simple: he treated everyone with sincere kindness. No matter the request, if anyone sought his help, Zou gave his all—never hesitant, never turning anyone away. 
But even a man like him had someone he'd been estranged from for seventeen years. 
Though calling it hatred was too strong—Yang never spoke of Zou, and the two quietly avoided each other whenever chance might bring them face to face. 
What no one knew was that Yang, the carefree storyteller, and Zou, the most admired senior among outer disciples, had once been inseparable friends. 

Seventeen years ago, the peach grove by the sparkling waters of Jadestream Valley had yet to bloom into the lush sea of blossoms it is now. 
In early spring, peach branches stretched gently over the water, their delicate pink buds like scattered rouge on vibrant green silk. 
Sixteen-year-old Zou walked deeper into the forest, a worn book satchel slung over his shoulder, his shoes damp from the morning dew kissing the grass beneath his feet. Suddenly, a clear, melodious voice drifted down from above:
"The east wind wakes the peach blossom rain,
The bright moon lights the jade-green waves." 
He paused, lifted his gaze, and spotted a slender youth perched among the branches of a peach tree. His faded blue shirt was worn thin and frayed at the cuffs, and he clutched a yellowed scroll of poetry. Catching sight of Zou, the boy smiled and raised the scroll. "You like poetry too?" 
Zou bowed politely, about to introduce himself. "I am Zou Yizhou…" 
But as he bent forward, a tiny wild boar poked its snout from the satchel. Blinking its bright eyes, the little creature clumsily scrambled free and darted off into the woods. 
The boy burst into laughter. "Hahaha! Who hides a wild piglet inside their book satchel instead of books? Truly one of a kind!" 
His laughter ringing through the grove, the boy gracefully leapt down, returning Zou's bow with a playful grin. Noticing ink stains on his fingertips, he casually wiped them on the hem of his robe. "I'm Yang Qianyan. Just tossing together a few stray lines of poetry. Looks like I've made fools of both you and your piglet friend." 
Zou watched the boar disappear into the underbrush, then glanced back at Yang, who was still chuckling. He hurried to explain, "I only tucked it in the satchel to keep it from running wild..." He couldn't help but laugh too—the idea of a book satchel turned pigsty was absurdly charming. 
When the laughter settled, Yang clapped him on the shoulder with genuine warmth. "Whether it's books or boars, you're the first I've known to carry a wild pig in a satchel." He waved the scroll playfully. "Those lines I just read aren't finished yet. You seem to have an ear for poetry—care to help me refine them?" 
For a thousand years, the Mohist Hill disciples prized mechanical ingenuity above all else—poetry, prose, and song had fallen into neglect. Because of this, the two young men connected instantly, as if old friends reunited. 
Zou confessed he lacked any real talent for mechanics but found joy in writing tales of legends, strange creatures, and the supernatural. To keep this secret from their master, he adopted a pen name. Still, he was caught and scolded for neglecting his proper duties. Yang laughed and said, "Funny enough, I'm a complete novice when it comes to mechanics, and even the master wouldn't take me in. All I do is write bitter little poems. If you want, you can use my name for your stories—I don't mind. I can even craft poems and notes to accompany them." 
As the sun dipped westward, Zou grew anxious—the little wild boar had yet to return. 
Yang took his hand and led him toward the forest's edge. "Don't worry—I saw it wander south earlier. There's fresh grass there; it's probably resting nearby." 
Sure enough, they found the boar curled in a patch of warm sunlight on a hillside by the fields, dozing with bits of grass stuck at its mouth. Zou gently lifted the creature, which softly snuffled and nestled against his chest. Watching this, Yang smiled and said, "Zou, I believe your first tale of legends should be about this wild boar." 
They laughed together, their joy echoing through the grove. 

From that day on, the peach grove became their treasured refuge. 
They dreamed of the day the mountain would reopen, when they could journey across the land like the great poets of old—one writing verses, the other composing replies. 
And they vowed to open a bookstore beyond the mountain, a place where their stories and poems could live and breathe, together. 
"I've heard Kaifeng City is the liveliest place around," Yang said as he copied out the latest manuscript. "When the time comes, let's open our bookstore right at the busiest street corner—and plant two peach trees at the doorway, ones we bring all the way from the mountains." Their stories had already become wildly popular deep within the mountains. 
Zou smiled and nodded, then penned four characters on the paper: Qian Jin Bu Yi—"Priceless and Rare." "That will be the sign above our shop." 
The "Qian" from Yang, the "Yi" from Zou. 
Together in one boat, priceless and rare. 
They were young then, believing such days would stretch on forever—that the peach blossoms by the crystal-clear Jadestream Valley would bloom again next spring—that they would share countless stories side by side—that the little wild boar would one day grow into a mighty beast. 
That was the spring seventeen years ago. 
Later, a few weathered, fragile scripts were found tucked away in a forgotten corner of Divinecraft Pavilion. The poems inside bore the name Yang Qianyan, and pressed between the pages were a few strands of boar's bristles. 
One disciple held the books and asked, "Senior Brother Zou, who exactly is this Yang Qianyan? Have you met him?" 
"I have. Long ago."

\n我本该死在那一日的。\n在那日之前，我是江南最负盛名的商贾上官家最受宠爱的嫡:
I should have died that day.

Before that day, I was the cherished daughter of the most renowned merchant family in Jiangnan, the favored young mistress of the Shangguan household.
My father cradled me in the palm of his hand, granting my every wish. Even if I had asked for the moon, he would have tried to fetch it for me.
I truly believed I would live out my life in such bliss.

One day, my father returned home from a journey, and everything changed. He brought back a girl my age, and from that moment on, he was no longer the man I knew. He told me that this girl, named Bai Yu, was his true daughter, and that I was merely the child of a lowly servant. That servant, seeking a better life for her own child, had swapped me into the family. The happy years I had stolen... were never truly mine.

I refused to believe it. I tried everything to prove my place, only to make a fool of myself again and again. Father did not cast me out immediately after all these years we lived together. But the warmth that was once in his eyes had turned to cold glances.

On my birthday, though perhaps it no longer belonged to me. The house was adorned with lanterns and banners, all to celebrate the true young mistress of the Shangguan family. Meanwhile, I was left abandoned and forgotten. Bai Yu found me, she stood before me in splendid robes and delicate makeup, draped in everything that once belonged to me. Yet she was not arrogant. She was gentle, yet tinged with sorrow. She said she could not bear to see me so pitiful, urged me to behave well at the banquet. If I did, she would plead on my behalf, and perhaps Father, remembering the past, might show me kindness once more.

I believed her. But the banquet became a nightmare. The pastries I had thoughtfully prepared nearly killed Bai Yu. As Father stared at his dying daughter, all the tolerance he had left for me is gone. He expelled me from the Shangguan household. I became nothing more than a rat in the streets, shunned and despised. With nowhere to go, I wandered to the edge of a dry well, thinking perhaps that was where my story should end.

But it was then that a man named A'Sheng got hold of me.

A Critique on the "Illustrated Evolution of Mohist Hydraulic Systems":

It is obsessed with completeness but clumsy in thought, biased toward the minute while lacking a grand vision. It exhaustively records a century's worth of mechanisms, rendering further analysis unnecessary, for the evolution of its principles has already laid itself bare.
Yet water is a thing of constant change; it cannot be confined to a single time or place. If one does not act, so be it. But if one must act, one must calculate the four seasons, delineate the square and the circle, connect ten thousand miles, and secure the eight desolate corners of the realm.
In antiquity, Yu the Great dredged the world's waters and left behind methods for ten thousand generations. As for us men of today, having inherited the wisdom of the sages and possessing the aid of mechanical arts, if we fail to establish an unprecedented legacy, have we not read our myriad scrolls in vain? We must rise and emulate his greatness!

\n按道理，阿九是不该和昙香这种醉花阴弟子走得太近的。\n这人处处招摇，处处留情:
By all logic, Ajiu shouldn't be growing so close to someone like Tanxiang, a Velvet Shade disciple. 
Tanxiang is a restless spirit—flamboyant and flirtatious, yet somehow careless. She appears suddenly and vanishes even quicker, leaving behind only a faint, lingering fragrance that stirs bittersweet longing. Take today, for instance: it was clearly Tanxiang who invited Ajiu to a quiet drink in her quarters, yet she still hasn't arrived. 
Ajiu has silently wrestled with her frustrations toward Tanxiang countless times. Yet each time, she catches herself thinking—after all, this is how Velvet Shade disciples are. Perhaps she's off meeting some secret beloved. What's the point in resenting her? And yet, inexplicably, it's Tanxiang who stirs the deeper waves of annoyance in her heart. 

One day, beneath the blossom-laden tree at Heaven's Pier, Ajiu witnessed Tanxiang trying to recruit a dashing wanderer into Velvet Shade. She intervened, gently urging the wanderer to join the Masked Troupe instead. But to her surprise, after that day Tanxiang began shadowing her, lingering close—sometimes commenting on songs and dances, other times rehearsing scripts at her side. Like twin blossoms, they grew inseparable, their days entwined. 
Within the Masked Troupe, mastery of dance and music is prized above all. But for Velvet Shade, song and dance carry a weight of emotion and longing. Ajiu usually heard Tanxiang's perspectives that diverged beautifully from the sober teachings of the Masked Troupe. 
Theatrical styles and customs may differ, but their spirit is unified. When Tanxiang critiques a performance or a script, she seems to shed her usual languid charm, revealing a keener, more vibrant intensity—almost as if she were someone else entirely. In those fleeting moments, Ajiu would find herself quietly gazing at her, struck by Tanxiang's complexity, leaving her heart guessing and yearning. 
Noticing her stare, Tanxiang looked up, a knowing smile playing at her lips: "Why do you look at me like that, sweetheart? Did I say something wrong?" 
Ajiu blinked, caught off guard. "No, you're right... It's just that when I see you like this, I find myself speechless." 
Tanxiang laughed then, a soft, genuine sound that seemed to melt into Ajiu's very soul as she leaned in—willingly close—no matter how she tried to gently push her away. 
Everyone in the Masked Troupe said Tanxiang's charm was merely a flirtatious trick—a playful game Velvet Shade disciples liked to play on unsuspecting Masked Troupe novices like Ajiu. Yet every time Tanxiang extended an invitation, all it took was one glance into those softly smiling, cat-like eyes for Ajiu's resolve to melt away. 
Well, perhaps it was for the best. To walk the world and taste its joys and sorrows—that was part of a Masked Troupe disciple's true cultivation. 

Outside the window, flower shadows danced in gentle chaos, petals drifting around the trees, stirred again by the whisper of the breeze. 
Ajiu frowned, eyes fixed on the dense storybook before her, but no matter how hard she tried, she couldn't focus. The love and longing in the words seemed to rise and scatter into the sky, while her heart was filled with something altogether different—something tangled and restless, impossible to unravel. 
Her gaze lifted from the crowded lines to a solitary petal drifting slowly outside, floating down to rest on the ground. Why had she arrived so late today? Was she not coming at all? 
Enough, enough! Ajiu scolded herself, shaking her head firmly. She couldn't let her thoughts wander this way, not again. 
—No. The story before her, the script in her hands—that's what truly mattered. 
"Ding-ling, ding-ling." 
The familiar jingle caught her ear, and she looked up without thinking. Tanxiang brushed stray petals from her robes, her smile gentle and radiant, as graceful as the first time they met—like a living statue carved from porcelain. 
In her hand, a single pure white pear blossom, carrying with it a soft, fragrant snowfall. 
Spring stretches long, and busy swallows soar across the sky. 
If she could spend a lifetime beside the woman in front of her, then how much of their bond was impatience, tenderness, admiration, or love—it no longer made any difference. In the end, it was simply enough.
\n时值暮秋，苦风萧瑟。\n他单衫草鞋，走在不熟悉的山路上，瑟缩慢步。\n“家”:
It was late autumn, and the wind had turned sharp and bitter. 
Dressed in a thin shirt and straw sandals, he made his way down an unfamiliar mountain path, shivering as he walked. 
There was no "home" left to return to. And the shed his distant relatives had given him wasn't even enough to keep out the rain, let alone the wind. 
Down below, the lights of the valley flickered through the mist, growing fainter the farther he went—as if he were looking up at the world from the bottom of a lake. 

He thought of the masked general on the stage, alone in a sea of soldiers, carving a path through countless foes. 
A song could not keep the darkness at bay. Worse, it might draw the attention of mountain beasts or passing bandits. 
But none of that mattered to him now. 
His heartbeat pounded like the war drums from that day, the general surging forward, fearless and unshaken. 

He ran—toward the distant glow of firelight. 
As the glow deepened, he began to hear it: the spiraling notes of a pipa, the cheers and cries of the crowd. 
It was his second time standing before the stage. 
Though the season was one of withered grass and falling leaves, the moment before he closed his eyes, he saw pear blossoms—thousands of them—snowing down from unseen branches. 

"We breathe lightning. 
I grasp thunder above my head, grind stone soft beneath my feet. Strength in my right hand, 
command in my left. When the sun sets in the west, the east rises silver as the moon. 
Beat the drums—let the long song roll." 

Gu Qiuhua, a native of Huzhou, was born with music in his bones. 
As a child, he was saved by Cheng Su of the Masked Troupe and later joined the Pavilion of Returning Snow. His talent was unmatched, his voice clear and bright—
and of all his performances, none surpassed The Prince Enters the Formation.
\n有墨者自北方来，称有救天下策。延广闻之，盛邀入府。\n\n初，墨者入府，处事:
A Mohist arrived from the North, claiming to possess a grand strategy to save the world. Hearing of this, Jing Yanguang lavishly invited him into his estate.

At first, the Mohist carried himself with arrogance, proposing several schemes to Guang. None were accepted, and he prepared to leave. Yanguang then made a wager: if the Mohist could recreate the legendary Deheng's Spectacle Puppet and have it run for ten days without stopping, his strategy would be adopted. The Mohist agreed and completed the work in a month. The mechanism ran for nine days without pause, but on the tenth day, when the Mohist asked for funds to repair the Yellow River canals, Yanguang laughed heartily. He led the Mohist to see the puppet; its gears had jammed, and the machine had collapsed. Bewildered, the Mohist inspected it, only to find a single wooden peg that did not fit the design. Yanguang made another wager: if the Mohist could drink a hundred jars of wine within the estate, his strategy would be accepted.

What a laughable farce! I wonder, did that Mohist manage to drain all a hundred jars?

Did Yanguang truly wish to save the world? He merely sought to present a novelty to the Emperor to regain royal favor!

Did the Emperor truly wish to save the world? Calling himself a "grandson" to the Khitans, gaining no real advantage yet recklessly provoking a war, all just to make a name in history!

Did the Mohist truly wish to save the world? The idea that clever trinkets and mechanics can save the world is unheard of!

Looking back, they were little more than liars driven by fame and profit, putting on an elaborate performance to deceive the commoners. National strategy? People's welfare? World salvation? What good does it do you? What good does it do me? It is all just a joke, like ramblings of a dream.
\n李筠给她做了她最爱吃的菜，招招手让她过来的那个下午，日光极好，她看向父亲的眼:
It was a sunny afternoon when Li Jun cooked her favorite dishes and beckoned her over. Gazing into her father's softer-than-usual eyes, she decided she wouldn't quarrel with him today. "What is it?"
Then she heard the absurd proposal: Her father had decided to give her a new father.
"Why not? You get along with Murong Yanzhao! You even call him 'Father'... We're father and daughter by fate, but we clash. You suffer with me..."
"I'm doing this for your own good."

She didn't understand.
But more than that, she wanted to share his hardships. She was used to them by now.
Her pride wouldn't let her say this. That night, she stormed out without glancing at her father or younger brother.

At first, she marched swiftly, then slowed, then began looking back. With every step, she never doubted someone would come for her. Surely her father would follow.
But no one came.

Two hours passed. Her legs felt leaden. After half a day, she forced herself not to turn around. As she trudged toward Mohist Hill, her anger cooled, and the spark of hope in her chest died.
Finally, she accepted the truth: she'd been abandoned. Her feet ached, but she shed no tears.

This road is so hard to walk, she thought.
No, it isn't the road. It's the waiting that hurts. The hoping. If I could just stop expecting someone to come for me, maybe the road wouldn't feel so long. 

From that day on, she stopped hoping. Hope, she realized, is harder to carry than the road itself.

\n狼山的第一场雪，还是落下了。\n魏芷昔蜷缩在背风的山洞内，耳边充斥风声与隐约:
The first snow of Wolf Mountain still came, in the end.
Wei Zhixi curled up inside a sheltered cave, the wind howling outside, faint cries echoing in the night.
But what she kept seeing, over and over, was the night she first met him, a rundown temple, wind and rain, dust swirling, cobwebs everywhere... a truly miserable beginning.
But that had all been by her own design.
Her father used to say that in troubled times, he couldn't protect her forever.
Her mother said a woman needed someone she could rely on.
That's why they arranged a meeting she never wanted.
She'd always scoffed at that.
Some birds, she thought, are born to fly.
No one can make them fall.

And yet, in this first snowfall on Wolf Mountain, she found herself thinking about that man again.
She remembered how carefully he chose his words, how cautious he was; she remembered the way the firelight flickered over his half-hidden face.
She hadn't really disliked him, even then.
He was nothing like her. He had grand ambitions, to govern, to bring peace to the world. She, on the other hand, only longed for freedom, to live by the sword and roam wherever she pleased.

But there was something steady about him, something that made her feel safe. Yes, steadiness. He'd listened patiently to all her tales of Jianghu, watched her ride off again and again without a word of complaint, always waiting for her return at every ferry. Even now, facing what might be their final parting, he remained the same.
"I have to get that Canglang Sword Manual. I won't be stopped!"
"How long will you be gone this time?"
"I don't know. If the snow blocks the mountain passes... who knows when I'll be back." She regretted those words as soon as she spoke them. She'd always left plenty of room for retreat, never once making a promise. But he'd always waited for her... and suddenly, she felt she shouldn't take that for granted anymore.
"Maybe... don't wait for me this time?"
Outside the temple, the rain poured down. Inside, the fire flickered. He was silent for a moment, then simply handed her a roasted sweet potato. "It's hot. Eat slowly."

That was the last time they parted. She never truly knew how he felt, but she'd made up her mind not to see him again when she returned. But with the Khitan invading and people displaced, she'd grown tired of her journey. And after exhaustion came longing.

The wind and snow still howled outside. But for a moment, everything seemed to pause.
Wei Zhixi felt it and looked up. The man who should have been a thousand miles away, who should have been leading his troops to pacify Huainan, was standing right there.
"I've come to take you home," he said.
Wei Zhixi was quiet for a moment, then smiled.
This time, the wild bird wanted to return to its nest.

\n第一次经过戏台的时候，父亲带着他，行路匆匆。\n见孩子停下了脚步，父亲皱眉叹:
The first time they passed the little roadside stage, his father was striding ahead, intent on getting where they were going. 
When the boy hesitated, the man stopped, frowned, and let out a long sigh. "...Fine. One performance." 

Masked Troupe disciples rarely visited a town this small. Whenever their music drifted through the streets, it brought more joy than the New Year ever did. 
But in times like these, when a full stomach was already a luxury, festivals had lost their shine. A single play, a single song—those were what comforted the living now. 
He was too young then to understand the story being told. 
He only remembered pear blossoms falling like snow, and in that snowfall, a general in violet armor—gold at his waist, whip in hand—dancing a lone, fierce dance of thrusts and strikes. 
When the show ended, the leader of the troupe—an older student, judging from his bearing—led the younger actors in a bow of thanks. Noticing the boy, he pressed a piece of pear-syrup candy into his palm. 

Soon after, his father took him to "stay for a while" with distant relatives in the next village. 
They braced against the spring chill with thin, fraying blankets, and day by day the air grew warmer. 
Under the harsh summer sun, the fields demanded tilling and hoeing, yet still no news came from home. 

He ran his fingers over the old whip scars on his arm. 
Now, with the autumn harvest in full swing and everyone occupied, no one was watching him. It seemed as good a time as any to make his way back. 

But when his parents saw him standing in their doorway, their eyes held only astonishment—and a certain troubled guilt. 
There wasn't enough grain. His younger siblings were too small. His older brother could work the fields. 
Sending him away had been the easiest choice, practically automatic. 
Even those who cannot read know how to weigh the cost of survival. 
A cast‑out dog might come back to its old home again and again—but a child needs only one look to understand exactly who was chosen and who was left behind.

The sky that day was surprisingly clear. The window in the room was half open.
There was a breeze in the courtyard—
even a few birdsong notes.

Shen Yu placed the flute gently on the table. Then she looked up, meeting the gaze of the bronze mirror before her.

For the first time, she truly studied her own reflection.

She looked at the face in the mirror—
and at the smile she had worn for so many years, unchanged. She recalled the surface of the pond when she was twelve.

But this time, there was no stone in her hand.

So, in silence, she lifted her arm—
and shattered the mirror. Then waited for the sound of footsteps.

She saw people come rushing in, startled by the noise, their voices loud, cluttered, questioning what had happened. But in that moment, those voices were so close yet they felt distant. Very, very distant.

Shen Yu said nothing. She simply stared at the shards of glass. In those fragments,
the false smile had broken into pieces—
along with her reflection, along with the girl she used to be.

Then she heard a voice, very close.

It was the old Shen Yu, whispering in her ear: 

"If seeing me brings you this much pain, then may you and I never meet again."

She raised her head and heard them asking about the flute resting on the table.
She raised her head again, looked at it calmly, and said,

"Tell Father to come."

"Tell him that today, I have a story to tell."

The Zhang clan of Roaring Sands built the Gourd Dike, offered white horses and jade to the river, and for generations tamed the waters by imperial decree, they became the River Master.

Young Zhang Yanling never believed in fate. To him, fate was a yoke, locking a man's spine and skull to the earth from infancy, leaving him no room to struggle. As a boy, he envied the heroes from storytellers' tales, those who rode through Jianghu with unbridled freedom, who came and went like the wind, leaving no trace. They never had to spend their days studying "Seven-Star Levee Ropes" by the Gourd Dike, nor memorize the Water Administration Code word by word under lock and key. And they certainly didn't have to descend into shadowed halls, treading on bleached bones, to tame... the dragon of Zhang clan.

Was this really fate? With that thought, Zhang Yanling went to the marketplace and picked out a fine white horse. He would flee to the desert's lone smoke in the far north, to the spring waters greener than indigo in Jiangnan. He would escape the Yellow River, whose veins dug deep into the heartlands, and every last trace of his predestined life.

The peach blossoms of the south bloomed fiercely, nothing like the barren banks of the Yellow River. But as Zhang Yanling rode, he brushed shoulders with a travel-worn woman in green. He returned the hat she'd dropped; she gifted him a pill she'd refined herself.
"What kind of medicine is this?"
"The life-saving kind."
"You've made so many. Who are you saving?"
"An entire city. Kaifeng."

"My beloved wife Yueniang: 

I wonder if all is well at home? Does father's leg still ache? How is your health? Has Xia'er learned to read yet? After two years with the army, I've only managed to save enough for this single Family Letter—truly my failing. 
However, last year I was assigned to serve under General Zhao Dejun. Fortunately, having learned some literacy from our father and with the support of my comrades, I was promoted to Platoon Leader. Perhaps in the future, I'll be able to send more Coins and supplies home. General Zhao's troops are exceptionally skilled, including a unit of Khitan cavalry riding grand Horses with silver saddles, fighting for us Han people. I've learned some mounted archery from them. Once I earn military merits on the battlefield, I may finally return home to see you. 

These years have been hard on you and father, managing the household alone. I've saved all my pay, waiting to bring it back to you. Please take care of your health and don't worry for me. 
"

You got the Mystic Bird Pendant? That deadly tomb—how did you survive? You've truly become a remarkable hero. Are you hurt? You remind me of my uncle.
In his later years, Uncle sought someone worthy to inherit Weiyang City. He even let me compete with his sons. I won because I had more at stake—to save my mom.
Before he passed, Uncle said there were two people like him: me, and whoever could bring out the pendant. He never met the second, but I do—someone so much like me. I just hope you never become my rival.
$N亲启：\n这十数年来本公子一直好奇，能从那吃人不吐骨头的疑冢里带出玄鸟佩的会:
To $N,

For over a decade, I have been curious—what sort of person could bring out the Mystic Bird Pendant from that man-eating Grave of Doubt? I just learned today that it was you. Now that I think of it, it makes perfect sense. The rumors say you are a creature of wolfish instinct—once you set your sights on something, you seize it without hesitation. Such a nature... is much like Uncle's.

In his later years, Uncle sought someone like himself to inherit Weiyang City. For that, he even broke tradition and allowed me to undergo the same trainings as his children. I prevailed over my cousins not because of strength alone, but because I was the most desperate—and the most greedy. I needed the title more than any of them. I needed it to lift my mother from her suffering.

Before his death, Uncle told me the secret of the Grave of Doubt and the Mystic Bird Pendant. It was his gambit to find the one who most resembled him to rule Weiyang City. He did not live to see his wish fulfilled. Yet in my lifetime, that person has finally appeared. It is a pleasure to meet you, my opponent—or perhaps... the one who is most like myself in this world.

To $N,
For years, I've wondered who could possibly survive that deadly tomb with the Mystic Bird Pendant in hand. You made it. You remind me of my uncle.
In his later years, Uncle sought someone worthy to inherit Weiyang City. He even let me compete with his sons. I won because I had more at stake—to save my mom.
Before he died, Uncle shared with me the secret of the tomb and pendant. He hoped this path would bring him the most competent heir to Weiyang City. Sadly, he never lived to see it. It's my honor to meet you—my rival, or perhaps... my closest counterpart in this world?

I've got great news: no school tomorrow!
The teacher says it's called "Respite," ordered by the Government. I must have been studying so hard lately that even the Government thinks I deserve a break!
Tomorrow, I'm going to sleep until the sun is up high, then fly kites outside the city all day long! Time for those storybooks and puppetry plays. Last, I will buy new Clay Dolls and gifts for Mom, Dad, and you at South Gate Avenue…

You... You really have divine powers... Oh my god... Master, please accept your disciple's bow!

Master, master, where did you learn all your magic? … A book of divine powers? There's such a book? … Then I won't talk. I don't talk much. Mmm, mmm.

81阶及以上等级的装备在完成定音后即可开放转律和变音。\n#Y转律#E：消耗转律:
Gear of Tier 81+ unlocks Retuning and Re-attuning after Attunement.
#YRetuning#E: Spend a Retuning Stone to replace one selected Tuning trait with a recommended trait from the chosen path. You may add a Quality Guarantee material. Each piece of gear can be Retuned once, and only one trait can be Retuned.
Tier 91 gear can reroll the Retuned trait multiple times, with a cooldown between rerolls. During rerolls, the originally replaced trait, the current trait, and any traites previously rolled from the same Retuning pool for that gear will not appear again.
#YRe-attuning#E: Choose an Attunement pool, then spend an Attunement Stone plus a Re-attuning Stone to reroll one Attunement trait from that pool. You can decide whether to replace the existing effect. Unchosen results are saved in Re-attuning History and can be reactivated for 20 Echo Jade. If you roll the same trait type again, its value will increase.
#YCustom Attunement#E: On Tier 91 gear, reaching a certain number of Re-attuning rolls grants one Custom Attunement chance. Normal and Arena Attunement are tracked separately. Custom Attunement costs no Re-attuning materials. You choose only the trait type, and the value is rolled using the same rules as Re-attuning.
Converting the gear into Relaid Gear resets the Re-attuning pity counter.
81阶及以上等级的装备在完成定音后即可开放转律和变音。\n选择倾向流派后，消耗转:
Gear at Tier 81 and above can be retuned and re-attuned after it has been attuned.
Select a preferred Path, consume a Retuning Stone to gain a random new Attribute from that Path's recommended library. The new Attribute will not be the same as the old one. Quality Guaranteed Materials can be added.
One Attribute can be retuned at most per piece of gear. Initial Attributes cannot be retuned. Gear at Tier 105 can further re-tune a retuned Attribute with no limit on attempts, but there is a cooldown between each re-retune. When re-retuning, any Attributes from the same Retuning Library that have been gained from previous retune attempts will not appear again.

Common and Arena Attunement can be performed simultaneously, but only one can be active at a time. Switching between them is free.
After selecting an Attuning Library, consume Attunement Stones and Re-attunement Stones to gain a random new Attribute from the corresponding library.
The new Attribute may be the same. You may choose whether to overwrite the old Attribute. Unselected Attributes are stored in the re-attuning Library and can be re-enabled by spending 20 Echo Jade.
If the same Attribute as the current one gets rolled from re-attuning, the value is guaranteed to increase.

Once Gear at Tier 100 accumulates a certain number of re-attuning attempts, you will have a chance to select an attunement of your choice. Common Attunement and Arena Attunement counts are tracked independently per piece of gear.
The attunement selection does not consume re-attuning materials. The Attribute type can be selected, but the Attribute value will be randomly generated according to rules.
Converting a piece of gear to Relaid Gear will reset the re-attuning count.

;你又梦到了那场追击，梦中刀光剑影，;凛冽剑锋擦过喉间，寒意刺骨。;自那场意外后: Once again, you dream of that frantic chase: flashes of blades and swords and the icy edge of a sword grazing your throat and sending a shiver down your spine. Your foster father has been missing since that night, and there has been no word or sign of him.
;你忍着伤口疼痛，;将王大负在身上。;好在一路相安无事，;你们回到了临时的居所┋: Despite the pain from your wounds, you manage to carry Wang Da on your back. Luckily, the rest of the journey is uneventful, and you both make it back to your temporary shelter. Exhausted, you collapse and fall asleep immediately, and the night passes without incident.
;只见一个白色光点飞速下坠;看这方向，似是砸向了村里;你的内心十分的焦急不安;于: You see a white streak falling rapidly from the sky, and it's headed straight for the village. Panic rises in your chest, so you exert all your lightness skills and sprint toward the village as fast as you can.
;夜里你躺在床榻上，想起白日里王大哥的神情，;总觉得他有什么事情瞒着你。;一夜浅: Lying in bed at night, you remember the look on Brother Wang's face earlier. It keeps nagging at you, making you wonder what he may be hiding. You toss and turn restlessly all night, filled with uneasy dreams. In the middle of the night, you catch the faint sound of something moving outside your window...

<信纸有火燎过的痕迹>\n\n晋安寨对战契丹，大败，赵将军降了。契丹人把我们汉军:
(The letter bears scorch marks along the edges.)

At Jin'an Fort, we met the Khitans in battle and suffered a crushing defeat. General Zhao surrendered. The Khitans have imprisoned all of us, Han troops and Silver-Saddle Khitan Regiment alike. They have also rounded up refugees of every sort, even deserters and beaten men from their own side. As yet, no one knows what they mean to do with us.
So long as I carry the peace charm Yueniang embroidered for me, I am certain I will survive this calamity.

There are five of us confined here together. Since we share one room and the same road between life and death, that too must count for a kind of fate. So I set down our names here.
Zhao Shi, from Luancheng's cloth workshops. At home he has his mother and a younger brother. His family once had a trade of their own, but he joined the army to defend his home.
Zhou Fugui, of Weizhou. He has no kin left. He joined the army to avenge his family.
Wo Tela, a Khitan from the Huang River. At home he has a younger brother and sister. He was captured by General Zhao and pressed into the Silver-Saddle Khitan Regiment. He says he asks for nothing, only to stay alive.
She Lang, a man of the Xi, from the Wolf River, married. Wo Tela told me that She Lang's tribe was raided by the Khitans, defeated and enslaved, then forced into service. He would not let the Khitans drive him to seize other men's land and kill other men's wives and children, so he deserted. His only wish is to return home and grow old with his wife.
Brother Zhao Shi said that if we ever escape, we should all go to Luancheng together and open a cloth workshop. She Lang said his wife is deft with the needle and could help.
Skilled though she may be, could she truly compare with Yueniang?
I wonder what Yueniang is doing at this very moment.

>页一（泛黄的纸张）\n#R却说那桃源乡中有三人，本为无名无姓之辈，皆因那山顶大:
Page One (yellowed paper)
#RIt is said that in Haven there once were three people, all nameless nobodies, who became sworn siblings because of the great tiger that haunted the mountaintop.#E
#GSince this is a storybook, just fighting a tiger is far too dull! Why not have them slay a fiend instead? Or battle the heavens! Let me think... some Chimei, the kind that prey on young boys and girls and wreak havoc outside Haven. What do you say?#E
#YHow can one speak so carelessly of such supernatural matters?#E
#RBut since Junior Sister wishes to write the tale, let it be as she says. Besides, such fiends need not truly be ghosts or gods. Sometimes it is human evil at work, borrowing the names of spirits and gods. That too has its own kind of interest.#E
>页三（泛黄的纸张）\n#Y桃小妹远涉蓬莱，仙人感其赤诚，赐慈悲、勇敢、智慧三道:
Page Three (yellowed paper)
#YTao Xiaomei journeyed all the way to Penglai, where an immortal, moved by her sincerity, bestowed on her three charms for protection: Compassion, Courage, and Wisdom. She then traveled west to Kunlun, where the Queen Mother of the West sent a three-legged golden crow to guide her on her way, and so she went, singing as she traveled...#E
#RSince when does Tao Erlang start telling tales of spirits and wonders too?#E
#YIf she can come back safe and sound, then perhaps even gods and Buddhas do favor the good.#E
>页二（泛黄的纸张）\n#G“居然识破了我的伪装！桃小妹，你以为这样就能救出你那:
Page Two (yellowed paper)
#G"So, you saw through my disguise! Tao Xiaomei, do you think that means you can save your two useless brothers?" The figure gave a wicked cackle and tore off the skin of the Chimei, revealing a face that was none other than...#E
#GAaah, I can't write this part... whose face should it be? I'm leaving it to you two!#E
#R...Tao Dalang has already been captured alive by the Chimei, and Tao Erlang has fallen for its trick as well. With a single sweep of your brush, Junior Sister, the two of us have become defeated foes. We are quite beyond helping now.#E
#YIt was Tao Erlang's face! So it turns out he had only pretended to fall into the trap. In truth, he made use of what was at hand: fir-white paper from the Chimei's manor, Lengyun wood, rice paste for glue, and the juices of various flowers, all boiled and blended together into a lifelike paper figure. He then set up a mechanism to lure the enemy, and the method was...#E#G Enough, enough! Deadly dull! Who wants to hear a storybook stop halfway through just to explain how to make a paper dummy?#E
>页五（近年的纸张）\n#G刀刃刺进那魑魅的胸膛，可却仿佛刺进了棉花一样。一阵金:
Page Five (more recent paper)
#GThe blade sank into the Chimei's chest, yet it felt as though it had pierced cotton. A flash of golden light passed before Tao Xiaomei's eyes, and there was no Chimei at all, only her two brothers. It turned out the pair had long since cut the creature down. This whole business had only been a puppet show they staged together to tease their little sister, putting on a scene so convincing that truth and falsehood could scarcely be told apart.#E

Page Six (more recent paper, stained with tears)
#GThe Three Swords returned to Haven. Because they had slain the Chimei, people from outside followed the trail there, and Haven became Haven City, then in time grew into the Kingdom of Haven. The people lived in cheer day after day, knowing neither hunger nor war.#E
#GAnd what became of the Three Swords of Haven? They hid their names away and grew old in Haven like the siblings of any ordinary household. Even when they had turned into three toothless old folk, they still sat together every day making up storybooks, bickering all the while, each adding a part, carrying on just like three children...#E

Signed: #RShi#E#G Qing#E#Yya#E

Page Four (more recent paper)

In November of the fifth year of the Qianhua era of the Later Liang Dynasty, it was a freezing winter day. A bitter wind howled across the northwest Gobi Desert, slicing through the air. Young Ding Pu found a collapsed man outside his home, blood soaking his armor—a blinding sight. With great effort, he dragged the man inside. Three days later, the stranger woke, laughing that fate had spared him. He taught Ding Pu martial arts but refused to take him as a disciple. When his wounds healed, he left behind a sword, a wine jug, and a martial arts manual, then vanished like the wind.

Even when his wife died in childbirth as their daughter Ding Mu'er was born, he vowed to protect the girl with everything he had. On Mu'er's full moon, he buried a jar of Daughter Red wine under the courtyard tree, to be opened on her wedding day. He taught her to read, to love her country, and to wield a sword—so no brat from the west quarter would dare bully her...

There's no right or wrong in life's choices, but he can't help wondering: Do I regret it? If he'd never stayed in Kaifeng, if Mu'er hadn't taken after him so much, would things be different? Yes, Mu'er was too much like him, and that was a curse. In the fourth year of the Kaiyun era, the Khitans invaded, and Mu'er died saving others. The grief drove him mad for fifteen years, daily waiting for her to come home.

Dreams fade eventually. When clarity finally returned, a flood of emotions surged through him, but all he could utter was a sigh. He ached with nostalgia, guilt, and rage. Guilt that his mastery of martial arts hadn't saved his daughter. Rage that madness had stolen fifteen years from him, years he could've spent avenging her. —No, he still didn't believe in fate. There were always paths to vengeance. Look, the northwest wind was rising again.

To yield would not only erode his prestige among the princes but, more perilously, stoke the Emperor's suspicions against the military, a recipe for imperial disaster.
"Press on. We shall not be the first to retreat."
Amidst the bustling streets, a masked woman gazes toward the horizon. This is Li Qingyun, Princess of the Realm. Upon hearing that her Fourth Prince brother is returning to the capital, she knows she must be the first to welcome him home. As she waits by the roadside, an imperial guard hurries over with urgent news: "The Crown Prince and the Fourth Prince are set to collide at the gates. Neither will give way. Bloodshed may follow!"
Li Qingyun furrows his brow, pauses thoughtfully, and then commands, "Send my carriage now!"
The princess's carriage speeds down the main street, drawing closer to the border troops. Startled at first, the soldiers swiftly fall into formation. The Princess leaps onto the lead carriage. Seeing her silhouette, the vanguard general laughs heartily: "The Flying General is here! Clear the way!"
The Fourth Prince spurs his horse forward, his booming laughter echoing as he greets her. As it happened, the Princess had once donned male attire and slipped into the Fourth Prince's ranks. It was only amidst the heat of battle that he discovered his "soldier" was his own sister. Together they charged through blood and fire, forging a sibling bond tempered by the anvil of war. Utterly unbreakable. While she was a paragon of riding and archery, she possessed a catastrophic lack of direction. In the chaos of war, she would charge blindly through enemy lines, earning her the mocking, yet affectionate, title of "The Flying General."
Their joyful reunion speaks for itself. Learning the border troops' steadfast resolve, Li Qingyun contemplated the situation before resolutely drawing her brother back into the carriage.
"The border legions have their grievances, but our Second Brother's seat is equally precarious. If you trust me, Brother, board my carriage. Today, I shall escort both my brothers into the Imperial City together!"
"In this den of vipers we call a capital, if I cannot trust my own sister, I have no one left to believe in."
The carriage races forward, pulling up alongside the crown prince's procession. Yet, within the Crown Prince's personal retinue, a snake lay in wait. Seeing the Fourth Prince and the princess arrive together, he realized the plan was falling apart. Panicked, he drew his bow and fired an arrow straight at the Fourth Prince's face!
The Fourth Prince, a veteran of slaughters, did not even flinch. He snatched the arrow out of the air with a bare hand, a terrifying, murderous aura erupting from his silhouette.

As the traitor reached for a second shaft, the Crown Prince, pale with horror, roared for his execution. The man was cut down before he could draw the string again. The princess sensed the danger and glanced at the Fourth Prince, yet the Fourth Prince only tightened his arm around his sister, shielding her from the chaos. Not a single shadow of doubt crossed his face.
"Is this the extent of the struggle for the throne? Petty schemes and hidden arrows? Qingyun, if the capital stifles you, remember, the frontier is always open to you."
Knowing the gravity of the slight, the Crown Prince descended from his carriage and bowed deeply. "The failure to discipline my men is mine alone. Fourth Brother, I swear upon my life. This treachery was none of my doing!"
The Fourth Prince spared not a single look for the future Emperor. His gaze remained fixed solely upon the sister at his side. Only when the Princess offered a small, reassuring nod did the Fourth Prince relent. "I do not trust your word," he said coldly. "I trust only her."
The three of them entered the gates together within the Princess's carriage, a tableau of sibling unity that would be told and retold in the teahouses of Chang'an for years to come.
Little did they know that within the depths of the Inner Palace, the new Empress was trembling in a cold, thunderous rage. With the Fifth Prince still in his youth, the Empress knew her only path to power lay in the ruin of the four elder brothers. If they ceased their clashing, her ambitions would wither.
At the princess's residence, the Third Prince is waiting for her. The moment Li Qingyun walked in, the formidable Third Prince, a man who commands the court with an iron fist, shed his armor. He reveals his true self, sprawled across the daybed.
"Tell me, are you truly my sister by blood? Or do you belong to that dull-witted Crown Prince, or perhaps that oafish soldier of a Fourth Brother?"
Li Qingyun gave him a shove with her foot and flopped down comfortably.
"Only you would dare treat me so! But alas, such is my fate for having but one precious sister." Grumbling, the Third Prince scoots over. He hovers nearby like a scolded puppy, watching over her. The April air has begun to simmer with heat. He takes up a fan and wafts it with rhythmic gentleness, careful not to let even the slightest breeze disturb her peace.
Just then, a servant delivered a note. The Third Prince took it, glanced at the sender, and scowled. It was from the Eldest Prince. It read: "The princess impressed everyone today." The Third Prince's face soured instantly. "The Eldest Prince?" he spat. "He's just a cripple marked by misfortune! Why do you soil your hands by associating with such an ill-omened creature?"
Li Qingyun shot up, anger flashing in her eyes. "Is that how you talk about our own brother behind his back?"
"Our brother?" The Third Prince's voice turned sharp. "You know full well he's in the Crown Prince's pocket. He's against me!"
"Then why must this war continue? You share the same blood!"
"Do you think we chose this slaughter? It is the Empe...! You wouldn't understand. If I do not seize the crown, I cannot be the shield you need!"
Li Qingyun shoved him toward the door and then slammed it shut in his face.
"Then I don't want to understand! And I don't need your shield! If you're willing to throw away brotherhood just to claw your way to the top, then fine. Go ahead. Go back to your den of scheming advisors. Fan them with your lies and leave me in peace!"
The Third Prince, a man whose word is law in the capital, can only stomp his feet like a petulant child before her closed door. "Withdraw! Every last one of you! My elite guards are wasted on a house that does not want them!"
Back in the inner palace, news arrived that the Princess's residence now lay unguarded. A cold, predatory joy flickered in the Empress's eyes. Seizing the window of opportunity, the Empress dripped venomous lies into the Emperor's ear: she claimed the Crown Prince and the Fourth Prince were joining forces in a treasonous coup. Bewitched and senile, the Emperor fell for her web of deceit. In his dotage, he surrendered the authority to command the Palace Guard to her hands.
With her personal guards gone, the princess stood no chance against the palace troops. Once Qingyun was dragged within the palace walls, the Empress gave a cold mandate: break the Princess's will and bend her to the Empress's service, or end her life.
Meanwhile, the Third Prince had already begun to regret withdrawing his men. But by the time he realized his mistake, the princess had already been taken. Without an imperial summons, he couldn't set foot inside the palace alone. Casting caution to the wind, the Third Prince dispatched riders in every direction, to the Eldest, the Crown Prince, and the Fourth Prince.
The Crown Prince arrived at the Third's estate in a whirlwind. Armed with the Heir Apparent's seal and authority, the two brothers stormed the gates together.
The Eldest Prince cast aside his facade of serenity. He unleashed his vast network of court officials, the "tongues" he had cultivated for years, to brand the Empress a traitorous usurper.
The Fourth Prince abandoned all caution. Defying the laws of treason, he marched his battle-hardened border legions into the city, sealing the Imperial Palace in an iron ring of steel.
The Third Prince's private shadow-guard, warriors raised for this very hour, breached the inner sanctum. They struck just as the palace guards raised their blades against the Princess. United for the first time, the four princes staged a swift, bloodless coup. A new sovereign was crowned, and the rot of the old court was purged in a single morning.

Gui Zhongyan was born in Chang'an at the end of the Tang Dynasty. He wasn't lying—he was indeed "from the capital." But life in Chang'an was harsh. From childhood, he wandered, scraping by one meal at a time. Having no home, Chang'an itself became his home.

His favorite haunt was the Three Bends Alley, a gritty district where fish and dragons mingled, perfect for his talents: cheating, scamming, and swindling. Everyone in the alley knew the sharp-eyed kid who ran its streets. But even scoundrels meet their match. Soon, he was hoodwinked by a master swindler into becoming his apprentice. Their relationship was far from "harmonious". Gui Zhongyan always felt he was the one getting played, and it grated on him. But even those turbulent days came to a brutal end.

In Zhengyue in the first year of the Tianyou Era, Zhu Wen destroyed Chang'an, forcing its residents to relocate at swordpoint. Homes were torn down, and the city wailed for weeks. Gui Zhongyan was among the refugees, but he didn't cry. He was numb. He had no home left, no family. His conman master had lied to him one final time. The old man had sworn he'd always stay, but he broke his vow. Gui Zhongyan tossed a pair of dice in his hand—his master had died for these cursed things.

A decade later, in Kaifeng, Gui Zhongyan cleaned out every gambling den in the city within three days, earning him the title "Gambler King". Life went on as usual for him, but not for others. His antics had drawn the attention of the authorities. To evade arrest, he slipped into Ghostlight Market and befriended its Dao Lord in a brawl, becoming a regular fixture there. For the first time in years, he felt he belonged somewhere.

He witnessed Khitan invasions, the Nine Mortal Ways' rise, the Later Zhou's overthrow of the Later Han, and the Yellow River's floods... Through it all, Gui Zhongyan saw it all and met countless souls. In the ever-changing capital, people came and went—some fled, some went mad, some died. But he remained unchanged: still the street-smart kid from Three Bends Alley, like an ancient tree weathering storms, accepting life's cycles of growth and decay. Except when he cursed: "Goddamn Wude Bureau! What 'Peerless Inn'? I'll...! I just want to go home!" Ah, no matter the dynasty, the authorities always had their eye on him.

"Ruby, go catch the kite!"
When the string broke, all the children at Heaven's Pier panicked as they watched the kite drift further away, landing in a distant hillside tree.
Ruby had broken the string. Biting her lip, she ran toward it.
"Wait here! I'll fetch it back."

She raced toward the kite as twilight deepened. By the time she had climbed the tree and retrieved it, the sun had completely set.
Looking down toward where the children had been, she saw no one—all had been taken home for dinner by their mothers.
By now... her father should still be working at the winery, not yet finished for the day.
Ruby clutched the kite tightly, afraid the wind might take it again. But the tree was so tall—climbing up hadn't seemed difficult, but now, holding the kite, she dared not descend.
The night grew thicker, the air turned cold with dew, and Ruby sat alone in her lofty perch, watching as lanterns lit up one household after another below.
She deliberately widened her eyes, letting the wind dry them completely. She was going to be a heroine someday—this was nothing!
Even if nobody knew she was here, even if no one came looking, even if she had to... had to spend the night in this tree alone, she wouldn't be afraid.
She, Zhou Ruby, feared neither darkness nor solitude!

After what seemed an eternity, Ruby had counted the evening lanterns of Heaven's Pier three times: two hundred and sixty-eight in total.
Cold and hungry, she curled into a tiny ball against the biting wind, drowsily thinking that she really would spend the night in this tree after all...
In her daze, she spotted a small lantern in the distance, seemingly the only light in these hills, bobbing closer and closer toward her.
"Ruby! Ruby!"
The lantern approached, somehow speaking.
"Ruby!"
...Hmm?
The lantern illuminated the kindest, gentlest face in the world, looking up at her with worry and care.
...Was this a dream? Ruby let go, and the kite floated down, caught firmly by the person below.
"It's you!"
She finally called out, her voice breaking with tears.

"Oh, little master, mind the scaffolding! If anything is not to your liking, just give the word." Uncle Zhou scooped up the boisterous child and set him down beneath the bamboo shade.
Settling only briefly, the boy grumbled about the lanterns being too thin and then scrambled onto Uncle Mi's back to fuss over a wooden chair. Finally, he squatted by Autie Tian, gravely critiquing the embroidered ducks and geese on the linens. In short, nothing in this new house was quite right for the little master.
At their wits' end, the workers cast their eyes toward their Mistress, waiting for her to intervene. This was the third house the little master had rejected. The first two had already been razed and rebuilt.
"Come here." Han Xiangxun watched the boy dashing about the yard, her grip tightening on her abacus.
The boy was growing up; it was time he had his own quarters. For this grand endeavor, the Blissful Retreat had been shuttered for nearly half a year. Yet the little master's whims changed with the tide, one day demanding narrow doors with stout furniture, the next, slender pieces with broad entryways.
Han Xiangxun had asked many times what he truly desired, but the child could offer no clear answer. So they indulged him, revising day by day, until three months had slipped away. She had meant to be patient, but with the third house nearing completion, the boy continued his fussing, still unsatisfied.
"The last time! One final change, and no more." Han Xiangxun shrugged off the boy's feigned wailing and walked away. That night, a "guest" at the Evercare Clinic awaited her routine rounds.
At midnight, beneath the full moon, she thought of the boy's daytime antics and how he had been frightened later that evening. She sighed at last.
Sitting by his bedside, she hummed a nursery rhyme from her distant home.
Beneath the quilt, the child lay curled in a ball, sobbing in his drowsy state.
As stars drifted and the moon paled, she caressed his sleeping face and tucked the corners of his blanket tight.
"...No new house... I don't want to grow up... I don't want to be apart..."
"Foolish child," she whispered. "You will grow up, and I shall..."
As if a thought struck her, she leaned closer. "When that day comes, even if you are left alone, you must fare well."
A softer murmur drifted up.
"Mother..."
As she moved to rise, the woman nearly lost her composure to tears.
Let him fuss for a few more months. Let her indulge him just a little while longer.
Before the day of parting, before that day which must inevitably come.

His parents died early, before they could even grant him a formal name. Thus, when he joined the army, he used only a crude childhood name.
They say a lowly name is easy to keep alive. He often thought his name must be too lowly; why else would Heaven refuse to take him?

"Your name?" This time, it was his turn to ask.
"My name is Zhao Buyi."
"Is your uncle named Zhao Shi?"
"Oh? You know my uncle, sir? He's been in the army for years. He's a real hero!"
He knew not Zhao Tie, but he knew Zhao Shi. A brother who had written his final words alongside him; one who fell at Jin'an Fort, never to emerge.
With every house in Luancheng at its loom, finding the Zhaos was no simple task. Yet the moment he saw the boy's face, he knew his search was over.
He drew out the letter that had long rested against his heart and placed it in Zhao Buyi's hands, to be delivered to Zhao Shi.
Zhao Buyi looked at the blood-stained envelope and then up at the man beneath the bamboo hat. A realization seemed to dawn upon him.
"Uncle... he... he isn't coming home, is he?"
Finding no words to answer, he merely patted the boy's head and turned to leave.
From behind, the young voice called out, "And you, sir? What is your name? Will I see you again?"
He gave a dismissive wave and tossed back a name: "Ding Xianzhen."
He remembered him, a lad no older than Zhao Buyi. Only... that one would never find his way home either.
Seasons passed, uncounted...
At the city gate, guards conducted their routine questioning of the departing crowd. 
"Your name?"
"Meng Kuan."
"Meng Kuan... Destination?"
"To the North." 
"Your business there?"
"To find a man. To deliver a letter." 
"Meng Kuan" tugged down the brim of his new hat, drifting into the northbound crowd. 
He knew many were still waiting for these names to return or for the closure they brought.
As for himself? For one whom no one awaits, a name is a luxury long since surrendered.

Yingying was a palace maid within the inner precincts. Quietly resolute by nature, she had a streak of gallantry in her as well.
One night, while making her rounds on watch duty, she heard tiles shifting overhead. In the next instant, a black-clad figure tumbled down before the steps, barely clinging to life. Yingying hid this intruder away in the Forlorn Palace, who turned out to be a famed grandmaster of the age and had risked entering the palace in search of a divine sword.
The grandmaster asked how they might repay her. Yingying asked them to teach her the sword. The grandmaster said, "You are already grown, and your frame has long since set. To train in the martial way is like rowing against the current. I fear you may never reach its heights."
Yingying bowed again and said, "Like Jingwei carrying twigs to fill the sea, so shall I. If one year is not enough, I shall give ten. If even this life is not enough, I shall have no regrets."
As her words fell, the cypresses in the courtyard rustled, as though ringing with the clash of arms. The grandmaster was stirred by her resolve. They clapped in praise and agreed to pass on their art.
From then on, sky and sea lay open before her, free for her to cross at will.
The grandmaster watched her departing figure with a thousand feelings in their heart. Yet Yingying said nothing. She merely turned and walked on alone into the jianghu.
Thus began the tale of how the jianghu came to know her as heroine Yingying.

A snowy night, a ruined temple. The two had been silent, focused on their blades until the aroma of the wine finally broke the ice.
Meng Kuan was here to deliver a letter. Over the years, he had repeatedly enlisted under false names, all to track down the kin of his old comrades and deliver their letters and back pay.
This last letter was for someone near the Wolf River, in Khitan territory.
He had set out with no expectation of returning, yet in this snow-swept wilderness, he encountered a fellow bladesman.
First, they fought over their blades, then over their horses, carving a path of blood and flight.
By the time they finally shook their pursuers and settled in this ruined temple, neither yet knew the other's name.
But by the laws of the jianghu, those who have shed blood and shared wine together are brothers.
The man gave a hearty laugh and introduced himself as Wang Qing. With that, he tossed over his half-emptied wineskin.
The aroma had long been parching Meng Kuan's throat. He downed three massive gulps like a thirsty ox. It left Wang Qing visibly pained.
Not for the man, but for the wine.
"One who drinks another's wine must mind his manners." Seeing this, Meng Kuan wiped his mouth.
"I am Meng Kuan, from... Hutuo. I've tasted brews from all over, but this... it smells potent, hits sharp, and finishes clean. I can't place it."
"Haha! This was brewed from the snows of Mount Taibai's highest peak. You'll find nothing like it elsewhere! But when I left home, I snuck out this many."
Wang Qing gestured with his fingers.
Meng Kuan scoffed, "Three jars? That wouldn't last the night."
Wang Qing shook his head, maintaining the gesture.
Meng Kuan: "Thirty?"
Wang Qing grinned. "Three hundred jars!"
Meng Kuan roared with laughter, clapping his hands. "Brother, you are a rare soul indeed!"
And so, in that ruined temple, over half a skin of fine wine, they talked the night away, wandering the world in their words.
At first light, the wine was spent and the fire dead. They mounted their horses at the door, one bound south, the other north.
"I, Wang Qing, take my leave. Farewell!"
"I, Meng Kuan, take my leave. Farewell."
Farewells said, Meng Kuan spurred his horse to leave, only to hear a shout from behind:
"Meng Kuan, next time we meet, I hope to hear your true name. Yah!"
Meng Kuan turned, but saw only the man's receding back as he vanished into the swirling snow.
He smacked his lips, as if savoring the wine, or perhaps at a loss for words.
"Now I owe the man a name."

"We swear! We'll survive together, and make Ever-Normal for All! Everyone will be free from hunger!"
The first time Shen Yilun heard this vow, he was barely twelve or thirteen. Back then, he didn't truly grasp what "Ever-Normal for All" meant. Perhaps even Zheng Ruan, who'd said it with such bright laughter, didn't either. Yet something in those words called to the boy's heart. And since following Zheng E had long been his habit, he nodded fervently, eager to match his friends' hopes.

He heard the vow again the following year, when the Later Han army collapsed and General Guo Wei seized the capital. Chaos bred famine, and families like the Shens faced starvation, until A'zheng and A'ruan saved them with their own rationed grain. Clutching the coarse bun they'd given him, he nodded even harder. Ever-Normal for All now tasted as sweet as this humble bread. Then his elder brother shattered that innocence.
"The strong devour the weak in times like these! If they don't die, how do we live?"
Shen Yiren and his Later Han comrades, hunted by Guo Wei's forces after defeat, had been starving in the mountains. At the sight of food, they seized A'zheng and A'ruan, stormed the Zheng estate, and left only ashes and blood behind.
That night, the Zheng estate burned in a blazing inferno. The screams and blood opened Shen Yilun's eyes to the weight of those words, "Ever-Normal for All," far heavier and harder than he'd imagined. And as he began to understand, he lost the right to turn back: A'ruan was dead, his brother was dead, and so many others.

Four years later, Shen Yilun left home. The Dawn-to-Dusk had ravaged eastern Kaifeng, and despite his efforts, he'd received news of A'zheng's death. Their vow to survive together had crumbled, leaving the boy consumed by grief and a desperate urge to move forward. He had to force himself ahead, even though walking alone, after years of following A'zheng and A'ruan, terrified him. He refused to let their promise become a joke, and now, he was the only one left to carry it. So the young Shen Yilun packed his bags, ready to leave his hometown. The night before departure, he visited his friends' graves again.
"We swore to make Ever-Normal for All and everyone free from hunger." He whispered to the departed, turning away with newfound resolve. Though he sensed the trials ahead, he never imagined this vow would consume his entire life.

...The story you have softly sung for a thousand years, in my life, from now on, no one is more precious than you, and for you, no one is more cherished than I. My admiration and passion for you have sublimated into my song of joy, never to be moved or changed.

……只可惜，想见的人，总也寻不到好时候相见。: …For the ones you want to see... there's never time.

……吃我一箭！呼……准头似乎够了……: ...Here goes! Whew, that felt like a solid shot...

……听不懂听不懂。: ...I didn't catch a word of that.

……复唐故地，一振国威。: and upholds the glory of the empire.

...Last week's accounting nearly drove me mad. Once again, I was at the very bottom. The elder looked at me as if I were a foul stone in an outhouse. I truly don't understand it—everyone else tricks people for a living, yet I'm the only one who never seems to earn a coin.
