Ordinary folk are tightening their belts just to survive. How much money could they possibly have? And I keep watching them day after day... What a complete waste of time. 
But people of the jianghu are different. Every sect has its own skill, its own specialty, which means its own way of making money. Their purses must be full. Kaifeng is full of wanderers from every school. How did I not think to make them my target? 
That's settled, then. Starting tomorrow, I'll visit them one by one. 

[Silver Needle] 
The moment I stepped onto the street today, I spotted a healer from Silver Needle. Her medical kit was set beside her, and the consultation fee sat on top, yet she was too busy to even look at it. So I slipped over, took two copper coins, and had just turned to leave when I heard her say to someone, "A full prescription only costs five wen." 
I stopped cold. All that hard work, all that running around—for so little? Those two coins felt unbearably heavy in my pocket. I dropped them into her box without a second thought. 
I will not take money my conscience cannot bear! 

[Raging Tides] 
I'm so angry! 
Finding someone from Raging Tides is easy—just walk into any tavern. I sat down with one of them, shared a drink, slipped a little something into his cup, planning to take his purse once he passed out. But who could have guessed he would drink himself into such disgrace? After only a few cups, he started getting handsy, reaching for me as though I were part of the furniture. Theft may not be an honorable trade, but it is at least a straightforward one. I will not let myself be taken advantage of by some drunken stranger! 
In the end, I kicked him aside and ran. What a loss—out of the whole ordeal, all I managed to take was a jug of cheap wine worth barely ten wen! 

[Velvet Shade] 
I've always known those at Velvet Shade were sharp, but having failed twice, I told myself that today I would try again, for I had nothing left to lose. 
Senior Sister A'xin taught me that if I wanted to get close to one of their disciples, I had to look the part—dress well and act like a man of means at Revelry Hall. I staked some money and borrowed a fine outfit from her. And honestly, once I put it on, I really did look respectable. 
The moment I stepped into Revelry Hall, a lovely woman from Velvet Shade greeted me with a voice sweet as honey. She showered me with compliments until I was completely dazzled. Ah... Being treated like a rich man felt wonderful—so wonderful I nearly forgot why I had come. 
After a few drinks and watching her dance, she even walked me out herself. Curiously, she didn't charge me for the wine. 
Had she realized I was actually penniless? Then why go to such lengths to flatter me? I couldn't make sense of it. 
Still... the fragrance she carried lingered even after she left. 

[The Masked Troupe] 
I left Revelry Hall thinking of her, and before I knew it, I had wandered to the stage at the Masked Troupe. And what a surprise—how can a human voice sound so beautiful? It felt like my bones softened amidst the voice. By comparison, mine is nothing but a broken gong. 
When she finished, a young girl came down to collect tips. Her bright eyes were impossible to refuse, and in a moment of impulse, I handed her the last few coins I had. 
So after an entire day of scheming... I ended up with nothing at all.

It was late autumn, and the wind had turned sharp and bitter. 
Dressed in a thin shirt and straw sandals, he made his way down an unfamiliar mountain path, shivering as he walked. 
There was no "home" left to return to. And the shed his distant relatives had given him wasn't even enough to keep out the rain, let alone the wind. 
Down below, the lights of the valley flickered through the mist, growing fainter the farther he went—as if he were looking up at the world from the bottom of a lake. 

He thought of the masked general on the stage, alone in a sea of soldiers, carving a path through countless foes. 
A song could not keep the darkness at bay. Worse, it might draw the attention of mountain beasts or passing bandits. 
But none of that mattered to him now. 
His heartbeat pounded like the war drums from that day, the general surging forward, fearless and unshaken. 

He ran—toward the distant glow of firelight. 
As the glow deepened, he began to hear it: the spiraling notes of a pipa, the cheers and cries of the crowd. 
It was his second time standing before the stage. 
Though the season was one of withered grass and falling leaves, the moment before he closed his eyes, he saw pear blossoms—thousands of them—snowing down from unseen branches. 

"We breathe lightning. 
I grasp thunder above my head, grind stone soft beneath my feet. Strength in my right hand, 
command in my left. When the sun sets in the west, the east rises silver as the moon. 
Beat the drums—let the long song roll."

Together in One Boat 

The night had deepened, yet Divinecraft Pavilion remained brightly lit. 
"Senior Brother Zou, still here? You should get some rest," a passing junior called out with concern. 
"He's still revising his paper—let's not disturb him," another whispered softly. 
"Senior Brother Zou, I'm heading off. I left the key where I always do. Don't forget to lock up." 
Zou smiled warmly in reply. 
Zou isn't the head disciple of the Mohist Hill. In fact, he's not even a core disciple, just an ordinary outer one. Still, whenever his name comes up, everyone from the elders to Buster speaks highly of him. 
The reason was simple: he treated everyone with sincere kindness. No matter the request, if anyone sought his help, Zou gave his all—never hesitant, never turning anyone away. 
But even a man like him had someone he'd been estranged from for seventeen years. 
Though calling it hatred was too strong—Yang never spoke of Zou, and the two quietly avoided each other whenever chance might bring them face to face. 
What no one knew was that Yang, the carefree storyteller, and Zou, the most admired senior among outer disciples, had once been inseparable friends. 

Seventeen years ago, the peach grove by the sparkling waters of Jadestream Valley had yet to bloom into the lush sea of blossoms it is now. 
In early spring, peach branches stretched gently over the water, their delicate pink buds like scattered rouge on vibrant green silk. 
Sixteen-year-old Zou walked deeper into the forest, a worn book satchel slung over his shoulder, his shoes damp from the morning dew kissing the grass beneath his feet. Suddenly, a clear, melodious voice drifted down from above:
"The east wind wakes the peach blossom rain,
The bright moon lights the jade-green waves." 
He paused, lifted his gaze, and spotted a slender youth perched among the branches of a peach tree. His faded blue shirt was worn thin and frayed at the cuffs, and he clutched a yellowed scroll of poetry. Catching sight of Zou, the boy smiled and raised the scroll. "You like poetry too?" 
Zou bowed politely, about to introduce himself. "I am Zou Yizhou…" 
But as he bent forward, a tiny wild boar poked its snout from the satchel. Blinking its bright eyes, the little creature clumsily scrambled free and darted off into the woods. 
The boy burst into laughter. "Hahaha! Who hides a wild piglet inside their book satchel instead of books? Truly one of a kind!" 
His laughter ringing through the grove, the boy gracefully leapt down, returning Zou's bow with a playful grin. Noticing ink stains on his fingertips, he casually wiped them on the hem of his robe. "I'm Yang Qianyan. Just tossing together a few stray lines of poetry. Looks like I've made fools of both you and your piglet friend." 
Zou watched the boar disappear into the underbrush, then glanced back at Yang, who was still chuckling. He hurried to explain, "I only tucked it in the satchel to keep it from running wild..." He couldn't help but laugh too—the idea of a book satchel turned pigsty was absurdly charming. 
When the laughter settled, Yang clapped him on the shoulder with genuine warmth. "Whether it's books or boars, you're the first I've known to carry a wild pig in a satchel." He waved the scroll playfully. "Those lines I just read aren't finished yet. You seem to have an ear for poetry—care to help me refine them?" 
For a thousand years, the Mohist Hill disciples prized mechanical ingenuity above all else—poetry, prose, and song had fallen into neglect. Because of this, the two young men connected instantly, as if old friends reunited. 
Zou confessed he lacked any real talent for mechanics but found joy in writing tales of legends, strange creatures, and the supernatural. To keep this secret from their master, he adopted a pen name. Still, he was caught and scolded for neglecting his proper duties. Yang laughed and said, "Funny enough, I'm a complete novice when it comes to mechanics, and even the master wouldn't take me in. All I do is write bitter little poems. If you want, you can use my name for your stories—I don't mind. I can even craft poems and notes to accompany them." 
As the sun dipped westward, Zou grew anxious—the little wild boar had yet to return. 
Yang took his hand and led him toward the forest's edge. "Don't worry—I saw it wander south earlier. There's fresh grass there; it's probably resting nearby." 
Sure enough, they found the boar curled in a patch of warm sunlight on a hillside by the fields, dozing with bits of grass stuck at its mouth. Zou gently lifted the creature, which softly snuffled and nestled against his chest. Watching this, Yang smiled and said, "Zou, I believe your first tale of legends should be about this wild boar." 
They laughed together, their joy echoing through the grove. 

From that day on, the peach grove became their treasured refuge. 
They dreamed of the day the mountain would reopen, when they could journey across the land like the great poets of old—one writing verses, the other composing replies. 
And they vowed to open a bookstore beyond the mountain, a place where their stories and poems could live and breathe, together. 
"I've heard Kaifeng City is the liveliest place around," Yang said as he copied out the latest manuscript. "When the time comes, let's open our bookstore right at the busiest street corner—and plant two peach trees at the doorway, ones we bring all the way from the mountains." Their stories had already become wildly popular deep within the mountains. 
Zou smiled and nodded, then penned four characters on the paper: Qian Jin Bu Yi—"Priceless and Rare." "That will be the sign above our shop." 
The "Qian" from Yang, the "Yi" from Zou. 
Together in one boat, priceless and rare. 
They were young then, believing such days would stretch on forever—that the peach blossoms by the crystal-clear Jadestream Valley would bloom again next spring—that they would share countless stories side by side—that the little wild boar would one day grow into a mighty beast. 
That was the spring seventeen years ago. 
Later, a few weathered, fragile scripts were found tucked away in a forgotten corner of Divinecraft Pavilion. The poems inside bore the name Yang Qianyan, and pressed between the pages were a few strands of boar's bristles. 
One disciple held the books and asked, "Senior Brother Zou, who exactly is this Yang Qianyan? Have you met him?" 
"I have. Long ago."

Dreams Returning to the Capital 

The zither's music spreads across the lake in gentle waves, a quiet sigh for how fate—not we—decides our meetings and farewells. In the capital, old bonds run deep, and through each lingering note, the stories of the past are softly told anew. 

Jiang Yi, though barely twenty, is already a virtuoso on countless instruments. By all rights, he could be arrogant—but he's not. To him, music is simply another language. What words cannot fully express, melodies carry with graceful ease. So naturally, he spends his days immersed in music, only gradually realizing others regard him as a "musical prodigy." Yet this language he speaks is rare, a dialect known to few, and most days, Jiang Yi feels like a wanderer far from home. 
That's why, when Velvet Shade invited him to perform at Revelry Hall and enjoy a night of music, Jiang was genuinely delighted. He knew Velvet Shade was closely connected with Grace Pavilion—a place famed for its masterful musicians and exquisite instruments—and so he hurried over without a moment's delay. 

It was a perfect day. On the flower-laden boat approaching Revelry Hall, Jiang could hardly contain himself; he stood at the bow, and the moment they reached shore, he leapt off the boat. Guided inside Grace Pavilion, he hadn't even caught sight of anyone before the sound of a flute reached his ears. 
His senses sharpened, yet a weight settled in his chest. The flute's tone was crystal clear, the technique flawless, and its timbre brilliantly radiant. But beneath that shining clarity lingered a profound sorrow, a hidden ache. Jiang didn't know who the player was or what trials he had endured, but the sadness in that music touched him deeply. 
He stood quietly behind the flutist, watching in silence as the melody unfolded. The man was slender, yet the breath behind his flute filled the room with a power that seemed to pierce through the skies. When the flutist finally turned and caught sight of Jiang, he startled, asking softly who the newcomer was. 

He had meant only to say, "I'm Jiang Yi, invited to perform at Revelry Hall," but the words caught in his throat, swept away by a sudden surge of emotion—like the quiet thrill of a boat drawing close to shore. Instead, he rushed to a nearby zither and let his hands speak for him. As the melody unfurled, the quiet ache he had heard in that flute earlier wove itself naturally into his playing. When the final note faded, he finally raised his head. The flutist was already seated opposite him at the zither bench, asking, "Does this piece have a name?" 
Jiang found his voice. "I just played what came to me." 
"There's the delicate longing of someone returning home, the vast breath of mountains and seas; a touch of the beauty in the moonlit sea, and the freedom of life flowing on through countless generations. What do you think of calling it ‘Dream of Mountains and Seas'?" 
Jiang considered it and then nodded. "It's a beautiful name." 
The man suddenly added, "So, you are Jiang Yi." 
"I am. And you, sir?" 
He didn't answer. He only smiled. "I named your piece. Shouldn't you name mine?" 
"I'm not good at naming things. I'm not good with words at all. That's why I let the music speak." 
"Ah. And you speak it well." The flutist tapped lightly on the hand Jiang still rested on the strings. 
"Master, how can you tease an honored guest like that!" A lively young voice cut in. A girl, still with a touch of youthful innocence, stepped into the room. "Master Jiang, you disappeared in an instant—I see you found the pavilion master all on your own." 
Jiang suddenly realized, "So this is the master of Grace Pavilion—no wonder the flute sounded so captivating." 
The master smiled, "Do you think you're on equal footing with me, Master Jiang?" 
Jiang quickly cupped his hands respectfully, "Far from it, Master Han." 
"Please, no need for such formalities—just call me Han Wei. Yuming, has Master Jiang's lodging been arranged?" 
"All taken care of," replied Ling Yuming, raising an intrigued brow. "Earlier, I caught the sound of a zither downstairs—bold and free, quite unlike your usual style. So it was Master Jiang? Truly exquisite." 
Han chuckled, "Are you implying my playing is stingy?" 
Ling teased gently, "Not nearly as grand as Master Jiang's." 
Blushing, Jiang hurried to interrupt, "You flatter me too much. I simply happen to know more instruments... As the young master of Grace Pavilion, Master Han outperforms me by far." 
Ling sighed with a smile, "Listen to that—‘just happen to know more instruments.' Hearing geniuses speak so modestly can frustrate the rest of us." 
Jiang's eyes widened as he waved his hands nervously, "No, no, not at all! Miss, your fingers are long and graceful—perfect for playing. You could never be ordinary!" 
Han laughed heartily, "Master Jiang may master many instruments, but he sure is shy of his words!" 
Taking their teasing in stride, Jian smiled softly, "Still, it's your flute, Master Han, that truly speaks—the words music cannot express." 
Han fell silent, a thoughtful look crossing his face. 
A delicate floral fragrance drifted through the hall. Before Jiang's arrival, rain had swept through the capital. Now, under clear skies and a gentle breeze weaving between the tall buildings, the lingering echoes of music filled the air. At this moment, the promise of the legendary "Ten Ballads of Pearlglow Lake" had yet to be made; Han was not yet withdrawn from the world; Jiang had not yet retreated into seclusion; and Ling was far from the wistful Flower Messenger she would become. Those unmatched melodies were still nameless, spontaneous creations, and the shadows of inevitable loss and sorrow lay quietly in wait, claws yet concealed. 
It was, in truth, a perfect day.

The Diligent Housekeeper 

Xie Qin, a Raging Tides disciple, was unlike most of his peers. 
While others drank deeply and carelessly, often soaking their clothes with wine without a second thought, Xie took a different approach. 
He carefully washed his garments with soap pods, scrubbing out every stain and drying them thoroughly under the sun on clear days. 
When his fellow disciples raised the wine jar for a round, each taking a sip, he would politely but awkwardly decline, saying, "I'll pass this time." 
In short, he was a neat freak. 

He carried himself with unwavering resolve, fearless in the face of life and death, wielding his spear as though it were his own tombstone. 
But there was no shame in wanting cleanliness, he told himself firmly. Even a Raging Tides disciple could value order and purity. 
With that conviction, he saved every coin meticulously, eventually purchasing a quiet, secluded courtyard. 
After a long life roaming the jianghu, he dreamed of returning home, tending the garden, and nurturing flowers. 
Someone once told him: to live well was to settle all scores. 

One day, returning home, he found something lying at the pristine gate of his courtyard— 
a filthy, ragged figure that was more a tattered cloth than a person. 
A chill ran down Xie's spine as he leaned down and checked for breath. The figure was alive. 
Drawing on his modest medical knowledge from his days in the army, he gently pulled this lost soul back from the edge of death. 

Once cleaned and slightly recovered, the stranger began babbling incessantly—nonsensical words spilling out like a broken river. 
"What nonsense is this? I am truly the son of the wealthy Yu family of Kaifeng! Wrongfully accused in a family dispute, meeting me is your lucky chance. Give me fifty taels of silver, and I promise a bright future for you." 
"I can no longer keep up the pretense—I was sent by the authorities. Lost my badge while pursuing criminals. Give me fifty taels, and I'll make everything right for you." 

Every week, on a certain day, voices echo with such incredible stories, as if a wild festival were taking place. 
Xie simply covered his ears, thinking that once his wound healed, he would go wherever he wished. 
When "Young Master Yu" was barely able to walk with a cane, a few visitors arrived at the gate. 
Xie handed over all the valuables from the house. 

"It's better to settle with me than with them," Young Master Yu said angrily. "What exactly do you owe?" 
Xie pointed to a jar of wine on the shelf. In the Raging Tides, debts between life and death are settled with wine and flesh. Drinking may cost a life; a life-draining debt may be repaid with wine. 
"I owe someone a life, but this jar of wine will never be used to repay that debt." 

Noticing the look in Young Master Yu's eyes, Xie added, "You don't owe me anything." It was a small kindness, done simply to keep someone from sinking deeper into hardship. 
The next day, Young Master Yu seemed transformed. 
Though his leg was still healing and his steps unsteady, he eagerly took up every task—from sweeping the floor to cooking—leaving Xie puzzled. 
"Because... I am an immortal. Heaven has taken pity on you and sent me to help. Understood? Now, give me fifty taels of silver..." 
Xie nearly fumbled his chopsticks. 
His cleanliness obsession was a hopeless habit, yet sharing a meal with someone brought an unexpected warmth. 

As the days grew colder, Young Master Yu's injuries healed swiftly, and he regained his spirited vigor. 
He paid no attention to Xie's subtle hints to leave, wandering in and out of the courtyard as though it were his own domain. 
Until one day, Xie spoke firmly, "This courtyard has been promised to another. Don't come back after tomorrow." 
Unable to repay the wine he owed to his fallen peers on the battlefield, Xie had instead bequeathed his modest family land to his living kin, hoping to find some peace in that. 

Young Master Yu dismissed all this, insisting on staying just one more night. 
By morning, both the wine and the man had disappeared without a trace, leaving behind only a sealed letter. 

With a heavy heart, Xie packed his belongings and set out for Kaifeng—both to recover the lost wine and to seek a new path. 
"Since you've caught me, I'll return the wine," Young Master Yu had said with a bright smile the day he was captured. "Don't judge me by appearances—I'm a man of honor who repays every kindness, endlessly." 
Xie gave a cold laugh. The wine was returned, but what of the rest? 
"Perhaps... you'd start by telling me your true name."

Although the original has been lost, the earliest surviving Song Dynasty copy is kept at the Palace Museum in Beijing. The artwork depicts Southern Tang's ruler Li Jing playing go with his brothers. Using the "trembling stroke" technique, the composition is ingeniously designed, featuring a screen within a screen—hence the name "Double Screen." Several copies were made during the Song Dynasty. As a realistic court painting, this work not only vividly captures the likenesses of the figures but also accurately depicts the everyday objects inside the room. This makes it an important visual resource for historians studying household items and palace life during the Five Dynasties and medieval China. 
Today, the painting is preserved at the Palace Museum in Beijing.

The bed is made from mulberry or pagoda tree wood, one chi wide, two chi long, with holes the size of chopsticks... Using the foot to press on it over boiling water, 'Water-Drawn' and 'Hele' noodles are made. 'Hele' noodles are kneaded to the size of a thumb, about five cun long. 'Water-Drawn' noodles are kneaded to the thickness of chopsticks, over one chi long. Both are kneaded until pliable, cut, placed into the holes of the bed, and pressed with the foot, causing them to fall into the water. Sought in the broth, they are done in a moment."

【三更天】\n其实三更天的钱我一早就在赚。有个三更天的阎王是我的老主顾：她找我打:
[Midnight Blades] 
To be honest, I've actually been earning from the Midnight Blades folk for a while. There's a living Yama who comes to me often: she asks for information, and I scout around for her. Today she came again, and I couldn't help complaining—everywhere else I make nothing, but at least she pays. 
She even brought pastries for me. 
But once she starts, she always returns to her talk about "saving souls"—how living is nothing but suffering, how early death means early release, and so on. 
I was eating the pastries she bought, but I still told her she was talking nonsense. What's wrong with living? If you're alive, you get to eat pastries. If that's her logic, my life has been miserable enough—why not "save" me as well? 
To my astonishment, she said she could. Her blade was quick, she said, and I wouldn't feel a thing. 
That startled me so much I lost my temper. I told her I wanted no part in that kind of work anymore. She simply replied, "Then I will seek someone else." 
So heartless—I truly thought we had at least a little friendship! 
Yet before she left, she still asked whether the pastries were good. I said yes. She said she would bring more next time. 
...But with the job already fallen through, what "next time" could there possibly be?
I really cannot understand what goes on in these people's minds. 

[Mohist Hill] 
Today, while searching through some discarded items—or rather, an old warehouse—I was hoping to find something useful when I happened upon a young girl collecting a pile of wood. 
I could tell right away she was from the Mohist Hill. Yet she shook her head firmly to deny it. Seeing how she treated even scraps of wood like precious belongings, I figured there was no real profit to be made from her. Oh well, no matter. 

[The Inkbound Order] 
I've always felt a bit intimidated by those at the Inkbound Order, and today was no different. I nervously wandered into the Hanlin Academy, where the scholars at the Inkbound Order were busy writing and painting, mumbling in a language I couldn't understand at all. I just stood there feeling completely out of place and awkward. 
Just as I was about to leave, a young scholar called out to me. I thought I was about to be told to move on. 
Instead, he handed me two steamed buns and ten coins, saying he noticed I'd been hanging around for a while and if I ever had trouble, I should talk to one of the disciples by the gate. 
The buns weren't very tasty—dry and bland—but free food is always welcome. The Inkbound Order guys are actually quite kind.

【孤云】\n今天特意收拾了一番才上街，却撞见个神棍，一开口就说我是九流门的，说我:
[Lone Cloud] 
Today I actually made an effort to tidy myself up before heading out, only to run into a wandering "seer" who declared I must be from the Nine Mortal Ways the moment he saw me. He pointed out six flaws he saw in me and claimed he knew at least ten tricks someone like me might use. I grew irritated—was he trying to ruin my livelihood? Before I could stop myself, I had already drawn my rope dart and given him a beating. 
Once he was on the ground, I checked his money pouch—it was completely empty! 
So I asked, "With all the books you've read, how is it you have no money at all?" 
He turned red and launched into a long explanation about "scholars' concerns," something about one star having eight different names. I couldn't see what good any of that did him! 
Still, I knew I shouldn't have been so reckless as to strike him. I helped him up as an apology and listened while he complained at length about how difficult it was to find work. That gave me an idea—since he could talk endlessly, why not work together? He could handle the fortune‑telling, I'd gather customers, and we'd split the earnings evenly! 
But he grew stubborn, insisting his star‑reading was meant to interpret the world's deeper workings, not be used for fortune‑telling. 
I replied, "If you can't do it, then forget it." 
He lifted his chin and said, "I can do it. I simply don't wish to." 
I said, "Which explains why your pockets are empty." 
Since he clearly had no money at all, I handed him a few coins for a meal before I left. 
Why is it that every time I go out, I end up spending money instead of earning it? 

[Well of Heaven] 
Everyone in the Nine Mortal Ways says the Well of Heaven disciples are as good as walking treasuries, but it would be far too embarrassing to ask them directly for food, so I refuse to do that. Still, while following them around today, I actually came up with a proper way to earn money. 
They visit the Springwave Pavilion every day, and they're all impressively built. If I could slip up to the window and sketch them through the cracks, then sell each picture for ten wen, I'd have no trouble finding buyers. 
It was a good plan, but I managed only two sketches before they caught me. 
Their leader questioned me. His grip was so strong that with one shake, I confessed everything. But to my surprise, after I explained, he said, "Why didn't you tell me you were drawing? I could pose for you." 
That's the Well of Heaven disciple for you—generous to the core. He even changed poses several times, and I finished ten sketches in one sitting. When I took them to the street and called out to sell them, they were gone in no time. A very good day's earnings! 
(Flipping a page) 
Today, the "walking treasury" sought me out again. He asked whether I could paint people I'd never met—just from their description. 
I told him I could. He tossed me a bag of money and asked me to paint several people. 
But he could barely remember what they looked like. His descriptions were things like, "I think there was a mole near the corner of the mouth," which wasn't much to go on. Still, since he paid generously, I didn't complain and simply did my best. 
He seemed troubled, so I assumed these were enemies and that he wanted the portraits to issue warrants. But instead, once I finished, he took the drawings to the backyard and burned them one by one. 
I couldn't understand it—why spend so much to have them painted, only to burn them? Yet as he burned them, he cried. It was the first time I'd ever seen a grown man break down in front of me, and it left me with a strange ache in my chest. Before I knew it, I had shed a couple of tears as well, though I couldn't say why. 

[Hollow Vale] 
I haven't run into anyone from Hollow Vale. And even if I did, I wouldn't dare approach—they might poison me without meaning to. 

[Nine Mortal Ways] 
Senior Sister A'xin read my diary and told me that someone with a conscience like mine will never earn money through trickery. She said I should stop thinking along those lines, and that she has better methods to teach me another day. 
I can't tell if she was praising me or teasing me, but her words still made me strangely happy. 
In any case, I've decided that if nothing else works out, I can always grind ink for those scholars at the Inkbound Order. The world's a big place; I'm sure I'll manage to get by.

[Warn] Spring Fever Spreads: Masked Troupe Reissues Love Ban!
Though Masked Troupe has always strictly forbidden romantic relationships among disciples, affections following spring fever bloom where they will. Lately, whispers of budding affection have stirred among younger members. In response, the sect has tightened patrols and once again issued a clear decree: No Romance Allowed!

[Thrill] Too Many Peepers! Taihu Lake Fish Demand Justice! Masked Troupe Must Take Full Responsibility.
According to an anonymous fish in Taihu Lake, no fewer than fifteen people have fallen into the lake this month while peeking Masked Troupe disciples rehearse. "It's all the Troupe's fault," the fish claims. "They're too charming and too reclusive. People can't help but peek. They should take full responsibility!"

[Shock] Masked Troupe Disciple Dines and Dashes. Innkeeper Denounces Their Basic Education!
A Masked Troupe disciple recently departed on a training journey and stopped at an inn without a single coin. Instead, he attempted to settle the bill with a song. Upon inquiry, it was revealed that the disciple had grown up entirely within the secluded grounds of the Masked Troupe and was unaware that food must be paid for outside. The innkeeper has since urged the Troupe to improve its disciples' basic knowledge of the outside world. As of now, the Troupe has yet to issue a response.

[Secret] Another Shady Fatcat Robbed? Eyewitness Says: No Way Did a Well of Heaven Hero Do It! 
Recently, another ignominious and unscrupulous merchant has been robbed of a large amount of wealth. At the same time, nearby poor families have received quite a few mysterious gifts. According to an eyewitness at the scene, it was definitely not the doing of a Well of Heaven hero! 

[Shocking] Well of Heaven Disciple Learns Fraud Prevention, Challenges Nine Mortal Ways, Loses 800 Taels Anyway
Due to the rapidly increasing number of victims of Nine Mortal Ways scams, Well of Heaven has instituted a anti-fraud lecture in the sect to teach disciples about detecting and preventing scams. One day after studying, a Well of Heaven disciple took it upon himself to challenge Nine Mortal Ways and ended up being scammed out of eight hundred taels.
【秘】墨山道弟子没有灭绝，有人问世\n近来，清河有村民在丹崖疑似目击到一只墨山道:
[Secret] Mohist Hill Disciple Spotted. The Sect is not extinct! 
A villager in Qinghe recently claimed to have seen a Mohist Hill Disciple roaming the Crimson Cliff, accompanied by a Automaton. The sighting occurred in an uninhabited area of the cliff. When the villager later returned with others, the disciple was nowhere to be found. 

[Secret] What is the Truth Behind Mohist Hill? The Secrets Revealed! 
So what is Mohist Hill? The question on everyone's lips. Countless rumors. Endless speculation. Today, we spill the tea. Buckle up! Mohist Hill...is a Sect! Shocking? Well, that's all we've got. Thanks for reading.

First, don't stay in Divinecraft Pavilion after Xu hour.
(Rumor has it that anyone who lingers past that time wakes up the next day naked in the plaza.)
Second, the pavilion only has one floor. If you suddenly see an extra floor, get out immediately.
(People say they've heard creaking noises upstairs, and then a new staircase appears. If you don't leave, you might never escape. Please tell me that won't happen to me!)

一、临安名菜：蟹酿橙\n食材选用：十月满膏母蟹，太湖蟹最佳；黄熟带顶大橙。\n烹:
1. Lin'an Specialty: Crab-Stuffed Orange
Ingredients: Roe-rich female crab in season, ideally from Taihu; deep-golden orange with the stem cap still on
Method: Cut a lid from the orange and set it aside. Remove the flesh, leaving a little juice in the shell. Fill the orange with the crab meat and roe, then replace the lid. Set it in a small steamer and steam with wine and vinegar until cooked through. Season lightly with salt and serve.
Tasting Notes: The orange fragrance lifts the crab and tempers its richness. The crab meat is creamy and full, balanced by the orange's gentle sweetness and fresh acidity. The only complaint is that there is never quite enough of it.

2. Kaifeng Winter Dish: Mountain-Stewed Lamb with Apricot Kernels
Ingredients: Ribs or leg from a young lamb; Shayuan apricot kernels, skinned and ground
Method: Cut the lamb into pieces and place it in a clay pot. Add scallion and pepper, and there is one secret to it: use a few pounded apricot kernels. Cook over a lively fire until the meat is tender and even the bones have softened.
Tasting Notes: The meat is tender but still holds together, and the broth turns white as milk. A little coriander at the end freshens the dish and lightens its richness. It is especially satisfying in winter, when it warms the body through. Do not overindulge in summer, though, as it can leave you feeling overheated and prone to heartburn.

3. Scholar's Table: Petal-Pasta Soup
Ingredients: Winter plum blossoms from Jianyang; Triple-sifted wheat flour; Aged ham
Method: Lightly steep the plum blossoms with a pinch of sandalwood powder, then use the fragrant liquid to make a dough like that for wonton wrappers. Roll it thin, stack the sheets, and cut them with a five-petaled iron mold in the shape of a plum blossom. Cook and serve in broth.
Tasting Notes: The dough pieces are delicate and almost translucent, with a faint plum fragrance that lingers on the palate. The broth is clear and fresh, and does not overpower the floral note. A refined dish, though a little too understated in flavor.

4. Winter Treat: Rosy Hotpot
Ingredients: Rabbit loin; Ginger citrus sauce
Method: Freeze the rabbit until firm, then slice it very thinly. Drop the slices into boiling bone broth and cook only until just done. Serve with the dipping sauce.
Tasting Notes: The slices are thin as paper and turn rosy the moment they meet the broth. The ginger citrus sauce brings brightness and fragrance, with a lively tartness that keeps the dish fresh on the palate. With a good wine alongside, the dish becomes finer still.

5. Signature Cold Dish: Crystal Aspic
Ingredients: Fresh sea bass; Fragrant fermented lees
Method: Blanch the fish slices very briefly in boiling water. Place them in an earthenware bowl with the fermented lees and ginger juice, then chill in a snow cellar until set. Cut into pieces and arrange with chilled lotus root.
Tasting Notes: Clear and glistening like amber, the fish aspic melts almost at once in the mouth. The lees give it depth and fragrance, while the lotus root provides a crisp contrast. Set it beside a bowl of hot rice, and you will not want to put your chopsticks down.

6. Kaifeng Morning Market: Spit-Roasted Pork Rind
Ingredients: Pork neck skin; Coarse salt
Method: Skewer the pork skin on an iron spit and roast it quickly over charcoal, turning constantly. As the fat renders, sprinkle with spiced salt. When the skin blisters and crisps, slice it and lay it over flatbread.
Tasting Notes: The rind is crisp, amber in color, with rich meat and fat beneath. The peppered salt draws out the smoky aroma so thoroughly that it can be smelled from several lanes away. The only trouble is that it depends entirely on careful control of the fire. Get that wrong, and all you get is a dry, joyless bite.

7. Lin'an Summer Dessert: Snow Pearls
Ingredients: Glutinous rice flour; Rock sugar; Plum syrup
Method: Roll the glutinous rice flour into small balls and boil until they float. Chill thoroughly in an ice well, then pour over sugar syrup and plum syrup. Garnish with carved preserved plums to make what is called the "Three Friends" ice-bowl garnish.
Tasting Notes: The dumplings are soft and chewy, set against crushed ice cold enough to sting the teeth. The syrup is clean and sweet without becoming cloying, with the crunch of the ice shards providing a delightful contrast to the soft pearls. A fine thing to eat on a summer afternoon.

8. Tavern Supper: Lees-Cured Lamb Trotter Slices
Ingredients: Lamb trotters; Fragrant fermented lees; Yellow mustard
Method: Cook the lamb trotters until tender, then remove the bones. Wrap in cloth and press into a square. Soak in lees brine for three days, then slice thinly and serve with yellow mustard.
Tasting Notes: The tendon and gelatin set into a glossy, firm slice. The lees fragrance runs deep, and the mustard gives the dish a sharp finish that cuts the richness well. It is a perfect dish for winter nights spent reading by candlelight.

一个人为了弥补一生的遗憾，愿意付出什么？——沈义伦的答案是：倾尽所能。\n他也的:
What will a man sacrifice to atone for a lifetime of regrets?
For Shen Yilun, the answer was simple: Everything.
And so he did. For twelve solitary years, he trudged toward that vision of "Ever-Normal for All". Until the Ever-Normal Granary rose tall over golden wheat fields. Until carts of grain from all directions filled them to the brim. For a fleeting moment, his friends' long-ago vow seemed almost within reach. Then the court handed Plainfield to monsters and rationed the grain for war. Cold reality doused the flames of idealism, leaving only embers. Still, he persisted. On his return from a southern inspection, he plotted memorials, strategies, and relief efforts until a sudden kidnapping interrupted everything. As he was seized, he braced for death, consumed by regret. Then, shocked, he recognized his "old friend".

From the moment he left Kaifeng, Shen Yilun had never dared to hope for a reunion with A'zheng. So when the initial shock faded, his heart was overwhelmed by grief at his friend's descent into darkness. But in a hidden corner, a tiny flicker of joy began to grow. Part of this joy came from the sheer miracle of A'zheng's survival, but another part was selfishly personal: for the first time, he saw a chance at redemption, a way to undo the mistakes that had haunted him for twelve long years.
Unfortunately, events soon spiraled beyond Shen Yilun's control. The towering Dawn-to-Dusk Blossom laid bare a cruel truth: the friend he remembered had been buried by chaos, by villains, and... by himself. Shen Yilun refused to accept the shattered promise, especially when it was his grown friend who'd destroyed it. So in those endless dark days, he sought and prayed, until fate led him to another honest, kind-hearted boy, just as it had twelve years before.
And so the towering flames rose again. Twelve years prior, fire had reduced the Zheng family mansion and the teenagers' innocence and kindness to ash. Twelve years later, an even hotter blaze consumed both present-day sins and past obsessions. Gazing at his disoriented old friend, Shen Yilun found that the man's shadow at last overlapped with the boy he had once known.
"From now on, you are the true Master of Grain."
With those final words, exhaled on his final breath, Shen Yilun knew: This is the end. When he'd begun this path, he'd been certain he'd give everything without hesitation. Yet now, with his wish fulfilled, what surged up wasn't peace, but regret. Regret and apology.
For as his eyes closed, he thought he'd stepped back into the past or forward into an unknown future. There, the "Master of Grain" stood alone in endless wheat fields, while young, kind boys laughed and raced through the golden waves, the air thick with the sweet, gentle scent of grain.

One day, He Jin went into the wild to pick Qianghuang flowers. The sound of a wooden arrow cutting through the air rushed toward her face. She dropped to the ground immediately, escaping the fatal blow. 
A man ran over from not far away, dressed like a hunter. He Jin pulled the wooden arrow out of the sand and handed it to him. 
Startled by He Jin's gaze, the hunter mumbled: "I thought there were wolves around, so I shot the arrow." 

"Then, do I look like a wolf?" 
"Such a fine lady, how could you be a wolf?" 
"Thank you. Next time, see carefully before you shoot." 
"I know! I was muddled. Wolves always come in packs, how could there be just one…" 

Before he finished speaking, the hunter suddenly shuddered. He drew his bow with trembling hands and turned around, only to see a man not far away staring firmly at him, walking slowly closer. 
So the other wolf had arrived late! 
The hunter barely had time to glance back and say a hasty farewell to He Jin before fleeing in panic. 

The wind picked up again. Feeling the threat behind him had disappeared, the hunter looked back. 
The two figures gradually blurred and faded in the wind and sand, shrinking into a distant dot, never to be found again.

One day, Pang Miao ran into a local ruffian on the street. 
To call him a ruffian was partly Pang Miao's own fault. 

The ruffian's name was Gao Er. That day, Gao Er was chasing chickens and dogs down the street, causing quite a racket. Only because Pang Miao glanced at Gao Er in the crowd did he happen to see Gao Er execute a perfect hawk flip down from a wall several yards high. 
That one glance convinced him: this was his new master. 

Gao Er impatiently chewed on a grass stalk, listening to Pang Miao's rambling. Gao Er had initially wanted to spit and leave, but then he heard Pang Miao promise ten taels of silver. So his eyes shifted, and he said, "For someone as mediocre as you, how could you be worthy of the name 'disciple of Gao Er'..." 
Pang Miao flushed red. "Yes, yes... Master, you are right." 
"But seeing your kind heart... fine. Complete three trials for me, and I'll accept you as my disciple." 
Overjoyed, Pang Miao agreed repeatedly. 
Next, Pang Miao repaired Gao Er's roof for him, carried his manure buckets, and bought over ten roast chickens. 
What awaited him, however, was a sudden kick to the chest from a now-hostile Gao Er, and the sound of mocking laughter fading into the distance. 

Gao Er had never found anything so funny. Just as he was heartily laughing at Pang Miao for being an idiot, a wooden mallet slammed hard into his shoulder. 
The carpenter, Old Li, roared, "How dare you bully my apprentice!" 
"And me!" The embroiderer, Third Lady Shen, grabbed her scissors and jabbed at Gao Er. 
"My apprentice is not someone you can make a fool of!" A huge abacus smacked him in the face. Gao Er saw stars. 
The wok-tosser, the fortune-teller, the bodyguard... Gao Er was beaten until he lay on the ground, begging for mercy. 

"Come, good disciple, get up. Let me have a look!" 
"Are you hurt? Come to my pharmacy. I have plenty of medicine." 
"My silly disciple, you mustn't be so trusting again!" 
Looking at the dozen or so masters gathered around him, Pang Miao smiled foolishly. In that moment, he finally understood what it truly meant to have "masters all under heaven."

The first watch has begun. Old Sun is on the clapper tonight. I can tell.
His clapper sounds lighter than other men's, light and faintly trembling. It was not always so. In years past he struck it hard and sharp, but after that day it was never the same again.
One strike, then another. Old Sun walks slowly, but the sound still drifts farther and farther away. He alone never looks toward the lattice windows of this hall. His eyes are empty, like a well veiled in autumn mist.
So are mine.
We were both soaked through in that rain.

It was in the autumn of 948. The rain that day was fierce, hammering on the palace tiles as though Heaven itself were beating a drum to cry out against injustice.
And yet inside the hall, the silence was more terrible still.
The officials stood there in a dark mass, like a stand of black trees. Their eyes sat high above, their hearts buried below.
They all knew why Lord Li had died.
He died for loyalty. He died for gratitude. He died in the ruin of factional strife.
But once the imperial will had fallen, his death had to be given another name.
"He endangered the altars of state, consorted in secret with traitors and villains, and plotted rebellion."
Word by word, they pressed him down into the mud. No one spoke again. No one could.
When wind and rain demand that bamboo bend, then bend it must, until at last it breaks. The whole hall watched it bend, watched it split, watched it be swept away in the mire. Then they turned in silence, and each raised his own umbrella.
I had an umbrella too. I gripped it so hard my nails bit into the handle.
But in the end, I did not step forward.
And so Lord Li's sigh dissolved into the sky above the palace, no different from the way the music of a grand ceremony rises and fades.

The rain kept falling, drop after drop, striking the bricks more clearly than even Old Sun's clapper now.
I was not wrong. I was only a young palace attendant. I could not even hold up the half inch of sky above my own head, much less contend with a judgment already sealed.
For two years now, I have whispered this to myself every night, like a charm to keep myself alive.
But no charm can quiet a dream. In the dream, the rain falls hard and never stops.
Last month I drank with Old Sun. The wine had gone cold when he suddenly said, "Lord Li... used to laugh most at the sound of my clapper." Then he laughed too, and the sound of it was uglier than weeping.
He used to say a man should live so that he could face his ancestors' tablets without shame. Now he says only that the wine has gone cold and ought to be warmed.
We have both learned to drink cold wine and speak warm words.

Drop by drop, that rain has gone on seeping through the years. From the cracks in the bricks outside the hall, onto the floor within, and into my very bones.
And still I write.
These words will be eaten by insects, buried in dust, perhaps never seen by anyone at all.
Then why do I write? To let myself hear them. To leave them for those who come after.
I do not know.
I know only that I am cold. Moonlight falls on the bricks at my feet, but it does not reach me.
Not on this night. Not on all the nights already gone. Not on all the nights still to come.

Ever since we parted years ago, there's been an emptiness in my heart. I thought we might find solace in each other when we finally met someday—never expecting that day would never come.
Our master often said, "One life, one price." Unfortunately, now with the flood looming and Aureate Pavilion closing in, I finally understand the weight behind his words.
If we fled, the enemy would seize our journals and the poison would rise anew. If we stayed, the city would be safe—yet at the cost of our lives.
So, I asked them for their opinions. Despite great grief, they all chose to stay, for their beloved ones. As you can see, one life, one price. For the sake of those we hold dear, for the peace of the world, we offer our own lives as the price.

I hope that one day you find this letter and understand my regret and desperation behind it. I hope you find the journal as well—pass it to the right hands to end this plague forever.
May you live in health and peace all your days.

A painter came across the torn remnants of an ancient scroll, its mountains, cities, and figures rendered so finely they seemed almost alive. He lost himself in copying it, and after some time he began to notice faint traces of ink appearing in the world around him, with voices that murmured like players reciting from a script.
One night, by the unsteady light of his oil lamp, he noticed that the wet ink at the edge of the scroll had spread beyond the paper and was seeping into the walls of his room. Seized with dread, he took up his brush, dipped it, and with a trembling hand added a single stroke to a corner of what he now thought of as his room. The world lurched. The walls shriveled and peeled back like rice paper, and behind them were the scroll itself and the wooden rods of its mount.
Only then did he understand. He and everything around him were nothing but a few drying drops of ink on some vast, unseen painting. A voice came from beyond the picture, low and even: "That stroke... was unnecessary." And with that, the painter and his room were wiped clean away, leaving behind only a small, unremarkable smudge of ink on the ancient scroll.

Thirteen years ago, in the Dingwei year, during a time of chaos, the Khitan army invaded Kaifeng, unleashing fire and slaughter. The people rose to defend their homes, and after a month of bitter fighting, the invaders were repelled. As the city rebuilt, an old tree in the northwest was found scorched by the fires of war, yet miraculously sprouting new leaves. Seeing it as a divine sign of resilience, the people named it the Immortal Tree.
Later, when the usurper Liu Zhiyuan founded his short-lived Han dynasty, his sycophantic court seized upon this story. Claiming the tree as a heavenly omen, they forcibly expelled the local residents and built the Garden of Auspicious Omen, adorning its burnt branches with paper flowers to flatter their emperor.
And yet, what came of it? The Liu Han dynasty collapsed in just two generations. A dynasty's fate is not bound to trinkets and omens. How can a ruler in troubled times dare to cast aside caution for arrogance?
Now, in the first year of Jianlong, with the founding of the Great Song, the realm remains divided. Our Emperor, taking this tale of hubris as a solemn warning, has decreed that the garden be remade. It is renamed the Garden of Vigilance and returned to the people, a testament to his vow to rule with virtue, to remain ever-cautious, and to protect the nation and its people.
Decreed and erected in the seventh month of the first year of the Jianlong era

Ding Xiao often sharpened his sword late at night.
No one knew that this man, so skilled in calculation, could only let his emotions flow at this moment.
Every time he sharpened his blade, he thought of his childhood. The crushing defeat at the frontier, his father and brothers branded as incompetent in death, and his own imprisonment. He thought then that he was no longer the young noble with a pen; when he was free, he should have a sword, a sword that could slice through injustice, pierce through grievances, and be more valiant and stern than his father's weak knives.
But all these years, as he hated and sharpened, the sword grew brighter, but his heart grew more lost, unable to see the path ahead...
Where exactly should this sword be pointed?
Until the clouds began to stir at Zhongdu Bridge, and he learned a distant truth.
Perhaps it was time for it to be unsheathed, pointed at past events that must be settled.

万无忧从来就不喜欢自己的名字。\n这名字属于开封绣阁里的富贵千金，属于山外云游四:
Wan Wuyou doesn't like her name at all.
It sounded like it belonged to a young lady behind embroidered screens in Kaifeng, or a wandering Daoist girl drifting beyond the mountains, anyone but her. Certainly not a dust-streaked girl who'd grown up in the shadowy folds of Mirkvale.
Wuyou, means "no worries" in Chinese... At twenty, she lay flat on a rooftop, cracking pine nuts between her teeth and chewing over those two words in her head. What did "no worries" even feel like? Even when she skipped work to steal a bit of peace, her heart stayed busy, worrying whether her parents would sigh again when she got home, worrying whether she'd end up like her father, hammer in hand, stuck in the same trade for life.
When the moon slid behind the western hills, Wuyou brushed off the dust and climbed down. The night breeze was cool, carrying with it a thread of unfamiliar scent.
It smelled like sparks leaping from her father's forge. Like summer nights when her mother hummed softly while weaving grass fans. The scent tugged at her until worries slipped loose, time blurred... The distant mountains seemed impossibly tall, and she was a ladybug resting among flowers. She felt herself becoming enormous, certain that if she reached out, she could lift the moon back into the sky.
Di Juan and Di Fu came running with lanterns, thinking thieves had broken into the storeroom. What they found instead was...
A girl sprawled on the floor, head pillowed on a jar of Mountain Pine Wine, clutching an empty cask marked Millennium Drunk, another jug pinned under her legs, sleeping like the dead.
"We haven't even opened yet. How did someone already get drunk?"
"Hush—Look at her. She must be having a dream with no worries at all..."

Third of March, overcast, windy.
Today I taught the weavers of Luan City the method of the loom. At the heddle, a worker surnamed Zhang suddenly said the method could be improved.
He said the heddle crossbeam is like an ox-cart, with rope and wood grinding together, causing great loss of strength. Why not imitate a well-side windlass, carve a shallow groove, inlay polished animal bone as a roller, and lubricate with tallow?
I thought his idea crude at first, but following his method, the pedal force was reduced by nearly 30%, and the heddle movement became much smoother. This method is excellent. I will record it in detail.

上\n一流的骗术，便是扮作别人且不叫人察觉。\n十七易容成为的第一个人是具无名女:
Part I
The finest deceit is to take another's shape so completely that no one ever sees through it.
The first guise Shi Qi ever wore belonged to an unnamed dead woman. She had died in a ruined temple, carrying a little silver and a letter meant for her younger sister. Shi Qi happened upon her, laid her to rest, and from that day on took her place in the world.
At last, she had become someone else. Shi Qi looked at her reflection in the water and was well pleased, then turned and went back into the city.
Yet when she stood before the house, she hesitated, until the girl rushed into her arms. That embrace was warm, and once it wrapped around Shi Qi, it held fast. Shi Qi did not dare return it. Her heart hammered like a drum.
Faced with her elder sister returned from afar, the younger sister was like a little bird, chattering and bright with laughter. Why were the words people spoke so gentle, so gentle that once heard, one longed to hear them again?
Whenever the girl smiled up at her, a tide would rise in Shi Qi's heart. Yet whenever she looked in the mirror, that face reminded her what she was: a fraud.
Happiness slips away in an instant. Lies are always exposed in the end. She knew that well.
Shi Qi could never sleep through the night, and often woke with a start. At such times, the girl would light a lamp and sit beside her. Even when neither of them spoke, her heart would slowly grow still.
A swindler knows most of the tricks in this world, and has seen too many eyes filled with suspicion. Only this younger sister's trust was so warm, so fierce, that it left her at a loss.
There was only one flaw in it all. The girl, too, had her unhappy moments. Whenever Shi Qi spoke of wanting a drink, her face would darken, as though she were about to cry.
Then, on the night of the full moon, the girl came back with wine. The cups were filled, and Shi Qi's delight brimmed over with them.
But by the third cup, she was no longer smiling. Little sister, who was it you were truly calling for?
The finest deceit does not merely fool others. In the end, it may fool even the one who tells the lie.
Perhaps she should have ended the charade sooner, told the girl that her true elder sister had long since died. But she had no such courage, nor did she wish to lose the only person in this world willing to light a lamp for her in the night. The moment she spoke, that elder sister would truly be gone, and Shi Qi would be nothing more than a blade of grass, something no one would ever stop to notice.
The wine left her heavy and drifting, dim and wavering all at once. Shi Qi wept as though the ripples in the cup had become waves within her. Human beings were strange creatures. Alone and with nothing to rely on, one could live freely enough. Yet once one had family, one began to suffer. No one could tell her why. The moon shone on two lonely souls, each with no one else in the world.
She raised her head, and through tear-blurred eyes saw the girl gazing back at her.

Part II
When a person is born into this world, life is like a river.
In the first half of that river, the two sisters clung to one another. The younger one's eyes followed her sister and the merchant caravan as they departed, quietly waiting for the day when that other stream would flow back to meet her own.
Her elder sister's embrace had always been warm. Whenever that hand came down in gentle pats upon her shoulder, her fluttering heart would settle.
At last, her elder sister's figure appeared again before the house. She flung herself forward and embraced her, but her sister stood stiff and still, like a stranger.
Her elder sister had changed. She had become timid and uneasy, often waking in the night. Whenever that happened, the younger sister would light a lamp and sit with her. As fear slowly gave way to drowsiness, the lamp too would gutter out.
Those eyes rested on her, and she knew every word they wished to say. Little sister, will we never be parted again? We are the dearest kin in all the world, are we not?
Just as in the old days, her answer was always the same. Yes.
Life ought to have gone on so, plain and quiet, yet little by little she realized that this was not the one she had waited for. Her sister had never drunk wine. This one craved it as though life itself depended on it.
The person before her was like some fragile little beast, curled beneath the light, her gaze full of fear and sorrow, as though she carried too many unspoken words and was only waiting for someone who could understand them.
Then one day a letter arrived from a distant place. The younger sister stood in the doorway with it in her hands, not knowing what to do.
Her elder sister would never return. The one who had come back was a fraud. Yet she wore exactly her sister's face. If she let her go, she would never again see that face.
When she turned back, "Elder Sister" was sitting alone in the little courtyard, looking unbearably solitary. She watched her for a long while, then tore the letter to pieces and went out to buy a jug of wine.
She filled one cup carefully and set it on the table, then looked up at the moon.
The second cup she placed before the one beside her. The drinker grew drunk easily, and tears slipped down her face.

In the first half of the river, the two sisters clung to one another. In the second half, the younger sister flowed on alone, sustained by a lie she chose to believe. Cruelest of all was this: people must die in the end, yet she had not been given enough time to ready herself for it.
In the wavering water was a face that wore her elder sister's likeness. She looked at the one holding the wine cup and said nothing.
Perhaps the deceit was simply too fine. Or perhaps she herself was willing to believe.

Your unfilial son Junhao writes:
I bow my head in shame, for years have passed since we last met, and I feel deep guilt before you, Mother. This winter is bitterly cold—are you well?
Should you ask about Father, I must confess: in my youth, I was mortified by his reputation as a thief.
That is why I left home to travel west, seeking enlightenment at the Well of Heaven, and now I have joined the Northern Vow to defend our homeland.
Ten years have flown by, and only now—through reflection and hearsay—do I realize Father's deeds were those of a chivalrous thief, not mere thievery.
I harbored resentment and misunderstood him for so long. If you receive this letter, Mother, please convey my apologies to him on my behalf. I write this in tears.
Forgive me for being unable to return home and serve you both at your knees.
Our land lies broken, and northern barbarians advance unhindered. I must be a barrier for the people, a bulwark for our rivers and mountains.
If Qinghe falls, countless families will be thrown into chaos.
Forgive my single-minded resolve. I entrust this letter to a friend from Harvestfall Village. Please, Mother and Father—do not worry or miss me!

Beneath the uneven leg of the table lies a stack of ten tattered silk edicts. They read:

19th Day of the Twelfth Month, 946 CE
The Han honored meritorious ministers, swearing oaths as enduring as the Yellow River. The Zhou esteemed their elder statesmen, granting them lands by the sea. It has long been known that Elder Raven of Mohist Hill is a man of great virtue and high merit. We therefore bestow rewards in his honor, namely gold, silver, vessels, brocade crowns, saddled horses, and the like, all as listed separately.

20th Day of the Twelfth Month, 946 CE
Elder Raven's heart and conduct are unlike those of ordinary men. Modest in virtue, keen in mind, broad in generosity, and rooted in benevolence, he once led the mountain folk into Haven and settled them there in peace, spending himself utterly in their service. Such conduct inspires reverence like a lofty peak, and We have long held him in admiration. He is hereby specially raised to the rank of Grandmaster of Mohist Hill and granted an iron charter. All affairs within the mountain are entrusted to his discretion. We hope that you will accept Our transforming influence and follow Our teachings, and that you will labor all the more for the sake of Our far-reaching designs, in reverent obedience to this gracious command.
...

28th Day of the Twelfth Month, 946 CE
Edict to Raven of Mohist Hill: We have come to govern the northern marches and bring peace to the four seas, ever dealing with others in sincerity, in hopes that all under Heaven may know peace. Yet the Mohists, for all the favor and rewards bestowed upon them, and for all the pains taken to win them over, still conceal hearts full of treachery. Once arrows fly, the worthy and the worthless are not easily told apart. Yet the gate of renewed fortune still stands open, and the will to spare life ought to be understood. You alone have spoken with Us and know the sincerity of Our intentions. Thus We issue this edict, trusting that you will understand.

Once, a besotted young master stumbled into such a forest. He wandered through the fog for a long time, only to realize he was walking in circles. He came upon a dozen ruined shrines. In this world, people change their names, their faces, and cast off the past—some for the future, some for the present, some for money, some for love, and some just to deceive themselves. But the moment he put on that black armor, he understood that leaving the past behind wouldn't earn him anything. To cast it off was simply to cast it off.

Cast off the past, the future, his name, his honor, and every thread tying him to the world.

He heard someone whisper:

"Once you put it on, you can't take it off."

"It's not a problem for me, but... it's such a shame."

Was it someone else who said it? Or had he said it himself? He couldn't remember.

He couldn't remember if, in that moment, he had looked up. Looked up toward the sky. No—there was no sky here anymore.

When a man lives on the surface, he looks up and sees the heavens. But when a man lives underground, when he looks up, all he sees is the world above.

And for him, in the next moment, there would be no difference between the two. Both were places he could no longer reach.

He couldn't remember whether he had looked back one last time at the world.

When each day becomes a perfect echo of the last, time flows like water, wearing down his memory to a smooth, blank stone. He would simply sit and polish his weapon. And sometimes, his gaze would fall to the old calluses in his palm, the faded scars across his hand. Sometimes, he would pause and stare at them for a moment or two. As though he were watching someone else's entire life.

Tactic Five: Bestow kindness before acquaintance; plan actions at the critical moment. 
<Before I even knew Li An, he sent extravagant birthday gifts every year, just like many others. He said it was to repay Father for a life-saving spear strike from years ago. But when I asked Father, he swore he'd never met Li An before.>

东海往北，为勃海。前唐张守节《史记正义》云，”蓬莱、方丈、瀛洲，勃海中三神山也。:
North of the Eastern Sea lies the Bohai Sea. Zhang Shoujie of the Early Tang wrote in Correct Meanings of the Records of the Grand Historian: "Penglai, Fangzhang, and Yingzhou are the three divine mountains in the Bohai Sea."
But this place is not known for myth alone. To the south runs the Yellow River. To the north flows the Hutuo River. Streams and rivers from every side come together here, giving the land a grandeur of its own.
Since ancient times, it had been a place for those who sought wonders, and a famed route for travel and pleasure.
Lately, though, the weather had turned vicious. Wind and rain tore across the sea, and the waves were so violent that even the fishermen had tied up their boats and stayed ashore.
And right at a time like this, two young men had taken a narrow skiff and headed straight for the depths of the Bohai Sea.
The one at the bow wore a scholar's cap and sang into the wind and rain. The one at the stern wore a crane-feather cloak and pulled at the oar through the crashing swells.
"The sea stirs the distant hills; the celestial rooster has crowed before dawn. Silver terraces rise in mirrored light; white waves roll like great whales!"
The boy at the bow sang so brightly that his voice seemed to pierce thunder and lightning and carry into the heaving black clouds above.
"Wow, even the storm can't drown out that voice of yours!" The boy in crane robes laughed aloud from the stern. He looked toward the dim, misty reaches of the sea and thought of how the two of them had ended up here: They were returning from their travels when, on a sudden whim, Lin Xiansheng had turned them north and brought them out onto the Bohai Sea in search of something.
The whim belonged to Lin Xiansheng. The one indulging it was Xiao Heyi.
Still, he could not help wondering what exactly Lin Xiansheng had come all this way to find in this empty stretch of sea.
An immortal mountain? No, surely not. Lin Xiansheng was not the sort to chase wild tales. They had seen the Luo River. They had gone as far as Zhongnan. As for all those stories of immortals and marvels, Lin would glance at them in passing, then let them drift off like mist.
Treasure, then? No, not that either. Leaving aside that neither of them cared much for pearls or jade, the two of them traveled light wherever they went: one book, one long sword, one brush, one inkstone. If it were money he wanted, there were plenty of easier ways to earn it than braving storms and monstrous waves for some perilous corner of the sea.
But Lin Xiansheng liked to keep people guessing. It was a common enough failing among the scholars of Inkbound Order, those learned men forever steeped in old things. And the less he said, the more curious Xiao Heyi became. Yet when he looked around, all he saw was the vast, empty open sea, with nothing in sight at all.
Lin Xiansheng knew exactly what was gnawing at him, but still, he would not give him a straight answer. He only kept singing: "Waves sweep Luoxing Bay," and "The moon is ringed; wind and mist seal the heavens shut." What he wanted was indeed somewhere in the sea. He had read of it in books, seen it named in histories, but had never beheld it with his own eyes. And now, having come this far on a fit of inspiration, why not see it properly, to his heart's content?
What he sought was none other than the legend of the sea: the whale.
On the road back to Inkbound Order, he had happened to hear an old farmer speak of it. Intrigued, he turned around and headed north, chasing the trail of that giant creature.
Lin Xiansheng had read widely since childhood. From The Commentary of Zuo to Li Bai, Du Fu, Han Yu, and Meng Jiao, there was no shortage of lines about whales.
But if one were to speak of who truly understood them, it might well be the fishermen of the coast.
When the wind and waves rose high, they said, that was when whales were easiest to spot. He had wanted to make this trip for a long time.
He wanted to see it. He wanted to see the whale of the poems, the whale of old tales, the whale that had lived in his mind for years. He wanted to see it with his own eyes, alive in the open sea. Even when the fishermen ran after him calling, "Young man, that great fish is dangerous!" it made no difference.
At that age, no one listens to warnings.
A hot, restless thrill surged up from the bottom of his heart, undimmed even by the perilous sea.
He had imagined meeting the whale in a hundred different ways. Passing close beside it, crossing its path, even being swallowed whole into its belly... From all the lines Lin had been muttering to himself, Xiao Heyi finally understood.
"Xiansheng, you're looking for a whale?"
His eyes lit up, even as he kept the oar moving.
"Tell me, what do you think a whale looks like?"
Lin Xiansheng thought it over, then said, "Cui Bao of the Jin writes in Records of Past and Present that the great whales run a thousand li in length, and even the smaller ones measure in the thousands of zhang. They pound the waves into thunder and fling up spray like rain. All creatures of the deep fear them, and no fish dares stand in their path."
"Ren Fang of the Liang also writes in Records of Strange Things that the pearls of the southern sea are the pupils of whales' eyes. They shine at night, and so are called night-bright pearls."
Lin Xiansheng paused, then went on, "They say that once you've heard true thunder, a drum sounds shabby; once you've seen a great whale, you know how small a tiny shell really is. But no matter how books describe a whale's form, in the end, you still have to see one with your own eyes."
Xiao Heyi looked out over that boundless sea, then back at his friend at the bow, chanting his way into the storm as though it were leading them onward. And before he knew it, he too had begun to long for the sight of the whale.
Let the thunder roar, let the waves rise, let the rain lash and the wind howl!

To prevent further collapses, the villagers of Horsehelm Village gathered to discuss and formulated three tips, which were implemented immediately. 
Now recorded in writing, all those involved in well digging must keep them firmly in mind. 
Firstly, personnel above ground must closely monitor surface wind and sand conditions. If strong winds are observed and the air feels piercingly cold, this is a sign of an impending major sandstorm. Immediately send someone down the well to notify everyone. All diggers must ascend to the surface without delay. 
Secondly, personnel below ground shall be divided into two groups. Group One continues digging the well, and Group Two follows closely behind, constructing the passageway. Regardless of the materials or methods used, the passage must be made sturdy to secure time for returning to the surface. 
Thirdly, no matter what important matters arise, internal strife is forbidden. 
Well digging is arduous labor, with uncertain outcomes and countless days expended. Anyone wishing to withdraw partway may go to the He family to receive a subsistence allowance and leave on their own accord.

九四六年的那天，刘娴回到这挂着“张家食肆“的屋子时，屋里还亮着灯，她摸了摸手臂上:
On that day in 946, when Liu Xian returned to the house with the sign "Zhang's Eatery" over the door, the lights were still on inside. She touched the scar on her arm. The skin there was wrinkled and puckered.
Her father had lost money gambling, come home drunk, and smashed a lamp on her. That's how she got the scar.
From the very first scar, she learned: if she came home from her odd jobs and saw the lamp still burning, it meant her father had been drinking and had already collapsed somewhere inside.
She was already skinny, and she'd scrunch herself up as small as possible when she walked in, looking as shriveled and fragile as the burn on her arm.
She would step as lightly as she could, lighter and lighter, until her footsteps were as weightless as her whole existence: barely there, easily overlooked.
She was always on guard, careful not to wake her father, and too scared to even look his way. So she would creep through the house, eyes locked on that lamp. If the flame so much as flickered, she'd freeze, bracing herself as if she'd been burned, not daring to move again until everything was completely silent. Then, she'd inch herself into the farthest, darkest corner from the lamp, praying for dawn, praying that when morning came, he still wouldn't wake.
She wasn't like her mother. Her mother had run away when she had only five scars; Liu Xian couldn't run.
She was just a seven-year-old girl. Inside the house or out, the world felt like a burning lamp she was terrified to touch.
She was still thinking about all this, pacing outside, when her footsteps must have caught someone's attention. The man she'd seen the day before, Zhang Ankang, came to the door with a lantern. She quickly hid the food she'd stolen and took a step back.
"Why don't you come inside?"
He looked like a good man, but she'd learned there were plenty of people who looked good, enough to make room for plenty of bad ones, too.
Inside, at the same old table under the same old lamp, was a bowl of steaming noodles.
She stared at it blankly. "What is this?"
Her confusion was reflected on his face. "Noodles, but there's just one bowl left. How about we share?"
For him, offering food to someone or waiting for someone to eat seemed as natural as breathing. For her, in this world, it felt as impossible as killing or being killed.
Liu Xian thought that, before this war, he must have lived a good life, to still be able to be a good person.

Exercise 1: Disciples from Nine Mortal Ways and Lone Cloud are gambling with dice at the market.
Each uses two regular dice (numbers 1–6). If their sums are equal, it's a tie. What's the probability of a tie?
Answer: 1 in 36. Why? The clever Nine Mortal Ways disciple brings two dice that always roll 6, totaling 12, while the Lone Cloud disciple rolls honestly, getting any sum from 2 to 12. Out of 36 possible combinations, only double sixes from Lone Cloud Disciples can tie, so 1/36.

Exercise 2: During tea season, Velvet Shade hosts daily tea tastings. Each day, guests are served one of three teas at Revelry Hall: Jing Mountain, Qujiang Thin Slice, or Xianya Stone Flower.
The chances are: 40% for Jing Mountain, 30% each for Qujiang Thin Slice and Xianya Stone Flower. So, how many days, on average, would it take for a guest to taste all three?
Answer: Simple calculation shows it's about 5.6 days. But, of course, you could always sneak into the kitchen of Revelry Hall and try them all in one go.

买春天，要多少钱？\n我当然知道她想买什么，但我不想让她知道我知道。\n于是我说:
"How much does it cost... to buy spring?"

Of course, I knew what she meant. But I didn't want her to know that I knew.

So I said, "Depends who you're buying. Miss Chen from the east wing? That'll cost a hundred strings of copper coins. Miss Li from the west? A thousand. But your Miss Chun..."

"Want... want..."

"She's our top courtesan," I said, holding up a single finger and giving it a wag, "Ten thousand."

She left, murmuring "ten thousand" under her breath. She really believed it.

I hadn't lied. Miss Chun truly had been the pride of our house.

But now... she was old, sick, barely able to move.

At first, when she started taking medicine, the girl would crouch by her feet, refusing to leave.

Later, when Miss Chun couldn't leave her room, she'd let the clients come to her. The girl would squat at the door like a little stone lion.

Then Miss Chun grew paler day by day, her makeup thicker, her prices cheaper.

The wounds on her body multiplied, and so did the copper coins she clutched.

The deal was struck on a winter's day.

I was wiping down the tables when I heard a loud slap.

She had slammed three bloody copper coins onto the surface.

"I have... only... three..."

"Exchange. Spring... Chun."

She said "Chun" so clearly, I almost believed it really was the first word she learned.

"You just want Miss Chun? No refunds, no exchanges."

"Want..."

The boss's eye twitched, and I understood why.

He shot me a look and waved me over.

"Waiter. Take her."

I'm the Waiter.

Out of pity, I gave her the last scrap of straw matting from my house, then took her to see the body.

I was waiting for her to regret it, to wrap the corpse in the mat, to bury it properly.

But she didn't.

She didn't use the mat.

The body couldn't walk, so she simply lifted Miss Chun into her arms.

Her dress was soaked in blood. So were the coins.

The three strings of bloodstained coins landed in my hand.

A poor bargain, by any measure.

A corpse not worth dirtying her silver, not worth dirtying her clothes.

But she didn't care.

She ran straight into the spring.

One night, Zhao Wu, a peddler cutting through the burial ground to save time, watched in horror as all the red silks snapped suddenly taut, jerking at the mounds until soil crumbled and fell. Dark, mottled hands clawed their way out of the earth, each wrist tied with a length of crimson silk, grasping blindly toward the moon.
"What wickedness..." An old villager seized the trembling Zhao Wu and dragged him away. Last year's drought, he said, had driven the village chief to declare that the mountain god wanted a bride. He had seized several young women from outside the village, bound them in red silk, and fed them into the mountain god's "embrace." The old man told Zhao Wu to leave and not look back.
That same night, fire broke out across the village. The flames curled around window frames like ribbons of silk. As the villagers struggled to fight the blaze, they saw dark, charred figures writhing in the fire, the red silk at their wrists still vivid and unburned.
By dawn, every villager who had played a part in the "bride offering" bore a red ring around their neck, appearing from nowhere. Within three days, twenty new mounds had been raised on the western slope, each wound tight with blood-red silk that glistened like an open wound.
