That was how the "Second Round" pancake stall opened. The owner was Master Jian, still stern-faced, still scowling.
He remembered mocking Heng'er once, "Peddling snacks is child's play compared to the study of Flight!" Now, staring at lumpy batter and a crooked sign barely holding together, he found himself oddly nostalgic for those punishing days of study.
But people live on food. He remembered how a single hot, savory bite had been enough to steady his heart on countless sleepless nights. So he brought the same stubborn dedication he once poured into flight, and turned it toward a griddle.
Too much water? Add flour. Too thick? Add water... Then, one fresh egg.
At last, a pancake spread into a perfect, full circle, round as the moon. Master Jian wiped the sweat from his brow. The steam rising from the stall seemed to soften the hard lines of his face.

Yi'er liked shepherd's purse. Rong'er liked ham. Ah Du liked zucchini. Ah Yang liked fresh lamb... He memorized every preference, inventing dozens of savory fillings.
The people here needed something new to look forward to.
Before long, business at "Second Round" picked up. Not just because the food was good, which was rarely good in No-Worries Cliff, but because people wanted to see it for themselves. To see how that once-lonely, aloof scholar now struggled earnestly to hawk his wares.
"Hot off the griddle! Savory and rich! One bite guarantees you'll be coming back for a Second Round!"
That's life, isn't it? Even if the past is dust... as long as you have something to look forward to, you can always start a Second Round.

The world, as Yang Qiang sees it, runs on two things: sharp blades and hard fists. With grit and muscle, he protects his siblings and defends his turf.
One day, he and his crew robbed a group of merchants. They were just getting ready to celebrate with meat and wine when an old refugee wrapped in tattered rags stumbled in.
Yang Qiang was annoyed. He got up, ready to teach the old man a lesson for stirring up trouble on his mountain. But then the man spoke, and his words landed like a rock to the chest.
"The invaders have taken Luancheng," the old man said. "How long do you think you can hold this mountain? Sooner or later, you and your siblings are next."
For the first time in his life, the wine in his hand lost its appeal. A cold feeling crept over him.
His mountain. His territory. The invaders were coming for it, for his home, for his brother and sister.
"Who do they think they are?" He jumped to his feet and smashed the wine bowl on the ground. The three siblings exchanged a glance, no words needed, just a shared understanding.
"Let's go meet those dogs," he said. "I'll show them whose blade is sharper."

In traditional celebrations, the eighth day of the Spring Festival often marks the end of the holiday break. 亲爱的游侠：\n岁暮天寒，今夜是除夕。在中原习俗中，无论身在何方，今晚都要围炉夜:
Dear Wanderer,
The year draws to a close in the cold; tonight is Spring Festival's Eve. In the customs of the Central Plains, no matter where one is, one must gather around the stove tonight and keep the lamps burning. This tradition is known as Keeping Vigil. The road of the Jianghu is long, and you may still be traveling. But this steaming "Spring Festival's Eve Dinner" must not be missed. May the lights of the city warm your weary journey. Farewell to the old and welcome to the new; tonight, we stay awake!
亲爱的游侠：\n年景过半，今日习俗为“挹肥”，即大扫除，寓意将昔日的晦气与贫穷统:
Dear Wanderer,
The Spring Festival is halfway through. Today's custom is the "Great Cleansing," symbolizing the sweeping away of past bad luck and poverty, which is a ritual known as "Sending Off Poverty." Please lighten your burden and discard useless clutter. Only by clearing out the weight of the past can you make room for the surprises and hopes of tomorrow.

To the people, food is heaven. Today marks the return of the "Kitchen God" to the mortal realm. The Kitchen God oversees the hearth and ensures the family is fed and warm throughout the seasons. Even a peerless master cannot go without a hearty meal. Please accept these delicacies. May you be well-fed and full of vigor in the new year.

"Five months," Shiqi answered.

"And if one acre yields two picul of grain per year, how much would five acres yield?"

"Ten piculs," said Lucky Seventeen.

Wei Renpu was overjoyed, "The sages spoke true!"
Seeing his joy, Shiqi clapped along with him and beamed with pride. 

After the death of Chai Rong, the Hanging Blade finally disbanded. Wei once said: "When ten thousand swords are forged, the day of return shall come." 

Lucky Seventeen, hearing this, asked innocently, "How long does it take to forge one sword?"

"A month," Wei replied.

"Then ten thousand swords will take ten thousand months. There are twelve months in a year..."

Shiqi did the math in his head and asked, "Once I finish forging them, will the Dragon keep its promise?"

Wei, though pained by the question, still answered.

"It will."

There's an old saying: among all trades under heaven, three are the hardest, poling boats, hammering iron, and making tofu.
Hu Sanli still remembered how it used to be, back when his father was alive. At early-afternoon, his father would already be preparing the next day's tofu. Making tofu wasn't brute labor, but a careful, fussy work, ten steps from start to finish. The first step alone took patience: picking through mounds of soybeans, choosing only the full, glossy ones. His father was an honest man who never padded the batch with bad beans. A full pile would pass through his hands, and barely half a basket would remain. Even then, the beans had to soak for more than ten hours in cold spring water drawn at dawn. Only after that could he stop and take a break.
At midnight, when the house had fallen into deep sleep, Hu Sanli would hear his father get up to grind the beans. The timing could not be wrong, not even slightly. Miss it, and the tofu would lose its true taste. In those days, grinding a single tub of beans took twelve full hours.
Now, at twenty, Hu Sanli straightened his aching back, drew a breath, and wiped the sweat from his brow. This was his second batch of the night. His father could make four before dawn. He could only manage two. Just where was he lacking in skill compared to his father?

什么是人？ \n铁甲人站在嗟叹崖顶，山下的动静在他鹰隼般的眼中一览无余。\n风:
What defines a human?

The Ironclad stood upon the summit of Gasping Cliff. Beneath his falcon-like gaze, every movement in the valley below lay exposed. The wind carried moonlight onto his mask, or rather, his face. That bronze visage, almost never removed, had long since become his true face. When bronze forms half your stride, half your spine, and half your very core, and when you can neither stand nor survive without the clatter of machinery, can you still be called human?
Yes.

He told himself that he was more worthy of that title than many born to it. One is born of man, yet birth alone does not grant humanity.

The child in the cauldron was not treated as human, and those huddled around the fire possessed no humanity to speak of. Nor did the guards who herded those starving beasts outside the gates to devour one another, nor the silk-clad elite feasting at lavish tables, nor the servants who discarded surplus grain and fine flour.

Years ago, his sister, too, was denied her humanity.

Does a cripple count? Does a fool? Is a witless child, fit only to squander rations and offering nothing in return, who recoils from the fire a heartbeat too late, truly worth the grain that could save a healthy life? Even cats and dogs know to flee the flames, yet your sister lacks even the sense of a beast! Open your eyes! People are starving to death before you, yet you waste life-giving food on a...
Yes.

His answer rang with the certainty of iron. Clutching his hard-won rations amidst the curses and pleas of the dying, he placed them into her unknowing hands.
Because his sister was human, too.

It was not until a wanderer descended upon an azure bird that he realized the world held more than men and beasts. It also held Immortals.
Immortals... What kind of humans were they?

They dwelled at the pinnacle of drifting clouds. Beyond their celestial peaks, the parched earth, wildfires, floods, and cold iron devoured human lives. Even the sun, moon, and stars seemed to open their ravenous maws. Yet within the mountains, bronze servants and stone maids walked the halls. Wooden oxen and gliding horses served without complaint. Even the elements of sun and moon, water and fire, had become faithful and submissive companions.
Overnight, his sister was transformed from one deemed unworthy of humanity into an Immortal by birth. She stood among them beneath the star-strewn skies, radiant and sublime, as though she herself were a goddess. Within those sacred peaks, he too found parents, a master, freedom, and glory. He mastered a blade art that became his pride, and he found companions whose hearts beat in harmony with his own.

The world beyond was too bitter, and he had been too young when it first scarred him. Thus, he buried himself beneath the sheltering wings of his newfound kin, allowing the storms beyond the mountain and the wounds upon his body to slowly fade. Until the day a falling sun reduced everything he loved to ash.
"Child, where do you intend to go?"
"To find her."
"To seek vengeance?"
"To protect her."
"...A heart of pure innocence. Someone like you should see what lies beyond these mountains before you return."
"...As you wish."

And so, the brother she once knew never returned. In his place stands the Ironclad of today, watching from Gasping Cliff as the wind carries the same question back to him: What defines a human?
Some are denied their humanity by their own kind. Yet those who refuse to see the humanity in others forfeit their own. Of this, he has no doubt.
But now, are these Immortals, separated only by a mountain's breadth, truly "human"? His sister and the entire celestial house were enshrined upon golden thrones. Yet those who reviled her as a beast and those who worshipped her as a goddess shared the exact same failing: neither ever saw the person she was.

If these Immortals understood that "humanity" is a myth, that there is only a creature who becomes a beast in purgatory, a god upon the peaks, and a "mortal" burdened by mundane woes in the world below, how would they view the so-called human race? And what of the one who broods over the nature of humanity, yet divides his fellow beings into ranks and castes, judging by his own decree who is "human" and who is not? Can such a judge truly claim that title?

For the first time in his life, the answer eluded him.
Until, with a thunderous roar, the sun flared and bloomed before him once more. In that instant, all notions of "human" and "non-human" evaporated from his mind. His limbs, his hands, and even the tears upon his face no longer obeyed the dictates of his logic.

He was but a common mortal, his heart torn apart by a thoroughly human grief.

Serving in the army, I am often moved to tears by news of comrades in the capital and across the realm striving for the cause.
Li Yin of Dingzhou, my childhood friend, is gentle by nature. Since assuming command, he has labored day and night, penning more than three hundred dispatches to the front, coordinating provisions and relaying intelligence to ensure that the border troops never suffer a shortage of grain.
Fang Qianshan and I studied under the same teacher. Though his views have long differed from mine, since the war began, he has set aside our disagreements, standing firm against opposition at court so that the soldiers under my command might at least have their fill.
Beyond the court, scholars such as Han Jiangzi, Mu Qi, and Feng Yunchang wield their brushes to awaken the world, undaunted by power; within it, officials like Sang Weihan speak with blade-like candor.
For the written word, and the principles it bears, is the backbone of a nation. It is through the steadfast efforts of such men, within and without the court, that the people of the realm may find, if only for a single night, a measure of peace.

On a bright, breezy day, the old shoemaker gently shifted the basket of boots balanced on his back and strolled slowly to the bustling marketplace. 
"Old man, are these shoes lined with gold? Why are they so pricey?" 
For over thirty years, he'd heard that question more times than he cared to count. But he didn't mind. Closing his eyes, he swayed lightly, basking in the warm spring sunshine. 

"How much for these shoes?" another woman's voice called out. 
"One hundred," he answered absently, without opening his eyes, assuming it was just another curious onlooker. 
"I'll take them." 
"If you can't afford them, just move along. That's the price... Wait, you're buying them?!" Startled, the old man opened his eyes and saw a young woman standing before him, her face serious as she carefully examined the shoes in her hands. 

Having traveled far and wide, the old shoemaker knew at once this woman truly appreciated the craftsmanship behind his work. A smile, warm and genuine, spread across his face—it had been years since someone truly understood the art of shoemaking. 
"These shoes feel so soft and comfortable, and the soles are thick but supple. How do you make them?" 
His eyes brightened. A fellow craftsperson? A kindred spirit! 

"Ah, my dear, since you know a thing or two about shoemaking, you understand it's no simple task. If leather is used for the uppers, it takes months to tan it properly. If linen, there are soaking and weaving steps to consider. And the thousand-layer soles? They require needles, awls, wooden lasts, and waxed thread to stitch through countless layers of fabric. It's painstaking work. This pair you hold is the quintessential thousand-layer sole—perfect for travelers. I spent a whole year making these." 
A whole year—that's a long time. The woman ran her fingers lightly over the shoes, lowering her gaze but her eyes drifting elsewhere. 

"To fit just right, the shoe's upper must be shaped and bent to the wooden sole with precision—off by even a fraction of a millimeter, and the fit's ruined. Shoemaking demands patience and care, don't you think?" 
Yes, she thought quietly—attention to detail is everything. 
Yet, what if this shoe was for a father journeying endlessly, alone, caring for a sick child in search of medicine? Such hardship couldn't simply be measured by careful work alone. 

"But in the end," the shoemaker said softly, gazing across the street at a father giving water to his daughter, "what matters most in shoemaking is heart..." 
"One hundred," Lan Ao said, placing the money in his hand. "Thank you." 
"Oh! You're too kind, young lady! Here, take it back—you don't need to pay so much!" the old man urged. 
She didn't reply, turning to walk away. 
Seeing she wasn't going to take it back, he called out, "How about two more pairs? These are good ones as well! Miss? Miss?" 
"No, thank you," Lan Ao paused, then added, "I make shoes myself." 

The old shoemaker stood holding two pairs in his hands, words failing him. 
She walked farther and farther away. 
For a moment, he thought he saw, in the distance, the man who long ago asked him how he made shoes—a memory stirred, as timeless as his craft.

今日是苏家老夫人七十寿辰，苏府上下铺红结彩，宾客满席，喜气盈天。熙熙攘攘的客席之:
Today marks the seventieth birthday of Matriarch Su. The entire Homestead is draped in festive crimson, a sea of lanterns and silks radiating joy to the heavens.
Guests huddle in hushed conversation: how did the Sus, of all people, secure the favor of the Dragon King of the Dragon Tide Clan? Word on the street is that by riding the coattails of the Dragon Tide Clan, they've seized a portion of the salt trade. That single move sent them soaring, leaving Xuzhou's local gentry scrambling in their wake.
Patriarch Su, a man of fifty who has yet to outgrow his hedonistic streaks, is lost in a drunken haze, his face flushed with the pride of a family reborn. The Matriarch shoots a scathing look at her useless son and then turns to her granddaughter, Su Wan, the true power behind the family. Only then does her gaze soften. But as her eyes drift to the outsider standing beside Su Wan, they narrow with venomous spite.
"Long Yuntian, Su Wan has serious matters to attend to. No place for an outsider. Withdraw to the guest wing now!"
This Long Yuntian possesses a sharp, ascetic face with eyes like distant stars, radiating a natural, frigid aura. His unkempt hair, bound loosely today, lends him an air of the wild, untamed jianghu. Despite the public humiliation, he remains silent. He is the matrilocal groom of the Sus. To the world, he is the greatest blemish on Su Wan's otherwise perfect life.
Long Yuntian's gaze falls on Su Wan, the woman who has once been cast aside by the matriarch but now stands at the center of power, the de facto head of the Su family. She acts as if he didn't exist, her face bright with charm as she shares a laugh with Luo Feng, the illegitimate son of the Vice-Governor, as if she'd completely forgotten who stood by her when she was thrown out of the Su Homestead in disgrace, who willingly took on the humiliating label of the matrilocal groom just so she could reclaim control of the family.
Long Yuntian raises his head, the suppressed dignity of his past resurfacing. His voice drips with cold irony: "Tell me, Matriarch, is this your plan? To pimp out your granddaughter to a bastard? I'm still Su Wan's husband, whether you like it or not."
A ripple of shock and murmurs sweeps through the hall.
Su Wan spins around, her eyes blazing as they lock onto Long Yuntian. Sensing the guests' prying eyes, Su Wan suppresses her fury. "Enough! For a matrilocal groom, obeying the Matriarch is the highest propriety. How dare you hurl such reckless insults on her very birthday?"
"Propriety? Ha! A fine word for it! Do you forget, Su Wan? When that old crone cast you out, claiming a woman had no place in the family business, who stood by you? Who took the brand of the 'matrilocal groom' just to fight that very 'propriety' by your side?"
The Matriarch trembles, her finger jabbing the air at him. "You insolent cur! Wan and I are of one blood; the past is buried. Now that she leads our house to greatness, how dare you, a mere outsider, to sow discord?"
The Matriarch glances at Su Wan and, seeing the anger flash across her granddaughter's face, finally relaxes.
"Blood is thicker than your lies. How dare you spout such filth against your elders? Bring paper and ink! Today, before all the honored guests, I, Su Wan, sever our ties. We're done from this day forth!"
To find out what happens next, stay tuned for the next episode.

He was the most ordinary of souls—no grand ambitions, no lofty dreams. The only thing he ever wanted was to follow his brother and walk the same path.
So he joined his brother at Inkbound Order, and when his brother left, he followed without hesitation.

Tian Qi was delighted when his brother took him back to their childhood secret cave to live in seclusion.
No matter what, he was the only one who had always stayed by his brother's side.
That cave, known to no one else, still held traces of their youth:
The crooked scribbles of their first attempts at writing, the bamboo sticks they once used for sword practice, a long-lost game piece they could never find...
Delighted, he showed each relic to his brother. But his brother only gave faint smiles, his attention buried in the books he had brought from Inkbound Order.
Ever since coming to the cave, his brother did nothing but read.
Those books held the purpose his brother sought, but Tian Qi never understood it.
It didn't matter if he couldn't understand—he just needed to follow his brother, Tian Qi comforted himself.

Until one day, his brother finished reading those books, decided to leave again, and destroyed all traces of their past.
What kind of great cause could be worth erasing all signs of their existence?
He had never understood his brother.

He finally realized that all these years, he had never truly walked the same path as his brother. He had always stared at the other's back, but had lost him in a distant moment.
Mediocre, insignificant, cowardly—he had foolishly believed the bond of their youth would last a lifetime.
He never knew that some who start together in hardship are fated to part ways along the road.
This time, Tian Qi did not follow.

他是个短视眼。\n\n打从他记事起，远山就是晕开的墨团，近树便是蓬松的绿云，人的:
For as long as he could remember, distant mountains were but smudges of ink, and nearby trees were nothing but soft, green clouds. Faces were veiled in a drifting mist, their features tucked away behind the haze.
His parents always smiled lightly, assuring him, "Being short-sighted isn't an illness; it's nothing to worry about." Yet behind their smiles, he saw the worn pages of medical books, tasted bitter medicines coaxed down in countless bowls, and even caught glimpses of talismans they burned in secret at midnight. They weren't as carefree as they pretended.
But he didn't fret. If the world was blurry, he'd simply lean in closer. When admiring flowers, he pressed his nose near their petals; in reading, his forehead was nearly pressed into the carved characters; and when looking at people, he longed most to peer into their eyes. Behind the same veil of mist, some eyes were dull as ash, while others shone like dewdrops.

Once, he leaned so close to the neighbor girl's face, studying her eyes with earnest curiosity, scaring her into a fit of tears. The next day, the family fled. He stood before their empty courtyard, a wave of guilt washing over him. From that day on, he learned restraint. No matter how captivating the face, he would hold himself back.

But Fang Bai... Fang Bai was an exception. That day, when he drew his sword and sent everyone fleeing, silhouetted against the day, his eyes seemed to burn brighter than the sun. How he longed to capture them in a painting, but the road out of the city was too short, their conversations too few, and he never got close enough to truly glimpse the light dwelling deep within those eyes.
All that effort, clinging to carriages just to slip him a note, hadn't been in vain. A letter finally arrived. Though filled with simple tales of rural life and trivial wandering adventures, to someone who had never left Chang'an, those words were nothing less than grand wonders. 
One day, as if possessed by a wanderlust demon, Chang'an could no longer hold him. He packed chopsticks, thinking they were brushes, and soap pods, thinking they were rations. His parents caught the bundle, tearfully unpacking the nonsense he'd stuffed inside. They replaced them with what he'd actually need, and tucked in the thickest, warmest winter coat they owned.
At the city gate, he looked back with bright confidence and said, "Mother, Father! I'm off to catch the wind!" Their voices faded on the growing breeze as home receded behind him, and the vast, open world beckoned, close, alive, and waiting.

He journeyed deep into the heart of the world, yet never drew close to Fang Bai again. The only time he did, it felt like a trick of the mind. Memory is always thus, a painting soaked in water, its ink bleeding away. What he truly remembered was racing through a hazy expanse, the jade box heavy and cold against his chest. The wind whispered past his ears, and while Fang Bai's back was to him, he seemed to tilt his head, just a fraction, and cast a glance back. Perhaps a look of encouragement, or a silent farewell.
In an instant, his sight was cured. The world turned sharp and clear as never before. He saw the delicate veins tracing through every leaf, the graceful flow of clouds across the sky, the subtleties in people's faces, some knitted in worry, others softened with kindness. Even the truth behind the neighbor family's abrupt departure, years past, unfolded before him: the clash of steel, the barks of command, and the muffled sobs... Now he finally saw what they meant.
His heart surged like a lion standing tall against the wind, propelled forward by an unyielding resolve to run, to fight, to save all those things he once failed to notice, blinded by his own limited sight.

He couldn't tell when the wind had finally fallen silent.
When he finally reached Chang'an, he found only a tomb of silence and ruin. Grand palaces, towering halls, government offices, humble dwellings, all reduced to splintered wood, too fragile to hold a single story, a single memory. The air hung thick with mist, the distant mountains kept their silence, and charred beams drifted aimlessly, tangling in the murky waters.

Lost and overwhelmed, he grasped desperately for an image of Fang Bai's face. There was only a blur, a darkness more absolute, more despairing than the ruin before him.
He loathed himself for being born with such short sight.

Ren Xiaoping would never understand Zheng Ran. Many children were fools, but Zheng Ran wasn't a fool. She was something stranger than a fool.
That day, another fool asked a stupid question: "We can see trees and rivers, but blind people only see darkness, so what do they actually see?"
Ren Xiaoping glanced at the child who asked, then at Zheng Ran. What an idiotic question.
"You mean blind kids? They see nothing, obviously."
"I can see!"
"Blind kid lies! What could you possibly see?"
"I... I can see... I can see—"
"Dreams!"
"When everyone sleeps, they close their eyes and dream. I asked before, and when that happens, people see darkness too, but they're just... dreaming."

Ren Xiaoping froze, unable to make sense of this logic, but that didn't stop him from bursting into laughter. "Blind kid says she sees dreams! Blind kid..." Before he could finish, his mother's palm smacked his back, lifting him like a chick by the scruff. Zheng Ran heard his "Help!" from a much higher position than before.
Ren Xiaoping's mother carried her son in one hand and held Zheng Ran's hand in the other, leading them home. The woman briskly asked what they'd been arguing about. Ren Xiaoping babbled an explanation—who knew if she understood? But as always, she delivered her verdict: "Ran is right. When she closes her eyes, she sees dreams."
"Dreams!"
"Yes, yes, Ran can see dreams." And so, Ran would live in dreams her whole life.

So what? 
As long as she could live in beautiful dreams forever, 
as long as someone was willing to let her live in beautiful dreams forever, then this world ought to have people who dwell in beautiful dreams. 
And Ran was a good child. Ran deserved to live in beautiful dreams. 

But Ran had one dream of her own. She didn't want to watch the people on this street disappear one by one. When she grew up, she wanted to stand in front of everyone she loved. 
Only... the fortune telling Daoists said dreams were always the opposite of reality.
But it didn't matter, Ran. If the world is a story that cycles endlessly, then perhaps dreams and reality share the same ending.

伏马庄厨娘的大女儿，向往江湖，最爱看话本中的侠客故事，给伏马庄的每匹马都起了江湖: Eldest daughter of Finesteed Hamlet's cook, who names horses after Jianghu heroes from storybooks.
伏马庄厨娘的小女儿，好奇心旺盛，喜欢躲在暗中观察庄子里的大人们。: The curious young daughter of Finesteed Hamlet's cook, who spies on adults from hiding.
伏马庄名马失窃，或是盗马贼所为。伏马庄庄主信誓旦旦，声称从其他马口中得知，盗窃者: A prized horse has gone missing from Finesteed Hamlet, and horse thieves are suspected to be the culprits. Master Qi of the Finesteed Hamlet insists, based on what he claims to have heard from the other horses, that the culprit is a mysterious man in a bamboo hat. The missing horse is brown in color. Master Qi also reports that another valuable horse was stolen earlier by someone who calls himself the "Horse Tamer," and its whereabouts are still unknown.
伏马庄名马失窃，或是盗马贼所为，望少侠前往探明真相！: A prized horse has gone missing from Finesteed Hamlet, and horse thieves are suspected to be the culprits. Please go there to get to the bottom of the case!
伏马庄外的陶翁总喜欢站在路边，双目无神地盯着来往行人，多去看他几次，定可遇上奇事: Old Man Tao, standing by the road outside Finesteed Hamlet, stares listlessly at passersby. Check on him a few times, and you will stumble upon something unusual.
伏马庄庄主，爱马胜过爱人，数月前曾忽然失踪，归来后与马儿们的感情更胜往昔，与人的: The master of Finesteed Hamlet, who loves horses more than people—vanished suddenly months ago, returning with a deeper bond to his steeds and growing distance from others.
伏马庄恰好有一名未央商会的商人，要不要将这封信交还给他？亦或是交给其他更有必要看: There's a merchant of Weiyang Chamber at Finesteed Hamlet. Should you return the letter to him, or give it to someone else?
伏马庄新来的这金乌缀雪似乎性子很烈？不过烈马也怕缠郎，多试几次，展开一段奇遇: Finesteed Hamlet's new steed, Golden Snow, has a fiery temper. But even the fiercest horse can be tamed by persistence. Try again and again to trigger an encounter.
伏马庄杂役，在伏马庄扫了二十年的马粪，心已经像陈年的马粪一样坚不可摧。: A 20 - year stable hand, his resolve as tough as aged horse dung from years of labor.
伏马庄李厨娘的小女儿阿骐古灵精怪，满脑子稀奇古怪的念头，近来她#a66829常在: Aqi, the lively young daughter of Chef Li at Finesteed Hamlet, is full of wild ideas. Lately, she's been #a66829wandering around the manor#E, seemingly searching for something interesting...
伏马庄来了一匹可通人言的马。但你发现这匹马居然是人变的。他因得罪了戏法师被变成马: A talking horse has appeared at Finesteed Hamlet, but you soon discover the truth: he is a man, transformed by a sorcerer he offended.
伏马庄牧马人祁阿五的妻子，丈夫失踪后常在不伏马场的树下等待他归来。: Wife of Qi A'wu, a horse herder from Finesteed Hamlet—she waits under a tree at Wildmane Ranch since her husband's disappearance.
伏马庄牧马人，专职给马儿喂草。闲时喜欢抠脚丫子，再用抠脚丫子的手给马儿喂草。: A Finesteed Hamlet groom feeds horses with hands that just scratched his feet.
伏马庄牧马人，专职给马儿盖房。虽然给马儿盖了无数房屋，自己却只能露天睡觉。: A stable builder who sleeps under the stars—he says, "Horses need roofs more than men."
伏马庄的一位马贩，原计划北上券马，未曾想渡河的船坏了，被困于苦海岸边，进退两难。: A horse dealer from Finesteed Hamlet who had planned to sell his horses in the north but got stranded on the shore of the Bodhi Sea because of his broken boat.
伏马庄的人告发，目睹了你偷盗了他们珍藏的驯马秘籍。: The Finesteed Hamlet reports you for stealing their prized horse-training manual.
伏马庄的猎户张刀疤数日闭门不出，听说是因为算命先生说他近日来会遭“报应”……: Scarred Zhang, a hunter from Finesteed Hamlet, has stayed locked inside for days. Word is, a fortune-teller warned him that retribution was near...
伏马庄的猎户张刀疤数日闭门不出，听说是因为算命先生说他近日来会遭“报应”。: Scarred Zhang, the hunter from Finesteed Hamlet, has been holed up for days. Rumor has it a fortune teller warned him that karma would soon catch up to him.
The lantern at Finesteed Hamlet is complete.
伏马庄的驯马人马老三近来似乎得了一匹十分通人性的好马……: The horse trainer Ma Laosan at Finesteed Hamlet has recently acquired a remarkable steed...
伐木烧山坏的是千年之计！若是任由他们将树木伐尽，不见山年年无樵可采，便无法自守山: If they continue cutting and burning like this, Hidden Mountain will be laid bare, and we will have nowhere left to stay…
休息之前，在奶奶家四处看看吧。: You decide to explore Granny Turtle's place before settling down for a break.
休息的不好，一段时间内精力消耗增加。: Poor rest increases energy consumption for a period of time.
Poor rest. Energy consumption increased for a period.
休息的不错，一段时间内精力消耗降低。: Good rest. Energy consumption reduced for a period.
休息组件不足，无法休息: Insufficient rest components; unable to rest
休想走！你当我三岁小孩！他已拿了一个灯，你又要跑，合伙赖账啊！: Hold it! You think I'm stupid? He took a lantern, and now you're running off. You two are in this together!
休想！！道不同不相为谋。: Never! We do not walk the same path!
休憩一晚后，女子已然不知所踪。她说过要去井口寻找什么，不如前去井口一探。: After a night's rest, the woman has vanished. She spoke of searching for something by the well. Check there.
休憩设施不足，匠客无法派遣到家业，是否前往摆放？: Insufficient resting facilities. Cannot deploy artisans to Homestead. Place now?
休憩设施不足，庄客无法派遣到家业，是否前往摆放？: Insufficient rest facilities. Retainers cannot be dispatched to the Homestead. Go place some now?
休整一番后，再继续探查。新的一日，也许燕会有新的消息。: Rest before continuing the investigation. A new day may bring new news from Swallow.
休沐……呵，无知刁民，竟妄图休息？!: Resting? Ha! You worthless fool, you dare slack off?!
休沐……理应善人岁岁休沐，恶人永世劳作！: Wind-down days… Rest the virtuous all year long and toil the wicked forever and ever!
休沐之时，可对是友非敌、道异心同之首领使用鹅之膝，不战而屈人之兵！: Use Goosy Slide to subdue without battle during the respite!
休沐了，可是大龙不在了……他们都不在了，没人陪小十七玩了。: But now he's gone... No one's left to keep me company.
休沐期间，请勿打扰: Rest period. Please do not disturb.
休沐的日子倒是比平日里更忙些，要检修兵器甲胄，巡视屯田。不过城里也更热闹些……: Rest days are even busier with repairing arms and inspecting fields, but the city feels more alive too...
Rest days are even busier—repairing arms, inspecting fields. But the city feels more alive too...
休要在此胡言！看清楚这里是什么地方！: Hold your tongue! Do you have any idea where you're standing?
休要多言，出手吧，同道。: Save your breath. Let's settle this.
休要扰我清净，耽误了我温书三百篇。: Go away. I still have three hundred pages to get through.
休要提这鬼神之说，辛匠已经在看了。: Don't go on about ghosts and spirits. Xin's already looking into it.
休要狡辩，我已亲眼所见！: I saw it with my own eyes. Don't bother lying.
休要猖狂，我都瞧见了！: I saw everything! Don't push your luck!
休要胡言……我们这是来……寻曲的！: Nothing like that... We're just here... looking for a tune.
休走！我正为木鸢烦心，你就撞上来了？: I'm already dealing with that wooden eagle mess, and now you show up?
休走！我看你形迹最为可疑！: You're the most suspicious one here. Stay put!
休走！我那物件可是要紧之物！: That was important! Give it back!
休走！此事与你脱不了干系！: You're not going anywhere. You're part of this!
休走！此事你必须给我一个交代！: You're not leaving until you answer for this!
众人争抢生金瓯，樊楼陷入混乱，这时，生金瓯忽然落入你的手中，尽全力保护生金瓯！: Revelry Hall descends into disorder as the crowd scrambles for the Gold-Making Vessel. It lands in your grip—do your best to safeguard it!
众人会合，与福禄寿交流藏身地情况。: You reunite with the three sisters at the hideout. Exchange information with them.
众人依次登录籍贯: Line up and register your origins.
众人先惊后笑，送了它“清河第一美雕”的称号，引得雕八爷十分开怀。: Everyone was surprised, but then they laughed and gave him the title of the most beautiful condor in Qinghe, and Lord Condor was happy.
众人只见中选者春风得意，而落选者就如这落花一般，多少悲伤，谁人知晓……: The people only see those proud, blooming chosen ones, while the ones that didn't make the cut get swept aside like fallen flowers, their tragedies unsung...
众人只谈开源，你能看到节流之重，是难得的清醒之言。: While others speak only of expanding revenue, you see the weight of reducing expenditure. This is a rare and clear-headed voice.
众人四散到大厅各处，拿起自己的乐器开始演奏\n廉道子穿行其中，听到了以不同乐器—:
The crowd disperses to various spots in the hall, picking up their instruments to begin playing. 
Lian Daozi moves among them, hearing the same song performed with different lead instruments—guqin, flute, erhu, and bili.
众人围攻一人激斗: A fierce battle of many besieging one.
众人对聚宝盆议论纷纷，想办法让他们买下聚宝盆。: You watch as the crowd gathers around the Treasure Basin. Find a way to convince them to buy it.
众人散去，燕欲在此等待鸟朋友探路归来，意外收到春花婶的热情邀请。\n鸰儿归山，你:
The crowd disperses. Swallow stays to wait for the Monocled Bird, while Aunt Chunhua offers a warm invitation.
Wagtail has returned. Go find Aunt Chunhua... and don't forget to unblock Big Feng's meridian.
众人正在围炉做活之时，“表叔”来访。\n随他一起来的，还有小磊。一家人竟在这个雪:
While everyone is working by the hearth, "Uncle" visits.
Lei arrives with him. The family is unexpectedly reunited on this snowy night.
众人皆拜 你为何不拜: They all bow to me. Why do you not?
Everyone gives, so I have to give too...
众人皆言此物已吸收东阙公子身上财气，少侠带一个回家，必定招财纳福，大吉大利！: Everyone said these basins soaked up the Ember of East's fortune. Take one home, Young Hero, and you're sure to bring in wealth and luck!
众位都是堂堂丈夫，不与官府暗通，才排在外庭就座。好不容易来此，连内堂都不入，不如: You're all here because you've got no ties to the court. You made it this far, so why sit out here? Let's take the fight inside!
众位，随我迎接公子秘使。: Everyone, with me. The young lord's envoy has arrived.
众佛之下，一个身影端坐于此。\n一声禅音仿佛从心间响起：小施主，你是想见我的法相:
Beneath the gaze of all the Buddhas, a lone figure sits in silence. 
A voice echoes, serene and inward: Little one, are you here to see my Dharma form, or the truth?
众侠客赴滹沱，入长夜。长夜虽暗，仍向明时。: Martial Artists head to the Hutuo, into the long night. Though the night is dark, it moves toward the dawn.
众侠齐聚欲争夺，宝物竟是大香蕉！: When life gives you bananas, make smoothies.
众多翠色身影汇成溪流，逆着乱世的洪流向北而去。一针续脉，一药还阳，他们于尸山血海: Verdant silhouettes stream north against the current of time. A needle brings back the pulse; a potion restores the spirits. Through mountains of corpses and seas of blood, they wrestle with Yama for every life that should not be lost.
众多饲养者齐心协力，提升管理，降低成本，#Y果味奶皮卷#E降价#Y{prop}#: The army has requisitioned large amounts of medicine, sharply reducing market supply. #YFruity Milk Skin Roll#E has decreased in price by #Y{prop}#E.
众多饲养者齐心协力，提升管理，降低成本，#Y驼奶酒#E降价#Y{prop}#E。: Breeders have worked together to improve management and lower costs. #YCamel Milk Wine#E has decreased in price by #Y{prop}#E.
众客齐聚共享休闲之乐，畅快诉说生活酸甜苦辣: Guests gather to share the joys of leisure and freely discuss the ups and downs of life.
众弟子 拔剑斩之: Draw my swords and fight back.

傅千里是王清从雪地里捡回来的孤儿，因是女儿身，后交由沈寒英抚养授艺。\n傅千里跟:
Fu Qianli was an orphan Wang Qing rescued from the snow. Because she was a girl, she was later given to Shen Hanying to be raised and trained.
Fu Qianli studied under her, practicing the blade most diligently and handling matters most thoroughly. She even learned ninety percent of that stern demeanor, cold as frost and snow. Gradually, she became that silent, reliable figure in the hearts of her peers.
When news from Zhongdu Bridge arrived, she saw her master standing alone in the courtyard, staring toward the north, her knuckles tightening and loosening on her sword hilt.
If the heart is tethered, the blade will hesitate.
Fu Qianli understood.
That night, she took her master's usual Heng Blade and left a single line: "Frost and snow can fall in place of the flower; this bridge should be crossed by the one from a thousand miles."
The person was gone before dawn. The burden on her shoulders was heavier than the blade.
傅千里第一次走那么远远的路，是从故乡到天泉。 \n朔风凛冽，积雪没膝，她每一步都:
The first time Fu Qianli traveled so far was the journey from her birthplace to Well of Heaven. 
In the biting wind, the snow rose knee-deep. Each step she took sank deep until she was half-swallowed by the drifts, only to be hauled out by her senior brother as he turned back.
Looking up, a boundless white expanse stretched to the horizon, meeting the heavens. Well of Heaven remained a thousand miles distant. 
Her senior brother smiled, pointing toward the faint, shimmering lights in the distance. "There it is," he said. "We're almost home!" 
Home. A new home. 
Everyone said she had a fine name. Qianli means a journey of a thousand miles. Her senior brother called it grand; her juniors envied its carefree spirit. She loved it herself.
Her thousand-mile journey ended at home, the best home imaginable. Practicing blades in spring, tempering physiques in summer, gathering pelts in autumn, and warming wine by the hearth in winter... The four seasons passed in steady, ordinary peace.
She no longer needed to wander from place to place, nor tread such wearying roads.
Yet, perhaps as a prophecy of her name, she eventually embarked on a thousand-mile journey once more. 
The Hutuo River stretched a thousand miles, and Mount Taibai lay two thousand miles distant, yet the corpses of Well of Heaven disciples were piled within a mere three paces.
Her Heng blade grew heavy; the scent of blood filled her senses. Yet the resounding voices of her juniors, as they petitioned their Master, echoed in her ears. 
Since finding home, only one cause could draw her a thousand miles away, and only one could make her never return. 
"Master's wish: of our three hundred disciples, not one shall be left behind." 
"Senior Sister... what if we cannot bring them back?"
"...Then we fight until the end. Three hundred disciples, not one left behind."

The once-kind young Wangshu had become the benevolent old man. 
He couldn't remember how many places he had walked, how many moons he had scooped up. 
But his song had become a legend. Every child in Hexi could sing: Moonlight bright, cast your net right... 
People said that eating a moon-turned-bun would make you remember your happiest memory. 
Old Wangshu would just smile, neither confirming nor denying. 
Perhaps peaceful lives had made people forget the simplest truth: to eat your fill is itself the happiest thing. 
But the children singing the rhyme had never known hunger, so they were willing to believe in the bun's magical power to bring joy.

A rabbit with a sprig of grass foretells joy and blessings. 

Rabbits were seen as symbols of fertility and abundance due to their prolific breeding. Among the Song populace, the word for "rabbit" (tu) was considered a homonym for "spitting out children" (tu zi), so porcelain often featured rabbit motifs to symbolize fertility. Rabbit patterns were widely used. One of China's earliest known trademarks was a copperplate design of a white rabbit for the "Liu Family's Kung Fu Needle Shop" in the Northern Song period.

In front of the Homesight Tower, the young man stared blankly at his rejected manuscript and the tael of gold. 
The princess's red annotation read: "The words are simple and lack rhythm, but they reveal sincere feelings. A reward of one tael of gold is granted." 
The young man couldn't believe it, but he still mounted his donkey and raced toward Skybrim Market. 
With this tael of gold, he learned to do business from the Sogdians and gradually became a wealthy merchant. 

Many years later, his caravan returned to Liangzhou. Passing the Cleardew Terrace, he seemed to see his younger self riding the small donkey to present his poem. 
He picked up his brush again and wrote "The Eleventh Scene of Liangzhou." He racked his brains and used all his literary skills to depict the princess's peerless beauty, calling her the eleventh magnificent scene of Liangzhou. When he finished writing, he happily sealed the poem in a golden casket and presented it to the princess living in the Homesight Tower, along with treasures. 
Soon after, a line of palace maids walked out of the tower. The leader returned the treasures and the golden casket to the merchant intact. Only on the golden casket were an additional tael of gold and another red annotation.

After death's long journey, return home. 
Fang Bai told her these lines meant that true lovers would find their way back to each other, and that after they died, they would surely be reunited. 
Such a beautiful promise. 
In those days of tender love, the poem was as sweet as honey to her soul. 

Summer days, winter nights. 
After death's long journey, return home. 
How comforting those words seemed... 
But in the endless nights of sorrow and pain that followed, when she finally released those harsh words and refused to look back, the poem turned bitter—like a draught of gall. 

Days without you burned like scorching summers; winters stretched endlessly, cold and unbearable. 
When I am gone, will you come to my grave? If I lie in eternal rest, will peace find me? 
The nights in Hollow Vale were cold and silent; loneliness seemed to envelop all around. She hid her soft weeping in the nightly winds. 

Wisteria wove through thickets of yellow spiny bushes; wild grapes sprawled across the deserted graves. My beloved rests here—who keeps him company? 
Wisteria wove through thickets of sour jujube branches; wild grapes sprawled across the deserted graves. My beloved rests here—who keeps him company? 
I was born into this world—where is pain not found? 
His pillow glows with polish; his embroidered cover gleams with grandeur. My love sleeps here—who shares his rest? 
I cannot be with you—when, then, is my heart not breaking? 

The breeze at Peach Grove Pass was soft, almost tender. Her plan, like the traps she'd woven, was flawless. 
Using the secret of Palm Master Fierceness as bait, she drew Fang Bai out—bound him with memories of their past love, subdued him with poisoned needles, and held him at swordpoint. 
When Lan Ao finally sheathed her blade, Fang Bai lay motionless on the ground. Perfect. Not once had she wavered. 
Yet, she did not claim the Golden Peach. 
Fang Bai would never yield. She knew him as deeply as she knew herself. 
Their love had been brief, yet it stretched across a lifetime—so intimately entwined, as if they shared the same resting place. 

She had failed to seize the Golden Peach, but even that treasure could not save her now. 
She was dying. 
What is death but cold, loneliness, pain—the utter despair of a future forever lost?  
If so, she had already died a thousand times, ten thousand times over. 
What was there left to fear? 
Alone amidst the peach blossoms, she thought of Fang Bai, who faced death without fear; of her father, burdened by shame; and of her own life, relentlessly hunted by death's shadow. 
A flock of birds swept overhead. 

Lan Ao told Xiaopan to remember her thus: 
When death came for me, I turned toward it, enfolding it in my arms. 
I left this world like a bird taking flight from its branch—not swept away by the storm, but standing resolute against it. 
The world is a cage, and with my death, I shattered its bars. 

Dressed in the robes of the Inkbound Order, she altered her appearance by disguise, ready to attend the banquet in Fang Bai's name. 
Even in this fortress, strong as iron and surrounded by foes, where danger lurked in every glance, her chance of success was slim—yet her resolve was unshaken. 
Better to act foolishly than to surrender without a fight. 
Without you, the winters stretch endlessly; the summers burn with unbearable heat. 
I shall be buried with my "Path" and my "Righteousness." Who will stand with me? 

Blades tore through her, and in her final moments, she thought she saw Fang Bai rushing to her side. 

Days without you burned like scorching summers; winters stretched endlessly, cold and unforgiving. 
My beloved will be laid to rest with his "Path" and his "Righteousness." 
Who will stand by him? 
I will.

养孩子是件麻烦事，寒香寻对此深有体会。\n此时此刻，她看着那孩子兴高采烈地抱着被:
Raising a child is a troublesome matter, something Han Xiangxun understood deeply. 
At this moment, watching the child's small back as he happily carried his bedding into his new bedroom, she suddenly felt as if a lifetime had passed... Ten years had silently slipped away just like that. 
Before the child could even walk, Han Xiangxun began taking care of him, she disliked Jiang Wulang's clumsiness, sometimes thinking he fed the child too much, other times complaining he dressed him too lightly. Three or four days out of ten, she would actively take the child to look after herself. 
Thanks to her, that coarse cloth swaddling stained with old blood was lined with a soft piece of red silk, originally bought by Han Xiangxun to make clothes for herself.... The jade-like, snow-white, adorable baby, wrapped in bright red soft cloth, would often fall asleep by the counter listening to the sound of Han Xiangxun's abacus. Blissful Retreat received guests from all walks of life. Daily, the sounds of finger-guessing games, laughter, and curses filled the air. Loud voices could make the mice in the secret compartments tremble in fear. Yet this little young master could clutch a corner of his blanket and sleep soundly, drooling, amid the full-room clamor. 
They say the more well-behaved a child is in childhood, the more they'll become a little hellion when grown, it's absolutely true. During the Ghost Festival when he was seven, the little hellion, holding a lantern, chased after a spirit-guiding banner. Not only did he singe two tufts of his baby hair on his forehead, he also knocked over the altar table... Later, punished by Han Xiangxun to stand under the eaves and reflect on his misdeeds, before even one stick of incense had burned, he was secretly carried away by Jiang Wulang who had returned from outside... 
... The most amusing was last year. Jiang Wulang, having done some unknown important business outside, returned so exhausted he collapsed and slept in the Bamboo Retreat for three days and three nights, the little hellion thought he had died. Sobbing, he ran to Blissful Retreat, begging Han Xiangxun to perform rites to summon his soul and give him a grand burial... This provoked even the usually impassive Jiang Wulang to suppress a remark: "You are quite filial." 
The past events were vivid in her mind. As Han Xiangxun recalled them, she couldn't help but smile secretly. At this moment, hearing the rustling sound not far away, she figured the little hellion was rummaging through his pile of tattered treasures, picked-up straight wooden sticks, colorful pebbles, clay pots and jars... This child had been restless since he was in swaddling clothes, yet today, when he said he wanted to choose his own room, he showed a hint of solemnity. 
"The incense burner Aunt Han gave me goes here, the little wooden sword Uncle Jiang carved for me hangs behind the door... My treasure chest goes by the bed, and my small stool goes in the corner..." 
After arranging the furnishings, he excitedly opened the wardrobe, which contained a small quilt made from his old swaddle. The outer layer was a piece of cloth torn from Jiang Wulang's clothes back then, and the inner layer was the red silk Han Xiangxun hadn't had time to cut into clothes. From infancy to a young boy, he had always held this quilt to fall asleep. 
A light wind blew through the tall tree branches, rustling them. The child excitedly stepped on the blue bricks to measure his new residence, his figure outlined by the moonlight already had the shape of a bamboo or cypress just taking form. 
Han Xiangxun suddenly felt grateful that the child had chosen this neither too high nor too low location, it allowed the young boy to look up at the Star River and imagine the martial arts world, and also let her see the warm light shining through the window paper with just a glance.

That day will never come.

27th Day of the Winter Month, at Dusk
Graduation draws near. Today I compiled the register of the graduating disciples and recorded each one's chosen path. Since their aspirations differ, the books to be gifted at graduation should differ as well, and I spent a long while choosing them. In the meantime, I heard Chengwu had arranged another match with Xiaomei. Perhaps he hopes to win just once before graduation. From the look of it, his chances remain slim.

28th Day of the Winter Month, Morning
A light snowfall today, a good omen for next year's harvest. Yet the fighting has not ceased this winter, and the people below the mountain suffer bitterly in the cold. Together with my fellow disciples, I went down the mountain to distribute firewood and help them endure the wind and snow. Qin Yuan and the others who study construction mostly took up repair work.

29th Day of the Winter Month, Evening
I heard from Master Su of Lone Cloud that Little Radish shows real promise in numbers and diagrams. Thinking back, the other masters at the academy have also praised the child more than once. When spring comes next year, Little Radish must be enrolled. Such talent must not be left to waste. Fu Xiao, Xiaomei, and Master Liu Sinong all think the same.

1st Day of the Twelfth Month, Morning
Luancheng has fallen. Many refugees fleeing from the north bear on their faces the tattooed words "Imperial Mercy," and the whole academy is incensed. More than ten among us skilled in mechanisms have asked to go to the Hutuo Camp. Hearing that our army is short of provisions, they have been told to bring as many devices as possible for hauling grain and clearing the way, in hopes of being of use. By dusk, the number of those volunteering for the camp had risen to thirty-seven.

6th Day of the Twelfth Month, Morning
Half a month has passed since the Master left. Only a letter has come, saying the fighting is dire. As he instructed, we began evacuating the villagers and dispersing the disciples, yet half refused to leave first, and instead asked to bring their mechanisms to the battlefield, saying, "Righteous men across the realm are all bound for the Hutuo. Now that we have finished our studies, how can we stand by with folded arms?" Before noon, the Master returned. Just as we had made ready and were about to leave for Zhongdu Bridge, Master Guan arrived with word that the enemy had already reached the foot of the mountain. At such a moment, they split their forces, bypassed Zhongdu Bridge, and came straight for the academy. What scheme could they be pursuing? Were they truly unafraid of being attacked from both sides?

6th Day of the Twelfth Month, Noon
The enemy burned and plundered all along the way, killing some and enslaving others. Yet when they reached the academy gates, they only surrounded us and urged surrender, demanding that the academy admit Khitan youths and teach Khitan script. They even claimed this would be the beginning of changing the hearts of all under Heaven, turning weapons into tokens of peace. Only then did we understand their design. They meant to make our academy the spearhead of their cause, to break the spirit of the worthy and the loyal in the Central Plains, and to replace the written tongue of our people. Their words are enough to sicken the heart. Now, by holding them here at the academy, we tie down their forces, blunt their claws and fangs, and strengthen the morale of our army.

10th Day of the Twelfth Month, Noon
The enemy poisoned the water and loosed toxic smoke... The academy's grain and fodder were utterly destroyed, and hunger now afflicts everyone within. I could not bear to watch the old and the young suffer, and tried to persuade them to leave the academy, but all answered as one: the enemy is given to burning and slaughter, and cannot be trusted. Thus not a single person would surrender.

10th Day of the Twelfth Month, at Dusk
I knew the Master's talk of the Myriad Engine was not the whole truth. When I asked him of it two days ago, he only smiled and said, "False, and yet true. I only pray it need never be used." But today, in the end, it was brought forth. This is the final entry.

11th Day of the Twelfth Month, Morning. Graduation.
Today I graduated together with my senior brothers and sisters, though I have not yet even entered school. I took with me Eldest Senior Brother's notes. Little Radish has already read them. Inside are many words once spoken by our senior brothers, senior sisters, and the masters. If one day I reach Hidden Mountain, I will deliver them to Master Crane's fellow disciples. If I fail to make it there, then I shall entrust them to some other wandering hero bound south.

Feng Yi never had a birthday. He'd lived a lazy life and never bothered to remember one. So in the end, he simply took Zhu Yu's birthday as his own. After all, whether it was A'zheng, Ruzhi, or A'cuo, whenever a birthday rolled around, it was always Feng Yi who ended up in the kitchen. Rolling out fine, slender Longevity Noodles, shaping plump little peach buns, gathering fresh seasonal greens for six dishes and one soup. Somewhere along the way, Feng Yi spent more time at the stove than wielding a sword. To the point when new recruits first joined the Dragon Hall, they even mistook "Boss Feng" for the head chef, causing quite the uproar.

Some things, he thought, are best not to trouble yourself over. And some other things, trouble yourself all you can. But when it came to Zhu Yu, trouble was always something to seek out for Feng Yi. What could he do? The fishmonger had latched onto the Red-Sleeved Fairy. Of course, to latch with persistence, the right tactics are much needed. If he'd tried the sappy nonsense from storybooks, he'd have been tossed out in three days flat. Thankfully, the brothers from Nine Mortal Ways taught him better: A fierce lady fears no brute, but can't resist a man who never leaves. If she needed to eat, he became the cook, simmering fresh watershield and bamboo shoots just to stir her homesick cravings for the South. If she wanted to travel, he became the groom, "borrowing" a white steed from Wan Shixiu, riding only to places where the Qionghua trees bloomed thick in the mountains, so she could admire the blossoms and gather medicinal apricot flowers along the way. As for the three little kids she brought... Fresh from the kitchen, Feng Yi wiped his hands, spotted yet another stray child, and, chuckling awkwardly, turned back to fire up the stove again. Using his Severing Wave technique, he sliced salted fish and brewed a winter melon soup rich with dried shrimp from distant eastern merchants. When the aroma filled the air, his booming voice would always drown out the rumbling stomachs outside:

"Hot food's ready!"

Handing over a clay bowl to yet another child, Feng Yi thought, "Ah, well. Where there are people, there is a home."

Once, Feng Yi believed that a man should live only for himself, free as the wind, coming and going without ties. Once, he couldn't understand her. Couldn't understand why Zhu Yu insisted on taking the burdens of the world onto her shoulders. He asked her, why smear herself with mud and gold to play the bodhisattva as an ordinary person? She smiled and said:

"A clay bodhisattva is still a bodhisattva, is it not? A clay bodhisattva doesn't melt away when crossing the river, it simply returns to the people."

Feng Yi pursed his lips, unable to fully understand the meaning. But without realizing it, his life had filled up, with her, with three children, with the bustling souls of the Dragon Hall. Maybe, in time, there would be even more. Ah, whatever. If she wanted to be a bodhisattva, then he would be the blue lion or white elephant that carried her. If the clay bodhisattva had to cross the river to save the world, then let him be the one to wade through the mud and mire.

The ones holding this blade were not just anybody. There were three heroes: Zhang Long, Zhang Hu, and Zhang Bao. Folks called them Dragon, Tiger, and Leopard, or the Beast Brothers. These three were famous for being strong, clever, and brave. When they joined hands, nothing could stop them.

Why call it Tiger Fort? Easy. Zhang Hu, the Tiger, said, "Let's use Tiger Fort." Long, the Dragon, agreed straight away. Bao, the Leopard, wanted his own name, but two votes beat one. That's how real heroes make decisions—straight and fair.

Create Room:
Players can create Training Terrace rooms and become the Host, managing members and matches. Ownership can be transferred or automatically passed to the most popular member if the Host leaves.

Formats:
The Host can set the Challenge Mode: Free Mode or Management Mode.
Free Mode: Players can freely select opponents or teams to issue Challenges or Targeted Duels.
Management Mode: Players or Captains sign up, and the Host decides the match-ups.
Victory Conditions: Best of 1, Best of 3, or Best of 5.
Training Terrace supports 1v1 battles.

Popularity and Room Heat:
Receiving gifts increases personal Popularity. More members, battles, and gifts increase Room Popularity. Both reset daily at @T[time_5].

Create Room:
Players can freely create Training Terrace rooms. Upon successful creation, they automatically become the host, with member management and battle arrangement permissions. The host can transfer host status to other members in the room. If the host exits directly, host permissions are automatically transferred to the member with the highest Popularity in the room.

Format:
The host can set the room's Challenge mode to Free Mode or Management Mode.
In Free Mode, players in the room can freely choose members or teams to issue a challenge or designate a challenge.
In Management Mode, after players or team leaders sign up, the host decides the opposing sides.
Victory determination is divided into three types: one win, best-of-three, and best-of-five.
Training Terrace currently supports 1v1, 2v2, 3v3, and 5v5 team battles; it also supports Perception Forest 1v1, 2v2, and 5v5 team battles.

Popularity and Room Heat:
Receiving gifts in the room increases personal Popularity. The more people in the room, the more battles and gifts, the higher the room's Heat value. Every day at 05:00 AM, the Heat of each room and the Popularity of each member in the room are recalculated.

The former Grandmaster, Halcyon.
Emaciated, with cracked muscles and bones. Judging by her remains, she has been dead for nearly three years.
Her location is the core pivot of the Derivation for Fate, where the reason for life and death also lies.

At the moment of crisis, perhaps she condensed her Qi to pierce the formation, using her body as a bridge – that searing heat capable of shaking heaven and earth was finally absorbed entirely by this mortal frame...

The former Grandmaster Raven retreated into the wilderness, settling in the Jadestream Valley. There, he built a hut as a school and taught the classics to enlighten the young. When he passed, his young disciples were sent back to Mohist City.
Rain and prayers, a rainbow in the west... Blessed by the east wind, may the harvest flourish.
May these new seeds keep the legacy alive.

Before he ever set foot in the Xuanyuan Cult, Deng Yideng was already someone of note.
His martial skills were solid, and his mouth even sharper. With those two alone, he could get by just fine wherever Jianghu took him.
He'd heard that the Xuanyuan Cult was full of true masters. How good could they really be? Better than me? Curious, nd a little smug, he set off to see for himself. He'd barely crouched atop a bamboo stalk on the hillside when a blast of Astral Wind from the cultists sliced the entire bamboo grove clean off. Every stalk but the one he stood on.
"Holy hell!"Deng Yideng scrambled away in a panic.
Xuanyuan Cult... From that day on, he repeated the name as he trained, from sunrise to sunset, night into dawn, driven by the thought that one day, he'd walk through those gates openly, and see just how many extraordinary people were hidden inside.
Eventually, he did get in. Out in the Jianghu, Deng Yideng could still make a name for himself. Inside the Xuanyuan Cult, though, his skills were only enough to earn him gate duty.
He did the job halfheartedly, craning his neck all day to peer toward the inner grounds.
Lost in thought, a pebble pinged precisely off the center of his forehead. The throw was precise: it hurt just enough to sting, without leaving a mark.
He looked up.
"Yo, brother. Up for skipping a few stones?"

It was the fourth year of Kaiyun. The Khitan invaded Kaifeng. But it wasn't just the Khitan raiding homes, there were Han traitors too, looting in the chaos, selling out their own comrades.

Bei Xiaoyu knew that Hong never built the Unbound Cavern to oppose the Nine Mortal Ways. He only wanted a place for those like himself, unwanted, outcast, a place to belong. Though their hands were stained with blood, he still believed time would mend the wounds. 

But the day Guo Wei's army stormed the city, the Nine Mortal Ways' schemes cost Hong his parents. And everything changed. He changed his name to Hong Si, expanded the Unbound Cavern, and welcomed scoundrels from across the world. He vowed to wipe the Nine Mortal Ways from the earth. 

Later, Hong Si left Kaifeng with a pair of siblings. And the one who stayed behind, Bei Xiaoyu, could only watch as Unbound Cavern turned into a haven for monsters. When the thugs cast him into the waters to drown, desperation finally took root in his heart. 
He knew all too well, there would be no hope in Unbound Cavern from this moment on.

十九岁那年，她跟着师父一行离开雾隐谷，来传闻中的机关之城不见山交流访学。\n\n:
At nineteen, she followed her master out of the Mist-Hidden Vale to Hidden Mountain, the fabled city of mechanisms, for an academic exchange.
Upon arriving at the Mohist Hill, she was captivated by the mountain's exquisite mortise tenons and mechanical wonders.
Soaring wooden eagles, earth-bound wooden scarabs, celestial chronometers, and the towering zipline anchors... Not to mention that perfect vantage point upon the Heaven's Threshold for stargazing!
Though far from home, the stars remained suspended in the heights, awaiting a mere upward glance.
It turned out that beyond the Mist-Hidden Vale, within the reclusive Hidden Mountain, there were so many others captivated by mathematics and yearning for the infinite void.
Together, amidst the Flower Expanse at Driftseed Moor, they observed night after night, eagerly sharing the truths they unearthed with all who turned their eyes to the stars.
When the exchange ended, her peers who had come to lecture and debate all departed. She alone remained, lost in her maps and surveys, staying on as a teacher of mathematics and stargazing.
By the time she came to her senses, she had found many kindred spirits and pupils who called her "Master." In time, she made this place her home.
But the stars... they are visible yet forever beyond reach. Why chase them at all? Much like those who rode the winds toward the firmament, they were always just out of her grasp.
Yet humans are such creatures: knowing full well the stars cannot be caught, we still cannot help but run a few steps, or stand on tiptoe... Even now, in her old age, when the paths home often slip her mind, she still finds herself wandering out the door, still chasing the stars.
Wait... Did she truly never reach them?
She froze for a moment. Her rough, withered hand was clasping a soft, tiny palm, as the little girl beside her prattled on without end.
Where were they going? Ah, right. They were walking home.
Xiao Yuelu... This is Granny's Xiao Yuelu.
"Xiao Yuelu, do you remember how we used to soothe you when you cried as a babe?"
"With stars?"
"That's right! I had a star-fishing rod when I was little, and you have one too. A pity that we can never truly reach the real stars..."
"Stars aren't out of reach, Granny, you silly. Don't the storybooks say so? The Lord of Clouds plucked the stars and shared them with the world, so everyone has a star of their own. If you don't believe me, I can give you many, many stars too.
Had Xiao Yuelu prepared more "stars" at home? Was it the Twenty-Eight Mansions this time, or the Northern Dipper?
But Xiao Yuelu is right this time. Granny has had many stars in her life.
She gently squeezed the child's tiny hand, the one she held now was the brightest star Granny had ever found.
Granny reached it at last.

Wei Xuan and his wife also met over a game of Piaoyao Battleboard. 
Piaoyao Battleboard demanded great physical strength, so the world mostly believed women couldn't master it. But that day, Wei Xuan, on a nine-win streak, was defeated by a gentle woman. She was bright and clever, like a blazing crabapple flower. 
"You fool, you lost. Hurry up with my prize." The young woman smiled, and Wei Xuan was instantly speechless. 
Later came endless efforts for their marriage. On their wedding night, after the guests had gone, Wei Xuan and his wife wordlessly took out the Piaoyao Battleboard set and battled delightedly until dawn. 

The world often spoke of mutual respect, of the husband leading and the wife following. But for the Wei couple, they were husband and wife, chess partners, and also teacher and student. 
Madam Wei had played Piaoyao Battleboard with her father since childhood. Though slightly weaker in strength, she excelled in angles and strategy, often achieving much with little—moves most men couldn't match. Wei Xuan begged his wife to teach him a few tricks, only to be met with her sly smile. 

Left with no choice, Wei Xuan made a pact with his wife: every day at four in the afternoon, if he was home, Madam Wei would instruct him in Piaoyao Battleboard. For Madam Wei, dusk was near by then, and having her husband home early was reassuring, so she agreed. 

Thus, the news of Wei Xuan being "henpecked" spread. Occasionally, Madam Wei would complain, saying she had guarded against everything, yet in the end, it was this Piaoyao Battleboard that had ruined her good name. Wei Xuan would just blush silently beside her. 
"Ah, forget it," Madam Wei would laugh. "The joy within this... isn't it greater than a spotless reputation?"

Wei Xuan was famously "henpecked." Strangely, Madam Wei was gentle, proper, and exceedingly clever—by all appearances a virtuous and kind woman. But ever since Wei Xuan married this lady, he changed. 
Wei Xuan was a Piaoyao Battleboard fanatic, often playing all day with others. But after getting a wife, whenever the watchman passed by at four in the afternoon, he would hurry straight home. Even if a game was unfinished, he would immediately drop everything and leave. His chess friends often teased him, calling him the "Time-Listening Donkey." 
Wei Xuan didn't mind. When people asked, he would just chuckle, his ears turning red with embarrassment. Everyone assumed the Wei couple was harmonious, enjoying marital bliss, which was naturally not for outsiders to discuss. 

Returning home, Madam Wei was already seated at the table. The candlelight reflected on her peach-blossom face, making Wei Xuan's heart skip a beat for no reason. 
"Husband, you're back a little late today. Did those chess friends not let you go?" Madam Wei blinked her autumn-water eyes. 
"That's right. My fault for keeping you waiting." 
"Then today, I must have my husband witness my skills—" It was charming, making one feel inexplicably weak. 
Madam Wei lifted the cloth covering the table— 
Revealing a Piaoyao Battleboard set.

Trey wasn't as strong as his older brother,
nor as cute as his little sister. 
He was the middle child, like a wild blade of grass by the rice paddy, unremarkable, but lives a life of transcent and leisure. 
Because of his low presence, he learned to live quietly and contentedly from a young age. 
The food Mama brought? Didn't need the best cuts, just enough to fill the belly. 
A cozy nest? Any place to lie down would do. 
Great ambitions? Living safely, simply, and peacefully. 
The world bustles. Humans come and go, cats weave in and out. 
He slips among them all, unseen and undisturbed. Isn't that its own kind of freedom?

Participate in the 5v5 Arena to make friends through martial arts. In this 5v5 competitive mode, players can form teams of five to engage in strategic battles.
 5v5 Arena is open daily, with entry available from 19:45 to 20:00. Be sure to join in on time.
 Once the match begins, up to four teams with similar ranking points will be grouped into a round-robin bracket. Each group will play three matches, with each match using a best-of-three format. Teams that win a match will earn season points and Activity Points.

 In this mode, healing effects are reduced by 70%. After a certain time in battle, players will deal increased damage while the healing effect is further reduced. Using Deflect consumes Endurance, while finishing Execute restores Endurance.

 Most player skills can be deflected. Defense-breaking Mystic Skills not only ignore deflect but also deal enhanced effects when hitting targets who are defending or deflecting. However, these Mystic Skills can be interrupted by any skill. Player skills, including Mystic Skills and Charged Skill, can interrupt Light and Heavy Attacks, but not vice versa. Effective use of Control-breaking Skills can turn the tide. The side that defeats all opponents first within the time limit wins. If the timer runs out without a decisive outcome, the winner is determined by the following priorities: 1. The side with more surviving players wins; 2. If the number of surviving players is equal, the side with the higher total damage dealt wins; 3. If the total damage dealt is equal, the side with the higher total healing amount wins.

Participate in the 5v5 Arena to make friends through martial arts. In this 5v5 competitive mode, players can form teams of five to engage in strategic battles.
5v5 Arena entry is available from @T[time_19:45] to @T[time_20]. Be sure to join in on time. Once the match begins, up to four teams with similar ranking points will be grouped into a round-robin bracket. Each group will play three matches, with each match using a best-of-three format. Teams that win a match will earn Season Points and Engagement tokens.

In this mode, healing effects are reduced by 70%. After a certain time in battle, players will deal increased damage while healing effectiveness is further reduced. Using the "Deflection" skill consumes Endurance, but successfully executing a finisher restores it.

Most player skills can be countered using "Deflection." However, Armor-Piercing Mystic Skills can't be blocked this way and are especially effective against defensive targets or those using "Deflection"—though they can be interrupted by any skill.

Various player skills (including Mystic Skills and Charged Skills) can interrupt light and heavy attacks, but not the other way around.

Mastering crowd-control removal skills can turn the tide of battle when at a disadvantage.

The side that defeats all players of the other first within the time limit wins. If the timer runs out without a decisive outcome, the winner is determined by the following priorities: 1. The side with more surviving players wins; 2. If the number of surviving players is equal, the side with the higher total damage dealt wins; 3. If the total damage dealt is equal, the side with the higher total healing amount wins.

Participate in 5v5 Arena to gain Martial Fellowship. In 5v5 Arena, wanderers can form 5-person teams for 5v5 competitive matches. 5v5 Arena entry opens at 19:45 on weekdays and stops at 20:00. On Saturdays and Sundays, entry starts at 19:15 and stops at 19:30. Please join in time. After the competition starts, up to 4 teams with similar scores will be matched together for a group round-robin tournament, totaling three matches. Each match is best-of-three. Team members who win a single match can earn season points and Engagement Tokens.

In 5v5 Arena, the arrow usage limit is 20, and healing effects are reduced by 70%. After a period of combat, player damage will increase, and healing effects will further decrease.
Most player skills can be countered with Deflect. Break-Defense Mystic Skills are not only immune to Deflect but also have better effects when hitting targets that are defending or using Deflect skills. However, they can be interrupted by any skill.

Various player skills (including Mystic Skills and Charged Skills) can interrupt Light/Heavy Attacks, but not vice versa. The control-breaking skill, Serene Breeze, can be used while being hit or under control. Using it wisely can effectively turn the tide.

Within the time limit, the team that defeats all opposing players first wins. If no winner is decided when time runs out, the following priorities apply in order:
1. The team with more surviving players wins.
2. If the number of surviving players is the same, the team with higher total damage wins.
3. If total damage is the same, the team with higher total healing wins.

The Dunhuang Melody Scroll was originally housed in the Sutra Cave of the Mogao Grottoes. Generally believed to be a pipa score, it dates to the late Tang or Five Dynasties period. 又到了一日的子时。\n无颜趴在暗房的地上，侧耳听了一会儿。她确信这是个逃跑的好时:
It was Zi hour again.
Faceless lay on the dark room's floor, listening intently. This was her chance. The guests had left, and the guards were asleep. If she could push open the door, follow the dim red lanterns, and crawl through that shadowy tunnel... she could escape. She'd mapped the route in her mind a hundred times, she had to make it.
With bloodied, mud-caked hands, she trembled to her elbows. The wooden pendant at her waist scraped the floor, making a faint noise. She froze, breath held, fingers crusted with scabs. Gritting her teeth, she tried again, but collapsed with a thud.
Her eyes fell to her legs, and she sighed silently. The Unbound Cavern had broken her left leg during her last escape, her right, the time before. A month had passed, and she'd thought the pain would ease. She'd overestimated herself.
The pain came swiftly, piercing to the bone. Tears and blood mingled as they streamed down her face, soon blurring her vision. She instinctively raised a hand to wipe them away, only to be met with even sharper agony. Then she remembered, yes, the time before last, in her struggle against those people, she had deliberately ruined her own face.
She propped herself up, momentarily dazed, but clarity quickly returned. No. She must escape. She had to get out. Broken legs could heal. A ruined face wouldn't make her mother love her less. If she could just get out... if she could just return to her mother's side... Gritting her teeth, she dragged herself forward. One painful crawl. Then another. However, the door burst open with a crash.

The dim red candlelight spilled into the room, swirling dust particles in the air. Faceless finally closed her eyes in despair... It felt like an eternity since she'd left home. Where was mother now? What was she doing? Did she still think of her? As these thoughts flooded her mind, a rough hand clamped around her jaw, forcing her mouth open as bitter medicine poured down her throat. A single tear escaped her eye.
This ditch of rotting shadows would be her grave after all.

A few more years passed. The sisters grew up, and Mo Xiaoyun reached her coming-of-age ceremony. 
After the ceremony, matchmakers came with proposals. 
Xiaoyun knew this wasn't something she could decide. But her parents had always doted on her, so surely her future husband wouldn't be too bad. 
Only, that day, Xini was very unhappy. 

When it was time to extinguish the lamps, Xini still sat on the bed sulking, hugging her quilt. 
Xiaoyun said nothing, quietly removed her hair ornaments, let her hair down, and lay down in her clothes. 
After a while, Xini huffily blew out the lamp and lay down with her back to Xiaoyun. 
For so many years, the sisters had been inseparable, sleeping together like when they were little. 
"What's wrong? Jealous that your big sister is getting married and will have a husband?" Mo Xiaoyun decided to break the silence. "Don't worry. When you come of age, Mom and Dad will find you a good husband too." 
"Big sister... if you get married, does that mean you can't... spend New Year's Eve with me anymore?" Xini's muffled voice came after a pause. 
She turned over. Two lines of tears fell onto the pillow. 
"We're a family who lives together, sleeps together... how do we suddenly become outsiders?" 
Mo Xiaoyun didn't know how to answer. She could only pat her sister's head. 
"It's always been this way since ancient times," she sighed softly. 
"But has it always been right?!" Mo Xini jumped up from the bed and stomped out.
