Deep within Mohist City, beneath the Divinecraft Pavilion, lies a hidden sanctum. Legend tells that here, Mohist sages once peered into the heavens to fathom the Great Numerals, deriving from them the myriad permutations of mechanism. Any who aspired to the Grandmaster would enter this place to challenge its arrays. Witnessing the shifting mechanisms, they would grasp the infinite depths of the Mohist Way. The Celestial Pivot of the array lies buried beneath the ninefold depths, aligned with the stars above and the Yin-Yang below. Save for those of transcendent wit and iron resolve, none may glimpse even a fraction of its essence.
Later, as the tide of Seclusion rose, a Grandmaster used this array to inter the Mohist martial arts and secret mechanisms, decreeing that they would emerge only when the age demands.
Thus, the sanctum fell into a profound silence, awaiting the footfall of the next seeker.
墨城的匠人，发现了蜜蜂萦绕山野荆条的奥秘。 甘醇的蜂蜜，得以在作坊里悄悄浮出身影: Mohist artisans discovered why bees swarm these wild brambles. Now, sweet honey quietly circulates in the workshops, hidden from the elders' watchful eyes.
墨城的小孩子们都说，小粟是个山外来的笨孩子。吃饭慢，走路慢，连说话也慢。\n幼麟:
The children of Mohist City all called Su the slow-witted boy from beyond the mountains. He was slow to eat, slow to walk, and slow even to get a word out. 

"Why have you not grasped it yet?" The master at the village school often sighed at him. His voice wavered, as though he had begun to doubt his own ability to teach. 
Su would simply scratch his head and offer a slow, sheepish smile. "Sorry..."

But every time Su apologized like that, Mi would grow angry. Mi would jab Su in the shoulder. "It is not your fault, so why are you apologizing? Master Raven said you are just a late bloomer, not a blockhead!"
Su would nod, then shake his head, clearly understanding none of it. Finally, he would give that same awkward smile. "Sorry... Mi."
Mi would stamp his feet in frustration, powerless to change him. In the end, he would simply drag Su off to find Xue for a game of hide-and-seek. 

Most children liked being the seeker in the game. Su did not. 
He was terrible at seeking, but when it came to hiding, no one could match him. He never hid beneath beds or behind doors, as those places were far too obvious. 
Su could squeeze into spaces no one would ever think to check. A giant pickling vat. The dry well behind the school. Or even the empty water tank behind the privy. 

One time, everyone searched for nearly an hour without finding him. 
Dusk was settling over the village. Mi had grown frantic, shouting his name everywhere. Then, he heard a faint rustling coming from the water tank behind the privy. 
Holding his breath against the smell, Mi carefully peered inside. The tank was completely dry. There lay Su, curled into a tiny ball like a little bean, fast asleep with the faintest smile on his face. 

Xue poked his cheek. "How did you manage to fall asleep in a place like this?"
Su rubbed his eyes, his voice slow and drowsy. "It is dark here. And quiet. I dreamed about what Master Raven said. How seeds rest beneath the earth just like this, waiting for the day they sprout."
"What else did you dream?" Mi asked. 
"I dreamed we grew millet. Giant grains of millet, taller than a person. It was all golden and shining. When the wind blew, it rustled like it was singing." His eyes lit up as he waved his hands excitedly. "I gathered as much as I could carry to show Master Raven."
"Wow. Then what happened?" Xue leaned in eagerly. 
"Well..." Su paused, his voice fading. "Then I woke up."
Hearing this, Mi could only stamp his feet in frustration once again. 

...

Because of this, when Mi asked if he would go to Jadestream Valley to help protect Master Raven's seeds, Su gave a rare, immediate answer. "Yes."
There were no questions. No stammering. Only a firm, heavy nod. 
He thought to himself that he had to get there early this time. He would take the back trails, find Master Raven's seeds, and hide them even better than he had ever hidden himself. No villains were going to get their hands on them. 

Master Raven had once told him he was not slow-witted. He carried those words close to his heart.

墨山道有内外门之别，入内门则探渊索珠，为千年计；入外门则专工其器，为万民益。\n:
The Mohist Hill distinguishes between inner and outer disciples. Becoming inner disciples means probing the depths, planning for millennia, while being outer disciples means specializing in crafting tools for the benefit of all people.
To many, "Is the distinction based on innate talent? Inner disciples for great talent, outer disciples for lesser talent." I think differently.
An outer disciple surnamed Mo, in a contest of mechanical devices against several elders, won three consecutive rounds undefeated, earning everyone's admiration.
His mechanisms emphasized practicality but were wild in form, originally looked down upon by the inner disciples.
After this contest, his fame soared. This rough, unrefined style actually became fashionable for a time, with disciples competing to take pride in the crude appearance of their mechanisms.
To this day, the old story has gradually faded, but this style alone has not fallen out of use.

At Mohist Hill, disciples are split into the inner and the outer sects. The inner sect digs into deep, long-term knowledge, while the outer sect focuses on practical device-making to serve the people.
Most assume this division reflects talent: the inner sect as gifted scholars, the outer sect as lesser. But that's a misconception.
During the Later Zhou's Guangshun era, an outer disciple surnamed Mo beat several elders in mechanical contests three times straight, earning their respect.
His mechanisms were built for utility, their forms rugged and unrefined, a style once despised by the Inner Sect. Yet after his triumph, his fame soared, and this "brutalist" aesthetic became an overnight sensation.
Though the story's mostly forgotten now, its influence still remains.

One day many years ago, just as Xu Shangqian had returned from his shift, he heard a clamor at home.
Pushing the door open, he found several neighbors in the courtyard demanding an explanation.
The Xu family's youngest son was mischievous. He had broken a tea jar in the Wang family's yard, drowning the Geng family's newly hatched chicks. Then he had climbed the Zhang family's gate wall to pick a persimmon and, swaying unsteadily, had knocked quite a few down. Lady Xu was apologizing profusely and offering compensation. A dull pain began throbbing in Xu Shangqian's forehead.
Seeing Xu Shangqian return, the group of neighbors swarmed around him again, chattering.
"I say, Fourth Brother Xu, don't you know how to control your child!"
"Killing living things at such a young age, he'll be murdering and setting fires when he grows up!"
"Our persimmons came from outside the region! I couldn't even bear to eat them myself!"
The rising and falling shouts made the pain in Xu Shangqian's forehead worse.
"My apologies, truly my apologies. I will definitely discipline my son. I've troubled you all. Whatever the losses are, I'll compensate, I'll compensate..."
After seeing off the neighbors, Xu Shangqian lowered his head wearily.
"You little troublemaker! Come here now... Wait, shouldn't you be at school today!"
Before the words had fully left his mouth, knocking sounded at the door again.
Opening it, the schoolmaster stood there, holding a ruler, furious.

"Master, you've been troubled. I will definitely speak to him sternly. Tomorrow, I promise tomorrow, I will personally take him to school. I won't let him skip class again..."
"Hmph! Rotten wood cannot be carved!" The master flicked his sleeve, snorted coldly, and left.

Xu Shangqian had almost lost all his strength. He just wanted to sleep.
He ordered his son to kneel in the courtyard and copy texts, forbidding him to sleep until he finished.

Lying in bed, before Xu Shangqian could even catch his breath, his wife came in, worried.
"Father wrote. The land lease at home is almost due, urging us to send some money quickly. Look at our family... we're not exactly destitute, but it's really..." 
Xu Shangqian felt dizzy. In the end, he could only heave a long sigh.
"Tomorrow I'll go ask if the academy has any copyist work. I'll copy a few more manuscripts..." 
His wife was still complaining by his ear, but Xu Shangqian only felt as if he were falling through clouds, sinking into a deep sleep.

Years later, floods once again stole the land's vitality. Murky waters spread and receded; the scorching sun baked the mud into hardness. Hunger and death once more stripped people of their dignity. 
Yet, for the first time ever, Mother steamed two white-flour buns and pressed them into Celestial Candle's hands. No matter how her little brother cried and fussed, Mother and Father only gave the buns to her. 
They were the most delicious things Celestial Candle had ever eaten. She couldn't bear to eat them both and tucked one into her clothes. At the same time, a wreath of grass was placed on her head. 
"From now on, learn to behave on your own." "If it hurts, don't cry out. Be obedient." 
Before the bun hidden in her clothes had even cooled, Celestial Candle was led away. She watched as her parents took another girl home. Thinking they had mistaken her for someone else, she cried and struggled desperately. But her parents never looked back. 
It was only many years later that she understood just how much luck was hidden within her misfortune. 
Selling children, trading sons to eat—hunger and death blurred the line between human and beast. 
The old man who bought her sharpened his butcher's knife again and again, then finally sighed. He dropped the knife, picked up a broken bowl and a bamboo staff, and led her west. 
The old man led Celestial Candle across the creek. She was too afraid to take a step. With a stern face, he harshly urged her forward, one careful move at a time. 
Once again, the icy, murky water rose over her feet, then her calves, her waist, her chest... Terrified, she struggled to steady her trembling, fragile body. But as she reached out, her hand found the old man's—quietly hovering just behind her, guarding her all along.

The two oldest Kaiyuan Tongbao coins were from the Tang Dynasty. She'd been a girl then, during endless wars. Her family had wanted to sell her, and she didn't blame them. She could still feel her mother's scalding tears falling on her hands as she pressed those two coins into them before the buyer dragged her away. She'd vowed that if she ever became a mother, she'd never be separated from her children.

Next to them lay Tiancheng Yuanbao... once her home. During the Later Tang, when the government suddenly raised housing taxes, she and her husband had sold their decent home for these coins, moving to the Forsaken Quarter.

The Tian Fu Yuanbao coins... she'd sent her eldest son to war with pride, only for a bag of mismatched coins to return in his place. Her husband had wanted to use them to buy a new house, but she'd refused. They were for Yingying, her daughter. She'd vowed Yingying would marry properly, not be sold like she had been. These coins would be her dowry, enough to open a shop and spare her poverty. But then the Khitans came. They'd demanded the coins, blood money from her son's death, and she'd rather die than give them up. Her meek husband had suddenly fought like a demon to protect her and Yingying. After the fire, they'd returned to ruins, finding only his cold, bloodied body still clutching a Tian Fu Yuanbao.

The rest were Tang Coins. These past two years, earning Song Coins had been hard. She'd risen before dawn and worked till dusk, only to watch the Tang Coins lose value faster than she could earn them. But she'd never lost hope, until Yingying... She remembered when Zhou Taizu's army entered the city, shouting "Massacre!" and "Loot!" Yingying had tried to protect the Tian Fu Yuanbao, running out... and come back pale, lifeless, covered in wounds... No, Yingying was here now, safe. Her eldest son would return from war soon. She'd read his letter telling them to stay alive for their reunion.

Wiping her eyes with a calloused hand, Granny Turtle dropped the coins back into the treasure basin, listening to their clatter. For a moment, hope flickered again.

A boy born in this joyful realm couldn't bear to see people outside the village suffer from hunger. He took all the moon-catching nets he could find and, step by step, walked out of his homeland bathed in clear light.

Unfated Tian never planned to raise two children.
Two children!
Not flowers or grass, not cats or dogs. You can't just half-heartedly raise kids.
Once you take them in, there's no turning back. You're tied together for life. You have to feed them, teach them skills, and drill morals into them. And if you do a bad job? Well, what if they grow up to be neighborhood tyrants?
So at first, Unfated Tian had no intention of taking these two in as disciples.
But the younger boy's face was a ruined mess, tears streaming endlessly, while the girl clung to Unfated Tian's sleeve, her eyes wide and pleading....
Fine, fine.
"From now on, you're Doudou, and you're Yao Yaoyao. Understood?"

As for why "Doudou" and "Yaoyao"? Unfated Tian put serious thought into it. Even if it sounded like a joke.
First, Doudou always looked so sorrowful. So he gave him three "dous" (to tease), ensuring he'd grow up laughing.
Second, Yaoyao was sickly as a child. So he loaded her name with "yao" (medicine), hoping she'd stay healthy.
Corny? Maybe. But it worked. Against all odds, Doudou and Yaoyao grew up just as he'd wished.
Unfated Tian wasn't a Buddhist, but whenever he thought about it, he couldn't help muttering a silent Amitabha.
Yaoyao shed her ailments, becoming a carefree girl who laughed at everything. Doudou, too, stopped moping like a little rain cloud. He even smiled sometimes, a proper, childlike grin, and was fiercely filial. Yet...Too filial, Unfated Tian sighed. That tiny heart carried too much weight. If only he'd learn to live lightly.

Unfated Tian poured his soul into figuring child-rearing out.
The worst challenge? Stopping nighttime crying.
One wailing child is bad enough. Unfated Tian had two in one house.
And they'd compete. One would start, the other would escalate, a duet of misery lasting half the night.
In those moments, alone on his remote mountain in Blissful Retreat, far from human noise, Unfated Tian truly understood the phrase: "It's lonely at the top."

Desperate, he even swallowed his pride to ask that insufferable Jiang Wulang for advice.
Great Hero Jiang, how do you soothe a child at night?
Jiang Wulang smirked.
Mine never cries....Jiang Wulang is the worst.
Luckily, through trial and error, Unfated Tian discovered a solution:
Telling jokes. Terrible jokes. 
The kind that'd make normal people shiver from sheer awkwardness.
But without fail, they silenced Yaoyao and Doudou.
Unfated Tian preened at his genius. Meanwhile, the kids would exchange a glance and burst into exaggerated laughter, playing along every time.

To the heroes of Well of Heaven,

I have heard that three hundred disciples are making for Zhongdu Bridge, and I am ashamed beyond words. Bearing the stain of one who betrayed the sect, how could I deserve such loyalty?
I know well that to lay down one's life in the cause of righteousness is the way by which Well of Heaven brings salvation to the world. I therefore earnestly beg you, heroes, to hasten to the front at once, and with this blade and this body, guard the realm from falling.

Excessive talent often breeds a spirit of sloth. Ye Zhuo had a habit of narrowing his eyes whenever he smiled, giving him the appearance of a perpetually drowsy, cunning fox.
The other disciples affectionately called him "Ye the Half-Immortal." Yet this nickname did not stem from any grand ambition to shape the cosmos. He simply helped his peers with their mundane troubles: how to talk their way out of being caught skipping class, how to unravel the puzzles their master had left behind, or what topics the elders might quiz them on.

He always seemed unhurried. With just a few casual words, he could untangle problems that had left the younger disciples in knots for days, elevating the art of saving effort to absolute perfection.
As for his master's intricate arts of springs and clockwork, he had mastered them long ago. Yet since his master never pressed him, he saw no reason to show it off, as boasting would only invite more lessons to learn.

All things in this world carry their own truths. There is no need to pry too deeply; knowing enough to get by is enough. To grasp but seventy percent of the wisdom hidden within the mountain is more than sufficient to weather a lifetime.
The greatest priority in this world, after all, is a good night's sleep. To dwell among mountains and streams carrying the title of "Half-Immortal" is surely the height of bliss!

But when his Eldest Brother came to entrust him with the affairs of the sect, he sensed a ripple in the still waters. His brother had always been a poor liar, and Ye Zhuo had never been an easy man to deceive.
His master had once warned him: "Among the five of you, you are the most adaptable. The Eldest is overflowing with righteousness but lacks flexibility. You must help me keep watch over him."

In the end, Ye Zhuo had let those words drift past his ears like the wind.
Fine. To descend the mountain is to be swept into the currents of the age.
The generals harbor deep suspicions, and old grudges have calcified. Factions intertwine like twisted roots, and the ambitious lurk in the shadows. To untangle such a web is truly the most vexing chore under Heaven!
But without me, I doubt any of you could even begin to sort out this mess. Could you truly prevail? Very well. I suppose I can endure a little more hardship.

"If you intend to descend the mountain and save the commoners of Chu, count me in."
How could a "General" march onto the battlefield without his "Strategist"? A mere mayfly of a man, reaching out to grasp the clouds.

Yet in the year they left the mountain, the rains of Neiqiu were far too cold, and far too long.
That Half-Immortal found not a single moment of rest. He exhausted his mind and poured out every ounce of his knowledge, yet in the end, he could not turn the tide for the weak against the strong.
Time flowed onward, and the world changed. That battle became no different from countless others before it, fading into smoke. Countless names were buried in the earth as though they had never drawn breath. The mountain's "Five Wonders" were spoken of no more, leaving their ingenious mechanisms to gather dust beneath the pines.

The historical chronicles, blunt and unforgiving, record it only thus:
"The Khitan general led tens of thousands of cavalry to invade the borders, assaulting Neiqiu. After five days, they failed to capture the city and suffered heavy casualties. Five hundred garrison soldiers rebelled, opening the gates to the Khitan forces. The garrison was slaughtered, and Raoyang fell."
History is a hard, cold stone. How many moths must fling themselves into the flames just to alter a single line carved upon it?

Kuikui was once the most promising pup in the Palace Guard kennels. Gou Ge prides himself on having judged countless dogs, and his eye for hounds carries real weight among the guards.

As one military text puts it: "Fearing the enemy may scale the walls at night, hang large lanterns every thirty paces along the wall's midline, and station watchdogs on the ramparts. Wherever they bark, reinforce the watch with oil-fed torches."
A sharp dog can scent trouble early and warn the guards to tighten patrols and keep prowlers out.

Kuikui is tall and long-legged, with a keen nose, quick instincts, boundless energy, and zero fear of people. Surely it was going to make something of itself in the palace.

One month later, Gou Ge admitted he had picked the wrong dog.

Day 3 (date redacted): hates being cleaned, restless and hard to handle. Scratched Guard Gou Di during a bath.
Day 5 (date redacted): started a fight during training. The other dog suffered minor physical injury and major emotional damage, then refused to report for duty.

On patrol, it's listless and low. Off duty, it's suddenly full of pep. Day after day, no improvement.

Woof woof woof, woof woof woof... (one thousand woofs omitted)

"Everyone calls me Kuikui. Yesterday I played with the person who bathed me again, but they didn't look very happy."
"So I licked their face to cheer them up, and they scrubbed their cheek raw with their sleeve."
"I raced Big Lu. Big Lu is weak. It lost and wouldn't play with me after. Boring."
"The palace is so fun. Getting picked up and brought here is the best!"

Gou Ge tried to reason with it: "I'm talking to you. Fix your attitude on duty!"
He watched the “miracle hound” he had pinned his hopes on, grinning with its tongue out, wobbling in place as it spun in circles.

Fine. Fine.
Miracle hound or not, as long as Kuikui is happy.

The day Khitan invaders stormed Kaifeng, Ni Laoshan was locked in a duel atop a cliff miles away.
"Rumor says you joined the Ghostlight Market and became Zhu Yousheng's honored guest," the Jiangnan Creepy teased, reclining against a pine tree. "Why waste time with an old friend like me?"
Drawing his long sword, Ni Laoshan laughed. "Heaven and earth may be vast, but martial arts reign supreme!"

Their battle raged for three days and nights, sword and blade clashing without end. 
It was only when the Jiangnan Creepy received a carrier pigeon message about urgent sect affairs that Ni Laoshan reluctantly stopped, still hungry for more.
Martial arts had been his life's passion. He'd met Zhu Yousheng through a duel and joined the Ghostlight Market initially just to test his skills against its oddball residents. But over time, he'd discovered joys beyond fighting.
"Xiaozhu loves tea, Xiaoba adores wine." As he approached Kaifeng with snacks for his friends, he joked, "They'd better not be mad at me for vanishing for three days."He never imagined he'd return to find them gone, all of them.

Five years passed. Then ten. Then fifteen... Ni Laoshan still wore his carefree grin, but he never dueled again.
In the dead of night, the grin would fall from his face, and he'd stare toward Sleeping Tomb Cemetery.
"Don't worry. This time, I'll guard this place."

Her earliest memory was a flame, a mass of encroaching fire.
Fire meets wood, and wood falls; fire meets grass, and grass melts; fire meets water, and water boils...
If fire touches my flesh, what then? This was her first inquiry.
Questions swifter than the blaze flooded her mind: Why, as fire touches all things, are its colors and scents never the same? Does fire have an end? What is its finality? Am I the fire? What makes me "I"? 
A cry shattered her reverie: "Sister, run!"
This was the first summons she ever heard. 
Hands reached her before the heat, sweeping her into a frantic flight. Fire fell behind, wind raced alongside; wailing echoed in her ears, and the firmament dawned ahead.
And so, amidst that first flight, the world slowly hummed into being. 
In that endless race, she came to know the one who pulled her along as "Brother." 
It would be long before she understood how the world described the fire she fled: wars unceasing, villages razed, lives reaped like weeds, and kin scattered like chaff. 
The displaced spoke of the wildfire with weeping and loathing: "Cursed be that fire! It was that flame that ruined our homes! It was that fire that took so many lives!" 
Then, she could not yet weave words into speech, only murmuring a few mimicked syllables: "People. Killing. Fire. Warmth." 
Her words were stones cast into a pool, stirring a greater clamor: "Fool," "Cursed cripple," "Burden"... "Better to cast her off and be done with it!"
She grasped not the meaning, but the truth of their gazes: they loathed her as they loathed the wildfire. 
"Brother" took her hand once more, shouting something at the crowd.
Then, he led her along another weary stretch of road. This time, the path had an end, and at that end stood a soul, one who possessed beautiful feathers, like a bird. The bird-like stranger took her other hand, just as her brother had, and said: "Come, let us go home." 
"Who are you?" she asked.
The figure replied, "Henceforth, I shall be your mother!" 
"Then, who am I?" she asked.
The figure said, "You? Oh, tell me, do you have names?"
They traversed a mountain of great height, yet the journey felt brief. For the road home is never long when it has a direction. 
Beyond the peaks, "Father" arrived to receive them.
After a night of deliberation, Father and Mother told her, "You shall be Ying Ning, and he shall be Ying An." 
From that day forth, she had a father, a mother, a brother, and a name.
From that day forth, she was no longer a stray wildfire; she was, at last, truly human.
Yet, this false deduction would claim its toll in the distant future.
Fire reclaimed all that the fallacy had granted: her "name," her "parents," her "brother," and even the very act of "running." 
She would revert to being fire once more. Yet, she felt a faint stirring: this time, it would be different.
She would not be like a wildfire, violently devouring all it touches. 
For while wildfire consumes the visible, what they left within her was a seed buried deep in the soil, waiting to crawl out from a heart and flow slowly from the eyes.

好侄儿：\n你父亲病逝一事，我们都很伤心，望你节哀，早日振作起来，重整商队。\n:
Good nephew,

We're gutted by the news about your father. Mourn him, but then you need to get back on your feet and take charge of the caravan.

I can still picture him, dragging us brothers out to Kingvine Village over and over, trying to get things going with the locals... A damn shame he never saw the Kingvine Wine get its name back.

He was stubborn, your father. Kept that Cleardew Terrace route open all these years, even though it was a money pit. We complained, sure, but none of us had the heart to turn our backs on the old folks still tending the vines there.

Well, he's gone now, and the rest of us aren't getting any younger. We debated all night and we've made a decision—we're done with that route. We can't afford it anymore.

These wars won't last forever. The world will find peace again... And when it does, everyone will know the name Kingvine Wine!

That day is coming. You can bet on it.

At eighteen, if someone had told Qiu Yuehai that he would become a heroic swordsman defending his home and country, the young man would have casually spat out the wheat straw in his mouth and waved them off. "Go cheat someone else out of their money."

He had imagined many possibilities for his life: maybe the fastest street runner in the world, a petty thief stealing gold in bustling markets, or a lazy fisherman who only caught one fish a day, just enough to eat. Either way, he'd be small, ordinary, unremarkable. After all, he had no extraordinary Martial Art Skills, just quick legs. This wasn't a storybook. Where did ordinary people get legends? Just live your life, he thought.

But years later, he learned that life isn't something you can simply "live well" if you want to. The raiders who stormed into his home, burning and pillaging, didn't listen to his pleas. "Please, I don't want to meddle in anything—just let me be!" Who did he think he was? Warhorses neighed, their iron hooves shattering soldiers' armor and crushing commoners' rooftop tiles alike.
So he buried the uneaten fish alongside the bodies of those who'd closed their eyes forever, gripped the last long spear in the village, nodded to a man named Lie Yan, and walked into the distance together.

"Hey, I'm Qiu Yuehai. From today on, count me in."

At Zi hour, Feng Ruzhi once again stood by the Yellow River, staring out at the sails fluttering faintly in the moonlit breeze, waiting for the one who had promised to come home.

She remembered. A long, long time ago, when she was still a little kid, there had been someone else standing by the riverbank, arms akimbo, waiting. That figure, chewing on a sprig of foxtail grass, hair tousled like the wind had scruffed it apart, was a little frightening under the moonlight. Back then, A'Cuo had still been timid, unlike herself, who was already bold and brash. Without a second thought, she had grabbed A'Cuo by the collar, barreled past the cook standing at the doorframe, and sat down at the table in one breath.

Three seconds. Within three seconds of sitting down, the jibber-jabber would start.

"How many times do I have to tell you? Do not stay out playing until it's dark!"

"With your half-baked skills, if you run into the Unbound Cavern, you'll end up sold to the Ghost Revelry Hall!"

"Don't you dare play dead! I'm talking to you, A'Ru! You too, A'Cuo!"

If "Fox" A'Zheng was around, he'd strike a pose and try to smooth things over:

"Master Pops, come now, don't stand in the doorway. I'll keep an eye on them next time. It's not good to keep the master waiting, either."

If Mother were to clear her throat and look toward the door, that cook would instantly droop his head and shuffle himself inside. That was the signal for another peaceful night.

The moonlight remained the same. But the people beneath it were gone.

Sun Letian had just laid out the sauce his mother had made the day before, wiping up the spilled drops when the first customer of the day walked in.
"Yo, got a new press?" The customer, a kindly-looking man in his forties, asked.
"Yeah, swapped it out years ago." Sun Letian smiled.
"I remember you were still helping your mother with the accounts last time. Looks like you're handling things on your own now. Good for you."
The customer ordered a simple bowl of He'le noodles with extra sauce. Sun Letian dropped the dough into the press, watching the noodles fall from the bottom in perfect strands, curling into the bowl.
When he was a child, he'd always found the whole process fascinating. A round ball of dough would turn into a bowl of delicate noodles, and with a little extra effort, you could make noodles in all sorts of shapes...
When his mother wasn't looking, he would sneak up on tiptoe, peering at the wooden shelf, eyes wide with anticipation, waiting for the noodles to spill out, almost like he was watching a trick.
If his mother didn't catch him, she'd simply scoop up the noodles he made, drizzle sauce on top, and hand them to the customer.
Sun Letian would stand by, eyes fixed on the customer's face, watching for any sign of satisfaction. A pleased look would send him into a quiet pride for the rest of the day, feeling that his small contribution had truly mattered.
The customers came and went, the press broke and got repaired, then replaced. But now, Sun Letian didn't find any magic in watching those long strands of noodles spill out.
Still, a kind word from a customer never failed to make him quietly happy.
He'd keep those words to himself, saving them for when he got home to tell his mother about it all.

Sigh... He let out a long breath. "A hero without wine is like a meat bun without meat. It's miserable!"

Who says Qi Zhao doesn't drink? That waterskin of his might very well hold...
Before he could finish, a waterskin flew into his arms, hitting its mark as precisely as if measured by a ruler.
Aha! Brother Qi Zhao is the one who truly cares for me! Meng Kuan looked triumphant. He shook the skin and pulled the stopper, ready to take a deep gulp. "Once this cap is off, I'll know: this must be the Forever Drunk from your place. Finally, a taste of..."
He stopped mid-sentence, his brow furrowing as he smacked his lips. "Darn it, why is it so weak? Did you water down good wine? What a waste, an absolute waste!"
Meng Kuan patted the scrawny old horse beside him and held the waterskin to its mouth. "Brother, this is thin enough for even you!"
The horse snorted and ignored him.
Just then, Fu Qianli approached from nearby. Meng Kuan's eyes lit up, and he tossed the waterskin toward her with a smirk. "Catch! Good stuff, don't drink it all at once!"
Fu Qianli caught it with one hand. With a slight toss, she knew it was more than half empty. Her expression remained unchanged; she gave Meng Kuan a flat look, pulled the stopper, and took two gulps. Then, with a flick of her arm, she threw the skin to Miss Xiu.
Who says fine wine is only for heroes? We daughters of the generation can hold our own as well.
Meng Kuan slapped his thigh and laughed heartily. The firelight stretched their shadows long and thin across the ground...

The art of craftsmanship flourished during the Song Dynasty, with porcelain-making reaching unprecedented heights. The five legendary kilns, respectively, Ru, Guan, Ge, Jun, and Ding, became celebrated across the land, each admired for its unique beauty. 
Tireless artisans pushed the boundaries of their craft, constantly experimenting to perfect their ceramics. At the Ru kiln, for example, craftsmen sought to create glazes "like jade, yet beyond jade," blending agate into their formulas to achieve a soft, luminous finish as "blue as the sky, smooth as jade, patterned like cicada wings, and as shining as morning stars." 
In their pursuit of color, these artisans masterfully controlled kiln temperatures and ingredient blends: iron yielded delicate celadon greens, copper produced vibrant reds, and cobalt brought forth deep, vivid blues. Through such innovation, they achieved glazes that became the stuff of legend—the ethereal blue of Ru ware, said to capture "the sky after rain breaks through the clouds," and the rosy hues of Jun ware, reminiscent of "sunset clouds after a storm." 
Countless masterpieces were born from this spirit of dedication and ingenuity. Through the devotion and skill of these ancient craftsmen, their radiant creations have been passed down through the centuries, a lasting testament to their artistry.

宗卿足下： \n\n\n金桃乃乾坤至宝，得者可驭天下。近闻李姓老贼亦谋此物，且欲:
To Zong Qing:

The Golden Peach is a supreme treasure of the universe; whoever possesses it can rule the world. I recently heard that the old thief surnamed Li is also plotting for it and intends to kill me upon obtaining it. Who does that wretch think he is, daring to compete with me? When my day comes, I will grind his bones to dust and scatter his ashes!

I order you to station at Brokegate Village. If he finds it first, you must seize it. If you fail and the situation turns dire, destroy it immediately. Most importantly: I would rather see it shattered than in the hands of others.
宗庙雅乐原本只有十二声，但王朴相公重定雅乐时对我们说，江湖庙堂本为一国，君民之声: The court's music originally only had twelve tones, but when Lord Wang revised the system, he explained that the voices of the emperor and his people should be heard as one.
宗珩...你叫宗珩......等等，你是晚蓉的弟弟，云溪的儿子？: Zongheng... You're Zongheng? Wait... so you're Wanrong's brother... and Yunxi's son?
宗珩？是不是一个五六岁的小男孩？我见过他！: Zongheng? A little boy, five or six? Yeah, I saw him!
宗琦？你怎么回来了… 你——: Zong Qi? Why'd you come back? You...
宗祠族叔: Clan Uncle at the Ancestral Shrine
宗贤哥，家主当真传讯说“万事齐备，所谋将成”？: Zongxian, did the family head really say, "Everything is ready, and the plan will go through"?
官人……这个，嗯……实乃天籁，小女子一时词穷……: Your... uh... heavenly music. I'm at a loss for words...
官人对折笑有救命之恩，一把嵇琴，何来不能碰之说？: You saved my life. Why shouldn't you touch my qin?
官人放心，小的记下了！: Rest assured, sir, I've got it all noted down!
官人看起来并不在意方才阿驮提及的询问象事之人？: You don't seem concerned about the person A'tuo mentioned. The one who asked about elephants before us.
官人，你看这两个陶人……: Sir, look at these two clay Men...
官人？官人盯着嵇琴做什么，可是要来一曲？: It's you? Why are you staring at me? Want to hear a song?
官兵不顾龟奶奶的痛心，依旧要抢夺唐钱，保护奶奶。: You see soldiers ignoring Granny Turtle's pleas and trying to take her Tang Coins. Step in and protect her.
官兵发现了你私藏唐钱，把你抓走了。: The government soldier discovers your hidden Tang coins and arrests you on the spot.
官兵将你和夜不脱押去面见虞侯。: The officers escort you and Night Vigil to see the Inspector.
官兵甲：完了大哥，他解开的容将军的机关……: Soldier A: We're in trouble, Brother. He solved General Murong's contraption...
官兵若有能耐，就不会是我先找到这儿了。: If the government soldiers were any good, I wouldn't have found this place ahead of them.
官印既已到手，就该与大侠说接下来的安排了。: Now that the seal's secured, let me fill you in on the next steps.
官吏甲：心血付诸东流，任谁都不好受吧，希望她不要过于伤心。: Official C: Anyone would be devastated. Her life's work just got destroyed. I hope she doesn't take it too hard.
Official B: Yeah... I wonder if General Murong is safe...
官员们围在木桶边似有所思，若加入其中，或能展开一段奇遇: Officials are huddled around the barrel in deep thought. Joining them might trigger an Encounter.
官员私下宴饮属个人行止，不宜过度干涉。: What officials do at their own tables is their own affair. Excessive interference is not warranted.
官员私宅宴请，不属朝堂议事范围。: A private dinner at an official's residence is not a matter for court deliberation.
官员行事影响市井民生，确有不妥，此事需严肃处理。: For an official's conduct to harm the people's livelihood is a serious failing. This matter must be handled with firmness.
官员陈笙正在仔细嘱咐运输粮饷的禁兵，提到近日从游春的人群中抓到了不少其他势力的密: Official Chen Sheng has been sternly briefing the guards escorting grain. Word is that several enemy spies were caught hiding among the springtime revelers.
官宦世家常觅良工制作成套金爵，雕文刻字，什袭世传，所谓玉壶金爵，雅容礼乐。传闻长: Legend tells of an official's eight chalices. After a decade under lock and seal, one vanished. The dust on the case was undisturbed. What else could it be but the otherworldly theft of a fox spirit?
官宦争相奔逃，朝野乱作菜场。: Half the court's already bolted. The rest are squabbling like fishwives at market.
官家不忍惨剧重现，遂在新朝建立之初，便将汴京城郊的赵家私田划为天下义田。: When the new dynasty began, the Emperor turned Zhao lands into charity fields to prevent another tragedy.

The flowers in the palace are exceedingly delicate and have to be tended every day. Watering, picking off insects, and keeping them warm...not one of these tasks could be left unattended. Yet for Her Majesty the Empress Dowager, such small, fiddly chores were one of the ways she liked to pass the time. At that time, her health was still fairly sound.

Among all flowers, Her Majesty was especially fond of peonies in the brightest, richest reds. She said they bloomed with such spirit, full and generous in form, with colors so vivid they delighted her at once. And so, whenever she took a fancy to flower arranging, she would always begin by choosing a peony.

That day, however, the first flower selected was a large camellia in full bloom. It was chosen by His Majesty. When Her Majesty saw that His Majesty and the Prefect had come to Shengping Tower, she bade the two of them join her in arranging flowers and passing the time in conversation. When she asked His Majesty why he had chosen that bloom, he replied that it was as big as his face, which surely meant it must be something precious, and so it ought to be chosen. Thus, the camellia took the center of the vase, where it would catch the eye at once.

As for Her Majesty, she had no need to deliberate. She simply reached out and selected several of her favorite peonies, placing them around the camellia like they were embrace it.

At the end of this elegant pastime, only the Prefect had yet to choose a flower. He looked at the vessel, already nearly full with those lush, brilliant blooms, and slowly circled it once. He frowned, then gave a quiet sigh before finally making his choice.

The Prefect chose with the greatest care. He examined each flower one by one, considering the variety, the color, even the length of the stem. His Majesty even personally recommended several cuttings of peonies he was particularly taken with, yet the Prefect chose none of them. Her Majesty, by contrast, remained entirely unhurried, and whenever the Prefect found himself uncertain about a bloom, she would offer her opinion as well.

After about a quarter of an hour, the Prefect selected a single stalk of white plum blossom. That plum blossom had been coaxed into bloom by prolonged exposure to warmth in a heated chamber. Slender and fine, white as snow and almost as delicate as snow, it seemed as though the lightest shake would send petals fluttering down. Yet even after the Prefect circled the vase once more before finally setting that stalk of white plum blossom into the embrace of the red peonies. It swayed gently while towering high above, but it never fell apart.

And so, by the hands of the three of them, camellias, peonies, and plum blossoms were brought together into a unique arrangement. If one were to say that each had its own beauty and that those beauties differed greatly, that would be true enough. Yet set together, they did not clash in the least, and instead seemed to rest in singular harmony. Only, such a pleasing scene was never seen again.

对战规则:\n1V1 竞技对决，需在限定时间内决出胜负：率先击败对方玩家即可获胜:
Combat Rules:
1v1 competitive duel—victory must be decided within the time limit: the first to defeat the opponent wins; if time runs out, the side with higher total damage prevails. To ensure fair play, no external assistance is allowed, and neither side may leave the designated combat area. The winner inherits the champion title, while the loser must exit the arena. Achieving consecutive wins unlocks exclusive rewards and honors.
Challenge Rules:
When the arena has no champion, players may initiate challenges in two ways:
"Open Challenge": Sends a duel invitation to all participating players, awaiting responses;
"Named Challenge": Selects a specific opponent from participating players to send a private duel invitation.

对芦花来说，春天是个看不见的客人。\n\n“娘，春天长什么样？”芦花歪着脑袋问。:
To Luhua, spring was an invisible guest.
"Mom, what does spring look like?" Luhua asked, tilting her head.
Her mother paused, her hands frozen beet-red as she fed handfuls of reeds into the fire. The crackling flames cast a crimson glow upon her face. "When the ice thaws," her mother said, "when fish leap from the water, birds return, and the reeds turn green, then spring will be here."
She could see birds soaring across the sky. She could see fish flicking their tails beneath the surface. She could see those seeds billowing like wave after wave in the wind as well.
But what did spring actually look like? Her mother still hadn't said.
Thus, in Luhua's heart, spring was like a guest from afar, one who only paid a quiet visit when the air turned warm. Bringing fish, birds, and an entire marsh of lush green reeds, enough to soothe her mother's cough and leave her own belly empty a few less times.
"If only this guest would stay just a little longer,"
Luhua thought to herself, huddling by the fire and nuzzling into the dog's scruffy fur.
For winter was truly, terribly cold.
It was the "tiny mouths" splitting open on her hands that bit her; the way her fingers stung at the slightest bend when she rowed. It was the "tears" that fell from her nose; the clothes frozen stiff as boards, and the house that shivered right along with them when night fell.
When she told her mother this, she would smile and say that in her own childhood, winter meant only white mountains and black waters, colder and harder to endure than this. But "it'll be fine once we pull through... when the ice thaws, the river will bring spring with it."
Only this year, winter seemed to stretch longer than any before.
First, the birds departed. In formation after formation, they rose from the water, circling the reedbeds a few times before plunging into the distant, ashen sky.
Luhua tugged at her mother's sleeve: "Mom, where are they going?"
"To a warmer place," her mother said, her gaze drifting away with them across the sky, only returning after a long silence. "They'll be back next spring."
Then, the people departed as well.
She watched as the villagers, like the birds, left in one group after another, boats laden with their belongings. When someone passed the reedbeds and shouted a few words to them from afar, her mother would only shake her head.
"Mom, where are they going?" Luhua asked.
"To a warmer place," her mother replied as before, though her voice had grown hoarse.
Later still, the river froze over.
Lying prone upon the riverbank, she peered down, seeing only a leaden expanse of grey beneath the ice. The fish had vanished. Each time she hauled up her net, it was empty, save for shards of ice and the frozen, stiffened roots of reeds.
"Have the fish gone to a warmer place as well?"
This time, there was no one to answer Luhua's question; only the wind whistled through the reeds. For Mother had gone out, and she had not yet returned.
Crack. A fissure split the icy surface of the river.
Plop. Something like a fish leapt from the water, only to vanish instantly into the shadows.
Was it spring returning? Was it that invisible guest, arriving at last along the river's flow? Had it brought Mother back along with it? Luhua did not know.
But she knew this: so long as one weathers the winter, spring will always be there, waiting.

(with a humble bow)

Hey there, friend!
Welcome to Kaifeng Talkin' School, where we learn to yack just like folks do down by the river and under the shade trees.
You're gonna meet Elder Bro Zhao, Second Bro Zhao, Sweet Xiang, Joyful Ni'er, and Wang the Gal. They're a lively bunch, always up for a good story or a laugh. We got Old Egg the dog runnin' around and Veggie the kitten snoozin' in the sun—you'll see 'em pop up here and there, causin' a ruckus.
Here, y'all will pick up local words, clever sayings, and try out some fun games. Might trip over a tongue or two at first, but stick with it and you'll be gabbin' like you grew up in Kaifeng!
Just a tip: don't go learnin' from folks hollerin' in a quarrel—those words won't help you none when it comes to talkin' polite or passin' any tests.
Ready? Let's get started!

Mi had been stubborn since the day he could walk. Tell him to go east, and he would head west just to spite you. 

His aunt always grumbled that it was because he was born during Grain in Ear. She said he was born full of prickles, just like the wild crops that sprout this time of year. 
Mi would shoot right back at her. "Then blame my parents for naming me Mi! Mi means grain, and grain is supposed to have prickles!"

The moment he brought up his parents, his aunt would fall silent. She would only mutter under her breath that she could not argue with him, and that once he was a little older, she would send him to Jadestream Valley. She hoped Grandmaster Raven over there could knock some sense into him. 

Mi did not understand why his parents were a forbidden topic. He had never met them and did not see what use they were anyway. He only knew his aunt wanted to get rid of him and ship him off. 

"I am not going! Master Raven? Sounds like some old crow. With a bird name like that, I am not learning a thing from him!"
"Ha. Well said."
"Who are you? I have never seen you before. Do not come any closer! My rattle-drum is no joke!"

A man stood beneath the old locust tree by the gate. He was long, lean, and tall as a beanpole. 
Mi clutched his drum and edged back a few steps. 

"Steady now," the man said. "Your aunt mentioned the mechanical ox had stalled again, so I came to take a look. I assume you are the one who took it apart?"
"It was not me! And I put it all back together anyway." Mi breathed a sigh of relief. 
"You did a clean job of it." Seeing the boy's guard drop, the man stepped inside. He crouched down to meet Mi's eyes. "Except for a few gears you installed backward."
"They are not backward! Who do you think you are, some Mohist Grandmaster?"

The man laughed out loud before replying. "It does not matter if I am a Grandmaster. But those ratchets you fumbled with have 'Forward' and 'Reverse' carved right into the metal. If you had learned to read, you would not have botched the job."

Mi rolled his eyes, knowing he was not stupid. "Then I will just learn those two words! What is the point of books? I would rather spend my days riding that ox across the hills."
"A fair point. But what if you could ride that ox while you learn? Would you come to Jadestream Valley then?"
"You... You are Master Raven? Then this rattle-drum... You made it?"
"I did. And not just drums. Mechanical oxen, wooden eagles, clockwork ponies... I build them all."
"Then... I want to learn from you!"

...

Seasons drifted by, and Grain in Ear returned once more. 

Mi clutched his rattle-drum and mounted the mechanical ox. He had heard the news. The seeds were at Jadestream Valley. He had to go back. He had to protect his master's seeds. 

If Grain in Ear passed, the time for planting would be lost for good.

To the Young Master:
It's been a while since I left home. Though the journey is arduous, my pen hasn't dared to rest.
Unfortunately, the winds along the way have been so noisy they've turned my brain into a clashing mess of gongs and mush. It's been days, and I haven't managed to squeeze out even half a decent page. So, I just lay in a small boat and let it drift. Accidentally, I wandered into a utopia. I asked around and found out this place is the legendary site of the Mohist, the main peak of "Hidden Mountain" itself.
Seeing how serene it is, I thought I'd borrow the elegance of the landscape to calm my mind, maybe unclog my inspiration. So, I took a stroll into the mountains. Little did I know, I was about to witness that there's always someone more anxious out there!
By the plank roads and under the stone cliffs sat several sighing Mohist disciples. One young man was clutching his paper so tight it was almost entirely crumpled, muttering in a daze, "Tomorrow's deadline is tomorrow's sorrow; today's deadline takes my life away." A few others were passing around a fortune slip. Somehow, it ended up in my hands, and written boldly across it was: "Repost this sign, and your exams will go fine"...
Haha! Seeing everyone else pulling their hair out puts my mind completely at ease!
I plan to stay in this wonderful place for a few more days. If the Young Master has time, you should take a walk here too and see the unique scenery hidden deep in these mountains.
Writing furiously, Lu Kangge

Young Master, come drink with me:
My heart is so heavy. If I don't have a few drinks and vent to you, I think I'm going to get sick.
Traveling abroad, I realized that only us folks from Qinghe are truly honest. I bumped into a heroine in Kaifeng who looked like a celestial fairy. I didn't even dare look at her, but she approached me first, saying I looked honest and she wanted to date me and settle down. I thought I was dreaming!
But after only a few days, she had her junior brother send me a letter, saying she was going to date Escort Leader Zhang from the west side of the city. She said the rules of the Velvet Shade require her to let me know "for my information."
I was baffled. What kind of sect rule is that? I ran to ask her, and she told me not to worry: "Big Zhao, the Velvet Shade rules say we can choose multiple partners, but if there's a new development, we must truthfully inform the old ones. It's out of respect for each other."
I thought it might be a misunderstanding and wanted to try harder, but not even three days later, I got another message saying she was going to date Scholar Li from the south side, again "informed as per sect rules."
I asked around and finally understood. It turns out I wasn't her only partner! Including me, she had five!
Five is fine, I guess, if that's just the Velvet Shade way... I was getting ready for us all to live happily as one big family, but then she weighed things up and said I overlapped with someone else's "type," so she optimized me out!
Young Master, can you believe this?! If you have time, you must come have a drink with me. I really need a heart-to-heart.

Yours, Zhao Dali

Young Master, a very happy New Year to you.
The firecrackers outside reminded me of Spring Festival's Eve long ago. My master said that children who keep the vigil until dawn will be the most blessed in the coming year. So I dragged you along to stay up all night with me, waiting for the light of day. Who knew we wouldn't even last until the third watch? Our heads were nodding like little chicks pecking for grain, thumping against the table... The truth is... I was simply terrified of those thunderous booms. I only insisted you stay so my heart could feel at ease.

少侠亲启：\n从清河离开后，俺顺路在周遭逛了两天。这不巧了，正愁没有人陪俺练拳脚:
Young Wanderer,
After leaving Qinghe, I wandered around the area for a couple of days. Just when I was starting to feel bored for lack of anyone to trade blows with, a few roadside thieves came looking for trouble.
Good thing all these years of practice were not for nothing. After a few exchanges, the young fools had lost all stomach for it.
They were strong, able-bodied lads. With strength like that, they could have made an honest living anywhere, yet they chose to block the road and play at being kings of the hill. Still, I could tell they had been driven to it by hard times.
So I pointed a few of them toward Kaifeng to enlist in the army. The others said the capital was too far and wanted to try their hand at small trade instead, so I sent them your way to Qinghe. You should be seeing them before long.
I also picked up some new wine along the way. We will drink it together when we meet.

When you were young, you were captivated by the tassels on the sword hilts of martial artists, and pestered Uncle Jiang for one. But he ignored you as if he hadn't heard. 
During sword practice, you'd stare blankly at the bare pommel, your mind filled with images of swaying tassels. Uncle Jiang would say with a stern face, "Your swordsmanship is lacking, yet you fixate on such trivialities." 
He punished you with a thousand practice swings, lasting until the sun set. That day, you didn't even have the spirit to sulk and fell straight asleep. 
The next morning, you were astonished to find a brand new tassel tied to the pommel by an unknown hand. Overjoyed, you showed it off everywhere. 
As you grew older, that small sword no longer suited you, and along with it, the tassel faded from memory. 
Only upon seeing it again today did you realize someone had treasured it all along, letting it gather dust only as the old residence fell into disrepair. 
Perhaps because the longing was never severed by time, after countless twists and turns, it finally returned to your hands.

Though she didn't fully understand, Ice Soul diligently managed her three little homes. 
Until one late night, her door was knocked upon. 
The visitor was a sweet-smelling elder sister. Stepping in on beams of light, the golden flower pinned in her hair shone brightly. 
"I knocked on many doors, but no one answered. You are the first to respond." 
"I am a traveler passing through. Thirsty and hungry late at night... might I trouble you for a bowl of water?" 
Ice Soul rubbed her eyes and politely invited the elder sister inside. 
Opening the cupboard, Ice Soul found this home's water and food long gone. After all, she hadn't stayed here much. 
Hugging the jar, she stammered an apology to the guest. 
"S-sorry, there's no water or food here. Please wait, I'll go find some!" 
"Take your time..." the guest smiled gently. 
It was strange. She was the host, yet the elder sister sitting on the chair carried an air of unshakable composure. 

Groping her way to the river behind the house in the dark, Ice Soul lost count of her falls. So strange—tonight's darkness was so thick she couldn't see the path. 
Ice Soul had to widen her eyes and prick her ears to barely hear the river's flow. She submerged the water jar. 
Suddenly, Ice Soul's eyes widened— 
Because she discovered the moon that should have been reflected in the water had vanished. 
Looking up, only blackness remained in the sky. Utter silence, even the stars had lost their voices. 
Only her own heartbeat and the murmuring water remained. Ice Soul cried out and hurried back home.

Dear Wanderer,
They say Meow Meow's Dragonfinder will lead you to the real treasure. Yet the rod remains silent, and Meow Meow is like a ghost without a trace. I skipped class for a full half month before I finally found its trail. A few of us from the sect followed it up the mountain for ages, but instead of treasure, all we found was you, fast asleep.
Could the treasure be on you? Or perhaps... Could you be the treasure Meow Meow was looking for?
As you remained in your deep slumber, Meow Meow wouldn't leave. Soon, disciples bound for Meow Meow Temple found their way here instead, offering scrolls and praying for smooth studies and successful exams. After a while, even the mountain monkeys started following suit, carrying wild fruit over in their mouths. Do monkeys worry about homework too? Or were they praying on behalf of us Mohist disciples?
Whether it was Meow Meow's grace, the monkeys' sincerity, or the fact that your resting place is a confluence of wisdom, those who came to pay their respects have indeed seen their marks flourish! Thus, we chipped in some Ink Tallies to get dried fish for Meow Meow, peaches from Jadestream Valley for the monkeys, and a small thank-you gift for you as well.

It's not much, just a few humble mountain offerings, but we Mohist disciples will always be grateful for this strange little stroke of fate that brought us to you!

Dear Elder Brother,

Lately, Chang'an is rife with gossip and mockery, all saying that a disciple of the Masked Troupe came to his end in a common brawl with street ruffians. Even our own records note your passing as "death in a street fight."
You lived your whole life with straightforward honor, and yet now you are left to be misread and sneered at by all. Though I know the truth of your staged death, I cannot rid my heart of the grief and indignation it has left there. You did what you did to recover the treasure taken away by the Prince of Wuwei, and you did it to save the world from ruin.
My illness grows heavier by the day, and I feel myself fading. In the idle fears that come with sickness, I find myself thinking: if you should one day return and find both the Master and me already gone, who will be left to speak for you and clear your name? I ask that you keep this letter, Elder Brother. Should the day come when you need it, let these words stand in my place and bear witness to your loyal heart.
I pray you keep well and take care.

I write today with glad tidings. Last year, a villager from Luancheng came to study at the academy, carrying his books on his back. He tills the fields and reads the classics, and has quietly devoted himself to the investigation of things. To my surprise, with gifts so plain and unadorned, he has touched upon something those before him had never brought to light. Beyond dyes drawn from plants, he has opened another path entirely, using the red earth of the Taihang in their stead. Whenever I watch the looms clatter and turn, and see lengths of crimson cloth emerge in ordered measure, it seems as though spring itself had quickened them into being. It is enough to make one clap in delight. To have gained a student such as this is comfort enough for a lifetime.
I still remember the resolve you once set your heart upon. Though the path you follow differs from mine, the Dao itself has never run contrary. Now that the first new shoots of the academy have begun to show, perhaps this may serve as proof of that old wish to know the people. If you were to see such wisdom of the common folk flowering within these halls, and find in your own path some new meaning as well, then I should be overjoyed. I only hope you may spare the time to come and see for yourself. I shall make ready and await you.

There was once a night when even the Dragonbend Academy, usually ablaze with light, was swallowed by utter darkness.
That day, the wind and rain raged, snuffing out the lanterns under the eaves one by one. With winter nearing, dusk fell early; the mountain nights were naturally ink-black, and should the Academy go dark, any wayfarer would be left with nothing but a trembling heart. After some counsel, the disciples resolved to take turns guarding a single flame. Both for their Master, who had been gone for days, and for any weary traveler who might, or might not, be out there in the dark. As for the order of the watch, for those so accustomed to bickering, there was only one way to settle it: they drew lots.
The bamboo tube rattled and clattered; amidst the storm, the sound seemed like a wondrous melody.
The first watch: Liu Sinong arrived. His hand was steady as he refilled the oil. A thin stream poured straight into the lamp's heart, and soon a halo of light bloomed. The rain fell like a cascading curtain. He watched it for a time, then drew a small bundle of coarse cloth from his breast. This object, kept pressed against his heart for years, was not something he showed lightly. It was earth from the graves of his wife and child. Yet now, amidst the raging storm, he cradled it firmly in both hands. He remembered how Miaowa had loved to watch the rain. In this solitary moment, he let himself pretend they were still here: the family, together again, listening to the rain.
The second watch: Luo Chengwu arrived. The rain had eased somewhat. Before his days at the Academy, he would have been awake now, lost in the clinking of cups and the chaotic charm of pipes and strings. His friends out there treated him well, speaking only the words he wished to hear. Not like here, where everyone has a temper, especially that Qin Yuan. A single word out of place, and it's a thousand too many... Strange. Why think of him now? Luo Chengwu refilled the oil and leaned by the window. To the rhythmic pitter-patter of the rain, he actually caught the faint melody of strings. These days at the Academy, it seemed, were no worse than his life before.
The third watch: the tempest reached its height. A pair of callous, scarred hands, knuckles distinct, steadied the lamp as it thrashed in the gale. Liu Xiaomei arrived; she was well pleased with these hands of hers. In her days as a bandit, she'd used these palms to deliver countless slaps just to survive. She knew her measure, of course: no mercy for the wicked, but for the good, a mere feint of a raised hand would do. Since joining the Academy, she applied that same decisive vigor to the carving of stone tablets. The third watch is the hour when demons and monsters are said to roam. But with Liu Xiaomei on guard, what evil would dare draw near?
The fourth watch: the rain slackened, yet a bone-chilling frost set in. Qin Yuan arrived. Shrouded in a thin quilt, he added oil with such care as if a single wasted drop were a transgression. The flame grew full again, casting a small circle of amber light. Only then did he draw a tattered book from his robe, bowing his head to read by the glow. Let it be cold. Since his family's decline, he had known straits far more desperate than this. To find refuge in the Dragonbend Academy was the greatest blessing of his life. Hunching his shoulders, Qin Yuan drew a fraction closer to the light.
The fifth watch: Tang Wenyao arrived. The deepest, most grueling watch of the night naturally fell to the Senior Brother. Thus, a little harmless meddling with the lots was surely no great sin. As the Senior Brother, though, he always felt he had come to this place too late. He often lamented, wishing he could have arrived years sooner. The rain outside seemed to hear his heart; it suddenly turned to a soft murmur, like a quiet consolation. You are not late at all. The days ahead are long indeed...
As the east paled with dawn, the wind and rain retreated.
A traveler walked the mountain path, yawning, his fishing rod still dripping wet.
He looked up at the Academy nearby. A lone, warm light still flickered there, so small, yet so steady.
The world was stirring to life.
He felt then that all the sunrises and grand wonders of the world he had ever witnessed were eclipsed by this single spark of light.
Truly beautiful.

Father, fine. Stepmother, fine. Younger brother, fine. Moving house, fine. Changing rooms, fine. Not speaking Han language, also fine. The house cat causing trouble was truly annoying, losing it was fine too. Clothes with holes, no one to mend them, just fine, one always needs to change clothes anyway. Having one less mung bean pastry in his bowl than his brother, fine, he didn't like sweets anyway. Reading one less hour of books each day to pick up his brother from school was just wonderful, he didn't want to recite that bothersome Confucian text with the teacher anyway. Younger brother taking over the Winter Solstice stove offering and ancestral hall worship... fine, whoever wants to get up in the morning can get up, he certainly wasn't going to. After enough "fines," his agreeableness became a daily routine, as regular as the sun rising. He had a rather beautiful old pipa, given by his grandfather. He couldn't play complete melodies, but he always held it. Perhaps the tuning pegs were too tight or too old, when he held the pipa, it would sometimes creak and call to him, and he would respond, "Fine, fine." He and the pipa got along fine, so everything was still fine. Father did once say it wasn't fine, that he stood without posture, was sloppy, indifferent, said "fine" to everything, not manly at all. He shrugged, replied "Fine," and turned away.  
Until one day, he returned home to find his pipa being loaded onto a merchant's cart. He rushed over, snatched back the pipa, his lips trembling, unable to utter a single word. His younger brother, however, clapped and cheered, while his stepmother urged him, saying he didn't play it anyway, it would just rot at home, wouldn't getting some silver for it be better? His father, as ever, scowled with anger, slapped him across the face, told him to take a good look at himself now, and to either put the pipa down or get out of this house.  
The pipa, aggrieved, nestled in his embrace, creaking and complaining to him. Mr. Agreeable, good Mr. Agreeable, don't say that word...  
He looked up. The sunlight was blinding.  
"Okay."

On the Lantern Festival night of the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong hung elaborate lanterns in Shangyang Palace, piling them like mountains and adorning with silk brocades as dense as blooming trees. From palaces to palace gates, the light shone as bright as day. 
At that time, the Taoist master Ye Fashan stood by and said, "Tonight's lantern festival is unmatched under heaven, only Liangzhou's comes close." 
The emperor was surprised, "Have you ever traveled to Liangzhou?" He replied, "I just came from there and hurried here at your call." The emperor was even more amazed, "I wish to visit Liangzhou, can we go?" 
Ye Fashan told him to close his eyes and hold his breath. At once, the emperor felt wind and thunder surging around his robes. 
In a moment, he touched solid ground. Opening his eyes, he saw thousands of lanterns glowing, fragrant dust covering the fields, red mansions stretching like daylight, and the quiet night shining warm as spring. Liangzhou's scenery unfolded before him in an instant.

This first Qingming since the mountain was open has kept the Bureau of Relief so busy that we barely have time to sit down for a meal.
Never have so many folk come to the mountain at once. We had only just finished reminding everyone to be aware of the flames when word came in that a Macaque had snatched someone's travel pouch. Visitors who came to admire the Spring view brought all manner of teas and treats we had never seen—even the Macaques were curious. Zhen has gone up the mountain to settle the score with those monkeys, so I finally have a moment to write.
That said, being a little busy is a good thing. It's far better than sitting idly and counting clouds, at the very least. Come to think of it, we still owe you thanks for putting the Bureau of Relief on the map, Wanderer. These gifts are what the folk from in and around the mountain have sent our way lately. Zhen and I thought we ought to share some with you as well. The skies are clear this Qingming—perhaps you could treat yourself to some fresh tea and pastries, take a stroll through the verdant fields, and enjoy the spring.
Finally, if you find the time, do come back to the mountain for a visit!

21st Day of the Eleventh Month, 946 CE
Today I went once again to Uncle's command tent to pay my respects, and once again he treated me with the same cold indifference. Then again, Uncle is a great minister of the court. So many seek an audience with him each day. Why would he spare a glance for some poor, down-at-heel nephew like me?
I know well enough that the soldiers in camp show me respect only to my face. Behind my back, who knows what names they call me.
Yes, I have borrowed Uncle's name, and wrapped myself in the hide of "Governor Du Chongwei's kinsman." But so long as I still wear that hide, those camp louts should show me some respect.
What right have they to look down on me? What right have they to make sport of me behind my back?
Only Ding Xiao, only he alone, has ever treated me with true sincerity.
When others mocked me for being useless and unlearned, it was he who wrote documents for me. When others pressed me and made a show of my ignorance, it was he who stepped forward on my behalf.
He... he ought to be true to me as well.
When he was reduced to slavery because his father and elder brother failed to hold the city, it was I who saved him.
When, marked by guilt and with nowhere to go, he lived from one day to the next, it was I who gave him clerical work so he could earn his keep.
Ding Xiao, you must not become like those who trample on me.
I have treated you as a brother. You owe me that much.

25th Day of the Ninth Month, Third Year of Kaiyun. Cloudy.
Today I went to court and had an audience with the emperor, where I presented my plan for driving back the enemy. As expected, it was not accepted. Worse still, General Guo was rebuked because of me. How bitter. How shameful.
At present, the only course left is to head north and visit Du Chongwei, in hopes of securing his support and using it as an alternative strategy to drive back the enemy. Yet I know well what sort of man Zhongwei is. I fear this journey will come to nothing, and am deeply troubled by it.
Before setting out, I was fortunate enough to be seen off by General Chai Rong. His words brought me sudden clarity, and I record them here to remind myself for the rest of my life.
General Chai said, "In former days, Emperor Taizong acted with ruthless resolve at Xuanwu Gate, and only then came the Reign of Zhenguan and a century of flourishing rule. A true man sets his sights high and sees a thousand li at a glance. Why should he waste words on creatures as short-lived as morning mushrooms and summer cicadas?"
What stirring words. What stirring words. Off I go.

The Zhang family's restaurant sign had been hung, smashed by troublemakers, refurbished, and finally stabilized after many twists. 
On the day they went to collect the new sign, Zhang Ankang was seven years old, only reaching his mother's waist.
He followed her across the street, past Harmonic Span. The towering horses loomed taller than him. The shops displayed wonders he'd never seen. His mother pulled him along, steering him clear of the bustling crowds and lavish storefronts, but though she dragged his body forward, his eyes lingered behind.
At the carpenter's workshop, saws and planes screeched, wood shavings swirling in the air.
His mother crouched to inspect the new sign, while he sat on a stool, looking around, at the sign, and at her.

The freshly carved sign was huge, the characters for "Zhang's Eatery" bold and imposing, making his mother seem even thinner, even smaller. Her old wooden hairpin, worn for years, swayed before his eyes, blending into the flurry of wood shavings, just another tiny speck in the storm of sawdust.
He stared longer than he had at the horses and fancy shops on the way here.
He remembered the customers at the eatery often saying to his mother: "Find yourself a supporter, at least then you could afford a new hairpin.
Zhang Ankang wondered: "What would a new hairpin look like?"
By ten, he understood.
A new hairpin was like the tall horses on the street, the exotic treasures in the shops, the grand new signboard in the carpenter's workshop. It was something bright and unmistakable, something that wouldn't disappear into a cloud of sawdust.
With it, his mother would become someone who "lived well", someone with backing, someone spared from the world's gossip.

On the way back, crossing Harmonic Span again, the horses still loomed over him, the shops still overflowed with strange, nameless wonders. His gaze shifted from his mother's wooden hairpin to a jewelry shop, where customers streamed in and out, and glittering hair ornaments lined the displays.
A shopkeeper called out, "Jin's Jewelry here..."
His mother yanked him roughly, "Watch where you're going, you scamp!"

张豹这一生最大的遗憾，就是寨子的名字没自己的份。\n\n自离开家后，三兄弟叱咤风:
Zhang Bao's greatest regret in life was that his name never made it onto the bandit stronghold's sign.

After leaving home, the three brothers had made a fearsome name for themselves. When they gathered to become bandits, even seasoned outlaws answered their call.
A name was essential for their stronghold in the jianghu. But since none of them were well-educated, naming it became a pressing problem.
"Enough dithering! Let's call it Zhang Clan Stronghold!" Eldest brother Zhang Long flicked a weed stem from his teeth.
"Too damn plain!" Zhang Hu wiped his broadsword disdainfully.
"How about... Three Heroes Fort?" Zhang Bao, the cleverest of the trio, ventured.
''Heroes? Who's a 'hero' here? You trying to curse us?'' Zhang Hu smacked Zhang Bao's head. ''We're named for the Long, tiger, and leopard—all fierce as hell. Why call it heroes?"
Knowing his brothers' limits, Zhang Bao swallowed his pride. "How about 'Claw & Spot Fort'? For the claws of the Long and tiger, and the spots of my namesake, the leopard?"
"Sounds clunky," Zhang Hu muttered, eyeing Zhang Long. "Tiger Fort—that's snappier!"
Zhang Long nodded. "Done. 'Tiger Fort'. Imposing. Memorable."
Zhang Bao's jaw dropped. "I'm still breathing here!"
"Ah, little brother! 'Parting Tears' has no tears, 'mooncake' has no moon, but by golly, Tiger Fort has a real leopard!" Zhang Hu tried to imitate patter of market square snake oil salesman with his forced explanation.
''Ugh, what nonsense is that!?'' Zhang Bao's beard twitched with anger. ''You two have been bullying me since we were kids! After Grandpa died, you'd have starved me to death if not for Mother!''

At the mention of their parents, the brothers fell silent. Their father, a butcher, had died young, probably from the ill karma of his trade. Their mother had raised all three alone, enduring untold hardships.
Zhang Bao knew life wasn't always fair. As the youngest, he'd always used their mother's favor to even the odds. After all, the baby of the family gets spoiled.
But this time, he was livid. They'd built the fort together, yet his name was being erased!

Zhang Long ignored him, ordering men to carve a huge signboard and spread the name Tiger Fort far and wide.
Zhang Hu agreed, oblivious to Zhang Bao's red-faced rage.
"Screw you both! I'm done with you two!" Zhang Bao kicked over a wine jar and stormed out, blade on his shoulder. Zhang Hu sighed.

That night, the fort was calm under clear skies. Zhang Hu stared at the moon, worried.
''Did we go too far?'' He still cared for his youngest brother.
Zhang Long, eyes closed, was tired. ''In this world, being bandits isn't a lifelong gig. If the fort ever falls, we might have to go down with it, but he shouldn't have to.''
''Bao's smart. He won't suffer, and he knows the way back.'' Zhang Long added after a pause: ''Send two sharp men tomorrow to check on him and bring him wine and meat.''
''Tell him no matter the fort's name, he'll always be our third chief.''

张错怕黑，至少很早很早之前的时候害怕。黑暗无边无际，既能吞噬一切，又没有尽头，黑:
Zhang Cuo was afraid of the dark. At least long ago, he had been. Darkness was endless, boundless. It devoured everything and led nowhere. In the dark, sound is the only thing he can still sense. His father's exhausted breathing. The crash of the door being kicked open. The harsh, alien shouts of Khitan soldiers. The clash of swords and blades. Fierce, desperate arguing. Then a long, long silence. And finally, the dull, heavy thud of something falling to the ground.

Zhang Cuo had understood nothing, and yet somehow, in that moment, he understood everything. He knew he had to run. Run from the ongoing carnage, from the eternal darkness, from everything. He stumbled blindly through the dark, first breaking his leg. Then he crawled on his hands and knees, scratching his palms. In the end, with his elbows, he dragged himself forward inch by inch. He heard a woman's voice just ahead, faint and blurred. He smelled the sweet, lingering scent of candied hawthorn. And beyond it, he saw the faint, long-lost glow of light.

A woman stood there, clad in green with crimson sleeves. She set down her sword, kneeling before him. She offered a few small, round healing pills. Zhang Cuo swallowed them. Then she handed him the candied hawthorn skewer that had long grown cold.

"Some paths," she said, "you have to walk yourself before you can understand. A'Cuo, this is the last lesson your father taught you."

"My name is Zhu Yu," she said, "and from now on, you'll be coming with me."
张错永远记得，与冯如之擦肩而过的那一刻。\n浊浪滔天，怒风呼啸，没能说动赤龙的青:
Zhang Cuo would never forget the moment he brushed past Feng Ruzhi.
The waves raged, the winds howled, but the azure flood dragon could not persuade the crimson dragon. 
It left the Yellow River to seek its own waters.
This was the second time Zhang Cuo left the place he once called "home."

The first time was during his childhood. When he woke up, the house was empty, just him, all alone. His fragmented memories were of a narrow cave, pitch-black tunnels, water seeping through rocky cracks that he could only lap up with his tongue, and the stench of raw rat meat. After barely escaping alive, all he remembered was a small hand at the cave's entrance, waving desperately in the light, as though summoning brightness for him.
That was his first meeting with Feng Ruzhi. It didn't end well. Every year on Feng Ruzhi's birthday, she would jokingly recall the feral little creature that had bitten her hard back then. At least it wasn't all bad. By now, Zhang Cuo had learned to turn away gracefully, coughing as he downed a cup of the notorious "Red Sleeve Special" amidst everyone's laughter.
"Why don't you bite back?"
"Next time, for sure."

The last of them had escaped the war outside and happened to flee into Hidden Mountain. His heart was filled with unquenchable hatred, and he used his knowledge to create various venomous insects, intending to seek revenge once his studies were complete. Seeing his improper intent, the elder never taught him his full knowledge.
Before the four senior disciples left on their travels, they created venomous mechanism insects to lure and kill the venomous creatures in the mountains using special sounds. They did this to prove to their master that venomous mechanisms could also be used for good.
