In the reign of Emperor Ming of Tang, the Master Ye Fashan was summoned. It was the night of the first full moon of the new year, the very hour when the Lantern Festival lights were displayed. Thereupon, he invited the emperor on a celestial journey, relying on wondrous arts. They were about to traverse the heavens when, in an instant, they departed the palace. The imperial phoenix carriage rose upon clouds, its emerald banners fluttering swift as a gale. Without relying on the art of riding the wind, they soared through the void in a flash. As if using the art of shrinking the earth, they halted in a moment. Soon, they felt the journey through Guanlong end, and the scenery of Hehuang unfold anew. 
Arriving at a bustling, prosperous place, they saw crowds of sightseers. A thousand silver lanterns glowed, fragrant dust filled ten miles of roads. Red mansions stretched endlessly, as bright as daytime, the clear night shimmered, as warm as spring. 
This prefecture was indeed Wuwei, its scenery like a fairyland. Colors flickered, reflecting the golden Buddha statues; light dazzled, outshining the jade toad in the sky. Wandering and enjoying, they wandered incognito here. No one recognized them, who could have expected the imperial visit? At that time, dew moistened the grass, and not a cloud dotted the sky. 
Golden duck-shaped incense burners radiated light, ice-like lotus lanterns held glow, connected like stars. The music was different from the Masked Troupe, yet flutes and songs filled the ears. The people were not from the imperial villa, yet silk and brocade filled the sight. Soon, the dipper shifted, and the silver arrow of the water clock marked the late hour. Wandering around did not fully satisfy the emperor's wish, viewing all still tired his royal attention. 
They mingled with people of high and low status, blending light with the common. Just as a phoenix hides its form among birds, and birds do not know it, a dragon conceals its shadow among fish, and fish do not see it. 
Soon homesickness crept in, and the emperor did not detain him. In a trance, he left the frontier, and in an instant, returned to the central plains. Unlike King Mu returning from the Jade Pool feast, or Emperor Wu coming back from the Bogu trip.

Once there were five hundred macaques wandering through the forest. Together they came to a great tree. Beneath the tree was a well, and in the well appeared the reflection of the moon.
When the macaque chief saw the moon's reflection, he said to the others:
"The moon has fallen into the well and perished. We must rescue it together and not let the world be plunged into endless darkness."
The macaques discussed it among themselves, saying, "How can we get it out?"
Then the macaque chief said, "I know a way. I will grab hold of the tree branch, and you will grab my tail. Then each of you can hold on to the next, one after another. That way we can pull it out."
So the macaques did exactly as their chief said, each clutching the next in turn. But the branch was too weak and snapped, and all the macaques fell into the well.

Once there was a woodcutter who heard that deep in the mountains there lived birds that kept hidden treasure, and so he went looking for them.
At the far end of the mountain, where there was nowhere left to go, he came upon heaps of gemstones. Beside them perched two birds, one a raven and one a swallow, and to his astonishment they spoke in human voices.
Swallow asked Raven, "This is neither fodder nor grain. What good is there in guarding it?"
Raven replied, "I would give it to all people under Heaven, so there would be no more divide between rich and poor, so all might live in halls of jade and wear robes of cloud-brocade."
Swallow asked again, "A worthy thought. Why then stop short of it?"
Raven sighed. "In the past, when the birds carried stones out of the mountains, the poor fought to seize them, even turning on their own kin. The rich, seeing birds that bore such stones, cast nets and loosed arrows, caging them for sport."
At this, both birds fell silent. After a while, Swallow spoke again. "If you know it cannot be done, why tell me of it?"
Raven answered, "To carry jade is to invite trouble. Better to hide it and wait for the right time. You leave in spring and return in autumn, and so have earned trust. You do not shrink from wind and rain, and so have earned constancy. Because you keep faith and remain steadfast, I entrust this to you."
Swallow said, "People know only that you keep your treasure to yourself. They do not know that you are waiting for the right time to bring it forth. Your body is worn down, your name diminished, and still the world mocks you. Do you truly accept this?"
Raven spread its wings and lifted its head. "People say Raven is a Mohist. If I am a Mohist, then so long as this heart remains, why should I care for praise or blame? The wants of men are endless, and still the Mohists feed them. When people ask for rice and flour, the Mohists cast iron ploughs and fashion wooden oxen to nourish the world. When people ask for wine and meat, the Mohists brew fine wine and raise fat hogs to feed all living things."

Spring's Gaze: Eternal Renewal 

"Xu Sanniang has a voice like silk. Surely she'll charm both the Emperor and the Noble Consort." 
Sanniang never dared believe the overseer's praise. 
"One wrong note, and His Majesty will hear it at once." The Masked Troupe existed by imperial will; in matters of music, no one surpassed the Emperor's ear. There was simply no room for mistakes. 
For first‑time performers entering the palace, lifting one's head was unthinkable. 
Sanniang trembled so hard she barely knew what to do with her hands and feet. 
"She's thirteen—still just a little one." 
The Noble Consort said, her voice warm and gentle, pitched with perfect grace. Sanniang risked a glance upward. She saw a soft, dimpled smile—like spring light spilling over a garden in bloom. 

The Emperor wished to present a new composition, a song he wanted the troupe to sing for the Consort. 
It was said to be based on a village tune collected by wandering song‑gatherers—a melody about a young man longing for the one he loves, sleepless and restless. 
A man who ruled the world, able to bestow treasures beyond imagining—yet here he was, imitating the shy earnestness of a common boy, offering his heart a little awkwardly. 

Sanniang sang with exquisite care. She knew she wasn't bad—but she wasn't truly good either. 
In the imperial troupe, "not perfect" meant "wrong." 
As she waited for judgment, the words came: "Child, come here." 
She nearly stepped on her hem as she stumbled forward. 
The Noble Consort let out a soft laugh and placed a bright red fruit into her palm, saying she was delighted. 

Whatever the Emperor said afterward faded into a blur. It almost sounded as though he was asking what reward she desired— 
his voice low, authoritative, yet tinged with something gentler, almost coaxing. 
Around her, performers bowed, accepted their stipends, and withdrew. Spring lingered in the Masked Troupe, its warmth left to the Emperor and his beloved alone. 

Born into a family of musicians, chosen for the Masked Troupe, welcomed into the palace—everything had unfolded as naturally as water flowing downhill. 
And as she stepped through the palace gates once more, Sanniang realized, quietly and to her own surprise: Perhaps she truly did love to sing.

A fine day for drying grain, the kind where you don't even have to turn it.
In the courtyard, Fang Bai gently swept, gathering stray wheat ears scattered by the breeze. The chicks followed at his heels, scrambling for the drifting chaff kicked up by the broom.
Across the fence, the neighbor's wife called out, chatting warmly but with a hint of warning that the wind's arrival would only make the days colder. Her words meandered, but the talk always drifted back to the fact that he had no soul to keep him warm.

Without missing a beat, Fang kept sweeping, a playful smile tugging at his lips as he nudged the chicks with his foot. "I've got plenty of ‘kin' here, squawking and fussing every day. What a headache. Add one more to the mix, and there'd be no peace left at all. Ah, maybe I should head out to the fields and breathe some fresh air."
He shouldered his hoe and made a swift exit, leaving the neighbors behind, shaking their heads with quiet sighs.

The scattered grains hidden among the furrows were nearly invisible to the human eye, but the sparrows always knew where to find them. As Fang worked the land slowly, he kept an eye on the lively birds flitting to and fro. Whenever one settled nearby, he'd gently wave a hand, sending it fluttering away. Only when they took flight would he stoop to gather the muddied grains, blowing off the dust before tucking them carefully into his pocket.

The last two Lantern Persimmons in the Leisure Garden had just been sold. This same scene has played out for days on end. Fang had grown used to it.
The sky shifted from a deep, velvety blue to a brilliant blaze of orange and crimson as he stared silently at the setting sun sinking behind the hills. Though he missed out on the persimmons, he caught a glimpse of the breathtaking evening glow stretching across the earth.
Lost in the quiet beauty of the dusk, he wandered without noticing where he'd gone until suddenly, a ripe persimmon dropped down, thudding softly against his head. The fruit was overripe, a sticky mess that matted his hair. He cupped the fruit in his hands, searching silently for someone to share this simple moment.
But all that greeted him was the quiet, solitary persimmon tree standing tall against the fading light.

A quiet loneliness drifted with him as he pondered adding an epilogue to the strange tale he'd been weaving. The story told of a spirit beast, its fur faded to a weary yellow, cast into a dog's womb and given the lowly name "Ahuang," yet it never forgot it was born a lion. Though its bones were trapped in a domestic yard, its behavior set it apart: it neither chased cats nor hares, refused scraps and leftovers, shirked its canine duties until at last, it was struck dead by celestial thunder.

Back at the stone table in his courtyard, ink stains still mingled with fallen grains of wheat that the chicks had left behind. Fang pinched a stray husk between his fingers. Moved by a sudden spark, he took up his brush once more. As Ahuang's remnant soul flickered, birds brought dew and shielded the dog with feathers, as if performing a rite of rebirth. In that moment, Ahuang's golden form dissolved into wisps of smoke, blending softly into the morning mist. Such a peaceful, tender farewell, surrounded by the warmth of those feathered companions, seemed... not so bad after all.

From afar, the clamor of a pack of youngsters broke the air. Their white robes were caked with mud and choked with dust. They clutched maps, their faces an unreadable mix of confusion and hope.
Fang was ready with a quip, but then he caught the vacant, shell-shocked stares in their eyes. The ragged youths' faces brightened suddenly, scrambling and tripping over one another, only to tumble into a heap at his feet.

"Master Fang! Uncle Fang! You're Master Fang, aren't you?"
As he recognized their attire, Fang Bai's heart tightened, though he feigned a gruff rebuke. "My dear Senior Brother... has he started recruiting nothing but airheads these days?"
Then the floodgates broke. Those tears... they were unsettling. The orange sky was now bled through by a sun the color of gore.
"Master... our Inkbound Order... it's gone..."
The wind had truly arrived. And it was only going to get colder.

When did it become like this? Xu Shangqian couldn't figure it out either. 
He had worked diligently all his life and studied the classics, yet never attained a high official post. He could only manage to get a position at an academy in the city. 
His wife was chosen for him by his parents based on a matchmaker's recommendation—a city girl. 
Her family had originally looked down on his humble origins. Fortunately, his wife believed in his steadfastness and hard work, seeing him as a scholar, albeit without rank.
He married his wife while living in his father-in-law's house. For two years, he endured no shortage of cold sneers from the old man. 
He worked steadily and diligently. Two years after marrying, he bought a small, remote house. A few years later, his wife bore him a son. 
He thought it would be a happy life for three. But the boy turned out to be especially unruly... 

By the time he reached thirty, he realized the burdens of life had long since worn away the stubborn, youthful spirit he once carried. 
Once, he too had been a young man galloping on hunts. He too had dreamed of roaming the roads of the capital, seeing all the splendors of Chang'an. 
But over time, many things were gradually forgotten. He no longer wished to speak of the grand ambitions of his youth. He just wanted to live well. 

Yet time's weight never lightens by even half an ounce according to human will. 
He only felt the burden on his shoulders grow heavier and heavier. Until he could no longer bear it. 
Only in dreams did he still ride a tall steed, holding a longbow, galloping across the hunting grounds. 
In the stands, his wife held their well-behaved child, cheering him on. 
Xu Shangqian knew it was a dream. But if a dream could let him escape the burden, let it wake a little later.

Dusk washed over the sky, and before they knew it, night had fallen. Jing and Da followed Uncle Zhang closely through the streets and alleys, finally turning into the Mahjong God Challenge arena. The arena glittered with gold and jade, so dazzling it was hard to keep one's eyes open. Da's sleeve accidentally brushed against a stone pixiu, which promptly clamped onto a half-exposed copper coin.
Suddenly, the clatter of rolling coins came from the eaves. They saw Uncle Zhang, Heng Blade in hand, slam it down on the blue bricks with a clang.
Uncle Zhang slurred, "The coin... spit it out! Spit all the money out!"
The two trembled with fear. Jing clenched his sleeve, muttering to himself, "What is Uncle Zhang up to now?"
Several bejeweled accountants gathered around, but Uncle Zhang paid them no heed, his gaze as sharp as a blade. "You two! Stop dawdling and get a move on!"
Their eyes met, a silent resolution forming between them: this time, no matter what, they would not be ordered around by this strange old man for nothing. They mustered their courage.
Jing gripped his sweat-dampened sleeve and stepped forward. "The weaklings we once were are dead! The ones standing here now—"
Before he could finish, the Prefect strolled toward them. Noticing the three acting strangely, he approached to ask what was happening. In an instant, the "voluntary labor" the youths had intended to refuse became a "military order."
"Alright... the ones standing here now... are even weaker than before..." Da said with a pained expression, the eggs stuffed at his waist digging into him.
Helpless, the two threw themselves into the challenge. After a battle of wits and courage, they won a hefty pile of chips. Just as they excitedly handed the chips to Uncle Zhang, he waved his hand magnanimously. "...The money... distribute it... distribute it... call the slaves over... and distribute it..."
Slaves? What slaves? The two looked at each other, utterly confused.
Uncle Zhang simply nodded with satisfaction, turned, and left, leaving them bewildered in the wind.
暮色苍茫，泾河水波如练。\n小盘目光远极处，船家余娘正撑船向渡口驶来。\n一片寂:
As twilight deepened, the Jing River stretched out like a ribbon of white silk.
Xiaopan's eyes traced the horizon, where Yu'niang, the boatwoman, was steering steadily toward the river crossing.
In the quiet hush, a soft, muffled groan suddenly escaped.
Xiaopan looked up at Lan Ao. Her face was ashen, cold sweat drenching her temples. She wavered on her feet, struggling to stay upright.
Xiaopan knew all too well the deadly poison that coursed through Lan Ao's veins, feared by all, and if anyone sensed something was wrong, it would only end in blood.
Not far off, the silhouette of Yu'niang's boat grew clearer against the river's darkening expanse.

"Be careful!" Xiaopan warned as Lan Ao suddenly leaned backward, and she caught her, hurriedly propping her up with her own body.

Reaching out, Xiaopan felt the dampness of cold sweat soaking through Lan Ao's clothes.
Quickly, she withdrew a pill from her medicine pouch and gently tilted Lan Ao's trembling chin, easing the remedy into her mouth. Stifled, ragged gasps mingled with the river breeze, brushing against her ear. Lan Ao's grown frame was far heavier than she could hold for long.

Lan Ao seemed to sense just how much strain Xiaopan was under and suddenly tried to pull away, but a sharp wave of pain robbed her of control, nearly sending her tumbling into the river. 

Without hesitation, Xiaopan dropped to one knee, catching her before she fell, even as her own knee slammed hard against the rough stones, sharp gravel biting into her flesh. Yet she held on with fierce determination, refusing to let Lan Ao slip any further.
This time, Lan Ao didn't resist or utter a sound. She simply surrendered to the moment, quietly allowing Xiaopan to ease her onto a nearby mound of stones.

"You don't need to struggle so much," Lan Ao finally whispered after a pause. "If anyone finds out... I'll deal with them."
Xiaopan met her gaze silently, catching a glimpse of the boatwoman's approaching silhouette near the shore.
"Well, you two have been waiting quite a while!" Yu'niang beamed at them, her eyes crinkling at the sight of the silver she could barely hold in her hands.
Xiaopan nodded in return, steadying the still-shivering Lan Ao as she helped her slowly step onto the boat.

The river's surface rippled gently, and between the three of them, only the soft splash of oars breaking the water filled the evening air.
Yu'niang glanced at the two young women, one tall, the other petite, both quiet and reserved, then smiled warmly and spoke up, "My, this young miss is more devoted than most. Your little sister, is she?" When no reply came, she didn't let the silence fall awkwardly. Instead, she murmured thoughtfully, half to herself, "Aye, in times like these, nothing beats a sister. Sisters look out for one another, not like living alone or even with a brother."
"She's my daughter," Lan Ao interjected out of the blue.

"Your daughter?!" Yu'niang exclaimed and then discreetly studied them both for a moment. "Well, you must've found the fountain of youth." 
"Found her," Xiaopan interjected plainly. 
Lan Ao shot Xiaopan a surprised glance and then continued, "That's right. And she's a dutiful one, at that."
"Oh, I see..." Yu'niang's gaze softened with quiet acceptance. "No different from one of your own blood, I'd say."

The river flowed endlessly beneath them, and before long, one of the young women laughed a light, genuine sound.
And the other, surprisingly, joined in, their laughter rippling out like the gentle waves. Feeling a warm glow spread through her, Yu'niang struck up a river shanty to the rhythm of their laughter.
Soon, the little boat echoed with joyous laughter. Just sisters at play, Yu'niang thought, the kind with a bond deeper than blood.
Having someone by your side to lean on and share the journey, and then, no matter where you started, you've already found home.

The young lady of the Cao family has a great affinity with Goddess of Mercy. 
She's heard this since childhood. The story first came from the temple her grandmother frequented. As a child, she was adorable, like a pink-and-white jade-carved doll, but often sick, barely able to leave her bed for more than a few days a year. Grandmother worried herself sick, running to the temple time and again, beseeching all deities. One day, Grandmother took her to pray before Goddess of Mercy. Just after they kowtowed, an unfamiliar nun emerged from behind the statue, touched her forehead with a willow branch, and then departed gracefully. The suddenness stunned everyone in the hall, only after the nun left did they think to follow. Sure enough, outside there was no one. From then on, her health gradually improved. The temple's master said she was originally a jade-carved acolyte under Goddess of Mercy reborn. Since her original form was jade, bloodless and fleshless, borrowing her parents' essence to gain a body made her naturally weaker than others. Thus, the Goddess of Mercy came specially to protect her. He also said it was best to include Goddess of Mercy in her name, so all minor ghosts would know she was watched by the Goddess of Mercy and dare not approach. Grandmother took every word to heart, complied item by item, commissioned golden statues, jade carvings, requested the abbot and masters to rename her, sent chests of offerings to the temple... Other Liangzhou families, hearing this tale, marveled and came to pay respects, so the temple's incense thrived. 
The subject of this tale was not much concerned. For a Buddhist temple to gain footing among Liangzhou's great families, it needed a hook. Sickly young children weren't rare, they often outgrew it. For the Cao family to stand out among the clans, they needed to make gestures to build momentum, show their single-minded devotion to Buddha. As for the fresh willow branch in deep winter and the unfamiliar nun... everyone needed a story, so the trick became truth. Xinzizai laughed at her for feigning clarity, teased that she really was jade reborn. So be it, jade reincarnation. Perhaps she was indeed born with a certain chill. Even having received divine grace, she still didn't believe in those ethereal things. So when she copied sutras in the temple, time and again, she never asked the Bodhisattva to stop the marriage. She did not beg gods or Buddhas, only relied on herself. 
Bodhisattva, I was wrong. 
The Goddess of Mercy, white as carved jade, hastily wrote a line on the back of her divine arts booklet. Her tears had not yet fallen before they were dried by the howling cold wind atop the high tower.

最恶浊的人学得所有，最璀璨的人却背乡远走。\n后来的无数个深夜中，蛤蟆长老常常于:
The most depraved inherited all the knowledge, while the most radiant were driven into exile.
Blessed with genius but barren of "The Way," Yanxi never deemed himself worthy of the Mohist name. He was but a hollow vessel, overflowing with technique yet empty of spirit. Scarred by the flames of war in his youth, his heart harbored a hatred that ran bone-deep. Those high-born predators, feasting upon the world, could turn millions to ash with a casual jest. Compared to the nameless millions of ants, the cost they paid for their wars was infinitesimal. This was the true rot at the heart of the world.
But a heart so full of vengeance had no place in the Mohist Hill. The brilliance of his seniors was a constant presence. It warmed his soul even as it scorched his conscience. Yanxi wore a mask of silence, gazing upward from the depths, straining to keep his place among those shimmering stars.
But the craft within his hands could tell no lies. Where others' fingers loosed soaring kites, his brought forth venomous, grotesque mechanical vermin. He thought only of how to harvest lives in silence. When they confined him to the Suspended House and barred him from the master's deepest teachings, he didn't resent it. He knew he could never be like them.
But in an instant, all light was extinguished. He had failed his last chance to hold back the person whose name he dared not even whisper in the deepest corners of his heart.
Facing a master who seemed to have aged a decade in a single breath, he realized that he was the one now forever sealed within the sect.
During the final three years of the Master's life, Yanxi finally mastered the forbidden arts he had once dreamed of possessing.
At the end, as the old man lay dying, he no longer spoke of the craft. He gripped Yanxi's hand, repeating a single, broken phrase: "What a bitter road you've walked... what a bitter road..."
Later, Yanxi donned the toad mask crafted for him by his Fourth Sister and ascended as the new Master of the Hall. After that year, the words "Junior Brother" vanished from the world forever. Everyone called him the "Elder Toad."

最美味的果子，生长在采撷者的梦里。\n这是从岭南快马加鞭进献上来的珍果，普通人看:
The choicest fruit grows only in the dreams of those who gather it. 
Rushed from Lingnan by swift horses, this rare delicacy was so precious that even a mere glance was a privilege denied to ordinary folk. 
While the troupe's musicians eagerly peeled back its snow-white flesh, Sanniang only wished she could keep it a secret, a treasure all her own. 

Later, the Emperor and the Noble Consort delighted in her singing—a tender folk tune from the southern lands. They praised her voice, saying, "Her clear voice sends echoes weaving through every street and alleyway." 
That timid child who once trembled before the imperial throne blossomed into Lady Eternal Renewal, a name on the lips of all Chang'an. 
Her song echoes beneath the bright moon atop the lofty pavilion, stirring courage in the joyful and wrenching sorrow in the broken-hearted. 
That lychee, gifted on a spring day, lay beside her pillow—cherished until it withered and decayed. 
The rot of the dynasty came no slower than that of the fruit. 
When the rebellion shattered the palace and scattered the sovereignty, she found herself adrift in distant lands. Her sorrowful melodies were met by tearful echoes in kind. 
Whether mighty generals or performers unmatched in skill, that night all were but solitary boats adrift on a stormy sea. 

The exiled soul carried memories of Chang'an close, and in quiet moments recalled a spring day, when pear blossoms fell like drifting snow. 
The woman from that day had become nothing more than a lingering fragrance on a barren slope. 
Sanniang would never again have the chance to ask her: "Did you truly love this song?"

Afterward, on my master's desk, I found a half-written manuscript. It broke off midway, as though some doubt had arisen in her mind. I believe she meant to verify a point or two before setting out, and in her haste climbed the mountain that very night, only to meet this calamity.
My master's sudden death is a grief I cannot lay down. The affairs of this world are ever uncertain. By what justice does Heaven ordain such things? Only this much is certain: the work my master left unfinished, I shall carry on even at the cost of my life.
After my master's death, Yuelu fell gravely ill. This too was my failure in caring for her.
After many difficulties, and with Master Raven's help, I have at last sent Yuelu back to the mountain. In its quiet peace, she will surely grow up safe and well there. I also hope she may keep the two of you company, and bring some comfort in your later years.
I bow my head and beg forgiveness. Your disciple was not equal to the charge of keeping my master safe. The kindness shown me by Mohist Hill and the academy alike is something I shall never forget. When the book is finished, I will present it, together with all that I have gained, to Mohist Hill, as a small token of my heart.

With another respectful bow.

Peaceward Camp was first built during the Dali period, originally serving as a reclamation and coin-casting site for the Anxi Army. Located beside Jade Gate Pass, it slopes from north to south. According to the surviving villagers, Peaceward carries three meanings.
Firstly, "looking toward Anxi." As a strategic hub, Peaceward Camp overlooks Jade Gate Pass. Garrison soldiers stationed at the tower of the coin-casting factory north of the camp would gaze east at Jade Gate Pass daily. Bugles at dawn and drums at dusk relayed messages. The lights of Jade Gate Pass burned bright, and the cooking smoke of Peaceward Camp curled upward. They watched over each other, never apart.
Secondly, "looking forward to peace." Peaceward Camp sheltered local people, whoever had nowhere to go could settle here. In the past, soldiers and civilians in Peaceward Camp lived as one, with doors left unlocked at night and lost belongings untouched on the roads.
The third meaning was left unspoken by the villagers. They only said that in the past, when the Tang court issued an imperial edict, the people rejoiced, and soldiers and civilians waited quietly for the imperial army to arrive from the east. Yet the army never came, instead, a sandstorm struck, scattering the soldiers and civilians, and collapsing the houses. Today, only a few households remain, clinging to life. The prosperity of the past can never be restored.

He laughed and shouted, "Khitan dogs! Witness my peerless skill!"
He fought with his Soaring Blade until the very end.

The old man was useless, dying before him just like his worthless father.
But the old man knew his craft; he said if they could hold, they would hold.
The two of them alone could hold Zhongdu Bridge and let the others cross safely.

They would die on this side of the bridge, and the Laid Bare Needles would remain nameless in the world.
But Zhao Jiu was delighted. He was willing.

Seeking Autumn in the Snow of Late Winter
末将拜见将军，大帅差末将，送虎符至此，并有一言，谓将军。: General. The Commander sent me with the Tiger Tally and a message.
本不欲与墨山道为敌，奈何你等偏要动手。: We didn't come looking for trouble with Mohist Hill. You forced our hand.
本不相识的三人，只因皆曾受过兵痞之苦而结伴相依。虽不知彼此名姓，却因身旁有人共对: Strangers to one another, these three were bound together only by the shared trauma of the soldiers' cruelty. Though they remain nameless to each other, the mere presence of a companion against the frigid night has kindled a glimmer of hope for the dawn.
本为储粮备荒以供应官需民食而设置的粮仓，如今守军早已变节，常平仓粮草只进不出，而: Originally built as granaries to store food supplies for officials and civilians during times of famine, these warehouses have long since fallen into disuse. The garrison troops assigned to guard them have turned traitorous. While supplies still come into the Ever-Normal Granary, nothing ever goes out, leaving the once-bustling storerooms empty and shrouded in mystery.
本为墨山道弟子，为隐藏墨山道所在奉命潜入天涯客组织，并揽下了绘制不见山区域舆图的: A Mohist Hill disciple who infiltrated the Wayfarers to conceal the sect's true location. Tasked with mapping Hidden Mountain, he deliberately creates accurate but rapidly outdated maps to protect his home.
本为墨门弟子，奉长老之命加入天涯客，负责测绘天陉舆图。自穷奇师势起，他总觉得那些: Originally a Mohist disciple ordered by an elder to join the Wayfarers to map the Heaven's Threshold. Since Qiongqi Artificer rose to power, he constantly feels they look at him strangely.
本为天子用以束忠臣，然被此物所囚者，非忠于皇，无忠于堂，惟忠于苍生耳。: Emperors use it to bind loyal ministers, yet those holding the tablet serve neither emperor nor court, but only the common folk.
本为皇家别馆，两年前，柴荣病逝之后，此处便已荒废，只余几个洒扫之人。如今荒废的别: An abandoned imperial villa left after Emperor Chai Rong's death. Few caretakers remain, but unexpected visitors have come. What secrets hide here?
本也没什么，只是此事的机缘不在我这里，而在东南角门里。我若横插一脚，事情反倒会生: It's nothing special. The opportunity for this matter isn't with me, but in the southeast Forsaken Quarter. If I interfere, things might change for the worse. Might not work out as intended.
本书以春秋时期青铜器莲鹤方壶为代表，详细讲解了不同时期青铜器、泥器的雕刻技艺。: Focusing on the iconic Lotus and Crane Rectangular Pot from the Spring and Autumn period, this book details the sculpting techniques of bronze and clay wares across different eras.
本书是音韵研究通俗读物，书中列举并解答了人们在学习音韵时遇到的困惑，譬如：何为十: A popular reader on phonology that answers common questions like: What are the Sixteen Sounds? How do they differ from the Twelve Pitches?
本书荟萃千年来近百位武林宗师的江湖经验，旨为读者揭示成为武林高手的上等秘诀！\n:
The secrets of 100 masters, finally revealed! This book grants you INSTANT mastery of forbidden arts, making you an unstoppable legend. Don't just dream it—do it! Start training NOW, hero!
—Chang Xiao
本书记载了某年秋季，入学弟子自研机关综述和导师点评。: A collection of mechanism research summaries by new disciples, complete with mentor notes, from one particular autumn intake.
本事不大，贼心倒是不小。: Not much skill, but plenty of nerve.
本事不济就别添乱: You can't hack it. Stay outta the way.
本人于墨城核心报刊《织网》发表论文十数篇，手握专利数十项。现寻有志于水力榫卯研究: I have published over a dozen papers in Mohist City's top journal, The Web, and hold dozens of patents. I am looking to settle down with a woman who shares my passion for hydraulic mortise-and-tenon engineering. Looking forward to your letters!
本人是刚入门的九流门弟子，前两天捡到一只小猫，本来一直好好的，忽然开始喜欢拿头蹭: I'm a new disciple of the Nine Mortal Ways. I found a kitten a couple of days ago, and it was fine at first. But suddenly it started rubbing its head against me, circling around me while constantly meowing, and flopping down in front of me every few steps. Fellow disciples, please help! Is my kitten sick?
本人楼梦月，肤白靓丽，楚楚动人。夫本江南富商，却意外失去……（被撕毁的痕迹）\n:
I am Lou Mengyue, a beautiful woman with ivory skin. My husband was a Jiangnan Wealthy Merchant, but... (Torn after this) 
Upon returning to Kaifeng, I decided to look for a tall, healthy, and handsome man to marry so I may one day be a mother. 
Should anyone be willing, please contact... (Scribble: Don't believe them! This is Nine Mortal Ways!)

本以为掌门大典会是门派难遇的喜事，谁能想到……: I thought the grand ceremony of the Sect Master would be a rare joy for the sect, who would have thought...
本伞虽不想淋雨。: I'd rather not stand in the rain, truth be told.
本公子与江南国主有约: With the Lord of Jiangnan's approval,
本公子今儿个去樊楼赴约，特意带了娘子赠予的花伞。: Yours truly is going to Revelry Hall for a rendezvous, and I made it a point to bring the painted parasol that the lady gave to me.

He remembered endless sandstorms by day, and at night, the wind carrying children's laughter, women's songs, and the flicker of candle flames.
He ached for it. Though its people, like those in the Central Plains, feared and hated him, there had been those who shielded and loved him.
But the vast desert stretched eternally. He could never return, never see those dear faces again.

In that damp, lightless prison beneath the earth, he paced and roared, a creature with no path back.
Until one day, a new sound threaded through the moaning wind: the flutter of wings, followed by a high, fragile chirp.

Had the gods heard his turmoil, sending this delicate creature as a salve?
He cradled the bird in his palm, nurturing it day and night, offering every scrap of beauty he could find.
He waited for it to grow strong.
He hoped it would soar free, to see the distant horizon for him, to hear the laughter and the flicker of flames in the wind.

Du Chenfei had been a bladesman his entire life. Only, in the first half of his life, he wielded a blade to kill; in the latter half, he lifted a cleaver to cut meat.
In his early years, when he wielded a steel broadsword, his only passion, aside from roaming the jianghu and robbing the rich to aid the poor, was eating meat by the mouthful. Having never suffered a loss in close combat, he was ultimately felled by a cold arrow from Khitan cavalry.
After sleeping in a groggy daze for who knows how long, he suddenly caught a mouthwatering aroma of meat. Opening his eyes, he saw an old man walking by, carrying strips of meat. Seeing him awake, the old man handed him two slices of dried meat and explained everything.
It turned out this place was called Toilgrain Barn, the main provision camp in the Hutuo region. The old man, surnamed Zhang, had run a meat stall here for over twenty years, and everyone called him Old Man Zhang. With the Khitan invading southward recently, the camp had heightened its vigilance. While patrolling outside with the camp brethren, Old Man Zhang had stumbled upon the unconscious wanderer and hurriedly dragged him back.
As Du Chenfei listened, he stuffed the dried meat into his mouth. He had never tasted anything prepared this way before, finding its unique texture greatly revitalizing to his spirits. He leaped out of bed with a kip-up, declaring that he still had silver in his bundle robbed from corrupt officials, and begged Old Man Zhang to teach him the recipe.
The old man waved his hand at him, saying that if he truly wanted to learn, he wouldn't charge a single coin.
However, this Five Flavor Jerky was an exclusive secret recipe. To learn it, he must inherit the old man's meat stall right here.
Du Chenfei touched the blade at his waist, thinking of how he had just been ambushed by the Khitan invaders; this was a score that had to be settled. The old man seemed to see through his hesitation and thus made a pact with him.
"Young lad, if you use this blade to kill another hundred foreign invaders, would you be willing to come back and inherit my stall?"
The savory aroma in the air grew even richer, and Du Chenfei nodded his head again and again.
"Deal."

Arguing can be toxic, but are we, the Four Silver Tongues, to shy away? Esteemed as masters of rhetoric, it is our duty to lead by example and offer three strategies to counter sophistry: lower, middle, and upper.
The Lower Strategy: Respond with force. Though clever words can win battles, not every dispute must be settled by speech alone. If reason fails, one may answer with strength. Yet this rarely convinces others, and so it is the lowest method.
The Middle Strategy: Ignore it. Sophistry may sting, but if you remain unmoved, you cannot be harmed. Let arguments pass like wind over the hills, indifferent and untouched. This preserves yourself, but changes little. Hence, the middle way.
The Upper Strategy: Reason with it. Sophistry may twist words, but it cannot stand against true logic. If all understand reason, empty arguments fall apart on their own. This is the highest approach.
(A line of tiny script follows)
Yet even with these strategies, hearts remain restless. The world admires eloquent speakers, eager to imitate them. If one can rival the famous simply by clever arguing, why toil in true study? What a pity...

Though arguing for argument's sake can be harmful, should we fear it?
As the "Four Great Masters," we feel responsible for curbing this endless quarreling. We propose three strategies for future guidance.
Use force. Words are weapons, but when reason fails, strength may prove the point. Yet this rarely wins true respect, making it the least admirable path.
Let it go. Without the urge to argue, one remains unharmed. Without clear right and wrong, disputes fade like wind over hills. This protects only oneself and is thus average.
Rely on reason. Though sophistry twists words, true debate rests on logic. If all valued truth, senseless quarrels would collapse like rootless trees.

The Dream Play

One night, a peddler lost his way and wandered into a wild persimmon grove. Drawn by flickering firelight, he stumbled upon a shadow puppet theater performing deep in the woods. Paper figures danced to haunting songs, watched by a dozen indistinct spectators, some laughing, others weeping. Mesmerized, the peddler grew sleepy and leaned against a tree, drifting into a slumber.

At dawn, the stage and crowd had vanished, replaced only by old, neglected graves. Rubbing his eyes, he thought it all a dream until he noticed the tree he'd rested against: a withered willow with drooping branches like flowing hair. Beneath it lay a faded puppet, its features matching those from the night's performance. Terrified, he fled.

I used to think people were just spinning yarns when they spoke of the world of the living and the dead overlapping. But perhaps those restless souls gathered one last time, replaying lost joys and sorrows. Thankfully, the peddler's sleep spared him from disturbing their fragile peace. Had he cried out, who knows if he would have escaped alive?

Under the pear tree, pear blossoms fluttered in the wind. 
Many petals had fallen on the stone table. Between the petals was a jar of wine, and beside the jar were two white porcelain wine cups painted with willow leaf patterns. 
Han Xiangxun had already poured the wine. 

Wei Zhixi didn't stand on ceremony with Han Xiangxun. She tilted her head back, drank the first cup in one go, and finally felt relieved. 
The only person in the world who could order her to do something like burying bones... was the woman sitting across from her. 
But there was nothing she could do, she owed her a life. 

She drank the second cup. Wei Zhixi touched the long sword on the stone table, there were still water stains on it. 
She hadn't wielded a sword in a long time after the Wolf Mountain Battle. Yesterday, she had come to find Han Xiangxun to drink and relieve her boredom. Unexpectedly, as soon as she entered the mountain, she saw Han Xiangxun chasing someone with a sword. 
 "Stop him!" 
"Okay." 
She threw a flying star dart, and the man knelt down and fell to the ground. Han Xiangxun caught up, raised her sword, and struck, clean and decisive. 
So she had wanted to kill him. Wei Zhixi touched the long sword at her waist. 
In fact, if Han Xiangxun had shouted "Kill him," she would not have hesitated to draw her sword. 
But she hated seeing blood, and Han Xiangxun understood her. That's why the sword hadn't shed blood yesterday. 
She had just felt bored while watching Han Xiangxun wash her sword in the river, so she used her own sword to stir up a few eddies... and received a few eye-rolls in return. 

She drank the third cup. 
Wei Zhixi thought it was time to leave. 
Before the Khitan spy died, they had extracted a lot of information from him. About Northern Han, about the imperial court... This information made her more aware of her path ahead. 
She had to climb higher, even higher. Only when standing high enough could she see far enough. She wanted to see how the knots tangled, how decay took root, and then use the sword in her heart to cut off the roots of evil born in this chaotic world. 
Han Xiangxun, however, thought it was time to stay. 
She had to get closer, even closer. Only when getting close enough could she see clearly enough. She wanted to do what she could in the present, protect those she could behind her. She wanted to save one person, then another, then another... Saving enough people would also make a corner of the martial arts world, a world of her own. 
Moreover, what those people had said about face-swapping, about Hidden Swallow... She looked down at her hands. It seemed time to put her skills on display. 

The wine cups fell onto the table. The two exchanged a glance, then stood up and took their leave. 
Three cups of wine, half a quarter of an hour. It was as if they had said nothing, yet as if they had said everything. 
This world needs a ferry boat to cross the river, and it also needs timely rain. They would part, but they would meet again and again in the hearts of everyone they had protected.

This musical score was lost in China but survives by name and anecdote in ancient texts. According to the Old Book of Tang: Treatise on Music and Extensive Records of the Taiping Era, the piece originated after Emperor Taizong defeated the rebel warlord Liu Wuzhou. The people of Hedong celebrated in the streets with song and dance. Soldiers adapted older military tunes with new lyrics to commemorate the victory, and thus the piece "The King of Qin Crushes the Enemies" was born, later entered the repertoire of the imperial music bureau. In the early Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong ordered Wei Zheng and others to revise the lyrics, while Lu Cai arranged the melodies and harmonized the composition. The finalized work became known as Prince of Qin's Triumph. 
Several variants of the song survive in ancient Japanese Tang-music collections. 此处墨渍晕开，已无下笔之地了……: The ink stain has bled around this spot, leaving no place to write...
此处实在诡异，我带着头盔进门，受到了将士热烈的欢迎，他们似乎把我认成了什么将军。:
The atmosphere here is eerie. Wearing a helmet, I stepped inside and received a hero's welcome from the soldiers—they must have mistaken me for a general.
Then, as I beat the war drum, I accidentally knocked the helmet off. Was that it? Was that the moment everything changed? Because suddenly, their warmth turned to steel, and every sword was drawn.

What secret does that helmet hide? I couldn't grab it in the confusion.
With such elite troops inside, I could investigate no further and was forced to return with nothing.

My investigation suggests this was an old Anxi Army garrison. An army base wouldn't have legendary treasures or martial arts.
And it certainly wouldn't be filled with beauties. That letter had to be a vicious lie!

A warning to the next soul fated to find this: Run.

此处山石崖壁形成了天然的弧形。站在回音壁下，无论何处发出声响，都会有清晰的回音传: The natural curvature of these cliffs creates a perfect arc. Stand beneath the Echo Wall, and any sound will return as a crystal-clear reflection, layered and lingering throughout the valley.
此处崖高林密，风清气爽，端的是个好景致。\n不远处似有琴声，听琴声哀愁，也不知是:
Here, steep cliffs tower and dense forests thrive, with clear winds and refreshing air—truly a fine view indeed. 
Not far off, there seems to be the sound of a lyre. The melody carries such sorrow—one wonders who could be playing it. 
Yet for those who truly understand music, perhaps someone might join the lyre-player in a duet, 
to pour out their feelings together and listen to the story hidden within the tune.

This is Wenming Hall, where the sovereign and his ministers hold court.
The last few times I came by, I saw only cleaning maids, palace guards, and a scattered few officials discussing business. Looking back, I must have come at the wrong hour.
I slept lightly last night, so I wandered the palace. Around the Yin hour, I saw carriages and mounted escorts file in through the palace gates and draw up outside the hall. Officials streamed inside, and the hall quickly filled with noise.
A few of them even got into a heated argument in the front courtyard, and when tempers flared their words turned downright coarse. Oddly entertaining.
The front courtyard is where officials wait for the audience hour. Once the Mao hour arrives, they head into the inner hall, leaving the courtyard empty and bleak, like the affairs of the former dynasty, gone with the wind while the halls still stand.
It is hard enough to slip past the guards and get into the inner hall, so there was no chance of overhearing what His Majesty is worrying about today. Ah well. What I caught from this corner will do.

武威山的风是冷的，雪是甜的，梅花是涩的。张淮深都尝过。\n他最爱独行策马登高。山:
The wind on Wuwei Mountain is cold, the snow is sweet, and the plum blossoms are astringent. Zhang Huaishen has tasted them all. 
He loves riding alone to the heights. The wind is fierce at the mountain top, squinting his eyes, Liangzhou City looks no bigger than the palm of his hand. 
A friend once invited him: "Lubo, when shall we view the mountains together?" 
"Next month." 
Which day next month? It didn't matter much to him or his friend. When the mood struck, he would casually throw on a fur coat, over the years, he had lost countless ones, left in the mountains after getting drunk, torn during sword fights with others, or given to shivering old men in the snow. 
He would carry a flask of River All Red in his arms. If he didn't meet his old friend at the top, he would pour himself a drink, to comfort friends who had already left, or to toast bosom friends who had not yet come. 
Before he set off, a little incident happened. His young brother Huaiding rushed over, hugged Zhang Huaishen's legs, and pestered him to stay. 
So he took him along. Laughing loudly, he lifted the young boy onto the horseback. The white horse neighed, shaking the snow off the branches. 
Everyone in Liangzhou remembered him. Few people had such a fast horse, or such sharp hearing. 
Zhang Huaishen's hearing was indeed excellent. The oaths of Sister Yue, Huaiding's coquetry, the worries of farmers, Zhang Qiu's recitations, Suo Jing's qin playing, and the cries for help from old men on snowy nights, he heard them all clearly. 
Gradually, more and more people became constant companions on his journeys: Huaiyue, Huaiding, Suo Jing, the old man, Zhang Qiu, and even bosom friends met by chance. Their weight piled up on the saddle, yet it never slowed his horse down. The white horse ran faster and faster, so fast that his young brother's exclamations were shattered by the wind. 
The scenery blurred all around. Shouts came, whether from within his embrace or behind him, now distant, now near, as if chasing or pleading, Zhang Huaishen could not be bothered to tell. 
"Brother, slow down!" 
"We need to go faster." 
Who in the world can stop a young man's fast horse? Who can put out a fire that is determined to burn brightly to the end, leaving not even ashes behind? 
"Where are we going?" 
"To keep an appointment." 
"With whom?" 
He smiled, raised his whip, and pointed toward the snowstorm covering the sky.

武威市磨嘴子汉墓出土。木俑为松木雕成。为两位跪坐对局的老者形象。二位老者间设二层: Unearthed from the Han Dynasty tomb at Mozuizi in Wuwei City. The wooden figurines are carved from pine wood, depicting two elderly men kneeling and playing a board game. A two-tiered chessboard is placed between them, with a black base and white lines forming grids on the surface. The remaining space beside the chessboard is used for rolling dice. Both figurines wear cone-shaped buns and cross-collar robes with right-side closures. Their faces and hands are painted white, with facial features, beards, and hair painted in black. The bodies are painted gray with thick white lines outlining the costumes, and the collars, lapels, and cuffs are painted with heavy black ink. Their gestures are slightly different, one places his right hand on his knee and raises his left hand to his chest; the other stretches his right arm forward and downward, holding a game piece. The two elderly men have focused expressions, ready for action, engaged in an intense chess match. This six-player chess figurine is full of charm, creating an atmosphere of imminent competition through simple yet intricate details, and is a masterpiece of Han Dynasty wood carving art.

Every night, after everyone fell asleep, Zhuge Ha would sit alone by the lamp, spread out the thick account book, and record every expense of the "Pocketrupt Circus". 
He would write for a long, long time, as if there were countless things to record. He would also mutter to himself as he wrote, as if every detail was worth caring about. 

——Expense: 2 qian of silver, purchased 20 chi of Sogdian red silk 
"Anzi's Immortal Rope is getting more and more worn out. This is her livelihood, she doesn't even mention it's old." 
"Running around all day, not even sending a message back. Making people worry about her nonstop!" 
Zhuge Ha muttered, and out of the corner of his eye, he saw the bamboo bird beside him, letting out a long sigh. 

——Expense: 500 copper coins, purchased several pots of Persian medicinal wine 
"That fool Qingqing, he never thinks about himself! He doesn't say a word when he loses money, when he's scolded by the audience, or when he gets hurt!" 
"Next time, next time he gets hurt again, I'll definitely not buy him such expensive medicine!" 
Despite his harsh words, his box was filled with empty medicine bottles. 

——Expense: 300 copper coins, purchased sugar melons, Salted Milk Curds, roasted lamb legs, hot pot dishes... 
"These two little monkeys, they're greedier than anyone else! They can't move when they see food! They'll eat up all our savings sooner or later." 
"Forget it, forget it, they're growing. Hmph, if I'd eaten this well when I was young, I wouldn't have ended up so short and stubby!" 
Zhuge Ha huffed, puffing his beard in anger, not noticing the crisp bell ring outside the tent at all. 

He closed the account book, blew out the lamp, picked up his pipe, and walked straight out. 
Once he was far away, two small figures sneaked into the tent. 
"Xiaoyin, I bet the troupe master wrote all his secrets in here." 
"Account... Xiaojin, how do you read this word?" 
"Ugh, it's not a diary... it's an account book... What a letdown!" 
"Xiaoyin, do you think the troupe master is the biggest miser ever? He even writes down every bit of food he buys!" 
"Hmm... He is a miser. So stingy that he never buys anything for himself." 
Jin and Yin Bells walked out empty-handed, dejected, even their bell rings sounded dull. 
The moonlight was bright and clear. Zhuge Ha leaned against a tree not far away, almost blending into the shadow. 
Only the faint red glow of his pipe flickered in the dark night, lighting up and dimming with his breath. 
He watched the two small figures crawl into their own small tent. Finally, silence returned to the surroundings. 
"A miser? Hmph... I'm happy to be one."

Every year at the reunion dinner, the children of Heaven's Pier keep one eye on the plate of candied fruit.
The adults never let them have much. Too sweet, they say. Bad for the teeth.
So of course the children wait for a moment when no one is looking, snatch a piece, and shove it into their mouths.
Then an adult spots them and calls out, "Hey, not that one. That one's gone bad."
But the child just keeps chewing, cheeks puffed out, and somehow it still tastes sweet.
Maybe the room is too warm. Maybe the laughter is too loud. Maybe everyone looks too happy for anything to taste wrong.

There are many stories of marriage contest in storybooks. Some tell of heroic maidens from famous martial arts families who, unable to find a satisfactory husband, hold grand arenas to seek the world's most talented man as their spouse. Others speak of poor girls in the streets who, though forced to sell themselves to bury their fathers, refuse to marry fools, so they hastily post notices for martial arts contests to find kindred spirits in the martial arts world. As a child, Feng Ruzhi loved these tales of knight-errant couples and martial arts grievances. She would chase after the storytellers from the Nine Mortal Ways, asking repeatedly, "And then? And then?" Then… many years later, on the stage of Verdant Hill Village, Feng Ruzhi also held a marriage contest. Not for knight-errant couples or martial arts grievances, but for one thing, money. 

She needed money to feed the brothers and sisters of the Bloodscale Hall, to repair the Huzhi Golden Dyke, to forge swords for the newly adult members of the hall, and to burn paper money for her mother… even that cost money. But the imperial court wanted to cut off the Yellow River's grain transportation, and money didn't fall from the sky. After much thought, she decided to get it openly from passersby. Hence, this marriage contest: first, to earn rewards and win money from wealthy young martial artists; second, to attract more merchants who would drink dogwood soup, bringing more business and commotion; third, to exchange martial arts skills and improve herself, making all this effort worthwhile; fourth, ahem… after fighting so much, she had disillusioned herself with the old storybooks from the Nine Mortal Ways. All that talk of knight-errant couples and martial arts grievances seemed tacky to Feng Ruzhi, downright vulgar. What nonsense love and romance! Nothing was as real as two copper coins. 

But that day, a reckless young hero jumped onto the stage, caught the silk ball, and looked strangely familiar… Though he didn't seem like a noble or wealthy man, there was something intriguing about him. Why not investigate? Feng Ruzhi put on a Nuo mask, held her spear, and turned around: "Next?"

Originating in the Southern and Northern Dynasties and flourishing during the Tang, Song, and Ming, it was a unique means for women to choose their husbands. Compared to Li Jun, who died in battle, and Murong Yanzhao, now shackled in chains, Shi Shouxin's fate seemed the most dignified. No life lost on the battlefield, no soul broken in captivity. He merely stepped from the light of generalship into the shadows of power.
He struck more decisively than Murong Yanzhao, adapted more shrewdly than Li Jun. He understood: one cannot cling to a book whose pages are destined to turn. Zhao Kuangyin was the next chapter, written in ink long dried. But his friends refused to see it, gripping the past until their hands were stained black with futility. Fools. Utter fools.

At first, he couldn't return to Shi Family Village or see his parents. He heard his mother still longed for him. Even though he was reviled as a traitor, she still ached for her son.
Then, he lost more friends. Some asked if his choices were worth it, some called him clever, some entrusted their children to him.
Later, he relinquished his military power, barely securing his life. Some said he'd fallen from grace, others praised his ability to "judge the situation".
Was he a wise man or a fool?

Such questions couldn't be answered by looking inward. No one thinks their own actions are foolish, otherwise, why take them?
Perhaps endless curses would follow him, but he couldn't hear the praises of the dead, nor the insults. Praise and scorn were irrelevant now. He didn't care to listen. Such voices served no purpose.

Standing outside the Martial Temple, his ears filled with the footsteps of artisans, their backs bent under the scorching sun, their work chants shattering the heat. These were the sounds of the present. The emperor's words in the court chambers, those were the sounds of the present. The floodwaters of Shi Family Village, the whispers of old friends, under today's sun, had faded to near nothing.

To Ruby, "jianghu" had once been just a distant word from storybooks.

She'd heard merchants passing through Qinghe talk about jianghu affairs—heroic warriors, secret manuals, enchantresses... The heroes were always dashing and handsome, while the enchantresses were always to blame for everything.

She thought these stories entertaining, but wondered how could one person be behind every bad thing. It didn't make sense, just like how her father always blamed her whenever something went wrong at home.

And she also had one big question: What exactly was this jianghu? It must be some enormous place to fit all those people and all those stories.

She used to imagine it as a massive, magical lake somewhere far away.

Qinghe had lakes too, of course, but they just had ducks and fishermen.

So in those days, Ruby never dreamed of venturing into this "jianghu."

A small girl from a small place like her would be better off focusing on practical matters—like how to sneak past her father and climb Moonveil Mountain alone.

Three years ago, on the night Madam Han left home, Ruby finally accomplished her great challenge, secretly climbing to Moonveil Mountain's peak.

But someone was already keeping watch at the summit—a person as mysterious as the night yet gentle as the breeze.

That day, Ruby witnessed the true jianghu. She realized that Qinghe wasn't so far from the jianghu after all.

Perhaps she too could explore this world?

From that moment, Ruby resolved to make her way in the jianghu, never backing down even after her father gave her a thorough thrashing upon her return home.

Next time, given the chance, she would go again!

A hundred times, a thousand, however many it took, she would sneak out again on that same night. No matter how hard it got, she'd become a true hero of the jianghu... or rather, a twin hero!

Why "twin"? Because she would bring the her cousin along, of course. Her most beloved, most cherished elder cousin.

Shen Yilun had always been the "quiet" child.
From childhood, people compared him to his bold, charismatic older brother, a natural leader who commanded attention. Yilun, by contrast, was slight and timid, perpetually shrinking into the background like a shadow. Others called him odd, and eventually, even he began to believe he was meant to dwell in solitude, swallowed by darkness.

On his first day at school, when the teacher asked about ambitions, Yilun's answer was painfully simple: "As long as I can eat my fill, any work would do..." The classroom erupted in laughter. He couldn't understand why his honest wish was mocked. School, it seemed, would be as lonely as the life he'd always known.

—He thought of disappearing again...

But fate had other plans this time.
Zheng E, a boy radiating confidence and charm, clearly born to privilege, approached him. Instead of joining the ridicule, he praised Yilun's answer, calling it "a revelation." Zheng E claimed Yilun's humble words had crystallized his own purpose.
How? Yilun wondered. It was just a joke to everyone else.

—"Let's make a promise. We'll ensure no one goes hungry. Peace will reign and famine will vanish!"
To Yilun, Zheng E seemed like sunlight incarnate. Everything he could never be. Friends with someone so radiant? Unthinkable. Yet here was this golden boy, insisting they were now "sworn allies" sharing a grand vision.
Yilun didn't fully grasp phrases like "peace reigns," but he understood the fire in Zheng E's gaze. For the first time, he had someone to laugh with, to walk beside.

—"When the time comes, you can't hide behind me anymore."
Changing his lifelong habits felt impossible. Yet... for Zheng E, and the dream they'd woven together, Yilun found himself willing to try.

The River Master's name carried weight in Kaifeng. But who the River Master truly was remained a mystery.

Some said the River Master was a member of the Zhang clan of Roaring Sands, once influential in the river transport trade since the Han Dynasty, only to fall from grace and serve the Khitan as dogs.
Others said the River Master was part of the Dragon Hall, wearing blue robes, red sleeves, and Nuo Dance Mask, skilled with both sword and fan, and known for healing the sick. This was the same Zhu Yu who had earned her fame in the Khitan wars.

Still, others whispered that the River Master was just a name, a cursed title that brought endless suffering. Those who carried it lived a life of toil, with no other path to follow. When people turned to see who dared speak such blasphemy, they found only a salty fish vendor, chewing on a blade of grass, wearing straw sandals, and looking half-asleep. "Just a market joke, nothing serious. Or hey, take a look at this salted fish, top quality!" The crowd burst into laughter, dismissing the vendor's words. After all, who would take a fishmonger seriously?

Feng Yi, for one, hated being confined. The jianghu was vast, meant to be roamed freely. Yet he couldn't escape his confinement, just as Kaifeng's people had been trapped under the blades of the Khitan. When the city fell, ordinary people were lucky if they weren't slaughtered like livestock. Heroes and outlaws stepped up to save lives, but what did that have to do with a mere fishmonger like Feng Yi? He could have laughed at himself for the thought, but as he wandered through the abandoned Verdant Hill Village, a Khitan warrior suddenly brought a blade crashing down on him.

Stories of heroes saving damsels in distress were common in the storybooks. But Feng Yi wasn't a damsel, nor a hero. The green-robed, red-sleeved woman before him deflected the Khitan's blade with a single stroke, then turned and stomped him into the ground. That was how the salted fish vendor met his match, pinned underfoot. It wasn't exactly romantic, though the sword that saved his life was unforgettable.

It was not until much later that Feng Yi learned that Zhu Yu had been exhausted that day, brewing medicinal soup with the Lamp-lighting Monk. And much later still, he would drink Zhu Yu's soup and join the Dragon Hall. The gang members under Zhu Yu were ordinary people: plain in appearance, average in skill, living lives as fragile as anyone else's. Yet their courage and ambition were anything but ordinary. Today, we drive out the Khitans. Tomorrow, we'll calm the Yellow River, bringing peace and ending the storms. Ordinary people wouldn't believe such words. But when Zhu Yu said them, they carried the weight of mountains, and no one could doubt her.

"Today, we drive out the Khitans. Tomorrow, we'll calm the Yellow River, bringing peace and ending the storms," Feng Yi murmured, unable to stop himself.

One can find wild eggs and stranded fish along the riverbanks. But A-fen had never seen a riverbank where books grew.
These books were soaked and wouldn't light.
These books were too thin to fill a stomach.
...
A-fen shook her head and was about to toss them into the river when she heard faint footsteps in the reeds.
Was it foreign invaders again? Or a deserter? In her haste, A-fen grabbed a thick book, ready to throw it.
The footsteps drew closer, pausing with every step. A-fen held the book higher, not daring to move.
The man pushed aside the reed curtain and revealed himself.
Don't be afraid, don't be afraid! Child, that book in your hand—could I have a look?
The newcomer appeared to be a cripple, walking with a heavy limp. He carried a bundle of books in his arms, looking much like the ones A-fen held.
Can these books... be sold for money?
A-fen stared at him suspiciously.
They can't be sold, the man shook his head. "But they must be kept. If they are kept, they become the most precious things of all."
A-fen only understood the word "precious." This book-picking business seemed worth doing; if he was doing it, she would too!

Fear gnawed straight through Yang Yishen. He was afraid that things would end very badly for him this time, and cursed himself for ever coming here.
Only when the waters had receded for half a day did he dare climb back down, legs shaking.
That was when he saw them... the fish. They were hurled inland by the flood and thrashed in shallow hollows. Their gills flared and collapsed as they struggled desperately to breathe.
They looked just like him. Exactly like him.
Every breath tasted of rot and death, yet they still struggle to survive.
The thought struck him with terrifying clarity: this was the Goddess's message!
When the flood came, even long-legged beasts couldn't flee, and neither could people. Only fish endured.
It could only be by the grace of the Goddess.
If people ate fish, surely some fragment of that blessing would cling to them as well and allow them to survive in the water!
Yang Yishen steeled himself. From that day on, he set up a small fish stall once more. This one, he told himself, is a gift returned by the Goddess.

Within the Hall of the River Master, Zhang Yanling carved tablets, tireless and unceasing. A hall filled with deities, drowned in deathly silence. Only the steady sound of the chisel striking wood remained, neither hurried nor slow. 

"Tok, tok, tok..."

"River Master Yu the Great."

"River Master Li Bing."

"River Master Wang Jing."

"River Master... Zhang..."

Each time he reached that surname, Zhang Yanlin's hand would falter, just slightly. Some names he carved, then destroyed. Carved to remember, destroyed to forget. To forget the boy who had once dreamed of roaming the jianghu. To forget the northern deserts and the southern peach flowers. To forget himself who had once tried to run from everything.

At the summit of Mount Tai, eighteen masters across the jianghu have gathered, their brows all knit in a grim gloom, for within this single year, the jianghu has been rocked by two brutal calamities.
First was the massacre of the Martial Alliance Chief, Yuwen Yue. His entire kin, along with over a hundred estate guards, were slaughtered overnight. Not a soul was left alive.
Then came the fall of Gao Qun, Master of the Tianhe region. A white-haired wraith appeared from nowhere and pierced his heart with a single palm-strike, killing him instantly. The white-haired madman seemed possessed by insanity, yet his martial prowess was as erratic as it was lethal. Though the remaining Gao warriors surged forward to hem him in, he shattered their formation with a surge of inner power and vanished without a trace.
With renowned luminaries falling in both slaughters, a shadow of dread has fallen over the jianghu; every warrior now fears for their own life. Should both atrocities be the handiwork of that white-haired fiend, he is nothing less than a demon incarnate!
Lu Yuan, a wandering disciple of the Mohist, stands amidst the giants. She gives a soft, rhythmic tap to the massive mechanical case strapped to her back:
"That demon... could it be you?"
Hidden within that case is the unconscious, white-haired patient she pulled from the brink of death days ago. His snow-white hair is too conspicuous, forcing her to conceal him within the device...
At first, the casket was silent. But after the others whispered for some time, the patient suddenly channeled his voice into a focused thread of sound, vibrating directly into Lu Yuan's ear:
"Leave now. There is a life I must take."
Lu Yuan is stunned. She has actually rescued the very demon. Before she can utter a word of protest, the demon erupts from the case. With a predatory lung, his fingers curve into a claw, snaring a man from the crowd. A single strike, and the life is snuffed out.
The masters spring to their feet and launch their attack, yet none can bring him down!
"That Mohist girl is his accomplice! There's foul play here. Seize her for questioning!"
Hearing that, the white-haired demon, who has already broken through the siege, plunges back into the lethal fray to shield Lu Yuan. Drenched in fresh blood and braving a rain of blades, he carves a path through the encirclement once more.
By nightfall, they find sanctuary within the crumbling walls of a derelict temple. Lu Yuan lashes out at the white-haired fiend, demanding how he could spill the blood of the innocent so ruthlessly. To her surprise, the man who seemed invincible in the daylight now only weeps in a heavy, hollow silence. Seeing the injuries he's suffered protecting her, Lu softens and presses him for an explanation.
"If I were to speak the truth... would you even have the heart to believe me?"
The demon is well aware that his unusual appearance makes it hard for others to trust him.

But Lu Yuan, kind-hearted and innocent, is already all ears.
"I am Yuwen Tianyin, son of Chief Yuwen Yue. On my mother's birthday, vipers bribed our servants to poison the feast. I awoke to see my father fall, shielding me with his dying breath. I fled through an inferno, the toxic miasma bleaching my hair to ash. The Gao Clan played the savior only to plunder our halls; they cast me into a lightless dungeon, torturing me for the secrets of our Cloud-Steering Palm. That fire-venom withered my youth, yet it forged my meridians anew. As my strength came back, I broke free, took down Patriarch Gao, and made my escape. Later, when I was wounded and unconscious once more, you saved me."
Lu Yuan studies his face. His words are raw with grief, the logic untainted by deceit. Her doubt softens; she believes him, at least in half. Since Tianyin has risked everything to save her, the remaining half of her heart follows suit. So she helps him piece things together:
"The timing is precise. The succession of the Alliance was at hand. He who covets the high seat most is likely the one with your father's blood on his hands."
After a fortnight of grueling trials, only five champions remain to vie for the supreme mantle.
Suddenly, the white-haired demon comes out of nowhere, and the crowd falls silent with fear. No one dares to face him. The five men exchange uneasy glances, unwilling to show weakness, and take turns launching their attacks against him. Even five against one, they can't overwhelm him.
"How did this white-haired demon get such overwhelming palm power?"
Just as one of them can no longer hold back, he spots a flaw in Yuwen Tianyin's Cloud-Steering Palm and lunges, driving his sword toward a vital spot.
But as the victor's cry dies in his throat, the truth is bared: the figure on the stage is nothing but a puppet. From the shroud of shadows, the real Yuwen Tianyin erupts. With a devastating strike of the Cloud-Steering Palm, he claims the villain's life.
The crowd, blinded by ignorance and fueled by rumors, surges forward in a frenzied assault. As the signature Cloud-Cleaving Palm is revealed, the four remaining warriors lunge at Yuwen Tianyin with lethal intent, despite Lu Yuan's cries.
"With the Yuwen line around in the jianghu, the rest of us will forever remain in their shadow!"
A chilling realization strikes Yuwen Tianyin: the annihilation of his kin was no solitary crime. The great sects, hungry for the supreme mantle, had woven a web of complicity, some through silent consent, others through active bloodletting. That day, through a storm of steel and blood, he carved a path for Lu Yuan and escaped the mountain's peak.
In the years that followed, Lu Yuan wandered in the jianghu alone. Yuwen Tianyin had vanished, yet no one dared to lay a finger on Lu Yuan. Whispers spread like wildfire: the world's most terrifying demon was slumbering within the case she bore upon her back. At the following year's Grand Assembly, Lu Yuan's rivals fled or surrendered before the first drumbeat. Without drawing a single blade, she ascended as the Sovereign of the Martial World. From her high seat, she washed away the infamy of the "White-Haired Demon." Her task complete, she abdicated her power and vanished into the mist. Their final destination remains a mystery, their names lost to the shifting winds of history.

Lu Yuan is stunned. She has actually rescued the very demon. Before she can utter a word of protest, the demon erupts from the case. With a predatory lunge, his fingers curve into a claw, snaring a man from the crowd. A single strike, and the life is snuffed out.
The masters spring to their feet and launch their attack, yet none can bring him down!
"That Mohist girl is his accomplice! There's foul play here. Seize her for questioning!"
Hearing that, the white-haired demon, who has already broken through the siege, plunges back into the lethal fray to shield Lu Yuan. Drenched in fresh blood and braving a rain of blades, he carves a path through the encirclement once more.
By nightfall, they find sanctuary within the crumbling walls of a derelict temple. Lu Yuan lashes out at the white-haired fiend, demanding how he could spill the blood of the innocent so ruthlessly. To her surprise, the man who seemed invincible in the daylight now only weeps in a heavy, hollow silence. Seeing the injuries he's suffered while protecting her, Lu softens and presses him for an explanation.
"If I were to speak the truth... would you even have the heart to believe me?"
The demon is well aware that his unusual appearance makes it hard for others to trust him.

But Lu Yuan, kind-hearted and innocent, is already all ears.
"I am Yuwen Tianyin, son of Chief Yuwen Yue. On my mother's birthday, vipers bribed our servants to poison the feast. I awoke to see my father fall, shielding me with his dying breath. I fled through an inferno, and the toxic miasma turned my hair white. The Gao Clan played the savior only to plunder our halls. They cast me into a lightless dungeon, torturing me for the secrets of our Cloud-Steering Palm. That poison altered my appearance, but it also broadened my meridians. As my strength gradually returned, I broke free of my shackles, seized the chance to kill Patriarch Gao, and escaped. Later, when I was wounded and unconscious once more, you saved me."
Lu Yuan studies his face. His words are raw with grief, the logic untainted by deceit. Her doubt softens; she believes him, at least in half. Since Tianyin has risked everything to save her, the remaining half of her heart follows suit. So she helps him piece things together:
"The timing is precise. The succession of the Alliance was at hand. He who covets the high seat most is likely the one with your father's blood on his hands."
After a fortnight of grueling trials, only five champions remain to vie for the supreme mantle.
Suddenly, the white-haired demon comes out of nowhere, and the crowd falls silent with fear. No one dares to face him. The five men exchange uneasy glances, unwilling to show weakness, and take turns launching their attacks against him. Even five against one, they can't overwhelm him.
"How did this white-haired demon get such overwhelming palm power?"
Just as one of them can no longer hold back, he spots a flaw in Yuwen Tianyin's Cloud-Steering Palm and lunges, driving his sword toward a vital spot.
But as the victor's cry dies in his throat, the truth is bared: the figure on the stage is nothing but a puppet. From the shroud of shadows, the real Yuwen Tianyin erupts. With a devastating strike of the Cloud-Steering Palm, he claims the villain's life.
The crowd, blinded by ignorance and fueled by rumors, surges forward in a frenzied assault. As the signature Cloud-Steering Palm is revealed, the four remaining warriors lunge at Yuwen Tianyin with lethal intent, despite Lu Yuan's cries.
"With the Yuwen line around in the jianghu, the rest of us will forever remain in their shadow!"
A chilling realization strikes Yuwen Tianyin: the annihilation of his kin was no solitary crime. The great sects, hungry for the supreme mantle, had woven a web of complicity, some through silent consent, others through active bloodletting. That day, through a storm of steel and blood, he carved a path for Lu Yuan and escaped the mountain's peak.
In the years that followed, Lu Yuan wandered in the jianghu alone. Yuwen Tianyin had vanished, yet no one dared to lay a finger on Lu Yuan. Whispers spread like wildfire: the world's most terrifying demon was slumbering within the case she bore upon her back. At the following year's Grand Assembly, Lu Yuan's rivals fled or surrendered before the first drumbeat. Without drawing a single blade, she ascended as the Sovereign of the Martial World. From her high seat, she washed away the infamy of the "White-Haired Demon." Her task complete, she abdicated her power and vanished into the mist. Their final destination remains a mystery, their names lost to the shifting winds of history.

At the summit of Mount Tai, eighteen masters across the jianghu have gathered, their brows all knit in a grim gloom, for within this single year, the jianghu has been rocked by two brutal calamities.
First was the massacre of the Martial Alliance Chief, Yuwen Yue. His entire kin, along with over a hundred estate guards, were slaughtered overnight. Not a soul was left alive.
Then came the fall of Gao Qun, Master of the Tianhe region. A white-haired wraith appeared from nowhere and pierced his heart with a single palm-strike, killing him instantly. The white-haired madman seemed possessed by insanity, yet his martial prowess was as erratic as it was lethal. Though the remaining Gao warriors surged forward to hem him in, he shattered their formation with a surge of inner power and vanished without a trace.
With renowned luminaries falling in both slaughters, a shadow of dread has fallen over the jianghu; every warrior now fears for their own life. Should both atrocities be the handiwork of that white-haired fiend, he is nothing less than a demon incarnate!
Lu Yuan, a wandering disciple of the Mohist, stands amidst the giants. She gives a soft, rhythmic tap to the massive mechanical case strapped to her back:
"That demon... could it be you?"
Hidden within that case is the unconscious, white-haired patient she pulled from the brink of death days ago. His snow-white hair is too conspicuous, forcing her to conceal him within the device...
