Evercare Clinic is quiet, and Unfated Tian enjoys the rare peace. He lies sprawled on a narrow bed, putting the ledger over his face and mentally calculates how much money he's made this month. Suddenly, the ledger is abruptly snatched. He sits up, annoyed. "Hey..." Then he sees who it is: Han Xiangxun. He turns his back to her and mumbles, "No patients today. I'm going back to sleep."

"Get up. I need a bottle of Priceless Antidote." Her tone is chipper, and his eyes light up. Business is business, and gold is gold. He flips over with renewed energy, already shaping a smile to thank his generous patron. But then a thought strikes him. There has never been any serious illness at Heaven's Pier that would call for this medicine. And she, stingy as ever, wouldn't be here unless it were for someone else. It has to be for him. Realizing that, the doctor drops his usual teasing. He turns to his desk and begins preparing the medicine in silence. Still, curiosity gets the better of him. As he grinds the herbs, he asks, "Is this for that swordsman again? That Hero Chu?"

"That fool throws himself into danger without a second thought. I'm just preparing this in case he winds up half-dead again. Someone's got to clean up his mess."
Unfated Tian clicks his tongue and mutters, "Fool? Who's really the fool here?"

Han Xiangxun shoots him a sharp look.

"Alright, alright. I'm the fool. Only a fool would drag himself out of bed at such a good time to make medicine for someone else's 'fool'." He pouts, voice soft and petulant.

Han Xiangxun turns away, saying nothing more. Silence settles over the clinic once again, broken only by the steady rhythm of herbs being ground beneath stone.

Could he face that forgotten place? Could he meet the hopeful eyes of his fellow warriors?
Still, the water's call continued as a quiet summons.
Following its flow would lead him home. He had to go back and deliver his report.
For Celestial Spring Station was made to bear messages.
Every message, whether truth or deceit, must find its final destination.
This would be the only false message he'd ever carry in all his years as a messenger.

I traveled a hundred miles along the river, setting up sieves amidst the waves at various points to examine the changes in sediment and currents.
My findings: the surface of the river flows swiftly, while the riverbed moves slowly. Where the river winds, the concave bank is deep and rapid, whereas the convex bank is shallow and gentle. A night traveler once passed by and saw a gaming table beneath the lantern light, with one of the four seats empty. Looking closer, two spirits and a peerless beauty sat there, her features as delicate as a painting, appearing like a wandering soul.
The traveler fell into a trance and awoke only at cockcrow to find nothing but lush bamboo shadows. Sensing the wick had burnt to ash, he realized it was no mere dream.

The shrine had once been a sacred place, built to honor a general who had stood his ground against the Khitan. It should have echoed with solemn prayers, a place of reverence and remembrance. But ever since the statue within lost its head, whispers of spirits and curses had only grown louder.

Drawn by curiosity or perhaps mere foolishness, a villager from nearby began sneaking out at night, hoping to uncover the truth for himself. He claimed to have seen flickering shadows, more than one, dancing just beyond reach. But by the time he rushed inside, the shrine was empty, silent as a tomb. In time, his story was dismissed. Now the shrine, worn by time and left to decay, stands alone in the wilderness.

清泉驿的铜铃在风里响了二十年，刘三杨“诶诶”的应门声也及时了二十年，来自长安的花:
For twenty years, the bronze bell of Qingquan Station had rung in the wind; for twenty years, Liu Sanyang's "Aye, aye" greeting at the door had been prompt; for twenty years, the variegated relay horses from Chang'an, spotted, plump, tall, short, had been led in and cared for by him; for twenty years, the sun had risen. 
The proud and diligent post riders of Qingquan Station didn't remember his name or face beyond Old Liu, it was as if he was born a grumbling, hapless old handyman. 
Old Liu, as the only person at Qingquan Station who wasn't a post rider, not of soldier stock, an ordinary man who didn't have to travel, his greatest skill was making himself disappear. 
He could always find the most inconspicuous spot when everyone gathered at night to eat and chat, when the post riders laughed and shouted "One station after another, the post horses like shooting stars!" while hugging people and forcing drinks, loudly boasting of their travels and dangers, letting the shadows perfectly cover his hunched back. The day Chen Zhong rang the bell of Qingquan Station and entered to announce he was the newly appointed station master, this old man, ordinary as a grain of sand, gnawing on a pancake, opened the door for the bell-ringer as usual.  
Old Liu was content with his day-in, day-out work. The horses were constant, the bronze bell was constant, the sand was constant. Being an inconspicuous grain of sand in the desert put him at ease, days unchanging like the sun put him at ease. 
But Brother Chen, that is, Chen Zhong, never wanted him at ease. Chen Zhong wasn't just a good man, he was a retired veteran of the Anxi Army. How could a man's back be so straight? The wind would break it. His sword was frightening too, a sword needed to see blood. And the aspirations, the drive that Brother Chen muttered about, they were as dangerous as his sword. Others couldn't see him, but Chen Zhong could see him. His skill of disappearing didn't work with Chen Zhong. 
This serious old soldier would always pull him from the shadows, bring him food, teach him to hold a sword, teach him martial arts, ask him what he wanted to do in the future. He knew Brother Chen meant well, but he also knew he wasn't cut out for anything. He didn't even dare hide from Brother Chen.  
He feared Chen Zhong would ruin him. And Chen Zhong did ruin him.  
Later, the bell rang less often, and the horses needing his care dwindled. The nightly gatherings, the post riders at the gatherings, the rations and copper coins in their pockets, the songs and poems floating in the night sky, all grew fewer. Old Liu numbly repeated his tasks. 
He always felt the sun overhead was also less. But he was just a grain of sand, destined to stick to someone's sole and be carried away.  
One day, the bronze bell at the door rang again. He went to answer as usual, and upon opening the door, the sun set.  
A young Tang soldier stood at the door, holding a heavy hemp sack and a dripping, bloody sword, eyes wide with fury, like a rock waiting to be shattered. Before he could scream, a gust of wind blew, and the Tang soldier dissolved into the sand.  
He didn't dare listen to how Brother Chen and the others argued. He only knew that day, Qingquan Station disbanded. In the end, only Brother Chen and a reckless young tough called Da Luozi remained. 
He was a commoner, not a soldier, but Brother Chen insisted he was a soldier, counted him to fill out a squad, and took him on the road. He didn't want to go, but Brother Chen promised to write him a transfer order after delivering this Burlap Sack to Chang'an, letting him stay in Chang'an with the sack, never having to leave home again.  
Go home. Go home. Go home...  
The road home was hard. The cart was lost. The horses were lost. Money, rations, and water were lost. Da Luozi lost his life. The seeds in the sack were lost until only less than half remained.  
Later still, Brother Chen was lost too.  
No one watched him anymore, urged him to gather strength. He could disappear again, like sand vanishing in the desert.  
Liu Sanyang took a step and kicked a Burlap Sack. The sack stood alone between heaven and earth, with no direction to go in all four quarters.  
"No one wants you either?"  
The sack, made of burlap, lowered its head in grievance, sagging in the sand.  
So, he shouldered the burlap sack.  
He was going home. 

A person is a grain of sand in the desert, blowing wherever the wind goes.  
But when the wind blows east, he'll strive to lift himself a bit higher, to float a little farther.

Dear Wanderer,
As the seasons turn and the snow gives way to spring, I wish you peace and health in this new year.
I take up my brush today because those three little ones, Fu, Lu, and Shou, have been pestering me relentlessly to write to you. As is the rule, children speak their hearts, and I shall record their words as faithfully as they fall.
Little Fu: Laoshan! This ink smells so sweet, can I eat it? ...Oh no! Don't you dare write that down!
Little Shou: Big friend, where have you been showing off lately? We've been waiting here for you forever!
...The children are chattering all at once; my brush can hardly keep pace. Enough, let me be brief and speak of the matter at hand.
Spring is here, and Kaifeng is ablaze with festive lanterns and flowers. The streets are full of acrobats, opera performers, seasonal sweets, and all the bustle of the holiday season. The children wish for you to wander the streets and capture the bustle of life and the city's spring beauty within your album. "To record the good times of the New Year"... Such an elegant pursuit is something even I look forward to.
Little Lu: Hey! I'm not done! Laoshan, write this: Wanderer, you've been everywhere and seen it all, so you must have the sharpest eyes! Once you've filled that album to the brim, don't forget to bring it back and show us. The three of us have also prepared a little surprise for you!

To the Esteemed Wanderer:
Time flies, yet the mountains and rivers remain unchanged. Recently, I've been traveling far and wide, collecting customs of the Qixi Festival and witnessing many interesting traditions.
Some places dry clothes and books under the sun, while others thread needles under the moonlight to pray for dexterity. Even the customs of eating Qiaoguo (festival pastries) vary—some prefer them plain, others only enjoy them fried with sesame. In some regions, people deliberately preserve them uneaten, drying and stringing them up as blessings for children, believing they can last until the New Year.
I accidentally bought too many and couldn't finish them all, so I thought of you. These taste different from what we usually have in Qinghe—some sweet, some slightly salty. Try them all.

A wanderer packs his bag beneath the cliff, waiting for his friend to fall. 
Just then, Young Yichao slides down, aiming straight for the wanderer's legs. The wanderer's head hits the packed bag; Chao kicks his waist—both narrowly avoid tumbling into the fire. 
Dazed, the wanderer sits up, clutching his side, staring at the laughing Nongchao'er. 

How come you're fine, but I'm the one falling apart? 
Not on purpose. 
You insisted on climbing with two broken blades, made me wait below—just to cushion your fall. 
Well, you did cushion it. Blades are broken, I'm done climbing. 
You're not passing through? 

Young Yichao plants the blades into the ground. 
Liangzhou is vast, the Hexi boundless. What use is passing through alone? In my lifetime, I'll find a way to bring everyone through. Let these blades watch Dasan Pass every day. 
He strides back toward Liangzhou. The wanderer hurriedly packs and follows. 

Bring everyone through? 
The wanderer glances at what he holds, then at his spirited friend ahead. 
Perhaps... this can be entrusted to him...

To the Wanderer:
Is everything going smoothly with the Homestead? We haven't exchanged news in a long time, and you are constantly in my thoughts.
Though the sights of the martial world are wonderful, traveling alone inevitably brings memories of the lights back home. Realizing it has been a long time since I last wrote to you, and fearing you might worry, I took up my pen to send these greetings.
I encountered a delightful coincidence in Apricot Village recently. While passing through, I met someone with the exact same name as mine. He is also a Well of Heaven disciple and is acquainted with a wanderer who manages an Homestead. Upon further inquiry, I learned that the wanderer is named $C$L#Y$PN#E$C, and he is remarkably similar to you: a fellow traveler who cares for all living beings and fears no hardship.
Though the world is vast, such a coincidence is rare. I suppose only "destiny" can explain it.
While we were talking, I noticed that the other Shi Jingtian seemed troubled. It turns out his friend often climbs cliffs and braves dangers to seek secrets and treasures, frequently snagging his clothes. By the time his friend returns home, he is always in tattered rags and looks quite disheveled. The other Shi Jingtian wanted to go to Silken Veil Society in Kaifeng to learn sewing himself, but he was always delayed by chores.
Since we are fellow disciples, why fret over such a small matter? I decided to make the trip to Silken Veil Society for him to ask the seamstresses for some sewing tips. If I learn anything, I might be able to share your burdens in the future as well.
This will take some time. If I return late, please do not worry about me.
Shi Jingtian

To the Wanderer:
It has been over a month since I left home and headed west. All that I have seen along the way has left me with profound mixed feelings.
In Kaifeng, Revelry Hall is brightly lit all night, echoing with endless songs. Yet, just around Forsaken Quarter, starving people with barely enough clothes to cover themselves huddle in the freezing wind.
By Jinming Pool, seeing the majestic imperial warships filled me with inspiration. But upon reaching the Mistveil Forest, I heard the young and old weeping over the poisonous mist that has left most homes empty.
The stark contrast of these scenes has left my mind deeply unsettled... I can only sigh that beneath the glory of this prosperous age, hidden wounds still fester. Having practiced martial arts for years, I wish I could use the Mo Blade in my hands to clear away this poisonous miasma and solve this crisis alongside other heroes of the martial world.
With such thoughts weighing on me, I picked up my pen to write, yet I know not what to say.
I originally intended to return early and talk freely with you over warm wine. Unfortunately, while passing the Grand Canal, I saw imperial soldiers whipping the laborers. I intervened, and consequently, ran into trouble with the authorities.
To avoid bringing disaster upon you, I will lay low for now. My return... I fear will be delayed. (The handwriting suddenly becomes sloppy here, as if written in a frantic rush with the other hand.)
Once the storm passes, I will definitely return to Blissful Retreat and drink with you until we drop.
Separated by a great distance, I hope you take care.
Shi Jingtian

游侠青览：\n风云际会，燕翼初程。天涯同契，共此清晖。\n自国际版启程以来，承蒙:
Dear Wanderer,
Winds gather and clouds stir as the swallow's wings begin their flight. Bound by an ancient pact, we share this same moonlight from every corner of the realm.
Since the global version went live, we have been profoundly graced by the favor of Wanderers worldwide.
Where Winds Meet, a tale woven from Chinese heritage, sailed westward across the vast seas. To our wonder, it has captured the world's gaze, achieving a brilliance beyond all expectations.
The commendation in the official financial reports came as a profound surprise, one we hold close to our hearts with eternal gratitude.
Looking back, we still cherish our time together: raising cups in Halcyonhe, roaming Kaifeng, drifting through the dreams of Hexi, and the solemn vow made in Hidden Mountain.
Those past days remain vivid as if before our very eyes. We seek to stand by your side like the everlasting winds, holding you in steadfast respect forevermore.
We present you with the Decoration "Home Longing." A marvel of Mohist ingenuity, it can soar thousands of miles into the clouds, yet it never forgets its roots in the ancestral soil.
Though the road ahead is vast, we wish to soar upon the clouds with you and behold the splendor of the Starry River.
With these humble words and a sincere heart, we bid you take great care.
游侠青鉴：\n自游侠告知兄长消息后，不熄心境开阔，渐生云游四方之志。此番原欲乘渡:
To the Wanderer:
Since you shared the news about my brother, my mind has cleared, and I have gradually developed a desire to wander the world. I originally planned to take a ferry north, but I lost my way. After many twists and turns, I stumbled upon a wondrous mountain when the mist cleared. The locals call it "Hidden Mountain."
The mountain features sheer cliffs towering thousands of feet, with suspended plank roads. You must watch every step... While passing a place called "Heaven's Threshold," I encountered a stone carver named Mo Ya. His skills are exquisite, but the contents of his carvings are baffling. For example, phrases like "So close yet so beautiful, let's spend our weekend in Hebei," "Looking for a wife," "Buff Nameless," and "Improve drop rates"... I don't know who commissioned these, but they are grandly carved right onto the cliff face.

Seeing this majestic stone screen, I suddenly thought of the people you often mention, like Shopkeeper Han and Hero Jiang. If longing could be carved into the cliff, perhaps it might be seen by fate. But then I realized outsiders rarely visit Hidden Mountain, so it would be hard to pass on any messages. I suppose the original intent of those carvers wasn't to broadcast news, but merely to entrust a wisp of untethered longing to these clouds and iron-like stones.
Though the mountain is treacherous, it hides a wondrous sight: dandelions blooming like a sea of snow, their seeds dancing like a tide of clouds. It is quite a nice place to visit. If the Wanderer has time, perhaps we could meet here.

Awaiting your reply, Lie Buxi
At Heaven's Threshold, Hidden Mountain

游侠，怎么了，是酿皮子味道不可口吗？: What's wrong? Don't like the noodles?

游侠，您也来比武招亲？: You here for the contest too?

游侠，您可莫要这般纵马了。: Please, not so fast on that horse.

游侠，您所在百业刚参与了百业战定级赛，特此发放奖励， 请查收。: Wanderer, your Guild participated in the Placement Match. Rewards have been issued, please collect them.

游侠，您来尝尝时令菜吗？: Seasonal greens today. Best you'll get all year! Try it out, wanderer.
游侠，您真厉害！刚才我都吓傻了，您随手一摆弄，那铁面先生竟然就笑了。: That was amazing! I was so nervous I froze, but you just put a few stems together and that stern face of his actually broke into a smile!
游侠，想切磋直说，不必如此。: If you want to spar, just ask.
游侠，想吃点什么？菜单上有的都能炒！: What can we get you? Anything on the board, we'll have it ready!
游侠，想学两手？撞人可不行。: Want lessons? Don't run into people.
游侠，想学啊？我教你啊。: Want lessons? I can show you.
游侠，想拿我练靶子啊？: You want me for target practice?
游侠，想摸点什么宝贝不成？: Want to lift something off me?

Dear Wanderer,

May the wind guide your steps, for a new journey is about to begin.

Thank you for participating in the event. Attached are your rewards. Please accept them at your earliest convenience.
游侠，愿意听我弹奏一曲吗？: Wanderer… would you be willing to listen to my music?
游侠，我、我不是故意的，你没事吧？！我看到个人影一直跟着我，还以为是坏人……: I'm so sorry, I didn't mean to! I saw someone following me and thought it was trouble...
游侠，我与家中二妹、三弟一同北上支援，想着虏人既擅长骑射，要是我们也能学会，到时: I'm heading north with my siblings to support the northern front. The Khitans are skilled in mounted archery. If we can learn their techniques, we won't have to fear them anymore.
游侠，我与师弟有要事相谈，劳烦暂避片刻。: Wanderer, my junior and I need to talk. Step aside, please.
游侠，我也想找你帮忙送个东西。: I have something I'd like you to deliver too.
游侠，我们两个腿脚不太行了，屋里还有些待客的果子，你要是饿了也自取吧……: We don't get around too well, wanderer, but there's some fruit inside for guests. Feel free to help yourself if you're hungry...
游侠，我们小姐梦到那那金簪正在一棵粗壮的梅花树下，旁边还有座亭子，何不去那里看看: Wanderer, our lady dreamed of a hairpin beneath a plum tree, with a pavilion beside it. Why don't we go take a look?
游侠，我们方才都商量好了，想给你演一出戏，算是答谢您，为了我们家的事劳神费力。: Wanderer, we're putting on this show for you to thank you for all you've done for us.
游侠，我们这便杀将进去吗？: You're going to storm in head-on?
游侠，我准备做些葡萄酱，到时候你别忘了来拿！: I'm going to make some grape jam. Don't forget to come and get it when it's ready!
游侠，我又欠你一个大情。往后有机会，我定好好报答你！: I owe you more than I can say, Wanderer. When the time comes, I'll repay you properly.
游侠，我娘亲说了，有时候只要一点甜，再多的苦都能过去！: My mama says a little sweetness can get you through any hardship!
游侠，我已寻到了你埋下的宝物！: Wanderer, I have found the treasure you buried!
游侠，我已寻到了你埋下的宝物，感谢慷慨分享，在此献上一个赞！: Wanderer, I have found the treasure you buried! Thank you for your generous sharing. Here's a like!
游侠，我师父和悟梵大师这些天一直念叨你呢！说你古道热肠，要我好好跟你学学！: Wanderer, my master and Master Wufan have been speaking about you. They say you're always willing to help others, and they told me to learn from you.
游侠，我想歇会儿了，就一会儿……: I think I need to stop for a bit. Just a little while...
游侠，我方才一番神游，发现此去离浆糊村不远处，有一家开粮铺的兄弟刚刚失去了活命的: Wanderer, in my wandering vision, I saw three brothers who run a grain shop near Riverlake Village. They've just lost the money they live on…
游侠，我方才一番神游，发现距破门村不远处，有一对苦命的张姓母女刚刚服毒身死……: Wanderer, in my wandering vision, I saw a mother and her daughter near Hearthfall Hamlet. They have taken poison and passed...
游侠，我有点怕……你说这个时候偷偷往外运东西的人，会是内奸么？还是……穷奇师？: Wanderer, I'm scared. Do you think the smuggler is a mole? Or worse, a Qiongqi Artificer?
游侠，我查到你和其他游侠一起拉粪撤离的最高记录是$T(18012)桶，你独自拉粪: Wanderer, I see that your highest bucket haul carried out together with other wanderers is $T(18012), and your highest solo bucket haul carried out is $T(18011)!
游侠，我的剑法如何？: What do you think of my swordplay, wanderer?
游侠，我的射术已好了不少，只是骑马仍有些不稳，可否再教我一次上马的技巧？: My aim has improved a lot, but I still struggle to stay steady on horseback. Could you show me how?
游侠，我看你就是咱们的东风啊！: Wanderer, I think you're the missing piece!
游侠，我真不是搞研究的料，不如收拾收拾，退出墨山道算了。: I'm clearly not cut out for research. Maybe I should just pack up and leave the order.
游侠，我瞧过了。这船虽看着破旧，但都是些小问题，我已经顺手修好了。: I've looked it over. The boat may look worn, but it's nothing serious. I've already repaired it.
游侠，我知道我漏了何物了。佛有佛的真经，人也有人的真经。: I know what I forgot. The Buddha has his scriptures, but some truths belong to the living.
游侠，我给你寄了美味可口的肉夹馍，记得一定要吃哦~: Wanderer, I've sent you a delicious rougamo. Make sure you eat it!
游侠，我见你气宇不凡，倒像与我门中宝物有缘。: Wanderer... you've got that look. The kind that attracts destiny. I'd wonder if you and our "treasure" are meant to meet.
游侠，我跟着大哥、二姐来前线，一道杀虏人去，可他们总说我还小，让我到时候跟在他们: Wanderer, I came to the front lines with my brother and sister to fight the Khitans, but they keep saying I'm too young and should stay behind.
游侠，我这宝物花了不少心思，可不能就这样浪费啊……: Wanderer, I put my heart and soul into that piece. It can't just go to waste!
游侠，手快有，手慢无，错过今日没处哭。: Catch it while you can, miss it and you'll cry.
游侠，找咱天泉啥事儿？: Wanderer, do you need our help?
游侠，救命啊！这鹅，疯了啊！: This goose has lost its mind! Help me!
游侠，新岁好啊！我……我也没想到，刚在山里忙完一阵，长老又把我派下山了。: Happy New Year! I didn't expect to be here either. I'd just finished a project back at the mountain when the Elders sent me straight down again.
游侠，易水砚师承班火热招生中……可有兴趣试试？: We're taking new students for the Yi River inkstone class. Care to try your hand?
游侠，是否要算一卦？: Care to have your fortune read?
游侠，是在帮老婆子我找东西？: Are you helping me look for something?
游侠，有事说事，别动手脚。: If you need something, speak up. Keep your hands off.
游侠，有些东西可碰不得。: Some things are best left alone.
游侠，有些东西是碰不得的。: There are things you shouldn't touch.
游侠，有话好说，先放开我。: We can talk about this. Just let me go first.
游侠，有话好说，先解开我。: Let's talk this out. Unseal me first.
游侠，有身好武艺，不该用在此处。: You've got real skill. Don't waste it like this.
游侠，来碗饸饹面暖暖身子吗？: Cold out there? Come warm up with a bowl.
游侠，来算上一卦吧！测字、占梦、相面、易卦，鄙人无所不精。: Want your fortune read, wanderer? I am proficient in everything from writing analysis and dream interpretation to face reading and divination.
游侠，此番多谢了。哎，我须得赶回墨城将此事禀报长老。: Wanderer, my thanks. I must hurry back to Mohist City and report this to the elders.
游侠，此番多谢了。恐怕门内还有其他的穷奇师，我必须赶快回去禀报长老。: Thank you, wanderer. There may be more of them inside. I need to report this to the elders right now.

游侠，瞧好了！这功法太公我只传授一遍——: Wanderer, watch this! I'll show this technique just once—

游侠，花蜜取来了么？: Wanderer, did you get the honey?
游侠，若将来茶余饭后与他人谈论起今日之事，还请莫要将我与那红拂女作比！: Wanderer, if you ever tell this story, please don't compare me to Hongfu.
游侠，若是无事，还请莫要涉险。: Unless you have urgent business, best stay clear.
游侠，虽然荒谬，但可能要麻烦你自己去找送你的礼物了……师兄现在实在不方便走动……: I know this sounds absurd, but could you go find your own gift? He really can't move right now.
游侠，要不我们一起来琢磨琢磨骑马射箭的功夫？: Wanderer, how about we practice shooting on horseback together?
游侠，见字如面。\n前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

游侠，解释一下你的手？: Mind explaining what your hands were doing?
游侠，诗歌传达情感的重任就等你了，灵感找的如何？: Wanderer, the burden of turning feeling into verse is yours. How goes your search for inspiration?
游侠，说真话也有错吗？: Wanderer, is it wrong to speak the truth?
游侠，谢谢你，帮我们做了那么多事。: Wanderer, thank you so much for everything you've done for us.
游侠，走路当心些，莫碰坏了我的花，也莫吓坏了我的猫！: Wanderer, watch your step! Don't damage my flowers or frighten my cat!
游侠，赶巧叫您碰上刚捞的鱼货，快来试试！: Just pulled these from the water! Perfect timing, come have a taste!
游侠，近来可好啊？我听墨门弟子说，你走山访水，开拓产业，定然遇到了不少奇人异事吧:
Wanderer, how have you been lately? I heard from a Mohist disciple that you've been traveling far and wide, opening up new ventures. You must have run into your share of strange people and stranger affairs. Just thinking about it makes my fingers itch.
As for me, yesterday I helped the Sun family's boy climb a wall to fetch his wooden eagle. The day before, I was running all over the streets chasing Aunt Xu's chicken. And before that... well, more of the same. This blade has sat in its sheath so long it may rust one day. I keep hoping for a real case, the kind where you hunt the culprit for a thousand miles and draw your sword to break the deadlock.
So I got to thinking, and of course I thought of you, Wanderer. No one is more reliable. You've seen more than most and your connections run wide. If I follow you, I'm bound to come across something worth my while. Rest easy, I'll bring my best and I won't slow you down. As for Constable Zhen, don't worry. I'll talk him into approving my leave.
游侠，还有什么事儿？: Is there anything else you need?
游侠，还有救吗？: Wanderer, can her condition be cured?
游侠，这一路辛苦了。: Wanderer, you've had a long road.
游侠，这个似乎不是放在这里的。: Wanderer, I don't think this piece goes here.
游侠，这可不是打招呼的礼节。: That's not how you greet someone.
游侠，这对的不太好，你再想想。: That line doesn't quite work, wanderer. Try again.
游侠，这就要走了？看来你的可以也不可以啊，哈哈哈……: Leaving already? Seems your "not bad" really was just talk. Ha!
游侠，这山中地形比我料想的还要险峻些，我们得抓紧时间，快些熟悉才好！: Wanderer, these mountains are trickier than I expected. We should get familiar with them as soon as possible.
游侠，这旗，你可愿接？: Wanderer... will you take this banner?
游侠，这是何意？: What do you mean by that?
游侠，这是我手抄本，是我答应给小安写的，请你等他醒来交给他好么？这金刚橛伴我多年: I promised the boy my manuscript. Give it to him when he wakes up. And take this Vajra Phurba. It's never left my side. Consider it as a thanks.
游侠，这机关可是已经破解了？: Have you solved the mechanism already?
游侠，这机关是个“念头”。漠夫人知道，这是漠师傅留给她的念头，便够了。: This mechanism is a keepsake, a thought left behind. All that matters is that Mo's wife knows the thought came from him.
游侠，这次多亏你了，我还忙着研究，就先走一步了。: Wanderer, you've saved me. I need to test this immediately.
游侠，这次我给你带了很多宝贝。: Wanderer, I brought you all sorts of treasures this time.
游侠，这次真是多谢你了！只要雪奴不闯祸，我很快就能开口问我娘要酬金了！: Thank you, wanderer! As long as Snowy stays out of trouble, I'll ask my mom about that reward.
游侠，这次要喝点什么酒？: So, wanderer, what are we drinking this time?
游侠，这继算机太神异了，你也来试试？: This Fengputer is amazing. Why don't you try asking it something too?
游侠，这虏人狡猾得很，咱们若要抢他们的财宝，现在的骑射功夫还有点悬……: Those Khitans are crafty. To take their spoils, our mounted archery skills still need some work.
游侠，选好了？如此便开始吧。: Made your pick? Then let's get you on the road.
游侠，速来鬼樊楼一叙！: Come to Ghostly Revelry Hall immediately for a meeting!
游侠，道儿这么宽，偏要撞我？: The whole road open and you hit me?
游侠，首先向您献上万分的歉意！\n本该于五日前向您发放录取通知，但本门突遭暗算，:
Young wanderer,
First, my sincerest apologies! 
We should have sent you a letter of admission five days ago, but we were ambushed. Our three elders and three hundred disciples are still unconscious, and I am the only one who has awakened. 
After some investigation, I discovered a large amount of fake wine in our cellar. Whoever brought these in must be punished! 
Due to our limited capacity, I have authorized that all matters regarding the Ragin' Tides shall be handled by the Nine Mortal Ways for the time being. 
Please go to the Nine Mortal Ways to start your training. Once the Ragin' Tides have awakened, we shall welcome you with open arms.
游侠，首先恭喜您，在本次又津馆的会考中拔得头筹。\n但又津馆众长老一致认为，您此:
First, congratulations on taking the top place in the Inkbornd Order examination.
All the elders have unanimously agreed your performance far exceeds that of a regular disciple. The current lessons at Inkbornd Order can no longer contain your growth.
We cannot bear to let someone like you slip away, so we've decided to make an exception and place you on the training path to become an Elder. Head to the Nine Mortal Ways to begin, and your costs have already been covered.
When you return from your training, it will be the moment the Inkbornd Order shines again. Best of luck!

游侠，香香甜甜的五色糕，来一块吗？: Five-color Cake, sweet and fresh! Want a piece?
游侠：\n 眼下就要到年关，终于要熬过这个冬天了。好在今年秋天收成不错:
Dear Wanderer,
The end of the year draws near, and at last, we are enduring the final days of winter. Fortunately, the autumn harvest was bountiful, and the village has stockpiled enough firewood and supplies to be spared from the bite of cold and hunger. How are you out there in the jianghu? Are you eating well and keeping warm?
Word has it you have headed north; we're wondering when you might return. Most of us were refugees from those very lands, so the news has us all a little worried. It is said some dwelt south of the river, gathering duck eggs amidst the reed marshes; others lived at the mountain's foot, tending to terraced fields... We all pray for your safety on this journey. When your travels bring you past our village once more, please stay a while to rest and share with us the stories of the north.
The villagers have been in high spirits lately, each household busy with preparations for the New Year.
Lingniang even made malt candy from grain, and the kids love it. It has been a hard year for everyone, and we all deserve a taste of sweetness at its end. We have saved a portion for you; if you've got time, do come back and have a taste.
On behalf of the entire village, I wish you a joyous New Year. May you remain free from illness and find peace in the coming year. Welcome home at any time.

游侠？是你吗，还是我的幻觉……: Is that... are you real, or am I seeing things?

A little calico kitten wove through the sea of people's legs a few times, but finding it all a bit dull, flopped onto the ground for a roll. As a result, its head and back ended up covered in scattered petals left over from the night before.
Spotting it through the crowd, the child crouched down and gently helped pick the flowers off its fur.
All around them, gongs and drums roared as lights and shadows danced. Yet, in this tiny patch of space, there was utter tranquility. The child held the gathered flowers, the kitten tilted its head up, and for a quiet moment, two pairs of eyes simply gazed at one another.
Then, the child reached out, selected a tiny pink blossom, and gently tucked it behind the kitten's furry ear.
"Now that looks pretty," he whispered softly.

At the lantern fair, there stood a beautifully crafted drum. Sadly, it went entirely unnoticed. The vendor simply set it aside, turning to chat with the neighboring stall owner.
A child tilted his head, gazing at it. He imagined how wonderful it would look if two vivid little figures in silk garments were to twirl upon the drumhead, spinning round and round on their tiptoes.
Yet, this thought merely spun for a moment before fading away. He figured that if those little figures truly had to spin up there day and night, they would probably get quite bored.
Unable to think of a better idea, the child furrowed his brow. Just then, in the distance, the gong for the cockfight struck with a sharp clang.
And with that clang, all his unresolved daydreams about the flower drum and the little figures vanished.

Yan Ying knew all too well that her family wasn't entirely pleased with marrying their treasured daughter off to a mere soldier. It wasn't just the hardships of daily life they worried about, nor the long stretches of separation; the battlefield was a place without mercy, where death could come at any moment, leaving her widowed at a young age. But fate had its plans. During the northern expedition, Emperor Shizong fell ill and soon passed away, and the once-proud Finesteed Hamlet began to decline. With the northern expedition armies disbanded, Yan Ying and a handful of comrades who refused to serve Zhao Kuangyin settled in Harvestfall Village in Qinghe, where he took up teaching. It wasn't much, but it was enough to give Qi Sheng a steady life. In time, Finesteed Hamlet gradually accepted him as one of their own. Yan Ying was a devoted husband, patient, and attentive. Qi Sheng was not a pampered woman, but she had a competitive streak when it came to chess, so Yan Ying often found himself walking a delicate line, losing just enough to keep her happy, but skillfully enough that she never noticed. Otherwise, her interest in the game might have faded.
Life had been moving along quietly until the issuance of the Jingbei Order shattered that stillness in Harvestfall Village. The northern expedition armies were to be reassembled, but was this just another campaign? Or something more? Sitting before the chessboard, Yan Ying found his thoughts drifting far from the game. His gaze lingered on the pieces, but his mind was not. Absentmindedly, he checkmated his wife with a few moves. Only when he caught sight of her stunned expression did he realize what he'd done. Silence fell like a curtain. Qi Sheng's pride was wounded. Without a word, she stood up and snapped, "I'm going back to Finesteed Hamlet!" Yan Ying opened his mouth, an apology hovering on his lips, yet when he finally spoke, the words came out sharp and cold, "Go, then! I won't stop you! Do you think being called Qi Sheng makes you some kind of chess saint? Well, just because I'm Yan Ying doesn't mean I'm weary of winning! If your brother hadn't told me not to upset you, I would've stopped holding back a long time ago! I'm done walking on eggshells!"
Qi Sheng cried. It was the first time they had truly fought since getting married and the first time Yan Ying had seen her in tears. Father,

It has been two years since I marched north with the army. All is well with me. I only do not know whether your health is sound, and whether Yueniang and Xia'er are both well.

Last year I came under General Zhao Dejun's command. Thanks to the few characters I learned from you in childhood, and with the help of the brothers in the ranks, I was promoted to the post of unit leader. But Father, do not worry. The men under General Zhao are all seasoned soldiers. I have heard there is even a troop of foreign cavalry, all Khitan riders on silver saddles, fighting for the Han. Most days it is not my turn to go into battle. Whenever I have the chance, I learn a little more riding and archery from them. I will take good care of myself.

I have asked Brother Wang to bring home this year's pay and grain stipend for me. I must trouble you and Yueniang to look after things at home for a little while longer. Once spring comes and the fighting eases, I shall surely be able to come home and see you.

Li Jingxing

Deng Yideng looked at the brothers before him and, all at once, memories of his old drifting days came flooding back. It felt like a lifetime ago.

The day Wang Daquan decided to leave home, Grandma's chronic headaches were acting up terribly. 
Many years had passed. Wang Daquan had grown into a fine young man. Such talent naturally chafed against the confines of his impoverished hometown. 
Grandma lay slumped on the bed, dizzy and faint, yet she clung to Wang Daquan's hand, her plea almost a whisper. 
"Just wait... let me steam a tray of buns for you." 

For the first time in all these years, Wang Daquan stayed to watch Grandma make the buns. 
The milled wheat flour needed sifting again—the wind was strong, and sand got in too easily. She mixed it slowly with clear well water, then pinched off a piece of old dough from the jar to use as starter, kneading it all together. 
The dough was left to rise under a breathable bamboo cover. She took a piece of fat from the house, chopped it finely, and set it outside to dry in the wind. 
Grandma's mouth didn't rest either. "Remember to eat on time, eat whatever you want." "Remember to dress warmly. If you need anything, write home." "Don't stir up trouble outside. If something looks wrong, just run"... 
Bits and pieces, murmured over and over. The dough rose; the fat dried halfway. 
Panting with effort, Grandma kneaded the dough while directing Wang Daquan to arrange the buns in the steamer. 
Sweat the size of beans pattered onto the board. For the first time, Wang Daquan realized: Grandma had aged. 
The towering figure from his memory now only reached his chest. Her face had grown gaunt, no longer what it once was. 
Grandma stacked firewood in the stove, then scattered the chopped fat over it. She added water, lit the fire, and started the stove. The fat crackled in the flames. The scent of wheat and meat mingled in the air, and steam clouded Grandma's eyes. 
"Good child... remember to think of your grandma."

Grandma furrowed her brows and snorted heavily through her nose. Wang Daquan was too scared to speak, just lowered his head and gnawed on the bun, only daring to relax when he heard Grandma push the door open and leave.
Outside the window, the wind grew stronger; inside, it gradually darkened. Wang Daquan lay on the rug and fell sound asleep.
Not long after, a subtle fragrance drifted into his nose. It was the scent of wheat and fat meat. Rubbing sleepy eyes, Wang Daquan's mouth watered at the sight of the bun before him.
"Eat. Fresh out of the steamer." Grandma's rough voice sounded. She picked up a bun, broke it open, blew on it, and handed it to Wang Daquan.

The day Wang Fen lost her daughter dawned bright with spring sunshine.
She'd spent half the day harvesting rice in the fields, planning all the way home what delicious meal she'd cook for the girl.
Her beautiful daughter, the loveliest girl in all the surrounding villages. Pride swelled in Wang Fen's chest, followed by guilt. She wanted to give the child every good thing in this world. Yet that thoughtful, sweet-natured girl never asked for anything. When asked, she'd say, "I just want to stay with Mother forever."
After days of consideration, Wang Fen decided: Perhaps it's better this way. The world beyond their home might wound such a gentle soul. If her daughter wished to remain by her side forever, so be it.

But when she returned, the girl was gone. Her husband's two brothers hung their heads in silence, her spineless husband wouldn't meet her eyes.
A chill running down her spine, Wang Fen dashed outside. Grannie Liu next door wiped her tears and told her. 
"She was sold. They sold her."
"Where?"
"No one knows."
Half a day had already passed. The wagon tracks had vanished into the wilderness, leaving no trail to follow.
Wang Fen stood motionless for a long moment. Then she turned, changed her shoes, and ran into the mountains...

Her beautiful, sensible, sweet daughter... she searched year after year, decade after decade.
Her shoes wore through. Kind strangers gave her new pairs. Those, too, wore through... Pair after pair, still she walked.
Years blurred into one, her feet carrying her nowhere and everywhere.
Singing the lullaby her daughter loved, Wang Fen stopped every passerby, asking the same question, over and over:
"I have a beautiful daughter. Have you seen her?"

生蓬户之侧陋兮，不闲习于文符。不见图画之妙像兮，不闻先哲之典谟。既愚陋而寡识兮，:
Born behind a humble gate of reeds, obscure and poor,
I never learned the written word in full.
No wondrous form of painting met my eye,
Nor ever reached my ears the wisdom of the sages old.
Dull and unknowing, of little wit,
By error I was brought into the palace halls.
This was no place for common grass to grow,
And so I lived in fear from day to day.
I bear the pain of longing in my heart,
And ten thousand cares for all that is to come.
Alas, these hidden sorrows deepen ever more,
Shut in alone, with no one there to hear.
My thoughts are troubled, desolate, and spent,
And longing winds more tightly still about my chest.
Through the long night I lie and cannot sleep,
My soul unquiet till the edge of dawn.
The wind stirs low on every side,
White frost lies thick along the court.
The sun is dim and gives no warmth,
The air is bitter, clear, and cold.
So laden am I with grief and sorrow
That tears must fall of themselves.

Think of Bo Yu, gentle and dutiful,
Who wore bright robes to delight his parents.
But I lament the cruel sundering of this day,
For now my kin and I are parted like Shen and Chen.
How can the distance between us be called far?
It is not even the span of a few paces.
Yet so cold and strict are the palace walls
That though I long to see them, I find no way.
I lift my eyes to the drifting clouds
And my tears fall, wetting my kerchief through.
Think of Qu Yuan and the grief he bore,
The sorrow of parting that he sang.
And those who wrote of towers and city walls,
Using sun and moon to speak of separation.
How much more bitter for those of one blood,
Now cast apart and cut off from each other.
Long have I carried grief and made my dwelling with sorrow,
Looking to Heaven and weeping tears of blood.

Envoy
Those bound to me by blood, my dearest kin,
Have become as strangers, lost to me afar.
In sorrow and anguish my soul returns in dreams,
And there I see the ones I long for.
But waking in alarm, I cry aloud,
My heart unable to endure the pain,
My tears falling without end.
So I take up the brush and set down all that stirs within me,
And with tears still falling, entrust it to this poem.

田英曾是文津馆的弟子，因为天资卓越而崭露头角。\n听闻，他翻遍了文津馆所有的藏书:
Long before this night, Tian Ying was a disciple at the Inkbound Order, famed for his brilliance.
 It was said he read every book in the Hall, yet in each, he read only three pages.
Hence, the nickname 'Tian of Three Pages' began to spread, eventually reaching Elder Chang Le, the venerable master of the Hall. 
Whether out of admiration or disapproval, he ultimately summoned Tian Ying and asked why he read in such a mean way.
Tian Ying replied, simply, "I do not seek knowledge. I seek the path in my heart."
What path he searched for in those books, no one knew. Perhaps not even Tian Ying himself. He simply kept reading, page by page, diving into the vast sea of ink.

Eventually, Tian Ying found what he was looking for; not in books, but in a man called Master Wei.
He once said, "Kindness, righteousness, loyalty, and courage are nothing more than words found in the Spring and Autumn Annals."
He burns like a torch, and anyone who encounters him will never forget, instead igniting their own flame.
And so, Tian Ying follows him, leaving the Inkbound Order behind.

For he has found his path at last.

田英者，清河人也。少时贫寒，而无所知名。求学文津馆，后事道济。道济甚尊之。\n及:
Tian Ying was a native of Qinghe. In his youth, he lived in poverty and remained unknown. He studied at the Inkbound Order before serving under Daoji, who held him in high esteem. 
When Emperor Shizong launched a campaign against the Liao Dynasty, the Liao ruler sent his uncle as an envoy to the Southern Tang. Daoji said to Tian Ying, "This opportunity must not be missed—how foolish to let it slip!" Tian Ying replied, "The Liao envoy can be assassinated. Although the Southern Tang has the Aureate Guards, they lack the power to command troops. By intimidating them in this way, what can they do to us?" Daoji praised him, saying, "This is not about espionage but state affairs. You understand my intentions." 
Later, the Southern Tang hosted a night banquet for the Liao envoy at Qingfeng Post . When the envoy withdrew to relieve himself after drinking heavily, he did not return for a long time—and was found decapitated. The Southern Tang ruler ordered the Aureate Pavilion to arrest Tian Ying, but he evaded capture. From then on, diplomatic relations between Liao and Southern Tang were severed, and Tian Ying was never seen again.

"Look at her, doesn't she look like a stray dog that's been cast aside?" Shangguan Yu laughed sweetly.

"She's not even worthy of being compared to a dog," A'Sheng advances step by step, a dagger in his hand, disgust in his eyes. "Fortunately, she's stupid enough. Otherwise, having to keep up this farce every night would have given me nightmares!"

I had nowhere to run, no strength left to resist. They severed the tendons in my hands and feet, then tossed me into the gutter of the Unbound Cavern. Even as my body fell, I forced my eyes to remain open. I wanted to see them, to etch their faces into my memory. Even if I became a ghost, I would never forgive them.

No—
I refuse to die like this.
I refuse!
I will claw my way out of this darkness.
I will crawl back into the light.
I will stand before them and take back everything they stole from me!

皎皎随信送来鞋子的时候，他跳了起来，桌角撞到了膝盖。\n时隔多年，他又穿上了女儿:
When Jiaojiao's parcel arrived with the shoes inside, he actually leapt up—hard enough to bang his knee against the table. 
After so many years, he was wearing something made by his daughter again. The stitching was fine as silk, but the fit—just a little loose. 

That evening, when he was slumped in a dim corner of the banquet, the heel slipped off just as the girl called Xiaopan edged toward him. 
Then the hall erupted. Through the chaos, he charged straight at Fang Bai. The two of them—future in‑laws who had met only once—locked eyes in the middle of that desperate moment. And in that single glance, they both decided to gamble. Fang Bai's Sage Palm swept toward him. He shifted back just a hair. The blow struck him, but didn't pierce through. He crumpled into a nameless heap in the corner—one more "corpse" no one would check, no one would mourn. Their gamble paid off. But his shoes were gone. 

Carried out with the dead, he drifted in and out, dimly grieving the loss. Even after he crawled out of the corpse pile, he was still thinking about them. 
Without those shoes, even a clear path betrayed him—blocked by a massive fallen rock. The thing sat there, shameless as a stubborn mule. He pushed, he slapped, he shoved with all the breath he had left. It didn't move an inch. 
Anger rose hot in his chest. If only he still had those shoes. 

A good pair lets a man find his footing. And this boulder—this lump—was nothing more than a scrap from his youth, a stone he could once shatter with half a palm. So why couldn't he budge it now? 
He must be hurt. Weakened. Had his hands... gotten smaller? 

And then it dawned on him. Age shrinks a man, the same way cloth shrinks when shoes are made. Jiaojiao had sewn for him so many times—it wasn't her stitching that had grown too large. He was the one who had grown small. 
When he was young, his wife had fallen for him at a single glance—broad‑shouldered, tall, unshakable. After she died, he carried his daughter from city to city in search of cures. She used to say her father was like a mountain. 
But now—when had that mountain crumbled into a small hill? 
He struck the boulder again and again. A lifetime of memories rushed past him. None stopped—Until one did. 

He remembered carrying little Jiaojiao to seek help from a famed master. The gates were locked tight. He waited so long that his knees nearly gave way to the dirt. 
But had he knelt? What held him back? His knees had hurt—was Jiaojiao calling him? What had she said? 
Lan Shouchi pounded the rock, searching the past. And suddenly he knew. The words Xiaopan had repeated earlier were the very ones Jiaojiao had said back then: 
"My father is the Palm Master Fierceness—the greatest hero in the world." 
"He—*cough, cough*—he'll never kneel to the likes of you!" 
Lan Shouchi straightened. He drew back his arm and struck. 
Jiaojiao said I'm a great hero. 
The boulder split. 
Half‑Palm Against the Tide—returned to the jianghu. 

In a heap of bodies no one looked at. 
In Peach Grove Pass about to drown. 

The waves were rising high—but he was Palm Master Fierceness.

They say a single day as husband and wife fosters a hundred days of grace. I was truly fortunate to have met you, my lord, to be wed in the warmth of spring, our fates bound as I came of age.

Yet our noble house fell in a single night. I intended to follow you, to shatter like jade, but word came from Hexi that you had cast me aside.
I know too well that your cold words of release were a shield to grant me life.

In this life, we may never meet again. Therefore, I must blaze a trail through this wasteland, carving out a chance at survival from this utter despair. Only then can I honor the sacrifice you made for me.

Reflecting on this life, I have crossed seas of sand and shouldered great responsibilities. If we should meet again in the Yellow Springs, I swear you will see me with new eyes.

Our fate in this world was brief, yet I pray for the next. I hold no regrets. May you always know this.

A respectful farewell,
Liu Si'an
盖闻前世同船渡，今朝共枕眠。\n上官何人竟遇柳氏思安。\n一日夫妻自有齐眉之意，:
It is said that a shared boat in a past life grants a shared pillow in this one. What great fortune, then, was mine to have met you, Lady Liu Si'an.

To be husband and wife for a day is to share mutual respect; for a hundred days, it is the bond of holding hands into old age. With you, I had wished to witness all of Chang'an's splendor, to sing long songs beneath the moon. To be a perfect couple, envied by others; to be true partners, celebrated by Heaven and Earth.

Alas, the passing years created a rift between us. Our lives were not our own to command, and the world is fraught with hardship and sorrow. You, Si'an, gentle as a willow, virtuous and kind, were yet unable to serve the elders above, nor manage the household below.

Today, I restore to you your freedom, hoping it brings you joy. I humbly pray that you, my lady, will find another good family. May you drink among blossoms and gaze upon the moon, with children and grandchildren gathered at your knees. May your family rejoice, and I, Shangguan, shall have no regrets.

This letter is set down as proof.

In Wannian County of Chang'an.

Respectfully,
Shangguan Ze

Li Zhenzhen finally learned the young man's name years later.
Tian Ying.
Her fingers traced the invisible strokes in the air, writing those two characters over and over, stroke by stroke.
Tian Ying, Tian Ying, Tian Ying...
A tinge of joy welled up.
The person she had searched for more than ten years had actually appeared before her on his own initiative.
Could this be fate?
All her life, she had hated fate, fought against it, refused to submit to it. This was the first time she wanted to thank fate.
Although he didn't recognize her, or perhaps he had never remembered her at all, it didn't matter. It was enough that she alone knew about this reunion.
As for the matter he had asked her to handle... she naturally agreed without hesitation.
Whether to be his sword, or his blood-stained hands, it didn't matter. As long as he needed her, she could become anything.
However, she wrapped her help in the shell of a deal, even though she was not interested in the thing related to eyes at all.
After all, if she agreed without reason, it would only arouse suspicion in a cautious person like him.

It never occurred to her that protecting the Khitan envoys was not the whole of his plan. He was going to Qingfeng Post to carry out another assassination.
Qingfeng Post, a territory of the Tang Dynasty, a place with heavy troops. How could he come and go freely?
Without caring about anything else, Li Zhenzhen insisted on adding another clause to the deal: letting her go with him.
Sure enough, there was hesitation in his voice.
What do you want to do in Qingfeng Post?
How do I know if you will come back after this trip? If you run away, where can a blind girl like me find you?
She made up a random lie. Fortunately, he seemed to believe it.
I said I would exchange eyes for you, and I will definitely bring the eyes. I, Tian, keep my word.
I don't believe you.
She put on a look of indifference without any trust. He let out a long sigh and said:
I will leave in three days. Don't wait if you are late.
Three days, that's enough.
Enough for her to pack her bags, get herself ready, and follow him to life and death without any worries, to protect him.
...If that accident hadn't happened.

When Li Zhenzhen died, why did she put on a wedding dress?
She couldn't explain it herself.
Perhaps it was because she knew that one day, someone would come to the bottom of the lake for a promise.
She had met him for the first time in a wedding dress, so she would also say goodbye in a wedding dress.
Maybe then he would remember, remember the day they met each other thousands of days and nights ago.
Finish your work.
Survive.
And... remember me.
Tian Ying.
It was the first and last time she called his name. The empty valley was quiet, and no one heard it.

Looking at the empty medicine jar, Yin Song lay back, resigned. Trapped by poverty and illness, his home was already bare. His son had gone up the mountain to gather herbs a few years back and fallen down a cliff. 
He didn't blame fate. He just didn't want to keep struggling on alone anymore. 

Yin Song came from Jingchu, where shamanism was revered, with soul-summoning rituals being normal. Hearing that the great shamans of the Miluo River had once used a sacrifice called "pepper and rice," Yin Song decided to emulate them, inviting the spirits to guide him to his son before he died. 

He searched every corner, finding only half a bowl of dried millet left in the rice jar. However, rituals for the spirits couldn't be slighted. He would go to the market to buy the finest Qin pepper. 
Speaking of the best Qin pepper in Skybrim Market, it had to be from Old Li's. The old man had a knack; his peppers were red and fragrant. Only such good stuff could please the spirits. 

But when he reached Skybrim Market, Yin Song saw that Old Li, the pepper grower, had transformed into the owner of a hot pot stall. 
Watching Old Li's face flushed with bustling joy, smelling the aroma of peppers awakened by hot oil, Yin Song clenched the hem of his clothes but couldn't help swallowing. 

"Hey! Old Yin! You came! Quick, sit, I'll make you a bowl of hot pot, you try it!" 
"No, no... Old Li, I... I want to buy some Qin pepper..." Yin Song took out his last few copper coins. "Look, just this much... just a little is fine." He paused. "Your peppers are good. I'll use them to cook an offering." 
"Brother, peppers are cheap this year, but with this..." Yao Zhaobu mentally calculated and knew this sale wouldn't work. 
"Say no more." Li Baiyuan cut him off. "Old Zhang, scoop a bowl of peppers. Sis, make a bowl of hot pot." 
Li Baiyuan then crouched, fiddled with something behind the stall, and handed Yin Song a cloth bag and a food box. 
"Here are the peppers. Open them at home, careful they don't spill." 
"This is the hot pot. There are two portions of guagua inside too. But this food box is quite valuable, please return it later, alright?" 
"If you like it, come again." 
Yin Song tried to refuse a hundred ways, but the others insisted he take it. Ashamed, he took the food box and left. 

If I die at home today, who will I trouble to return this box? 
Yin Song thought for a moment. Better to return the box first, then go find my son.

A tiger that knows better stays in its cage; a leopard content hides in the mist.

In traditional Chinese culture, mist and leopards share a natural bond. One, because leopards hide well in mist; two, because they often appear together in hermit poetry. The prototype traces back to Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women, where a black leopard stays in the mountains for seven days without eating during rain and mist. It is often a metaphor for scholars living in seclusion.

破门村来了许多江湖人，王小手突然明白了为什么先生要走了。\n他和爹娘说，爹娘只叫:
When Brokegate Village was filled with swordsmen, he finally understood why the master had left.
He told his parents, but they only told him to stay out of trouble. With no master to scold him, no classmates to play with, even the old men from next door and upstairs kept their doors shut.
So Wang Xiaoshou sat alone, setting up the pieces just as the manuals showed. He was about to play left hand against right when a shadow fell across the board.
"Hey, kid. Playing?"
It turned out these wanderers were alright. At least they didn't bully kids or loot the village. Mostly, they just sat down to play him... and beat him soundly.
Wang Xiaoshou liked asking about the Jianghu. Some answered, some stayed silent. Some flipped the board in a fit after losing, then others quietly set it back up and kept playing.
"Great hero," he asked once, "where is the Jianghu?"
The man across from him tipped his hat lower.
"Where you stand is the Jianghu."
Wang Xiaoshou snorted.
Before these guys start walking the Jianghu, they must all go to the same school. Something like "Jianghu 101."
Otherwise, why do they all sound exactly the same?

破阵乐源自唐初的秦王破阵之曲，最初为军歌，后演变为唐朝的宫廷乐舞，用于宴享、祭祀: The piece originated from the early Tang Dynasty's Qin King's Battle Music, which was first composed as a military anthem and later evolved into a form of imperial court musical dance performed during banquets and rituals. Grand and thunderous in tone, it embodied martial valor and ceremonial majesty. During Emperor Gaozong of Tang's reign, the Divine Power Battle Music, and under Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Lesser Battle Music, were both derived from Prince of Qin's Triumph, originally commissioned by Emperor Taizong of Tang. Though this version has vanished within China, others survived in ancient Japanese transcriptions, offering a rare glimpse into the splendor of Tang court music. Yet deciphering these old scores proves extremely challenging, and efforts to reconstruct the original pieces remain arduous. Today, this modest rendition of sixteen tones is offered as a humble start. May it inspire all who share this passion to continue the work.

now roasted to golden perfection.

神仙渡的小孩，个个都觉得自己是蹴鞠大王。这倒也不怪他们——\n村里的大人们，见了:
Every child in Heaven's Pier was convinced they were the local cuju champion. And honestly, you couldn't blame them.
The adults encouraged every single one of them.
"Beautiful kick!" "So I'm the best, right?" "Of course you are!"
From one end of the village to the other, they all got the same answer.
So by the reunion dinner, the whole table was packed with "number one players."
"I kick the farthest!" "I've got the best moves!" "I'm the real cuju king around here!"
The room was so loud it sounded like they might bring the roof down. The adults just smiled and listened, sneaking extra bites of greens into their bowls while the children argued.
Children only have so much attention to spare. If they're busy yelling, they're not paying attention to what's in their mouths.
神仙渡的居民，为猫痴狂，自称育有一女，名曰踏雪，是只颇为可爱的小猫咪。: A cat-obsessed resident of Heaven's Pier, self-proclaimed parent of an adorable kitten named Snowy

To the western side of Heaven's Pier lies a trading dock, once used for river transport. 
Every year, during the opening of Parting Tears, merchants gather here to ship the famed brew far and wide. 
This once-secluded mountain village has gradually reconnected with the world thanks to the peace that now reigns.
神仙渡的酒工，热情大方，勤勤恳恳。: A wine maker at Heaven's Pier, warm-hearted and hardworking.
神仙渡的闹鬼传闻背后，竟是两只发情的猫咪捣鬼。所幸，你找到了真相，神仙渡又能睡一: Behind the rumors of Heaven's Pier being haunted lie two cats in heat, causing the disturbance. Fortunately, you uncover the truth, and the people of Heaven's Pier can once again sleep peacefully at night.

Behind the Brewery of the Heaven's Pier Winery lies a small workshop courtyard. 
Well-stocked with tools, it's a favorite spot for locals to repair broken wares. A very convenient spot.

They say fine wine is best shared with a kindred spirit—perhaps he's still waiting for the right one to appear. Talk to him to find out more.
神仙渡酒肆坐着一个喝闷酒的独饮客，每当你想与他交谈的时候他都把你赶走，直到第三次: A lone drinker sits in the tavern of Heaven's Pier. Each time you try to speak with him, he drives you away—until the third attempt.

神仙渡酒肆的小二，他们一共有九人，按照排行，他为老大，故称宋一。: The waiter at the tavern in Heaven's Pier. There are nine waiters in total, and as the head, he's known as Song Yi.

You wish to help her, only to discover she has caused those children who mocked her to suffer the same fate of disfigurement.

Heaven's Pier was unknown in olden times, for some ten-odd years ago, it was a place of seclusion. At that time, when the Khitan plundered and committed untold atrocities, refugees from Qinghe were fortunate to be taken in by Madam Han of Heaven's Pier, whose shelter spared their lives.
Heaven's Pier now has two great specialties: one is the fragrant drink named Parting Tears, and the other is a Pear Blossom Grove whose blooms fall like snow. When the Drunken Immortal Month arrives, this place becomes a splendid scene on earth—truly a delight to behold.

祭者，真能通神？\n祝娥不知道。至少，在她历经数次改朝换代的祭师生涯之中，她从未:
Can those who perform the rites truly commune with the gods?
Zhu En does not know. Throughout her life as a Fangxiang Ritualist, spanning the rise and fall of countless dynasties, she has never once heard the voice of a god. The only voices to reach her have been human.
The voices of the dead, burdened with unfulfilled wishes; the voices of the living, offering prayers for fortune... Through the Nuo Rite, these human voices converge in her ears. They are the very reason she ascends the altar and performs the Nuo Dance.

Some ask: Does she not fear the weight of so many voices?
Fear? What is there to fear?
If they speak of ghosts, what is there to dread? They are but the final slivers of obsession left by the departed, voices and faces that serve as the last evidence of their time on earth. Once the obsession fades, they too depart.
And if they speak of gods, what fear is there to be? The Nuo Dance is a rite for the divine, yet the gods remain unseen and silent. It is humans who built the altar beneath her feet, and humans who carved the myriad masks. Even she, as the Fangxiang Ritualist, is but a mortal donning a mask.

Whether a ritual can truly alter the course of fate, Zhu En cannot say. She only knows that when the sick are healed, it is through the doctor's care; when grand halls arise, it is through the artisans' toil; and when laughter endures, it is because people still cherish hope for what is to come. For the sake of that hope, they labor and persevere through every day. They never cease despite the hardship or exhaustion.
In every matter she has witnessed, Zhu En has seen only human effort. Thus, to her, rather than fearing the power of ghosts and gods, it is far more terrifying to imagine commoners who have lost all hope amidst disaster and war. If toil yields no echo, and if tomorrow offers no light, then no matter how grand the annual Nuo rites or how the drums may shake the heavens, it is but a hollow illusion, a play in which no one believes.
Now, the clouds part to reveal the moon as fresh snow descends. In a fleeting moment of clarity, she seems to hear a sound, one she has awaited for a lifetime.

Scruffy sat too, staring blankly.
The tree was massive. He remembered the trees outside the palace walls: starving like him, withered and dry, unlike this lush canopy.

Clouds drifted by, petals fell. Rustle. The water of the Rear Garden lapped against the shore.

Father fell in a pool of blood, but this time, he shouted for her to run faster, run faster.
Xiuxiu held back her tears and could only keep running forward.

Master Zhang, a merchant who made his fortune on the road, always kept two bed-warming maids to serve him at night. At midnight, hearing a rustle beneath his bed, he feigned sleep and peeked. From under the bed crawled a fox as large as a hound. Its eyes glowing a blood-red hue, it stood on its hind legs like a man. With claws like withered branches, it pulled back his quilt, lifted his left foot, and began gnawing on his little toe. Strangely, the two maids slept on like the dead.
The pain was excruciating, yet Zhang's body went completely rigid; he could neither scream nor move. He could only watch the fox chew vigorously, emitting eerie rasps from its throat, its teeth glinting with blood. After the feast, the red glow in its eyes dimmed. It flashed a hideous, human-like grin before diving back under the bed and vanishing.
When Zhang finally regained his movement, he found his little toe nearly severed into a bloody pulp. The strange thing was, after the wound healed, that toe became as cold and hard as stone, completely devoid of feeling. As for the two maids, they remained entirely oblivious to the night's horrors.

The first time Yi Dao met the little one of Han Xiangxun, he scoffed. 
Where did this clueless kid come from? 
Not only did the kid not run when he saw the infamous Killerblade, but he even dared to draw his own sword. 
Gutsy, Yi Dao thought. But let's see how long those guts last against a few of my swings. 
They fought, with blade against blade. The kid was no match for him, but when Yi Dao struck, there was no blood. 
The kid stared at him in shock. Yi Dao had used the back of his blade. 
He realized then that this laughably clumsy swordplay was familiar. 
So Han Xiangxun raised a kid this naive? She was never an easy one herself. 
The kid seemed to know all sorts of people. The kid might be more useful alive than dead. 
Still, he needed to teach the kid a lesson that Jianghu was a dangerous place. 
Yi Dao sheathed his blade. 
"Hey, take me to Blissful Retreat." 

Just showing the way, there is no need to be so cagey about it. 
As soon as he went ahead to scout, the little kid predictably slipped away at the first chance. 
Yi Dao always kept his word. If he said he wouldn't kill, then he wouldn't kill. 
And yet, the kid still didn't trust him. Did he really think Yi Dao would go looking for trouble with Han Xiangxun, that troublesome woman? 
But honestly, a kid who's barely out of childhood, even with some wits, was no match for a seasoned old hand like Yi Dao. 
In the thick fog, Yi Dao called out half-heartedly, then swaggered after the panicked, fleeing figure ahead. 
Seriously, as if anyone could escape the Killerblade unless he let them! 
He couldn't help but grin smugly. 
Run, kid, run! The faster you go, the more you're giving your Aunt Han away!

Grand Artisan Gull sighed; such chronicles already spanned twelve full volumes.
Mechanics and cuisines follow diagrams and recipes, but for the rearing of a child, no such schematics exist.
When a mechanism malfunctions, a firm thwack or a complete teardown usually sets things right. If the hearth-fire falters, one merely endures undercooked rice or charred cakes. A stomachache for a day or two, and life goes on.
But a child allows for no such sloppiness. No one taught him the precise meters of a hug, nor at what age spoon-feeding ought to cease.
Was there ever a mechanism more vexing than this? Grand Artisan Gull was unconvinced. After a lifetime of deciphering sacred Mohist Texts and forging complex wonders, could he truly be bested by a single, picky waif?
Consequently, the workshop, once cluttered with gears and axles, became a hoard of bizarre and exotic ingredients.
And thus, the Grand Artisan of the Mohist Hill embarked upon the journey of no return: the study of ancient gastronomy.
Research, after all, was his forte. Once the data was codified, surely raising a child would be as systematic as any other craft.
"By then," he thought with a swell of pride, "none in Mohist City shall surpass my mastery of fatherhood." And with that, he plunged back into his scrolls.
...And yet, the child had refused to grow according to the dictates of his books. Her palate shifted, and her temper proved just as fickle. She had even mastered the art of outmaneuvering her father, employing stratagems within stratagems, and diversions of the most subtle kind...Yet, watching Xiaoxiao wield a rice paddle longer than her own arm, expertly flipping the fish in the pan, a surge of pride, relief, and humble contrition rose within him... a flavor that no culinary scroll under heaven had ever dared to record.
Grand Artisan Gull resolved to commit this to his journals, for this was a nascent recipe that no soul had yet composed. Perhaps all it required was a measure of time, a constant presence, and a pinch of patient grace. Then, those nameless, nebulous emotions would bloom naturally from the child, quietly intertwining themselves within the father's heart.

The birth of Xian'a was a marvel in the hidden village deep within the sandy valley. 
Even though the village itself was something of a legend, facing an infant born in the body of an old woman, everyone was still horrified. 
The village chief sighed. "The moon waxes and wanes, cycles endlessly. Perhaps she is just a step ahead of us." 
Kind villagers scooped up a moon-bun for her. She hadn't yet grown teeth, so they had to soak the bun in hot water until soft and feed it to her bit by bit. 

The stronger the wave, the faster the shock subsides. Soon, everyone grew accustomed to this young old woman. 
Xian'a sat on the doorstep, looking dazed, watching the villagers come and go. They would stop and greet her kindly. 
One day, a boy recklessly came to her side. 
"Do you know how to scoop the moon?" The boy's flushed face startled Xian'a. Flustered and shy, she shook her head. 
"Everyone in our village knows how! I'll teach you!" The boy stood up eagerly, pulling Xian'a towards the clear spring. 
The nimble, agile boy overlooked her unsteady, toddling steps. Xian'a lost her balance but was steadied by the boy's firm hold. 
"Bro... ther..." she babbled, instinctively gripping the boy tightly, step by step walking towards the water brimming with moonlight. 

That day, she still didn't learn how to scoop the moon. Even though the moon-catching net was light and handy, she couldn't find the right angle to throw it. 
But she remembered the net the boy tossed out again and again, and that clear, ringing song.

As fine as needles and packed densely, too numerous to count. 

In the Song dynasty, grass carp made up a significant portion of freshwater fish farming. People dug ponds, constructed buildings beside them, and often cultivated economic crops like lotus root, gorgon fruit, and wild rice, creating an ideal environment for fish to thrive. They would then release fry as fine as needles into the ponds and raise them with great care. Some fry were too tiny to count accurately, so the ancients inserted bamboo markers and used portioning methods to gauge the density of fry in a container. This shows that measurement tools for counting fry already existed in the Song dynasty.

Those scholarly purists, who once prided themselves on unblemished virtue, have long since been banished to forgotten corners, while someone like me—pragmatic, clear-eyed, and adaptable—has steadily climbed the ranks.

First, the art of speech lies in adaptability. 
Never bind yourself to a single stance; always leave a margin for retreat. 
When factions clash, begin by acknowledging, "Both sides have their merits." Then, in private, gently confide to Party A that Party B can be overbearing, and to Party B that Party A is somewhat harsh. But be careful never to leave words that could be twisted against you. When the dust settles and power shifts, you can easily align yourself with the new victor, moving like water conforming to every shape.

Allow minor, harmless transgressions under your watch—they will serve you well later. 
Let a subordinate collect small bribes. When your superior arrives unannounced, feign shock and sorrow: "I have failed my duty and allowed corruption to spread!" Then, with feigned heartache, root out a minor, insignificant official and make a public example of him. Once your superior's anger subsides, seize the moment to praise his wisdom: "Thanks to your keen oversight, the vermin were uncovered." In doing so, the dignity of your superior remains intact, and your own position strengthens. Pruning twigs does not harm the tree—instead, it makes the trunk appear all the more robust. 
#YSide note: Seems to make sense, doesn't it? #E

Third, pursue gain, avoid blame, and protect your reputation. 
Be the first to claim success; the last to admit failure. 
If a task falls apart and you face accusations, begin by expressing heartfelt regret. Wipe away tears, choke back emotions, then lament, "Everyone made mistakes," subtly casting blame on others without ever implicating yourself. Thus, someone else will shoulder the burden. 

Fourth, accept gifts under a veil of refinement. 
If you must receive gratuities, cloak them in culture and grace. 
When a merchant offers a "family heirloom painting," respond solemnly, "Such a treasure belongs in the public collection." If a wealthy patron presents a rare manuscript, sigh and say, "I will safeguard this precious volume for now." Should inquiries arise, point to your shelves full of "items held in trust," earning you a reputation for nurturing talent instead of greed.

Autumn's Solemn Chapter: Formation Entry 
The first time they passed the little roadside stage, his father was striding ahead, intent on getting where they were going. 
When the boy hesitated, the man stopped, frowned, and let out a long sigh. "...Fine. One performance." 

Masked Troupe disciples rarely visited a town this small. Whenever their music drifted through the streets, it brought more joy than the New Year ever did. 
But in times like these, when a full stomach was already a luxury, festivals had lost their shine. A single play, a single song—those were what comforted the living now. 
He was too young then to understand the story being told. 
He only remembered pear blossoms falling like snow, and in that snowfall, a general in violet armor—gold at his waist, whip in hand—dancing a lone, fierce dance of thrusts and strikes. 
When the show ended, the leader of the troupe—an older student, judging from his bearing—led the younger actors in a bow of thanks. Noticing the boy, he pressed a piece of pear-syrup candy into his palm. 

Soon after, his father took him to "stay for a while" with distant relatives in the next village. 
They braced against the spring chill with thin, fraying blankets, and day by day the air grew warmer. 
Under the harsh summer sun, the fields demanded tilling and hoeing, yet still no news came from home. 

He ran his fingers over the old whip scars on his arm. 
Now, with the autumn harvest in full swing and everyone occupied, no one was watching him. It seemed as good a time as any to make his way back. 

But when his parents saw him standing in their doorway, their eyes held only astonishment—and a certain troubled guilt. 
There wasn't enough grain. His younger siblings were too small. His older brother could work the fields. 
Sending him away had been the easiest choice, practically automatic. 
Even those who cannot read know how to weigh the cost of survival. 
A cast‑out dog might come back to its old home again and again—but a child needs only one look to understand exactly who was chosen and who was left behind.

Bustards are ground-dwelling birds with sturdy bodies. They favor warm, dry habitats such as meadows, farmlands, and bushes. Due to the significant size difference between the male and female, ancient people believed bustards were all female and could only reproduce by mating with other bird species. This misconception led to the term "lao bao (old bustard)" being used as a euphemism for aging madams of brothels.

胡二饼是从一场地震中逃出来的。\n随身的只有一只老狗，还有剩下的几块烤馕。\n老:
Hu Erbing escaped from an earthquake. 
All he had with him was an old dog and a few remaining pieces of baked naan. 
The old dog didn't understand what wandering meant. It only knew to walk with its master. Where the master was, there was home. 
Crossing the sea of sand, the road was endless. Hu Erbing divided each piece of naan in two. Though man and dog weren't full, they were inseparable. 
Until the pack was empty, and man and dog had walked a long way further. 
Hu Erbing collapsed in the desert from thirst and hunger. In the end, he only saw the old dog anxiously pawing at him, then barking wildly and running off. 
Go on, old friend. Remember to fill your belly... 

Hu Erbing woke up in Karez. 
The villagers said they had found an old dog suffering from heatstroke lying at the village entrance, tongue lolling, gasping for breath. Seeing people approach, it struggled to stand up, tugged at their pant legs trying to lead them into the desert, then wobbled and fell again. People followed the direction and found Hu Erbing unconscious in the desert. 
Hu Erbing asked, where was the old dog? 
The villagers were silent, leading Hu Erbing to a shaded shelter. Seeing Hu Erbing arrive, the old dog used its last bit of strength to lift its head, wagging its tail and panting. 
That day, Hu Erbing talked to the old dog for a long time, until the old dog's tail gently drooped and moved no more. 
Hu Erbing blamed himself. In the end, he hadn't even let the old dog leave on a full stomach.
