胡厘：要下雨了。\n董夫子：是啊，要下雨了。我曾听闻，狐身于巢便知风起，鼠居于洞:
Hu Li: It is going to rain.
Master Dong: Yes, it is going to rain. I have heard that a fox knows the wind from its den, and a mouse knows the rain from its hole. I suppose you must be either a fox or a mouse.
Hu Li: You know me?
Master Dong: No. But I have been waiting for you... waiting for you to come and kill me.
Hu Li: Are you not afraid of death?
Master Dong: No, I am afraid of death. But there is something I fear far more than death itself. I believe you feel the same, do you not?
Hu Li: Oh? Then what is it you fear?
Master Dong: You should know, though I am a scholar of Confucianism, I have also studied the Hundred Schools of Thought.
Hu Li: Why?
Master Dong: Because I wanted to find a Great Way, a path that could bring true and lasting peace to the world.
Master Dong: I studied Legalism. Yet, the First Emperor used harsh laws to rule the six directions, cracking the whip across the realm. His majesty shook the four seas, but the people never found joy.
Master Dong: Then I studied Daoism. In the early Han Dynasty, they ruled through the ways of Huang-Lao, letting the people run free like unbridled horses without guidance, but the powerful and wealthy never restrained their greed.
Master Dong: I also studied Mohism. But the Mohists preach universal love and non-aggression; they suppress human desires and sacrifice themselves for the benefit of others. How many in this world can truly achieve that?
Hu Li: So you believe that among the Hundred Schools, only Confucianism is the Great Way?
Master Dong: Confucianism? No, it is not.
Hu Li: Then what exactly is this Way you are searching for?
Master Dong: I had a dream. I dreamed of a world two thousand years from now.
Master Dong: In that world, Confucianism serves as the spine, establishing eternal moral fortitude; Mohism serves as the blade, protecting the lives of the common people; Legalism serves as the ruler, balancing the boundaries of all things. The Hundred Schools merge into one stream, and the hearts of all people are united. There is no fear of famine, and no suffering of war and separation.
Hu Li: You want to merge the Hundred Schools! Are you not afraid of being spat upon by your own Confucian peers?
Master Dong: Just now, you asked me what I fear. Now I can answer you. I fear that this is merely a dream.
Master Dong: The morning mushroom knows not the turning of the moon; the summer cicada knows not the passing of the seasons. One who has not seen the high mountains cannot comprehend the flat plains; one who has gazed upon the vast ocean can hardly be captivated by a trickling stream.
Master Dong: A decade can plan for temporary prosperity; a century can plan for the rise and fall of a dynasty; a millennium can plan for the continuation of a culture. My friend, you and I stand in the eternal flood of time. Why not cast our gaze across a thousand years, and plan for an era that spans ten thousand?
Hu Li: How do you intend to do this?
Master Dong: To bring peace to the world, the Royal Way must unify the Hundred Schools. But this act will inevitably clash with the Mohist ideal of universal love.
Master Dong: Therefore, I brazenly seek to borrow a thousand years from the Mohists on behalf of the world. For the next two thousand years, the first millennium shall belong to Confucianism, and the second shall return to Mohism. Thus, the world shall reach the Great Harmony.
...
Hu Li: And how do you intend to borrow it?
Master Dong: By asking the Mohists to die.

胡小旭最开心的回忆，就是那个溜出去偷看嫖姚棋比赛的下午。\n那天，爷娘有事要出远:
Hu Xiaoxu's happiest memory was that afternoon he sneaked out to watch the Piaoyao Battleboard tournament. 
That day, his parents had to travel far. Before leaving, Lady Hu carefully instructed Xiaoxu not to go out. 
Xiaoxu only dared to give a vague promise. Because he had overheard his parents chatting: today, a lively Piaoyao Battleboard tournament was being held at the nearby market. Anyone who won ten matches in a row would win a brand-new Piaoyao Battleboard set. 
He knew his own skill wasn't enough to compete. But just seeing so many people play would make him happy enough. 

After his parents left, Hu Xiaoxu waited another two hours. 
Then, gathering his courage, he climbed over the wall. 
He didn't know the way to the market and wandered around, taking many wrong turns. 
Stepping onto land outside the courtyard, smelling unfamiliar winds, seeing strange goods and all sorts of people, Hu Xiaoxu felt dazzled, his steps lighter than ever before. 
He saw laborers by the well using wooden mechanisms to easily draw up bucket after bucket of water. 
He saw children under fruit trees using long bamboo poles to catch chirping cicadas, tying them to strings to play with. 
He heard the loom creaking, the shuttle flying back and forth, spinning out soft cloth. 
He saw one new, unfamiliar thing after another. 
Until his parents caught him and brought him home, scolding him for a long time. 

So strange—he hadn't even seen any Piaoyao Battleboard match that day, yet Hu Xiaoxu was extraordinarily happy.

胡辣汤\n胡辣汤是中原早餐摊上当之无愧的王者。正宗的胡辣汤汤底由牛肉汤或羊肉汤制:
1. Hulatang (Spicy Pepper Soup)

Hulatang is the undisputed king of breakfast stalls in the Central Plains. A proper bowl starts with beef or mutton broth, fragrant with rich stock, then comes with pieces of meat, wheat gluten, tofu skin, and other add-ins.

Even so, it varies from place to place. Some say the hulatang they grew up with was yellow and thick, with the spice taking center stage. Others swear by a darker, thinner version that leans more numbing than hot.

Either way, it's delicious. The kind you end up craving again.

胡辣汤豆腐脑两掺\n谁说阴阳不可调和，谁说泾渭必须分明，谁说黑白注定对立？日月尚:
3. Hulatang and Tofu Pudding, Mixed

Who says opposites cannot mix? Who says black and white must stay apart? The sun and moon can share the same sky, so why not hulatang and tofu pudding?

Street stalls in the Central Plains know a thing or two. If the soup is too fiery, add a spoonful of pale, fragrant tofu pudding. If the tofu pudding tastes too mild, stir in a spoonful of hulatang, spicy, savory, and numbing.

Heaven and earth hold up the same world. A king and his queen belong together. So do these two, once you mix them. If you are not the kind of well-off, big-appetite adult who can finish two full bowls, just ask the vendor for a half-and-half.

In one bowl, black and white mingle, and all kinds of flavor open up. In the end, most of us are simply chasing a life that hits the right balance, salty and mild, wanting both and getting both.

Though far from home, I too spend my days at the academy observing the heavens and drawing star charts. I often think of the four of us wandering together in years past. Beneath the River of Stars, once our charts were finished, we would play verse games. Now we are scattered, and such games can no longer be played. It leaves me full of longing.
The food and drink beyond the mountain are plentiful enough, though they soon grow dull. There are all manner of noodles here, Lily Bulb Noodles, Radish Noodles, Fresh Fish Noodles, Chicken Noodles, and many more besides. The wines too are many, Blood Red, Spring's Sip, Parting Tears, and countless others. Yet they are only fresh at first. After three or five tastings, one quickly tires of them. None can compare with Father's home-cooked dishes, nor with Mother's Forever Drunk.
In the past, I was forever finding fault with the food and drink at home, quick with some careless remark, always thinking there was room for improvement. Only now do I understand that the meals of home may be eaten a thousand times, ten thousand times, and still never lose their savor.
And now that I think on it, several years have passed in the blink of an eye since I left home. For several years now, I have not tasted a meal from home, nor drunk a cup of wine brewed at home.

Yet life at the academy has its own pleasures.
Xu'er and I came here in the name of teaching, yet in truth we have gained much ourselves. There are many truly learned people here. Trade and farming, histories and classics, all may be discussed, and with great delight. Just the other day, Xu'er came to know several disciples of Lone Cloud, all highly skilled in mathematics. I had meant only to exchange a few thoughts on celestial calculation, yet somehow I found myself drawn into one of their debates, on how the weight of feeling between a man and a woman might be measured. I could not bear to treat what lies between Xu'er and me as though it were some cold thing to be weighed and reckoned, so I said nothing. Yet by saying nothing, I was somehow judged the victor, and rewarded with no small number of mathematical texts.
There are many more such amusing incidents, too many to set down one by one.

Only after leaving the mountain and coming here have I truly understood how vast Heaven and Earth are, and how small a single person is within them. It is like a mayfly gazing upon the sea, no different from when, as a child, I lay in the courtyard in the evening cool and counted the stars.
Ah, but the River of Stars alone remains unchanged. Though we are far apart, we may still look up at the same sky. Is that not some comfort?
And when one day we are together again, we may compare which chart was drawn at what time, set them side by side, and speak of the longing of these years apart. Would that not be a joy?
This sheet is small, and household trifles too many to tell in full. When the day comes that we are reunited, I shall sit with you by candlelight and tell you everything.

If you wish to know what the Mohist Voice is, you should first ask Mohway. Yes, that black furball usually curled up asleep at Yu Ge's grandfather's desk.
Grandfather often said that all things have a sound. During the years he spent developing the voice box, he created countless noises: the crisp snap of bamboo slips, the rustle of paper meeting ink, the low hum of turning gears. Yet Mohway was never disturbed, sleeping soundly through every sound. Grandfather would tiptoe to the cat, holding the voice box near its furry cheek to capture its rising and falling purrs. Sometimes as faint as a child's breath, sometimes as steady as water simmering on a stove.
Grandfather found it amusing and would occasionally ask, "Mohway, Mohway, you sleep so much; have you heard a wonderful sound in your dreams that I cannot?"
Mohway would only curl into a tighter circle, as if all the world's complex noises were merely background for its dreams.
Grandfather couldn't help but remember the day he found Mohway. A faint meow from the wall harmonized perfectly with the rain he had just recorded, forming a melody of its own.
In this life, he might never discover what the true "Mohist Voice" was. But this kitten and he were meant to be.
Once, Mohway suddenly woke from a dream.
Grandfather was practicing his old training verses alone. Mohway walked over softly, nuzzled Grandfather's hand, and let out a meow that was captured forever by the spinning voice box. According to Yu Ge, that was Grandfather's final duet.
Later, Grandfather was gone.
Mohway still sleeps until the sun dips low.
The house no longer holds the old bustle. Logically, with no one to disturb it, the dreams should be more peaceful.
But now, every time Mohway wakes here, the silence of the room feels louder than all the previous sounds combined.
It licks its paws and lets out a meow to the sky.
This cry is louder than usual, as if by instinct.
As if waiting for someone to answer.

Should one ask who gives the finest lectures in Mohist City, every disciple would offer a different name. Yet, as to who renders the Mohist Texts most captivating, eight out of ten disciples would nominate Grand Artisan Gull.
When the Grand Artisan Gull expounds upon the texts, he not only draws from vast classics with effortless clarity but also weaves culinary metaphors into his teachings, whetting every appetite. From the meager rations of Mozi's travels to the grand banquets hosted by kings, Grand Artisan Gull meticulously chronicles every morsel. In his words, Mozi had fifteen disciples, and their spiritual progeny were many. Whether they dined on mountain potherbs or rich meats when they wrote "Heavenwill Declared" is, of course, a fundamental question of the Mohist soul.
Furthermore, the mechanical diagrams of old differ but little from those of today; true novelty is rare. Recipes, however, are a different matter entirely. The richness of ingredients, the diversity of pairings, and the complexity of flavors align far better with the Mohist principle of "Transformation from the Heart" than any mundane device. Beyond his duties, he upholds the Mohist path of empiricism, seeking out lost recipes. He tests the ingredients, the temper of the flames, the balance of spice...
Nor are the disciples idle; every three watches, they take turns seeking his counsel. Not out of tireless studiousness, but because the failure rate of his culinary experiments is truly tragic. Without oversight, he might well collapse amidst a heap of bizarre ingredients, babbling in a fever dream.
Gulltside, the mists disperse as the mountain fowl herald the dawn. In the courtyard, disciples steadfastly recite: "Universal Love, Mutual Benefit." They debate the latest mechanisms of Mohist City, or argue from dawn till dusk on mountain expansion or seclusion.
Grand Artisan Gull has entrusted this "cookbook" of the Mohist Texts to his disciples, letting them add their own bitterness of dawn vigils and the toil of earnest labor. They stir in the piquancy of fierce debate and the subtle sweetness of walking the same path as peers. Others prefer to cast in heavy handfuls of salt, or dilute it with the river waters of their vast wanderings...
"Take up the plane, or the ladle; what matters most is crafting a dish that is truly your own." With that, Grand Artisan Gull ducked back into his den, leaving his disciples to exchange glances over a pot of... highly dubious stew.
At such moments, the senior disciples couldn't help but pine for the days before Grand Artisan Gull strayed from the "Righteous Path." Why would a man so learned and steadfast abandon a lifetime of mechanical mastery to immerse himself in the esoteric world of ancient recipes?
To this day, it remains a mystery unsolved by his disciples.

荧渊对无相皇来说，是起点，也是归宿。\n他在幼年之时，随父母入渊，后来父母病亡，:
Gleaming Abyss to the Void King marks both a start and an end.
As a child, he entered the Gleaming Abyss with his parents. But when they passed away, a slender woman, as graceful as a willow branch raised him.
Yet, in the end, that woman too was taken from him. When she died, the flowers of Gleaming Abyss fell like snow, drifting endlessly through the air. Amidst the sea of petals, the white-haired man stood, silent and still.
It was then that he spoke to the man for the first time.
The man, embodying the very essence of Formless Reign, gave him a name. From that moment on, The Void King has become his.
For once a beast is named, it belongs to its master.

Ever since the Void King followed his master out of the Gleaming Abyss, defeat has never again been his companion. There was only one exception: a single loss to a man carrying a child.
His master's face remained impassive, but the disappointment in his eyes was undeniable. 
No, my lord, please don't be disappointed in me... I am still the Void King Reign you want. I am still the Emperor of Warriors.
Since then, he has been back in the Pond, vowing to guard the tomb of that woman, swearing never to leave until he claims a thousand heads.
More than a decade passes. He is just one head away, one step from fulfilling his vow and proving himself worthy to his master once more.
He has to prove that the Void King deserves the name bestowed upon him. That he has not failed his master.
But why...
The Void King collapses heavily, staring at the indistinct figure before him. He reaches out, desperate to touch that far-off shadow, but in the end, he is consumed by darkness.

萧史从萧府逃跑的那一刻，他看着前头救他的那位江湖人，后头是追来的家仆，笑了起来，:
The moment Xiao Shi fled the Xiao estate, he looked ahead to the jianghu man helping him escape, and behind him to the servants chasing him, and he laughed. The wind rushed past his ears, his robes flaring wildly. There's a kind of illusion that comes with running into the wind, an illusion of freedom. He felt like a bird loosed from its cage. Not flying to the sky, but into the jianghu.

He only stopped once on the road to freedom by the Shen estate.

He disliked places where the wind didn't stir, and the Shen estate was clearly one of them. The rear courtyard where the Shen family's young lady resided was far too lifeless. He recalled the smile she always wore when they met, always the same, never changing. She was pretty, that he remembered. 

But the more he looked, the more she seemed... unreal.

Later, he realized what she reminded him of. Like the ornate rockeries set in noblemen's courtyards. Like the finely carved jade displayed in the great hall. Like the velvet blossoms that never wilt, no matter the season. Every wealthy household wanted one, but they were things that never changed, never moved.

People collect jade. But no one falls in love with it.

That impression stuck with him so strongly that when Shen Yu, whom he had always thought to be just like the lifeless stones and rockeries, suddenly opened her window without a smile, told a lie, and casually used birdseed to tease him, he froze.

That tiny spark of life in her cast him out. He stood outside her window for a long while, confused.

"She wasn't like this before," he thought.

But then, what was she supposed to be like? Like a rockery? Like a piece of jade?

No. She was a person. She was always supposed to be like this. Because people shouldn't be like rockeries. They shouldn't be like jade. People should be like people.

But too many in this world... don't know that.

萧誉默默地清扫着柴房前的落叶，几位弟子聚在不远处，毫不避讳地对着他指指点点。\n:
Xiao Yu was silently sweeping the leaves outside the wooden shack, while nearby, a few disciples huddled, pointing and snickering without the slightest pretense of privacy.
"So this is the 'top blade' of our sect? Look at him now, reduced to a woodshed servant."
"Haven't you heard? He dabbled in some dark arts and backfired his Qi. Now? He's nothing but a spent husk!"
"I knew it. A low-born stray like him reaching those heights? Must be some crooked trickery. Bah! A total disgrace to the Fierce Blade name."
Xiao Yu shot them a cold glance, and even now, the weight of his former name was enough to shut them up. Just as he bent down to keep sweeping, a voice cut in from behind.
"Hmph. A toothless cur, still barking to scare the juniors?"
It was Song Baishu, the senior disciple. The spineless lot rushed to Song's side, showering him with sycophantic praise. Xiao Yu ignored them all and kept sweeping.
Song Baishu sneered. "Your Senior Brother is here. Where is your salute?"
Xiao Yu replied flatly, without even looking up. "We are both disciples, and I've been struck from the scrolls. Why should I bow to you?"
In the blink of an eye, Song Baishu blurred forward like a bolt of lightning. He clamped a hand over Xiao's face and slammed his head into the dirt. Xiao Yu, already too weak to fight back, hit the dirt hard. Blood seeped from every orifice. A brutal sight.
"You think you're in any position to lecture me? You pathetic cripple!"
Song pulled back, wiping his fingers with a white handkerchief in feigned disgust. Then he ground his boot into Xiao's head as if he were nothing but a stray dog.
Xiao was barely holding on. His breath grew even shallower. His lips quivered as if struggling to force out a final word. Curious, Song leaned in closer. Bad move. Xiao spat a mouthful of blood right in his face, followed by a roar of defiant laughter.
Song lost it. He was about to end Xiao right then and there when a girl rushed into the courtyard and threw herself in front of him. It was Wang Xun'er, the Sect Master's daughter. She'd just gotten medicine for Xiao.
"Junior Sister, the man is a renegade. Why shield him?"
Wang helped Xiao to his feet, fury burning in her eyes. "Xiao Yu and I are betrothed. And this is how you treat my fiancé, Senior Brother? Leave now, or do not blame me if my blade shows no mercy!"
Song's face darkened. "The Master has annulled that marriage pact! Why cling to this shell of a man? I shall petition Master to grant your hand to me instead!"
He was about to keep pushing when he noticed Wang's hand moving toward the sword at her waist, and the killing intent suddenly locked onto him. Forced to yield, he feigned retreat, only to whirl around with a sudden strike, aiming to knock Xun'er senseless. Though his powers are gone, Xiao Yu's eyes remain keen. He shouted a warning just in time, and Wang barely managed to dodge.
Song stopped holding back. "Xun'er, enough! This traitor corrupted our sacred styles and leaked them to outsiders. His execution is Master's direct command!"
Xiao furrowed his brow. When had he ever committed such a crime? But Wang didn't care. She grabbed his hand and bolted toward the back mountain. The Sect's intent was now bared for all to see. A tide of pursuers swarmed the mountain paths. Outnumbered and overwhelmed, Xun'er fought a desperate retreat toward the edge of a cliff.
The pursuers didn't want to risk hurting the Sect Master's daughter, so they held back, but blades had no eyes. Xun'er was soon trailing blood from several shallow gashes. A fierce wind whipped around them, Xiao's blood-soaked robes snapping in the gusts. He looked at Wang, guilt and anguish written all over his face.
"This is far enough."
Before she could utter a word, Xiao flung himself into the abyss. In that final moment, everything clicked into place. His shattered meridians were no accident; it was the Master's design. His honesty in pointing out the flaws of their style had been his own death warrant.
The Fierce Blade Sect was never worthy of him. If fate granted him another life, he would show that stagnant old Master the meaning of true mastery!

After Xiao's fall, Master Wang sought to betroth Xun'er to Song Baishu. But she would sooner die than submit, leaving Wang with no choice but to drop the matter. As the years weighed heavily on Master Wang, the reins of the sect slowly slipped into Song's grasp. Before Song attained the secret legacy, he seethed with envy as Xiao Yu surpassed him and mastered the core techniques first. Yet once the techniques were finally his, he found them... underwhelming. He grew slothful, using sect business as a pretext to abandon his training. He became a frequent, if secret, guest of the entertainment quarters. Neglecting his inner cultivation, he relied on gold to buy hollow prestige. It was a house of cards, a brilliant blaze fed by nothing but oil. The old sect master tried to admonish him. At first, Song maintained a respectful front. Eventually, he dropped the mask entirely, snarling that the old man was a fossil who had achieved nothing, a failure who couldn't even rule his own daughter. In fits of rage, he would even withhold the Master's meals. Cowering under the abuse, Old Master Wang fell into a fearful silence. Three years slipped by in that strained, suffocating silence.

One day, a youth in straw sandals came to challenge the most "renowned" sect in the land. Seeing only a nameless nobody who looked easy to bully, the disciples scrambled to be the first to strike. Yet none could withstand a single blow. Before long, the courtyard was littered with fallen men. No one dared to rise.
Just when the sect's reputation had taken a serious hit, things went from bad to worse. The Heavenly Sword Sect, irked by Fierce Blade's unearned fame, came to issue a formal challenge.
Song Baishu couldn't stand for that and stepped forward to face their warrior. Seeing the hosts were occupied, the boy in straw sandals retreated with an easy grace, clapping his hands in amusement:
"A clash of masters... Seems my journey wasn't in vain after all."
But while Song held the legacy, he didn't grasp the soul of the technique. His forms were incomplete, his strikes unable to find their mark. And due to years of slacking off, his stamina was giving out. A split-second lapse in concentration, and his opponent's blade sent him reeling.
"I haven't even drawn upon my Sword Intent, yet you are already at your wit's end. This 'Fierce Blade' is all bark and no bite. How dare you even fly a sect banner?"
Song's face went pale with rage.
"Lies and slander!" Despite his clear defeat, Song launched a desperate, dishonorable strike. The Heavenly Sword warrior's eyes turned cold. The Intent manifested. In a flash of cold steel, the blade cleaved through Song's arm in one clean stroke. Before Song could even cry out, the blade was already arcing toward his throat.
In a blur of motion, their blades clashed. The youth in straw sandals had snatched the fallen blade, parrying the lethal blow with effortless precision.
"Steady now, brother. Mercy is a virtue of the great. Why stoop to killing blows in the jianghu?"
The Heavenly Sword warrior eyed him warily, sensing this boy was no ordinary fighter. Reluctantly, the warrior lowered his sword. "The man is a craven; he struck after his defeat. And this sect? It's a fraud, lacking true mastery, yet preying on the hopes of young aspirants."
The youth thought for a moment. "The style itself is not without merit, but this man has missed the mark. Allow me to demonstrate the true essence of the Fierce Blade."
He took up the Fierce Blade stance, and it was like watching an entirely different martial art. Every strike felt like a mountain crashing down. The warrior found no opening to counter, his very spirit crushed by the overwhelming pressure. Had the boy not stayed his hand, the man would be a corpse by now.
The warrior bowed in genuine submission, humbled to have witnessed such mastery. Song Baishu, gritting his teeth against the pain, was about to stammer out his thanks when another figure appeared at the gate. At the sight of the newcomer, the boy's formidable aura vanished, replaced by a childlike glee as he rushed to greet his master.
"How did you know I would be passing this way?" The young man in the bamboo hat asked, his voice soft as he ruffled the boy's hair. The boy grinned; he hadn't. Left to his own devices, he simply grew restless for a fight and sought out this sect to test his mettle. The man shook his head with a faint, resigned smile. He surveyed the wreckage of the courtyard as his disciple filled him in.
Song Baishu, one arm lost, his spirit shattered, finally recognized the man. A hollow, bitter laugh escaped him as he collapsed to his knees.
It was indeed Xiao Yu. Against all odds, he had survived the fall and chanced upon a mystical method to recover his shattered meridians. After three years of cultivation, he had returned. Revenge was never his aim; he came only for Wang Xun'er. He had plucked a beggar boy from the wayside and taken him as his disciple, the very youth in straw sandals.
Xiao had no heart for vengeance: he came here for Xun'er, and her alone. And who was Song Baishu to stand in his way? The old Master wept tears of bitter regret. He lamented the day he traded his honor for lies, all for the fear that exposing the flaws in his craft would cost him his legacy. But the dust of the past had already settled; Xiao no longer cared for old grievances. In the years that followed, many sought his tutelage. He and Xun'er roamed the jianghu, righting wrongs and leaving a legacy that would be whispered in every tavern for generations.

Xiao Heyi set out to travel with two swords and his friends.

Along the way, they squandered fortunes in bustling markets to bid on a sinner's belongings and were hunted for it.
They also found themselves penniless, huddling in the corners of foreign alleys to beg.
They climbed the frigid peaks of Mount Hua and witnessed the legendary three sword intents.
They nearly drowned in the water formations of Dreamy Marsh, soaked to the bone and mocked by the local girls.
But the second sword never left its sheath.

Until the defeat at Zhongdu Bridge, when chaos descended.
Lin Xiansheng fled in a wretched state. Du Chongwei, the Khitans, the mysterious figure in the tent—they "defeated" none of them.
As the Khitan soldiers struck in their moment of victory and the refugees stood defenseless, Xiao Heyi threw that sword to wake his friend.

It was a gift they had exchanged as children. A precious blade for a friend, to walk the path together.
"I promise: as long as you stand, I will not fall."
"Leaving home, roaming the world, heading to the front—no matter the task, I am with you."
Then, sword light surged like the endless cycle of Tai Chi; with two blades, they repelled an entire army.
A new sword formation was born, and many lives were saved.
Later, the world of martial arts would say: "What luck to have such a pair of rising stars."

Nicknamed the "bubble fish," the river pufferfish lives in freshwater. With its rounded body tapering to a narrow tail, it has long held a dangerous allure. As early as the Qin and Han dynasties, it was said: "To eat it is to risk death." Yet its soft, snow-white flesh is considered a supreme delicacy. So much so that scholars and nobles have praised it across the centuries, willingly gambling with fate for a single taste. Lan He journeyed south through Jingchu, gathering inspiration and composing music, losing all track of time.

One day, he noticed the local music shamans all wore red tassels and asked them why. "Cinnabar is the purest yang," one replied, "able to commune with the God of Music. Red cord wards off evil and draws the god's favor."

Longing for the Snowplum siblings, Lan He bought cinnabar to dye silk and crafted a tassel each for the guqin and the flute, stringing several silver bells from their ends.

Months later, he returned to the Ba Bridge, but the old friends were nowhere to be found. He hung the cinnabar tassels on the gnarled boughs of an ancient plum tree and left.

The next day, the siblings arrived and heard faint music drifting from the branches. The wind had stirred the bells, drawing out a sound like the hollow breath of a flute. They took down the tassels and fastened them to their own instruments, knowing then that though their friend was far away, he had not forgotten them.

For those whose hearts are in tune, words are not always needed. The world is wide enough to be a home, and when the spirit finds its echo, the kindred soul will come.

Cai Jingxing had thought about dying more than once. Each time the thought grew near, the faces and voices of his old regulars stopped him.
"Cai, with hands like yours, even if the oven's gone, you'll still be a fine cook."
Right, even if his meat bun stall was smashed, even if he couldn't cook meat, he could still make some vegetarian dishes, porridge, and rice. In such a vast world, as a cook, he could always make something for everyone to eat. A good cook feeds whole families. One life keeps dozens alive.
So he fell in with the refugees. At first, there were still rabbits in the brush and fish in the streams; he could rustle up something to eat and keep hope alive, thinking the war would end before long. Then the Khitan took Hutuo River. No more fishing, no more game. He began making soups from wild greens, telling himself that when the plants ran out, the fighting would be over.
But the plants ran out, and the war did not. People started digging for any roots they could find; they scraped at clay from riverbanks. Some of those roots and soils were poisonous. Men who ate them would convulse, foam at the mouth, and never wake again.
After a lifetime at the cutting board, Cai knew enough to recognize names and symptoms: the so‑called "Guanyin clay," the bitter, life‑binding broths that ate at the body.
He understood what those things would do. He also understood what not eating them would do. Hunger was immediate and absolute.
But there was no choice, neither for him nor for the people who followed him.

Cai Jingxing felt the same way. From a young age, he had been learning to make meat buns from the old master in the village. Cai Jingxing just smiled, saying he wasn't going anywhere. For him, the greatest happiness was simply staying right here, keeping his parents company, staying by the villagers who had watched him grow up, and making delicious food for everyone every day.
Cai Jingxing held onto this kind of happiness for over twenty years. He was so happy that he sometimes thought it wouldn't matter even if he remained a bachelor for his whole life; so happy that he believed these peaceful days could last for another twenty or thirty years.
Until the warhorses of the Khitan trampled his stall to pieces with a single hoof, and set the entire village ablaze, including, of course, the home he had lived in for over forty years.

By the time I hid away this silver, you had already been with me for years. I watched you grow from a tiny little thing into a fine young man taller than I am. It seems "Little Coin" was a fitting nickname all along. Just like my strings of coins, you kept growing longer by the year.

Now that you are all grown, you need a proper name to match, just as I, Qian Duoduo, have one of my own. That day when you came to ask me about it, you said perhaps you should take the shopkeeper's surname and call yourself Qian Chizi. Rich enough by the sound of it, you said. Stubborn boy. Not a bit of flexibility in you. You never cared much for keeping accounts, and were always fonder of riding horses. Why insist on taking a name after me?
To my mind, Chi is a fine character, so I secretly wrote it down and tucked it beneath your pillow. Whether you ever found it, I couldn't say.

You were always saying your shopkeeper was too stingy with you, that your monthly wages were pitifully small. Hah. That only showed how green you still were. I was teaching you to save.
What I gave you was more generous than what you would have gotten anywhere else. It only looked like less in your hand because I had already set part of it aside for you. Money for sickness, money for a house, money for your old age. One must start saving early, so that money may in time make more money, and a man may go through life free of worry.

Enough. By the time you read this letter, I expect I will already be old, and you will have made a name for yourself. When that day comes, if fame is yours and this windfall has also fallen into your hands, remember to thank me properly for my foresight. And do not call me stingy ever again.

During the Tang and Song dynasties, when fisheries flourished, tender perch became the favored choice for this refined delicacy. The art of raw fish reached its golden age then, defined by freshness and flawless knife work.

Sogdians never make losing deals. Back then, she spent the caravan's entire savings to build the Pearl Boat, having secured channels with the Bodchen, Utuk, and others. All she needed was the protection of the Tang garrison. She heard that army was dirt poor. If a deal could be struck, profits would multiply a hundredfold. 

Yet the Tang people actually doubted Sogdians' business acumen.

"How can you not believe me?" Kang Zhenzhu blocked Guo Xin at the pass. "Your meager pay is useless! Give me your silver and your army's seal, and I'll trade jade to the Utuk. Tenfold returns, I promise!"

"Kang, you can't win forever in this world."

"General Guo, you lead troops to victory every day. Why doubt I can turn a sure profit?"

"Battles can be lost too... When they are, we defend with our lives."

"..."

Kang Zhenzhu swallowed her anger, reminding herself: This man is her pass on the Silk Road. She needed to please the Bodchen, grease palms in Utuk, and never offend the Tang...

She forced a smile. "General, rest assured, not a coin of tax will go unpaid! I only want to make us both rich..."

"Even if we lose money, I'll sell everything to make it right!"

"Pay your taxes. But no investments, no seal."

Guo Xin's expression didn't flicker.

That night, Kang Zhenzhu hauled a jug of wine up the city wall. Moonlight stretched the general's shadow long. Cups clinked as they drank, round after round, calling each other "friend" with every toast... 

Yet still, the deal fell through.

Instead, half-drunk and hazy, she signed a new contract: she, a rootless Sogdian merchant, would fund well-digging for the Tang! The wells were for her fellow traders, sure, and the watered oasis would become a Sogdian hub. But that Han general's talk of moons and homelands felt like flatbread forever out of reach. Who knew if she'd profit or lose?

Was Sogdian business prowess truly to fail this time?

Drunk, Kang Zhenzhu leaned against her camel. Through the haze, she seemed to see poplar shadows dancing in the moonlight. And suddenly... she felt certain this deal would pay off after all.

He was only ten when he was brought back to Dragonbend Academy. That was the age for running wild and going wherever your feet could take you. Instead, he was holed up there.
The more he thought about it, the more it annoyed him. He had already done the hard part. He had lured away the trafficker named Ma, gotten those children out, and led them along the river. If they had just kept moving, they could have reached safety in a few days. He had talked the whole way to keep them from crying, joked until his throat went raw—and in the end, a man named He appeared and took them all off to this supposedly better place.
And yes, Dragonbend Academy was fine. The food was good. The rooms were good. It was also painfully boring!
So he immediately started looking for a way out.
During lessons, he bent over his paper and drew maps instead. Before long, he had the whole academy laid out in his head and was already thinking through the best way to sneak away. While the others trained, he climbed onto the roofs and watched the clouds and the mountain ridges, trying to judge which direction he should go once he was free. People were always telling him he couldn't sit still. In his heart, he only thought one thing: the world was far too big to spend a lifetime living in one place.
That winter, he found his chance. He stole a horse and rode off alone. He made it a fair distance, too—until he came across a village struck by disease. He couldn't just leave it like that. Maybe he understood too well what it meant to be trapped with nowhere left to go. In the end, he turned back and went to Dragonbend Academy for help. By the time he returned, both he and the horse were worn thin. He had already prepared himself to be punished. Instead, He placed a letter in his hand and told him another path had been arranged for him.
Before they parted, He told him: "Go. The world has its fair share of what's clean and what's foul. You ought to see both for yourself."
He left in high spirits, quick and light on his feet, and tossed back only one bright shout: "Farewell!"
That was how he joined the Wayfarers, and at last won the life he had wanted—the freedom to walk the world on his own two feet. From then on, people called him Bingshen.

But that kind of life did not last. Before he had gone far enough to really know the world, he was sent to Toilgrain Barn to wait for someone.
He waited too long. So long that all the noise around him seemed to pour straight into his head without end: merchants shouting prices, women weeping, children crying, hoofbeats pounding down from the north. He was nearly frantic, but he still had to stay where he was. So he started drawing. Roads that might still serve as retreat routes. Passes that might still be defended. Troops that would arrive too late... The more he drew, the whiter his hair became. In the end, even drawing was no longer enough. If he wanted to know the land, he had to go out and see it for himself. So he set off for the Hutuo River. And when the person he had been waiting for finally arrived, he barely cared anymore. Fine. Take the map. Let that be the end of it.
It should have ended there. But all along the road, people kept stopping him, people with nowhere left to run—old men, women, children.
Every time he pointed one group toward safety, another gathered around him. Every time he told himself he had to leave, someone else begged him to show them a way out. He couldn't bear to do nothing and leave them out to die. Just a little farther, he kept thinking. I'll get this group through, then I'll turn back. I'm fast. I can still make it. So he kept going. And by the time the last group had been settled, everything was already lost.
Zhongdu Bridge had fallen. The academy was gone. Even He—the man who had always seemed to know what to do—was dead.
And in the end, Bingshen was the one left with nowhere to go.
What clean and foul was there left to speak of in a world like that? There was nothing in front of him but ash.

He returned alone to Moonlit Knoll.
That was the very place where he had once left Dragonbend Academy behind. If he had not left back then, would things have ended differently?
The rain came down in sheets. He shut his ears, closed his mouth, and stopped moving. Since there was no answer to be found, then he would walk no farther.
So he stayed there, and the rain kept going. Until one day, someone came.
He didn't look up at first. And yet before that person, even the pounding rain seemed to fall in silence. Only when his long hair was cut away did he finally look clearly and understand. The road to Zhongdu Bridge that he had failed to take had been taken by someone else in his place. And when that person left, they told him to go back out into the world—just as his old teacher once had.
The parting he had regretted all his life had, in the end, led him to this meeting on the road.
When the rain finally passed, the wind rose behind him on Moonlit Knoll, as if gently urging him onward.
Why shouldn't a man become the wind? The wind has no fixed home, and yet everyone who comes and goes can still feel where it has passed.
So he chose to walk again. This time, he would go where the wind went, and open a road toward a better world.
And this time, instead of farewell, he said only, softly, in his heart: Till we meet again.

Perception Forest has special combat rules: Players' own development attributes and items will not take effect inside the match. 
You need to pick up weapons, Inner Ways, Mystic Skills, medicines, and other items inside the match to strengthen yourselves. There are four qualities of various items: white, blue, purple, and gold. The higher the quality, the stronger the effect. 
As the match progresses, the area where players can move will shrink, and the miasma outside the area will spread. Players who enter the miasma will continuously lose HP. To defeat other players, you'll need to equip high quality gear, coordinate your skills, and choose reasonable movement paths based on the style of battle. 
At the same time, the items in the bag will be converted into Sin Leaves according to their quality and quantity at the end of the match, which can be exchanged for rare rewards in the shop.

However, in the 4th year of the Kaiyun Reign (947 CE) of the Jin Dynasty, when the Khitan attacked the city, this area was pillaged and burned, causing countless civilian casualties. Subsequently, constrained by lack of manpower and resources, it remained unrepaired, gradually becoming a dilapidated settlement for the poor. The city's elite shunned it completely. Moreover, due to a "corner gate" in its southeast, it earned the derogatory name "Forsaken Quarter".

记录人：丁小柳\n监查对象：鸿胪寺少卿 吕从善\n事由：前朝留用官员，需观察可有:
Recorded by: Ding Xiaoliu

Subject: Lyu Congshan, Deputy Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial

Reason: A holdover from the previous dynasty. Watch for any sign of disloyalty.



Second Month, Day 4

Started tailing Lyu Congshan today. The chief says he might be hiding something.

From what I can tell, he is not hiding anything. He is just sick in the head.



Today he was attending Lord Wang at the Privy Council. Lord Wang thought the tea was too hot and snapped a curse under his breath.

Lyu Congshan jumped like his tail was on fire and started fanning the teacup with his sleeve.

He fanned so hard the dust flew right into the tea.



Lord Wang took one look and his face went green. He flicked his sleeve in disgust.

Lyu Congshan was standing so close he got knocked flat.



Did he get mad? No.

He rolled once on the ground, popped right back up, and praised, "My lord, what power in your arm. One sweep like that, and you show the might of Great Song!"

Lord Wang stared at him like he was an idiot and walked off.



Second Month, Day 14

This morning I watched Lyu Congshan pawn a family jade pendant, all to buy a painting.

He carried it to the residence of Hanlin Academician Li Mingyuan.



He waited at the gate for two hours in the freezing cold, nose running the whole time.

Lord Li glanced at it and called it "third-rate" and "vulgar beyond measure."



Lyu Congshan froze on the spot. He clearly wanted to praise the thing, but he did not dare argue with Lord Li.

He stammered for ages and could not squeeze out a single proper sentence.

In the end, they got tired of him and threw him out.

I was up on a roof beam watching, and even I felt exhausted for him.



Third Month, Day 1

Today was even worse.



At Sun Yang Tavern, Lyu Congshan ran into an instructor from the Palace Guard.

The man was drunk, bragging that his boots were filthy and no one ever wiped them for him.



Lyu Congshan did not hesitate. He squatted down and started polishing the man’s boots.

In broad daylight. With people staring from all sides.

If I did not have to stay hidden, I would have dragged him away myself.



The instructor sobered up halfway, probably realized how it looked, and kicked Lyu Congshan off.

Then he cursed him for being spineless and a disgrace to Great Song.

I cannot say he was wrong.



Third Month, Day 15

Nearly two months of watching is enough.

Conclusion: no treason in him, and no ability for office either.



He claws at every powerful sleeve for one reason only: to stay alive.

He wants a master to tie himself to, because he thinks that is the only way to be safe.

Annoying to watch, but not dangerous.



Further surveillance unnecessary.

话说这江湖上凡是读过话本子的， 恐怕鲜有几人未听过“太湖梨膏糖”的声名。“太湖梨:
In the jianghu, anyone who's read a storybook or two has surely heard of the name "Taihu Pear Syrup." Famous for their keen grasp of martial world gossip and masterful storytelling, Candy Lady created beloved works like Tyrannical Warrior: Dao Lord and I'd Gladly Be a Hound for the Lady of Nine Mortal Ways. Yet ever since the sudden rise of Lament Scriptorium, Candy Lady's popularity has been in decline every day. To compete with Lamentation Heavens, Candy Lady picked up the pace and churned out tale after tale. Only to unwittingly reveal clues to their true identity between the lines.

After countless secret investigations conducted by devoted storybook fans, the truth finally came to light: the romantic wordsmith behind Candy Lady was none other than Han Yanluo, the famed "Ice-Faced Fairy" of the Masked Troupe. The news stunned the jianghu. Then again, in hindsight, "Candy Lady," "Masked Troupe", the hints were there all along. Since its founding, the Masked Troupe had been devoted to dramatizing the legends of the martial world, crafting countless poignant classics. Yet in recent years, their output dwindled, overshadowed by the Lamentation Heavens. As a direct disciple of the Masked Troupe's master, how could Han Yanluo not be anxious? Her feverish writing was likely her way of proving that Masked Troupe is still the king of all storybooks, an effort both lamentable and admirable.
话说这陈子奚刚与江晏相识不久，便发现他总在读一本书。江晏白天读、晚上读、喝酒时读:
Shortly after meeting Jiang Yan, Chen Zixi noticed his constant reading. Day and night. While drinking. Every spare moment. Assuming it must be thrilling martial arts tales, Chen grew offended. Keeping such entertainment to himself meant Jiang Yan didn't consider them friends! The outrage! Thus, Chen had no choice but to demand a look.

"Sect secrets are not for outsiders." Jiang's refusal was firm, which only made Zixi more curious. Was it some scandalous sect history? Forbidden knowledge? The itch of not knowing was unbearable. So when Yan was asleep, Zixi stole the book from his pack. No title. Worn cover. Utterly unremarkable. Then he opened it. Page after page of densely packed blade techniques. This was what had Jiang so obsessed? A manual of blade skills? The man was either fascinating or painfully dull.

The next morning, Jiang opened his book to find new annotations:
"Note: Are you sure it's not 'Book of Heaven'? This is incomprehensible."
"Note: Even if you shared this, no one would care. Rest easy."
"Note: I finished it. Still don't understand. No need to keep reading."
"Note: Drinks, Jiang Yan?"

Jiang frowned and looked up at Chen. Zixi fanned himself lazily.

"Drinks, Jiang Yan?"

诶，真是可怜见的。瞧瞧我的花儿，都被你糟蹋成了什么样！: Oh, such a pity. Look at my flowers. What a mess you've made of them!
诶，石家大闺女是不是去墨城好久没回来啦？: Hasn't the Shi family's eldest girl been in Mohist City for ages? She hasn't come back in a while.

诶，等等！二打一？: Wait, hold on! Two against one?
诶，算了，你先把这些钱拿着。: Oh, forget it. You take this money first.
诶，给你准备的可是最后一碗了。: Hey, this is the last bowl just for you.
诶，老大是大侠，我是小侠，这么一说，我这女侠的称号，也非浪得虚名嘛！: A great hero and a small one! I didn't earn this heroine title for nothing, you know!
Hm... A great hero and a younger one... You know, I didn't earn this heroine title for nothing!

诶，药药你看，咱们就按这个方子来！: Yaoyao, look! Let's follow this recipe!
诶，要的要的，大侠，请。: No no, I insist! After you. Please!
诶，记住了啊，下值后来此处找我，好好教教你！: Remember to come find me here after your shift, and I'll show you the ropes.
诶，说不定人家相信后人的“智慧”呢！再说了，你管他怎么想的呢，替别人瞎操什么心，: Hey, maybe he believes in "future wisdom"! Besides, why do you care what he thinks? Don't worry about Song's business. The higher-ups mustn't know!
诶，说了多少次，我没这么想，阿娘也不根本不在乎。: Aw, I said a bunch of times, this isn't what I wanted. Mother doesn't care about this one bit either.
诶，诶……坐着，坐一会儿就不疼了。娘去跟人家换个鞋回来。: Ah... sit down for a bit. You'll feel better once you rest. I'll go see if I can trade something for a pair of shoes.
诶，诶呀，二位御史大人怎么来了？这个时候你们不是应该……: C-Censors? What are you doing here? You're not supposed to—
诶，诶！亲家实在不必如此……这孩子本性不坏……: Whoa, whoa! There's really no need for that... He's not a bad kid at heart...
诶，诶，你可别又给我哭鼻子。: Now wait, don't go crying on me again.
诶，诶，小祖宗们哟~天哥儿往这儿来，来……: Hey now, my little masters. Come here, Tian'er...
诶，诶，诶！小后生，那曲谱可看不得啊！: Hey, hey, hey! Hands off that music score, young one!
诶，谁叫我等了这些日子，能与我共奏的人就你一个呢？: Oh, whose fault is it that I waited all these days? Now the only one who can play with me is you...
诶，谁说不是呢！整个营地的车马都我一个人修，骡子都不敢这么使！: Ain't that the truth. Every busted wheel, every lame horse in this camp... me. Just me! I'm telling you, they wouldn't work a mule this hard.
诶，还是得看上一看，才知道那异宝是何物啊！: Well, we'll only know for sure once we take a look!
诶，这不是重点！要我说呀，少东家你是真的细心: But that's not the point! What I'm saying is, you're really thoughtful.
诶，这个手绢……是陆婆婆做的吗？: This handkerchief... did Granny Lu make this?
诶，这么一说，好像是有些道理。那你打算怎么做？: Actually, that makes sense. So what's the plan?
诶，这位兄台，今日辽人比武的擂台设在何处啊？: Hey there, could you tell me where today's Liao martial arts matches are held?
诶，这便要走了吗？这场群英会还未至高潮，你便不再看了吗？: Leaving so soon? The Heroes Assembly has just begun. Won't you stay and watch?
诶，这儿怎这么多石头？: Why are there so many rocks here?
诶，这后面是官差休息的班房，可别走错啊。: Ah, the back rooms are for officials. Don't wander.
诶，这玉鸭子有意思。: Hey, this jade duck is intriguing.
诶，这腰饰也是新买的吗？真是凸显少东家非凡的品味呢！: Is that belt ornament new too? It shows off your taste, really!
诶，这身行头——你是武德司的？: Hold on, that uniform... you're with the Imperial Service?
诶，这里可不一样！这条溪里的鱼儿，肉肥刺少，附近的小猫精得很，试了一口就知道排队: Oh, this spot's special! Fat fish, soft bones. The local cats caught on quick. One taste, and now they queue up like proper little gentlemen!
诶，这里怎么走出去？: Hey, how do we get out of here?
诶，这里果然暗藏玄机。: Just as I thought. There's something hidden here.
诶，那哪有逗你有意思？: Hey, that's nowhere near as fun as messing with you!
诶，那边屋顶怎么摔下个人？这身影……: Did someone just fall off that roof? That silhouette...
诶，那边的小哥稍待——！: Hey, you over there! Wait a moment—!
诶，都说男儿薄情，女儿薄幸。: *Sigh* It's like they say, men are fickle with affection, and women unlucky with love.
诶，马老板那我可就直说了——我的情况您也知道，外头来开封讨生活的，根不在这儿。: I'll be straight with you, Ma. You know my situation: I came to Kaifeng to make a living, but my roots aren't here.
诶？$T(2001)，你是不是也对我们的计划感兴趣？: Hm? $T(2001), don't tell me you're interested in our plan too?
诶？不再考虑考虑了么，还有呢……: Are you sure? There's more to see...
诶？不是威业么？怎么今天的货送完，来这里喝酒啦？: Huh? Weiye? You're drinking here? Finished your deliveries?
诶？不是说要较量……？: Eh? Didn't we say we'd battle it out...?
诶？什么声音，好像有人在唱曲？: Huh? What's that sound? It's… someone singing?
诶？你听殿前那啥动静？又在为年尾那大典操演了？: Hear that from the front hall? Are they rehearsing for the year-end ceremony again?
诶？你是……？少侠，是你吗，是我，冯继升！我被关在那石窟后面！: Eh? Young wanderer, is that you? It's me, Feng Jisheng! I'm trapped behind the stone!
诶？你是怎么把门打开的？！先前唤人来修，都说得将门给拆了，这才迟迟没修呢！: How did you get that door open?! The repairmen all said they'd have to tear it off the hinges, and that's why nobody's fixed it!
诶？你是认真的吗？好不容易得来的缘分……: Eh? Are you serious? The bond we worked so hard for...
诶？你看到康延了吗，一个穿着黄绿色衣服的年轻窣利人，他刚才念念有词地往沙丘那边跑: Hey? Did you see Kang Yan? A young Suli man dressed in yellowish-green clothes. He was chanting something as he ran towards the sand dunes...
诶？你说，会不会你姐姐也去找她的师父鸦去了？: Hm? Do you think your sister is looking for Master Crow?
诶？你身后的那个是宝剑吗？！你有宝剑！你是大侠？！: Huh? Is that a sword you're carrying? You have a sword!? Are you one of those great heroes?!
诶？你还帮我……呸……帮我也捡啦？谢啦！呸呸……: Huh? You picked up my things too? Thanks!
诶？别走啊！不喜欢哪里咱可以改……: Wait, don't go! We can change whatever you don't like...
诶？千年渡的仙人吗……小云知道，小云知道！: Huh? The immortal of the Millennium Crossing? I know, I know!
诶？卖浆的小贩呢，怎么没有看到了？: Huh? Where did the juice vendor go?
诶？咱荷包呢？: Huh? Where did my purse go?
诶？哦哦。（浮夸）诶呀我的脚~好痛啊~: Ohhhhh, my foot! It hurts so much!
诶？大侠！大侠！你是来救我们的吗！: Huh? Hey, Great Hero! Are you here to save us?
诶？大侠，你回来啦~你了解完容鸢姐姐了吗~: Oh! Great hero, you're back! Did you learn more about Sister Murong Yuan?
诶？大侠，你怎么看？: Huh? What do you think, wanderer?
诶？大坏蛋，还妮儿的宝贝！: Hey! You villain, give back the girl's treasure!
诶？少侠不知道么，都是巴蜀给咱大宋进贡的东西。: Huh? Don't you know? It's all tribute from Shu to our Great Song.

诶？怎么走了，我话还没问完……: Why are you leaving already? I still had more to say...
诶？您还没问，我也没答，怎么就……: Wait. But you haven't asked, and I haven't answered. How did this happen?
诶？我的墨筹呢？怎么又不见了。: Where are my Tallies? They're gone again.
诶？我的荷包怎么在这？: My purse! How did it end up over here?
诶？收铁钱？你从哪里听说的？: Collecting iron coins? Where'd you hear that?

诶？是撞到我了么？: Did you just bump into me?
诶？武德司的大人，您来得正好！: Oh! Someone from the Imperial Service, just in time!
诶？神、神神神神神鹅，这这这……是什么意思？: F-f-fish? D-Divine Goose, wh-what does that mean?
诶？竟然发生这种事。: Well, I never thought something like this would happen.
诶？老大你去哪儿？不管那个怪花了么~: Huh? Where are you going? What about that odd flower?
诶？诗诗，你不弹琴了？: Huh? You're not playing the zither anymore?
诶？还真是，怎么方才没发现……: Huh? You're right. How did I miss that before?

诶？那个留信说，要请我吃饭的人就是你啊。: Wait, the one who left that note about buying me a meal? That was you?

诶？那石头上是不是有一只妙妙喵……？又找着一只。: Hey, is that a Meow Meow on that stone? Found another one.

诶？阿奶？……你怎么……睡在地上……: Granny? Why are you... sleeping on the ground?
诶？鹞长老，你没把我们偷跑出来的事告诉鹏长老吧？: Wait. Elder Harrier, you didn't tell Elder Peng that we snuck out, did you?
诶？默契这种事，还是要加强一些哦！: Hmm? Your coordination still needs work though.
诶？！师妹，快看前面，前面的路自个儿连上了！: Look! The path ahead just connected on its own!

Dear Mountain Dwellers and Fellow Disciples,
A strange mystery solved, and one less thing to worry about.
Have you noticed? The strange noises in the mountains have been gone for days now.
Some have asked whether I was the one who solved it. So let's clear that up: not quite. The mysterious sounds were caused by the renovation of the Harmony Troupe, and with help from #Y$N#E, they've finally come to an end.
.

Yu Ge: "...We never meant to disturb the peace of the mountain. Our humblest apologies. Those strange noises came from my grandfather's Voice Box. They weren't meant to scare anyone. From now on, we'll rehearse in a proper designated place. Oh, and our club president is #Y$N#E, who's both musically gifted and incredibly kind. We'd love for everyone to join us and share in the joy of singing."
...
In short, this little mystery is now wrapped up. The Bureau of Relief is happy to see the Harmony Troupe back on its feet, and we wish them all the best going forward!

贺家先祖贺怀智曾为唐玄宗时梨园乐师，为坐部伎之首，擅琵琶。安史之乱后，贺家来到湖:
He family's ancestor, He Huaizhi, was an excellent pipa player who led the seated musical division in Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's Masked Troupe Orchestra. After the An Lushan Rebellion, the He family went into seclusion in Huzhou, turning to farming as they grew increasingly conservative. He Huaizhi's stone pipa was sealed in a cellar, forgotten until the eldest son of the He family discovered it.

The son had rebelled against tradition since childhood. Disdaining poetry and classics, he obsessed over operatic tales and the line, "A smile brings eternal spring, a tear invokes endless sorrow." He cast off his given name, insisting everyone call him "Wanchun". Intrigued by the pipa's peculiar aged appearance, he struggled to pluck at its strings, only to find them made of an unknown and impossibly tough metal. Despite being too weak to play a single note, he grew determined. Sneaking into the cellar daily, he strained to play until, after days of effort, he accidentally vibrated the thinnest string. Its melody lingered, deeper and more resonant than any he'd heard, captivating him utterly. Soon, he could play all five strings. He played recklessly, unaware the harmonics pierced the cellar walls and startled the village. During the family's mourning period, his conservative father flew into a rage, ordering the pipa smashed. But its body resisted rocks and fire alike, so he threw it off a cliff outside the village to curb his son's musical obsession. Wanchun fell gravely ill, fueling rumors that he was a pipa spirit in human form. His father grew distant, and Wanchun withered, losing his childhood plumpness.

By some twist of fate, an opera troupe came to perform in the village. When Wanchun went to watch, he found himself increasingly drawn to the performers during their conversations. Realizing he was overlooked and unappreciated at home, within the clan, and in the village, he decided it was better to strike out with the troupe. With a flick of his sleeves, he left home and wandered the world with them.

At a musical contest in Weiyang City, a theater master unveiled a Tang Dynasty pipa, carved entirely from stone. He Wanchun recognized it instantly: This was his family's pipa. He demanded its return, but the theater master, having paid a fortune for it, refused. As they argued, a man in his thirties appeared with a smile. "The true owner of this pipa can play it," he said. "Since both claim it, let each prove it with a song." The theater master, confident in his skill, went first. But the stone pipa was impossibly heavy. He could barely lift it. Propping it against the ground, he plucked at its strings, succeeding only in cutting his fingers. He Wanchun laughed, hoisted the pipa onto his shoulder, and strummed wildly. The notes rang for miles, though hardly melodious. Humiliated, the theater master ordered his men to seize the pipa and break He Wanchun's hands. Outnumbered, He Wanchun fought back, until the stranger intervened, revealing himself as Hu Changyi, acting master of the Masked Troupe.

Hu Changyi purchased the pipa and told He Wanchun that if he wanted it back, he must return to the Masked Troupe with him. He Wanchun had no choice but to agree. Upon arriving at the Masked Troupe, he first began studying music but ended up snapping 300 pipa strings and breaking 50 ramskin drums. He damaged every instrument in the Dewfall Barge: flutes, guqins, ruan lutes, panpipes, ramskin drums, bili pipes, yu pipes, fangxiang, pipas, and clappers. The Dewfall Barge's music master finally lost patience, deciding the boy had no musical talent and transferring him to the Snowswirl Barge where He Wanchun trained in song and dance with junior disciples, but his tone-deaf singing wrecked every melody. After several disasters, the dance master ordered him to focus only on group performances. His muscular build and gangly limbs made him anything but "light as swirling snow" in dance, and his powerful movements often meant accidental collisions with his partners. He managed modest success only in sword dances and character formation dances, while his peers avoided him like the plague. The Snowswirl Barge's dance master concluded he lacked rhythmic talent altogether. Noticing his strength, they assigned him to carry instruments and set up stages across the pavilions.

He Wanchun grew deeply frustrated, thinking he might as well return to wandering with his old opera troupe. That night, he carried the stone pipa to the lakeshore and played, pouring all his pent-up frustration into the music. Unaware of how much louder the stone pipa was than ordinary ones, his playing rippled across the water, disturbing the entire Masked Troupe's sleep and awakening Hu Changyi, who was drinking at Zephyr Pavilion. Following the sound, he found He Wanchun and learned of his struggles. Astonished, he tested He Wanchun and discovered his long, powerful fingers, keen ear, and sharp memory, ideal traits for a musician. How could the Dewfall Barge masters declare him untalented? The truth emerged when he understood He Wanchun's history with the stone pipa: Crafted by He Huaizhi, its extreme weight and rigid strings had taught the boy only brute force as a child, preventing him from mastering the subtle control needed for other instruments. His talent had been stifled by starting with the wrong tool.

Thereafter, Hu Changyi ordered He Wanchun to return to the Dewfall Barge, but with a strict condition: He must hold a chicken egg in his hand while playing. If the egg broke, it meant he was using too much force. He would only be allowed to formally study music when he could complete a piece without cracking the egg, and he was forbidden from touching the stone pipa until then. It took a full year for He Wanchun to play an entire piece with the egg intact. From there, his progress surged as he mastered every instrument and score in the Dewfall Barge. Once he could play ordinary instruments with skill, Hu returned the stone pipa to him, again requiring the chicken egg to be held. Three years later, He Wanchun finally played a piece with the stone pipa from start to finish without breaking the egg, and Hu Changyi declared him fully trained. The closest He Ran ever came to General Wang Qing was the day they met. A group of beggar kids stumbled into the path of a general's procession, horses tall and gleaming.
 Back then, they were all more or less the same. One might be half a head taller, another had a few extra bites of steamed bun. Jiang Yan was just one of them, a hot-tempered boy, maybe a bit shorter than the rest.
 But when Jiang Yan stepped forward, clutching his wooden sword, brash and proud, he seemed the sort least likely to survive in this world. Yet the general, seated high on his horse, favored him.

 Years later, He Ran would chew on Jiang Yan's words over and over again. In dreams, he returned to that day. But this time, he was the one who stepped forward, said those words, stood before the crowd. This way, he would've become the boy chosen by the general, instead of Jiang Yan, wouldn't he?
 He would've stood at the general's side. And unlike Jiang Yan, he wouldn't chase cats around the courtyard and come back filthy. He'd be the obedient one. He wouldn't drink. Wouldn't cause trouble. Wouldn't leave the general frowning at constant complaints, helpless to defend him. He would've done much better than Jiang Yan. He knew it.

 In the dream, he looked up, and the general was smiling at him, calling his name. He smiled back, instinctively, about to answer...
 Rain fell from the eaves, and the dream shattered. He woke up, leaning against the wall of a ruined temple. The puddle on the ground mirrored a blood-smeared face.
 A long sword in his grip, one that cut off a head today. A gunny sack by his feet, with that head in it. He stared blankly at the drying blood on the blade. Yes... it was one of the men who killed the general. He remembered now.
 Three days ago, his general had died.

 He leaned on his sword and stepped outside. The rain was still falling.
 Inside the ruined temple, rain dripped silently from the roof. Each bead of red-streaked water splashing against the floor like tears from the earth.
 He knew dreams couldn't change fate.
 He just didn't understand why even the sky, full of rain, refused to let him keep a single dream whole.

Jumper was a stray who found his purpose as a guard dog. He still carries the faint memory of that rainy night when a boy carried him home. The house was warm, dry, and smelled of meat. Jumper had only ever watched such a place from a distance, never daring to approach.
His favorite game with the boy was "Jump High." No matter how high the little hand reached, Jumper would leap and tap it, steady every time.
Years passed. The boy grew up, and Jumper went from pup to old dog. His master no longer stayed home all day. He left each morning and returned at night, sighing, rubbing his back, worn thin by the world.
But every day before leaving, he would look back at Jumper. At first, Jumper thought it was time for Jump High; he'd try to leap, though his strength was failing. But his master never raised his hand. Instead, each morning, he bent down and held Jumper close.

Once across this river, she would be home at last.
Xiuxiu gazed at the flickering campfires on the far bank, lost in a daze. Seldom had she looked upon her home from such a vantage.
Beyond lay the old well at the village entrance; there, the narrow path leading to her door; and there... the river flats where she used to bide her time, waiting for her father.
In years past, when Father came to the south bank to reap the wheat, she would sit there and wait. Whenever fear found her in her solitude, she would sing the tune he had taught her. Hearing it, he would harmonize with her, never pausing in his toil.
"Who planted the Sal tree in the heavens high? Who carved the Yellow River beneath the sky?"
It was upon these same river flats, on that night of flight and chaos, that she raised her voice in that song once more.
With the distant thunder of hooves and wailing still echoing, she knew not where to turn, nor what remained for her to do.
Gazing at the wheat fields on the far shore, she unconsciously hummed the familiar air.
The waters still echoed; the wind still joined in. Yet her father, who once sang back from across the river, was gone forever.
"The Queen Mother planted the Sal tree high; The Dragon King carved the river beneath the sky."
A faint voice nearby suddenly took up the refrain. Could it be Father? But he...
Xiuxiu traced the sound, only to find a child separated from his kin. Hearing the tune, the child realized she was no foreign invader, but a fellow villager.
Throughout that night, Xiuxiu's song drifted fitfully along the bank. More and more souls recognized the melody, slowly huddling together by her side.
"To the encampment!" Xiuxiu cried. Beholding her neighbors finding one another in the moonlight through that shared song, her restless heart found a new wellspring of courage.
The melody drifted from the north bank to the south.
Within the encampment, those who listened grew in number, as did those who joined the refrain: children roused by the thunder of hooves, unable to return to sleep; valiant warriors wounded in the struggle against the foreign invaders; and the aunties who labored beside her over the soup kettles...
"Lift your voice in song, and stride boldly forth!"
Xiuxiu recalled the words Father always spoke upon his return from the fields. That air had done more than banish her own dread; it had guided a multitude through the vast, endless night.
Some, heartened by the song, took their rest and found the resolve to journey further south.
Others, singing in cadence and marking the beat, drank deep and found strength in their grip and then turned toward the north.
And thereafter...
She looked upon those standing at her side. From every horizon they had gathered, ready to bridge the river and reclaim her homeland, inch by bloody inch.
They stood in hushed reverence, listening to her voice.
"Who stands watch beyond the Three Great Passes..."
Father, I have met many heroes and heroines. By their side, I... I, too, shall slay the foreign invaders. I will lead them northward to avenge you and to avenge all we have lost.
"Who left their home, ne'er to return..."
Father, once I reach the north bank and stand upon our soil, I shall rebuild our home stone by stone. I will plant wheat before our door; when you catch the fragrance of the grain and hear this melody, you will surely find your way back to us.

This Archery Jade named Perseverance was made by Raven, a parting gift for Halcyon when she left for the first time.

"Dear Halcyon, I know not when you will return. I only wish that this will remains unchanged... this heart unwavering."

Thus, when Halcyon wore this jade ring down the mountain, she was full of ambition.
With the martial art of the sword, with the skill of Mohist defense, she would surely protect the peace of a region.

Outside the mountains, she met a little mute. The little mute had no name, thin as a withered blade of grass in the wind. Yet the "withered grass" still struggled in the wind.

The little mute was very clever and very sensible. She never asked Halcyon where she came from, where she was going, or if she would ever return. She just studied desperately, studied desperately.

In just three days, the little mute could already make some simple traps. She gestured happily, meaning she could catch rabbits, wouldn't starve, and the big sister could leave with peace of mind.

A withered blade of grass like her, even nourished by rain, could never grow into a big tree.

Halcyon didn't understand why the little mute wouldn't go with her. But just then, she had matters to attend to outside the mountains. Before leaving, she thought and thought, then finally took off the jade ring and gave it to the little mute.

"The one who gave me this jade ring said wearing it helps keep the heart steadfast and the will clear. I'll lend it to you for a few days. If you change your mind and are willing to go with me, wear it to find me on the day I return."

But when Halcyon returned to the mountain, Raven didn't see the little mute mentioned in Halcyon's letter.

Halcyon said she went back to look, but the little mute was gone. The villagers said the little mute ran out and was bitten to death by wolves. But... but why was that jade ring being worn by someone else?

Raven looked at Halcyon's reddened eyes and asked no more.

He simply split the original jade ring in two, half for Halcyon, half for him.

"Willing to share half your burden."

Together in heart, together in mind, together in burden.

这里本该有多美啊，她真希望遍地都是红枫叶。\n可现实留给她的，只有满地染血的盔甲:
How beautiful this place should have been. She truly wished the ground were covered in red maple leaves.
But reality left her with nothing but blood-stained armor scattered across the earth.
Standing all alone upon this scorched earth, for a fleeting moment, she genuinely doubted: Does the Haven sought by the Mohist Hill truly exist in this world?
If one seeks it, can it actually be found? And even if it is, by then, will there be anyone left to share in the joy?
Human lives felt as fragile as withered leaves, unable to even survive the autumn.
A quiet, lonely chill crept into her otherwise unyielding heart.
Master once told her that life is like the four seasons, and autumn is always the shortest.
No matter how bitter, it will always pass swiftly.
She raised her head and gazed toward a place thousands of miles away, wondering what autumn must look like in the Hidden Mountain.
Were they, at this very moment, standing beneath real red maples, waiting for her just as they always did?
With that thought, she felt she could endure this autumn after all.

Lost, lost again! 
Left is wheat, right is wheat, front is wheat, back is wheat too! How am I supposed to tell north from south? Whoosh—there are always people sleeping in the wheat field day and night. I couldn't see clearly at night and stepped on someone by accident. She yelled "ghost," and I yelled "ghost" too. What a damned mess! 
But it's a funny way to make friends. I've stayed with the local villagers for days. Their high-rotation waterwheels move with water power, and those wheat baskets and sickles are so interesting! I helped them with loads of farm work—my back is killing me! But the food they gave me tasted amazing. 
They said Gracetown ahead serves Lily Bulb Noodles and Scallion Pancake. It's also Community Festival time! After finishing this baked pancake, I'm heading there. 
Heaven help me, don't let me get lost again!

Players must abide by Where Winds Meet General Tournament Rules. See the "General Tournament Rules" section on the official Where Winds Meet Tournament Center website. 

"Tempest" uses a Fair Balancing Mode. Wanderers can freely customize Skills, Inner Ways, and Mystic Skills. Stats are not affected by character progression (characters use unified fixed stats; Skills are Level 95, Inner Ways are Tier 6, Mystic Skills are Tier 6 Stage 9; Gear Sets, Tuning, and Attuning Effects are inactive). After the challenge starts, you can switch Skill loadouts and Divinecraft during the preparation phase.

In the Qualifiers, players must challenge 3 designated Bosses in order ("Puppeteer - Overture", "Nameless General", "Yi Dao"). Each Boss has 3 challenge attempts. You can only unlock the next Boss after completing the challenge for the current one. The shortest time among the 3 attempts is recorded as the best result; the Martial Arts combination used for this best result will be locked and cannot be reused in subsequent Boss challenges. The total score is the sum of the best times for all three Bosses.

In the Elimination Stage, players must consecutively challenge three fixed Bosses (Elimination Bosses: "Coffin Master", "General Nameless", "Yi Dao"). HP and medicine counts are inherited throughout the single run and do not reset. Completely different Martial Arts must be used for different Bosses (restriction applies only within a single run). Martial Arts and Divinecraft can be switched via Training and Bag during each Boss's preparation phase. Combat starts automatically after preparation. There are 3 challenge attempts, with the shortest total time taken as the final score. 

The Finals follow the same rules as the Elimination Stage. The final Boss will be announced on the day of the Finals.

Team Ranking Criteria (Priority):
Participants are ranked by wins (higher is better). If wins are equal, compare Net Score (Net Score = Total Game Wins - Total Game Losses); higher Net Score ranks higher. If Net Score is equal, compare the Head-to-Head result.

If three or more players have equal wins and Net Scores, calculate results only among these players using the rules above. If still indistinguishable, compare time taken for wins in the small cycle; shorter time ranks higher.

The Jade of Way once belonged to Murong Yuan's mother, Chu Yun, a former disciple of the Mohist School. 
In the chaos of war, a young girl lost everything. Clutching the wooden eagle her mother had crafted, she clung to life by a thread. With help from a kind soul, she learned to survive in the world. 
But the world is cruel. The one who once shielded her from the northern snows would eventually entrust her to someone else on another snowy night. Confused and hurt, she buried her doubts and turned her heart fully to the path of tool and craft. 
With talent and relentless study, Murong Yuan restored the very wooden eagle that once carried her to safety. 
In her pursuit of mastery, she scoured the land. 
When she learned that the Jade of Way she carried was an antique of the Mohist School, she realized she had found her path forward. 
She believed that one day, her flying eagle would soar in the sky and never fall again.
