On that night, a heavy snowstorm fell on Liangzhou, lasting three days and three nights. 
The spring water at Clear Jade Shore froze solid, and the bell of Purity Pagoda grew hoarse. Even the camels that could cross the Qilian Mountains couldn't withstand the extreme cold, freezing to death by the roadside of Jade Dew Terrace. 

Someone saw the princess holding a glazed candle holder, dressed in plain white with light makeup, walking step by step into imperial capital, never to look back. 
Frost and ice engulfed the entire imperial capital. In the end, the princess never returned to Chang'an, the city she missed day and night. 
Outside the Crane Retreat, the palace maids also dressed in white mourning clothes, holding hands and walking into the depths of the frozen Jade Pond. 

The heavy snow raged for three days, covering imperial capital in black ice. Three days later, concerned about the princess's safety, the people gathered at Chalice Peak by Jade Dew Terrace and called out to her loudly. Under the moonlight, imperial capital stood still like a glazed coffin. When the wind blew, the holes in the pagoda tower let out a whimpering sound. 
Grieving, the crowd tried to break the ice with sharp blades and enter. But there was no sign of the princess in imperial capital, only an elegant hairpin. 

Grateful for the princess's kindness, people regarded imperial capitak as the place closest to the moonlight. A winemaker tried to climb the tall tower and finally left his wine here. 
The elders, moved by the palace maids' loyalty to their mistress, erected a statue at the Crane Retreat by the Jade Pond in their memory.
那一天，我也在。\n我们老家有句话，只有死绝了的人，没有死绝了的买卖。\n仗打输:
I was there that day.
Where I come from, we say there's no such thing as a dead trade until every last trader is dead.
So what if the battle was lost? Broken swords can be melted down. Jade can be pawned. Armor can be cleaned and sold again. Pull a few wounded men out while you're at it, and they'll call you their savior for the rest of their lives. Only a fool leaves a battlefield empty-handed.
That said, even I knew not to push my luck. If I could come away with a good blade or two and keep breathing, that was good enough.

By the time I reached the north bank of the Hutuo River, rain had started falling. The air smelled of rust, wet dirt, and death. I looked over the bodies and remembered I'd killed men myself before, the foreign invaders, with nothing grander than a woodcutter's knife. People talk as if killing is simple. It isn't. A man's neck is tougher than it looks, and your own hand is softer than you'd think. Never mind that.
I was just about to start picking through the dead when I noticed someone still standing in the rain. He wore Jin armor and stood straight as a spear, but something about him was wrong. Too still. Too stiff.
Then Jiang Yan appeared. I dropped flat immediately. He had spared me once before, and if he caught me still making a living this way, I doubted he'd do it twice. He came through the rain with that plum-blossom sword in his hand. Fine steel. Beautiful blade. If I could get hold of it... well, great men always have more ways to live than the likes of me. Hard times are hard times, and I still had mouths to feed.
So I watched the sword and waited for my chance.
As Jiang Yan came closer, I finally got a clear look at the man in front of him. His eyes were wide open, but the pupils had gone gray. His face had turned a dead blue. He looked worse than the bodies at my feet. Even so, I knew that face.
Then I remembered. Back home once, the whole street had turned out to catch a glimpse of a hero. I'd done the same. It was Wang Qing. The man righteous folk admired, the general ordinary people trusted. That Wang Qing.

And then Jiang Yan drew his sword.
A sword does not leave the sheath for no reason. But seeing a good blade raised against a hero nearly made me break cover. People said Jiang Yan could kill a man in fewer than ten steps. That day, though, he walked so slowly it hurt to watch.
The rain hammered the ground between them. Five steps remained.
On the first step, General Wang shuddered and raised his head. For a moment, he looked almost alive again.
On the second, I heard a wet rasping sound. I couldn't tell where it was coming from. Then I saw something gray-blue moving in his throat.
On the third, his armor split open. That was when I understood. If Jiang Yan waited any longer, there would be nothing left of Wang Qing to save. That was why he had come. But if he drove that sword home, what would be left of Jiang Yan?
On the fourth, Jiang Yan raised the blade. Slowly. Too slowly. And somehow, through the rain, I saw him more clearly than ever. No matter how famous a swordsman becomes, he can still just be a young man. I had never seen a killer's face look like that before. There was no thrill in it. No rage. Only grief. A sword follows the heart, and his heart was shaking. So was the blade.
Then came the fifth step. General Wang moved first. With everything he had left, he stepped forward just enough to meet the sword himself, just enough to guide it into his own heart. He leaned in and said something to Jiang Yan. I strained to hear it, but the rain swallowed every word. All I knew was this: it did not look like murder. It looked like one man placing something precious into another man's hands.

Then General Wang fell, and the rain came down harder still.
That was the day I learned there are different kinds of killing.
Some men kill with tricks, ambushes, and knives in the back. By the time they are done, they've turned themselves into ghosts.
Some men kill by cutting away the cleanest part of their own heart with their own hand. And when it's over, they are still heroes.

The rain stung my face. Everything blurred. I watched Jiang Yan walk away until he was no more than a speck. Where he went after that, I never knew. As for me, a bastard who made his living picking through the dead, I could not get up for the longest time. The rain that day felt too heavy to stand under.
Much later, I finally forced myself up. As I passed General Wang, I looked at that sword again. It really was a beautiful thing. I could take it, sell it, and buy myself comfort for the rest of my life. That was what I was thinking when I bent down and reached out.

What I picked up instead was a tiny wooden sword, barely a handspan long. Round, blunt, childish. A little good-luck knot still hung from the hilt, stained red with blood.
Greedy little thing. Came to a battlefield and still brought this along.
Maybe that was for the best.
I tucked it inside my coat. The sky was still dark, and the rain still had not stopped.

The child's first cry rang out at the very moment King Qin drew his final breath. 
Li Jun knew the man was gone. Without hesitation, he turned and fled north, the infant swaddled in his arms. 

It was a long, uncertain road. But the child he named Yuan was lively, cheerful, full of chatter, she became a joy that belonged to him and him alone. 
But as the child grew older, Li Jun had wandered the land for far too long. He had no home, no rest. 
He had to make a choice. The right choice. For himself, and for the child. 
The Murong family, born of generals, steeped in honor, upright in heart. 
It would be a good place for the child to belong. 

Leaning on his silver spear, his body half-covered in frost and snow. 
The child cried again, not far behind. 
Once more, he turned away. Just like he had on that distant night, years ago. 
The road ahead is long. And if storms were to come, let them fall upon him alone.

It was a dark, blustery night. That is how this account ought to begin.



But the Imperial Archives has a proud tradition: the day shift shows up at noon and clocks out by Shen hour. I would not dare smear my own institution with such baseless slander. So, truth be told, it happened on a perfectly pleasant afternoon.



The spring weather was mild, ideal for a nap. Everyone found a good spot to doze off. Only the birds kept calling in the courtyard now and then.



Then, all at once, I jolted awake in the covered walkway. The sun was still high, not yet sliding west, and the courtyard had gone dead quiet.



A gust passed.



I heard someone shout, "That technique! You are of the Inkbound..."



Bamboo leaves whispered. Another voice answered with a bright laugh. "I have left the hall. I am no longer one of you. I cannot go around borrowing my old master’s name."



The first voice snapped, "Then why stick your nose into jianghu business?"



The other laughed again. "Because jianghu walked straight into me."



The bamboo blind trembled. Then came a long stretch of silence.



I counted to twenty before I dared lift the blind and steal a look.



At first, there was no one. Then my eyes caught him. His blue-green robe was nearly the same shade as the bamboo, so close it was hard to make out at all.



A green robe. That meant... someone from the Archives?



Rustle.



The blind I had lifted dropped on its own. I raised it again, and he was gone.



There was nothing left but a cool breeze and the bamboo.

He remembered almost nothing of it now, except that color seemed to be involved somehow. He neither accepted the name nor rejected it. She did not care either way. She called him Goshawk once, then again, and before long it had simply become his name.
After watching the iron flowers for a while, she stretched lazily. Goshawk immediately ran over to her.
"Will you teach me martial arts now?"
She scratched her head. "Not yet." Another burst of iron flowers went up. When the show reached its climax, she clapped and cheered all over again.

So he went, with nothing but his youthful gusto. That very night, he came back with a boar slung over his shoulders. He had once tried to rob her on the road, and he had lost. By the rules he knew, the strong preyed on the weak. If she wanted to kill him, she could. He would not run.
He gnawed on boar meat, breath steaming through his nose, eyes locked on the woman.
"You shouldn't be this strong."
To him, it was obvious! She was not ruthless enough. Not hard enough. Not guarded enough. Every time she stepped in, it was over something that brought no benefit at all: a beggar on the roadside, a sick old woman, children fighting in the street. None of it gained her anything! He had grown up brawling in the streets and taking food by force. He knew the rule people lived by!
The weak died. The strong lived! And so there was only one thing he wanted: to become stronger!
She looked at him for a long time. At the boy sitting before her, whose joy and anger had been worn away, until all that remained was a stubborn will to survive. Then, very gently, she placed a hand on his head.
"You don't have to rush so hard to become strong. One day, you won't need to."
Later, she taught him martial arts. Later, she left the temple. And later still, Goshawk learned to strike iron flowers.
He never really understood what use the craft had. You throw molten iron into the air, risk getting burned, earn a few gasps of amazement—and then it's over. The sparks die. What burned bright turns black and dull again. It all seemed pointless. And still, he kept doing it, telling himself not to fear heat or flame. Because somewhere inside that blaze, he was still searching for the truth behind his master's strength—a strength that was more than the simple law of the strong preying on the weak.

郭昕出身华阴郭氏，满门忠烈，伯父郭子仪曾立下赫赫战功，官拜中书令。\n当年在长安:
Guo Xin hailed from the Huayin Guo clan, a family full of loyal martyrs. His uncle, Guo Ziyi, had achieved illustrious military feats, rising to the position of Secretariat Director. 
Back in Chang'an, Guo Xin was also the young general who "galloped his horse joyfully in the spring breeze, viewing all Chang'an's flowers in a single day." 
Filled with fervor, his sole desire was to follow his uncle to the battlefield, slay the enemy, and restore the realm. 
In the first year of the Yongtai era, Guo Xin was ordered to patrol and pacify Hexi and Anxi. 
When bidding farewell to his uncle in Chang'an, his uncle used a broken arrow as a hairpin, entrusting Guo Xin to break rather than bend. 
Guo Xin looked back at Chang'an, this city once piled with splendor, then trampled by iron hooves. He clasped his fists, turned, and rode west.  
He never imagined that this glance would be his last at Chang'an for a lifetime. 
The northwest was a perilous place. 
Enemies loomed outside, and no reinforcements came from within. Grain and pay ran out, and his troops were defeated in Ganzhou. Cut off from east and west, they were stranded in a distant land. 
In the second year of the Jianzhong era, the Tang court's imperial edict finally arrived: 
"The Four Garrisons of the Northern Protectorate, governing the fifty-seven Western Xia tribes and ten surname clans, have since the dynasty's founding served with dedication. After Guanlong fell, east and west severed, the loyal and righteous have defended with blood and tears, cautiously securing the borders, upholding rites and teachings, all achieved through the mutual efforts of marquises, earls, and garrison commanders governing together. The officers and soldiers may be promoted seven ranks." 
Seven ranks, can they replace grain and provisions? 
Seven ranks, can they replace troops and horses? 
Seven ranks… seven ranks… In Anxi, these seven ranks were nothing but a fleeting hope, gone before long. But having hope was better than having none. 
Decades in the northwest, tens of thousands of lives, countless tears and blood of soldiers and civilians. 
He could barely remember. Now with white hair, Guo Xin stood at the city gate, gazing at his dozens of gray-haired soldiers. 
Behind him were soaring flames and tens of thousands of enemy troops. 
Arrows rained down like a storm, but he felt no pain. Guo Xin only thought of one person. 
That old friend from years past, with whom he had severed ties, once asked him, "Do you regret this life?" 
At that time, Guo Xin had replied firmly, word by word: "I would die a hundred deaths and never regret it." 
But now, he regretted it deeply. He regretted failing here, failing these dozens of gray-haired soldiers behind him. 
He could no longer defend the Great Tang, the love of his life. 
"Great Tang… Chang'an…" 
No one knew these were his last words before dying in battle. 
Guo Xin, born in Chang'an, died in Kucha, held Anxi, never retreated.

Wang Sheng of Pine Bend, a man devoted to drink, often stumbled home through the dense pine forest. One night, amid the towering trees, he heard rustling behind him. Turning, he saw only his shadow under the moonlight and dismissed the sound as a mouse. But the rustling grew louder and closer. A chill ran down his spine, sobering him enough to flee. Behind him, eerie laughter chased him through the woods. In his panic, he dropped his wine pouch. Safely outside, Wang Sheng glanced back to see a shadowy, otherworldly figure licking the spilled wine before dissolving into a wisp of smoke.

Elders say the spirit is that of a drunken man who died in the forest, his soul forever bound to the wine he loved, now dwelling in an ancient pine. Though fearsome in form, it harms no one, and is only driven by its thirst. By leaving his wine behind, Wang Sheng unknowingly granted the spirit's longing.

From then on, travelers crossing the pine forest at night offer a sip of wine to honor the restless spirit within the ancient trees.

Velvet Shade has always been a place of joys and sorrows, none more so than in the days surrounding the finalization of the Heroes Assembly performance list. The Flowers often dismiss such petty worries with a scoff, but the gentle Ruo Lan is different. She always takes time to listen. One night, by the west pond of Nimbus Tower, she encountered a young woman dancing alone in the moonlight. Ruo Lan simply stood and watched in the silver light, but the girl started in surprise when she noticed her. "My fault," Ruo Lan interrupted the girl's bow. "Keep practicing, and may your wishes come true in the audition." Her encouragement was as sincere and soft as her smile. But the girl's eyes filled with tears.
She had already guessed she would fail. How could she not? The assembly's theme was the "Skyward Dance," and she lacked natural talent. While her peers mastered moves in one try, she needed countless repetitions.
Through tears, the girl poured out months of frustration. She didn't expect special treatment, just some comforting lie like "hard work beats talent." But after listening, Ruo Lan looked puzzled.
"Wait, you're auditioning for dance, not singing? I followed your voice all the way here!"
It was not the response the girl expected. She froze, tears drying mid-fall. Seeing her confusion, Ruo Lan continued gently, "Music and dance are two halves of the same coin. Your singing is lovely."
The girl pondered this. When she looked up again, the tears had vanished, replaced by a new light.

Amid the girl's grateful bows, Ruo Lan drifted away. She climbed to the Fragrance Pavilion of Nimbus Tower and retrieved several old dresses from a rarely opened bottom wardrobe. Though the peony patterns were faded, the intricate weaving and beaded jade trimmings hinted at their former splendor.
It was hard to imagine the modest Ruo Lan, who adorned herself with only simple fragrant herbs, had once loved such ornate clothes. Just as tonight's encounter had reminded her: she too had once obsessed over peony-themed invitations and once resented her master's choices. But Song Ruyan, like a wilting peony, had seen through her struggles.
"A single bloom does not make a spring. A thousand colors do," the older woman had chided her. "I want each of you to make me proud."
Yes, 120 days of floral beauty, 24 cycles of flower winds. Who says orchids cannot rival peonies? A peony without orchids is less vibrant.
Gazing at the old dresses, Ruo Lan smiled that familiar, serene smile. She closed the wardrobe, shutting away a past of obsession and doubt.

里头危险，进去时候小心些。: It's dangerous in there. Watch your step.
里头可是我们歇息的地儿，别想乱闯！: This is our resting quarters. You're not welcome here.
里头可都是外头来的贵客，别惊扰了他们哪！: Important foreign guests inside—Don't disturb them!
里头在修登云梯，大家伙都是来送建材物资的。: They're repairing the Cloudstair. Everyone's delivering materials to help rebuild it.
里头多是些冶矿工匠，能有多难对付？你就放心吧。: It's nothing but miners and smiths in there. How much trouble can they be? Relax.
里头有人……你！啊！（打晕的音效）（换衣服的音效）（开门的音效）: Hey, I'm still in here... You! Ah! (thwack) (rustling of clothes) (door creaks open)
里头的人，赶紧束手就擒！: Those inside, surrender yourselves at once!
里头的老爷们悬了五十两买硬闯者的舌头。您猜他们是要用来泡酒还是风干？: The gentlemen inside have put a fifty-tael price on the tongues of any intruders. Do you think they want them for wine or to dry them?
里头装得是磨碎的艾草、菖蒲和少许雄黄，用来驱虫防潮再好不过。: They're stuffed with ground mugwort, calamus, and realgar, which help keep insects away and the air dry.
里头记载着他这些日子以来的飞天实验。: This journal is filled with sketches, calculations, and observations from his relentless pursuit of flight.
里头还有好些老客人，都是寒娘子的老友，你每年都见的那些……: The usual crowd is inside, all of Madam Han's old friends. You see them every year.
里头那位又摔碗了，快去收拾收拾。: The one inside is breaking things again. Go clean it up.
里头那四人，神秘的很！至今都没人知道他们到底是谁，只知道他们各个神出鬼没的。: Those four guys are mysterious. No one really knows who they are. They move like shadows, here one moment, gone the next.
里头那阶下囚，怎这么多事？都这天气了还要加衣！: Why are there so many prisoners down here? And why are they asking for more clothing in this weather?
里头，好像有动静？: Did you hear that? There's noise coming from inside.
里有桔梗、射干、胖大海、地黄、石斛等药材，可生津利咽、清音亮嗓、健脾益肾。: Contains platycodon root, blackberry lily, malva nut, rehmannia, and dendrobium. Helps moisten the throat, clear the voice, promote fluid production, and strengthen the spleen and kidneys.
里边儿住着几只辽狗: Holed up in there are a few Khitan dogs
里边装了好些钱，我也不知道丢在哪了……我们好不容易才……: The bag had some coins, but I couldn't find it anywhere... We've been working so hard...
里里外外都翻了十几遍了，还有什么地方没找过呢？: We've turned the place inside out a dozen times over. Where else is there left to look?
里间有人，还请客官留步。: It's occupied. Please do not enter.
里面不过是一群墨门弟子进行普通研究，什么事也没有。: It's just a group of Mohist disciples in that house. There's nothing unusual going on.
里面东西都倒了，哪有空让你们再进！都等着！: Everything inside just toppled over. Nobody's getting in until we sort this out! Wait here!
里面似乎是名贵字画，价值连城。: It seems to contain priceless calligraphy and artwork, worth a fortune.
里面似乎有人？这个时辰，竟真能遇上……: It looks like someone's inside. I can't believe I might actually meet her at this hour…
里面似乎装满了异域珠宝，价值不可估量。: It seems to be filled with exotic jewels, their value immeasurable.
里面是怎么了，为何要封起来？: What happened in there? Why does it have to be sealed?
里面是王家第三十八代传人的故事，大婚之夜，他被背叛了，流落巫山！: It's about the thirty-eighth heir of the Wang family. Betrayed on his wedding night, he fled to Wushan!
里面曾经装着一些普通的吃食，被人视若珍宝。: Once held ordinary food, treasured by someone.
里面有人？出来吧。: Someone in there? Come out. It's safe.
里面有他给徐明穹的话: What Xie Ruhui couldn't say in life, he entrusted to ink for Xu Mingqiong.
里面有动静，去看看。: I hear something inside. Better check it out.
里面有好些我们的守卫，莫误伤了你。: There are plenty of guards inside, so watch your step.
里面的人，你已经被包围了！你的诡计，已被我看穿！: Hey, you in there! You're surrounded! Your scheme ends here!
里面的快点！一早上就占着不出来，还让不让人活了！: Hurry up in there! You've been hogging it all morning! The rest of us have needs too!

Record of Rebuilding the Cloud Ladder

These mountains feature towering cliffs, making paths hard to find. 
The Mohists reside in Peaceful Village, while Flying City sits atop the Heaven Path. The old Cloud Ladder ascended via stone steps into the clouds, built by ancients who carved rocks and laid timber for passage.
After the Qiongqi disaster, the stone steps collapsed, becoming dangerously steep. Travelers had to detour for miles, enduring arduous treks.
As a vital north-south route, its ruin inconvenienced the people. Funds were gathered to hire skilled stonemasons. They carved firm rocks from Mount Taihang into steps, linked them with iron chains, and placed wooden beams in perilous spots to ensure safe passage. The work took a month. From dawn to dusk, hammer blows echoed in the valley, and stone dust filled the air. Spared by wind and rain, the construction was swiftly completed.
Once completed, the ladder stood seventy rods high, winding like a dragon straight into the clouds.
Travelers climbing from Deep Pond can reach Heaven Path in half a day. Descending from Heaven Path to Peaceful Village is effortless. Disciples and commoners save thirty miles of travel, and pilgrims avoid rugged paths.
On clear days, looking north from the ladder, the picturesque Mount Taihang blends with the clouds—a true spectacle. Recorded on this date.

Three Khitans were found dead on their beds in an inn at Sangma, each with a gold leaf next to them. 
 Several small red punctures, possibly caused by being stabbed with a hairpin, were found between the end of their eyebrows and their ears (but the holes indicated that the strength of each stab was different, almost as if an amateur was looking for a pressure point). Liu, Landlord Chen's housekeeper, woke up one morning to wash clothes and found a grass-woven gold leaf in the manor's well. According to Liu's testimony, several skeletons were exhumed from the well. A small gate was also found behind the feigned landscape of the garden, indicating that someone had been coming and going through this gate.

Making money isn't as hard as you might think. 
Learn a few key techniques, and there's no money in the jianghu you can't get your hands on! 

Technique One: Getting Started – Practice at the Inkbound Order 
Among all the jianghu sects, the Inkbound Order is the easiest target. The scholars there wear multiple layers of clothing—missing a layer doesn't seem odd to them. From my experience, their money pouches are usually hidden in the second and fourth layers, and the third layer usually holds a book. If you sense something's off, reach for the third layer, pretending you want to read—their eagerness to teach will give you the perfect chance to act. If you get caught, just share a heartfelt story about your hardships—you'll at least get a simple meal. If you're new to this, this place is the best for gaining experience. 
But if you want to make real money, don't settle for just a meal. Disguising yourself as an Inkbound disciple to blend in is the way forward. This method is more challenging and requires mastering a special skill called the "Thousand-Character Classic." This isn't written down anywhere; those interested should seek out Xu Jinwen for direct instruction. 

Technique Two: Roaming the Streets and Alleys to Earn Easily 
Who knows the streets of Kaifeng better than the Nine Mortal Ways folk? Who's more familiar with every alley? You can turn this knowledge into cash! 
All you need is a charred stick to map the routes and alleys you've traveled. Then, find Midnight Blades disciples dressed in red and black. With your "Intelligence Map," you can charge a fee for guiding the way. As your drawing skills improve and your knowledge of people and places deepens, you can create even more detailed maps. Eventually, you may earn money simply by selling these maps without even guiding anyone. If fortune favors you, you might also gain two free bodyguards. 
Give it a try! 

Technique Three: Combining the First Two to Make Big Money 
Once you've mastered the first two techniques, it's time to attempt this—becoming an informant for Velvet Shade! 
As everyone knows, the beauties at Revelry Hall love gossip from everywhere. Record and map these rumors and where they come from, and exchange this information for a fee with Velvet Shade disciples. 
After all, the Inkbound Order scholars are just bookish types, and those from Midnight Blades are unpredictable. Once you're skilled at gathering information and drawing maps, Velvet Shade will offer you a steady income! 
But remember—don't spend your earnings on them again. The worst mistake in the jianghu is letting your feelings get involved, especially when it leads to spending on drinks! Keep this in mind! 

Master these three techniques, and you won't just earn steadily—you'll be well off in no time. 
Want to make even more? The next volume contains secret methods!

Money can make more money. 
Learn these techniques, and you'll have money coming to you! 

Technique One: Face Reading 
In the jianghu, when it comes to disguises, the Nine Mortal Ways leads the way, with Mohist Hill coming second. 
That said, the disguises from Mohist Hill aren't very convincing. With a bit of face-reading skill, you can easily spot several Mohist Hill disciples. Once identified, you can get them to do simple tasks like diverting water for villagers or fixing wells in neighborhoods, charging a modest fee for their work. With very little effort, this can earn you around 300 wen a month. 
No need to worry—they'll get more motivated the more they work, especially if you encourage them with praise like "great skills" or "sharp minds"! 

Technique Two: Brewing Technique 
A Mohist Hill disciple once confirmed that adding the right amount of water to wine can actually improve its taste. That means for every ten jars of wine, you effectively get an extra jar. Scale that up to a hundred or a thousand jars, and that's a lot of extra wine—and profit. 
There's a risk, though: this method might attract attention from the Raging Tides, who don't take kindly to such tricks. 

Technique Three: Partnership Strategy 
Everyone knows Well of Heaven is famous for robbing the rich to help the poor. Begging along their road has become a steady source of income for us, but that's only a little money. To make serious cash, here's the trick: 
During festivals, markets and shops get overcrowded, and the authorities are stretched thin. That's when you team up with Well of Heaven, using the promise of a peaceful outing to lure wealthy merchants into secluded alleys. When the Well of Heaven disciples strike, the merchants lose their purses—and we take a nice cut of the haul. Even small shares add up to big earnings! 

In short, there are many ways to make money, but this is all I'll cover for now. 
I hope the next generation will take these lessons further and go even deeper on the path to wealth. 

Appendix: 
Looking back at the earlier notes, I realized there was a gap—mathematics. 
Counting small amounts like one or two wen is easy, but adding up thousands gets tricky. 
To fix that, I invited a disciple from Lone Cloud to teach me some arithmetic skills. Now I'm no longer afraid of handling big sums. 
If you want to learn, find Fang Guochun at the base.

To my Bro:
Before I left, I kept nagging you, saying it was boring to travel alone and wanting to drag you along. But you said you were too busy and kept making excuses not to go.
And look what happened? Even the heavens couldn't stand it! Not long after I set out, they practically shoved a partner into my arms!
Bro, do you know a guy from Qinghe named $C$L#Y$PN#E$C?
No? Well, that makes sense, because I don't know him either. My new partner is a retainer under him called Li Laizuo. (That name sounds weirdly familiar, like I've heard it somewhere before.) But that doesn't matter. What matters is that my partner leads a miserable life! His young master doesn't treat him like a human. Every day before dawn, he's ordered out of bed to work, rising earlier than a rooster and sleeping later than a dog.
Man, that's not even the half of it. He doesn't get a penny of wages, and if he doesn't work well enough, he gets locked in a dark room and whipped on his butt with a little leather strap!
Bro, we're both young masters, but this jerk named $C$L#Y$PN#E$C is just a total scoundrel compared to you!
Anyway, Bro, my brother is currently in terrible trouble. I want to save him, but he says his contract is still in $C$L#Y$PN#E$C's hands. If he runs away and gets caught by the authorities, he'll be beaten to death and have no way to seek justice.
At this point, you surely understand why I'm writing. You're usually a good talker, so how about you go talk to $C$L#Y$PN#E$C and get him to set my brother free?
Whatever price he wants, let him name it! I already gave my brother 100,000 coins. If that's not enough, 200,000 or 300,000 is fine too. Of course, if he insists on being stubborn and won't let go... hmph, then don't blame me for trying diplomacy before force!
Yours, Fang Xu
铁铁收：\n铁铁，最近咋样啊？\n从前搁咱家有钱花不出去，我老五脊六兽的了，大宅:
To my Bro:
Bro, how've you been?
Back home, I had money I couldn't even spend. I was bored out of my mind! Big mansion? Bought it. Grand carriage? Got it. Revelry Hall? Been there... I got sick of all those fancy things ages ago. Do you know the pain of having too much money? It's downright suffocating!
But coming to the Nine Mortal Ways is a whole different story. The people here are all so talented, and they speak so nicely. I freakin' love it here.
Take the day before yesterday. A guy in rags, leaning on a crutch, told me his five brothers and dad all died in battle, his sisters-in-law were taken to the army camp and never returned, leaving an eighty-year-old mother and a bunch of nieces and nephews to feed. He asked if I could help. Hearing that, my eyes welled up with tears, and I gave him a huge handful of coins. The guy was so happy he threw his crutch away and ran off, hollering: "The great benefactor gave me money!" Man, a warm heart truly can awaken medical miracles!
I counted. In the days I've been at the Nine Mortal Ways, I've helped 28 Nine Mortal Ways disciples, spending a total of 1.08 million coins. Bro, the folks at the Nine Mortal Ways really have it rough!
There's just one thing that rubs me the wrong way. A few days ago, I kept getting love letters at my door. Some Nine Mortal Ways disciple named Fan Qicha kept calling me "big bro" in the letters, saying things like, "Big bro, want to date this little kid?" Seeing how sincere they were, I agreed. But when we finally met, I found out it was a burly, broad-shouldered dude! I was so mad I ran away instantly. Swindle my coin if you must, but don't play with my heart!
Bro, I'm hurting! Say no more, come find me at the "Money Hole" in the Nine Mortal Ways. I'll give you all my remaining coins. Just come keep your bro company and chat for a bit, boohoo!
Yours, Fang Xu

Fengying grew up and married. Her mother-in-law was Madam Zhu's old childhood friend. The two families had lived in the same village for generations. Her husband, Tang Ming, was someone she'd known since they were little, a playmate who had never quite left her side.
They were deeply in love. Tang Ming was gentle, a perfect match for Fengying's sharp efficiency.
Fengying never lost her gift for making food. The buns she steamed and the meat sauce she simmered sent rich, comforting aromas drifting down the entire lane.
People praised Madam Zhu for raising such a capable, virtuous daughter. Yet in her heart, she was still that little girl on the doorstep, gnawing on a bun while the neighbors laughed.

She and her husband built a small farm with their own hands. In time, they had a daughter and named her Yiduo.
Raised among clear water and rich grass, Yiduo grew bright and carefree, like an early spring flower opening to the light.
Rooted in land that was gentle and free, even her laughter seemed warmed by sunshine.

Fengying never forgot the look her mother once gave her at the doorway, nor the quiet pride she felt the first time she kneaded a dough so smooth it gleamed.
"Yiduo, come help Mama knead the dough," she said now, guiding her daughter's small hands. She spoke softly, almost to herself.
"Don't force it, use skill. Knead it through, until it's smooth, not sticking to your hands or the bowl..."
After just a few presses, Yiduo pouted. "Mama, this isn't fun. I don't want to knead dough."
Fengying froze for a moment, then heard herself ask the very words she once knew so well. "Then what do you want to do?"
Yiduo's answer came tumbling out. "I want to herd sheep and raise chickens! I want to ride a big horse! And pick mushrooms! Oh—and I want my own farm too. A huge one!"
In that moment, Fengying was carried back to a long-ago afternoon. Had her mother looked at her the same way: part relief, part surprise, and something like hope quietly blooming beneath it all? If this was what her daughter wanted, how could she ever say no?
"Well then," Fengying said with a smile, her voice warm and sure, "you'll be the greatest farmer in the whole wide world."

In the great cold of Chang'an, snow piled six feet high. 
The blind musician siblings, Seren Snow and Plum Melody, played the guqin and flute under the ancient plum tree at Ba Bridge. When passing by, Masked Troupe Disciple Lan He stopped to listen and then took out his bamboo flute to join in harmony. Without exchanging a single word, their notes resonated, as if sharing a heartfelt melody. 
The three drank and discussed music under the tree until it was deep into the night. Lan He, flushed with wine, said, "Though perfectly skilled after learning the bamboo flute for three years, I remain puzzled by one thing. The bamboo flute creates melodies with the wind, but the wind is the most elusive force in the world. How can one control it?" 

Hearing this, the flutist Plum Melody gave a cloth pouch to Lan He, saying, "Blind since childhood, I am sensitive to the wind's movements, able to 'see' its flow. Knowing not how to describe it to others, I visualize it this way—burn the inner membrane of reeds to ash and place it inside the hollow of the flute to clearly show the flow." 

Lan He tried it and saw the ash dance with the music: when he played the Gong note, the ash flowed like threads to the gong note, scattered like dust to the Shang note, and surged like a spring, blending with a thousand sounds to the Jue and Zhi notes.  
"After years of studying, now I realize the truth—human melody aligns with the rules of the universe," sighed Lan He. 

Discussing all night long, they composed the "Winter Trio." The sections for pine and bamboo came naturally, except for the plum blossom section. They agreed to meet later to complete the plum blossom melody. 
As dawn approached and snow cleared, they parted, leaving the lingering echoes among the trees.

Immortality is tediously quiet. We might be stuck at the bottom of this abyss for a hundred years, and all I can do to pass the time is write down my own story.
I'm no Immortal of Longevity. I am but a man named Ba Wu.
Granny told me "Ba Wu" means "child blessed by the Deer Goddess," so I've worn a deer mask all my life, straining to hear her whispers.
But others say the mask is meant to hide how different I look.
Granny raised me in a hut shared with the Toad King. Every day, venomous swarms from miles around would crawl to it, bearing fresh herbs at its feet like offering tribute. The Toad King liked me. It was my only friend. The villagers believed the Deer Goddess had truly blessed me, that the poison in my veins could subdue any venom.
Word spread, and outsiders branded me "the Immortal of Longevity." Granny scattered herb powder around the village, warning that we must never be found. She was hiding from some wanderers.
Jianghu, or the martial world, sounds poetic. But it was because of the wanderers that we fell into this abyss, cursed with this endless life.
Our only hope now lies with Chen Huaiqing's formula.
The one that might free us from longevity.

Question 1: How did I manage to get picked exactly zero times in the Autumn Selection?
Ever since I heard Baoci Palace was running a "Laughter Recruitment," I've been drilling jokes in day. And in the end, I didn't even get to see Sister Qiu.
They say she only let a handful of girls she liked the look of move on, and that "luck is part of strength"...

Reply 1:
Don't be so down. Being a nobody your first year isn't always a bad thing.
Stick your head out and you'll be the first to get clipped. Lie low for now and get a solid skill under your belt. That's what counts.

Reply 2:
Forget "make my lady proud." Think "make my lady unable to do without me."
I bet everything on double-sided embroidery back then. Now if my lady's robe so much as snags, it waits for my hands. Even the female clerks in the Crafts Office can't fill in.
Sisters, know your core advantage.

Reply 3:
You got this, you got this. Keep your head straight.
Honestly, not getting picked might be a blessing. At least you won't be on edge every day.
For small fry like us, making it safely to the day we leave is the best fortune there is.

Reply 1:
If you're as "passionate" about food as the sister who posted about su shan... I mean, if you truly love food, you might have a shot.
Key thing is people need to see you can take hardship and do heavy work. The Culinary Office looks nice, but someone's still hauling flour sacks and chopping firewood.

Reply 2:
You want in? Enthusiasm isn't enough. You need to have an eye for work.
We need people who care about food. When you have time, go help out at the Culinary Office back gate. Pick vegetables, dump slop buckets, make yourself a familiar face.
Last time a little one peeled garlic for me three days straight. I only asked for her because her hands were quick and she didn't complain.

Reply 3:
Transfers take time. Take care of your health first.
The Forlorn Palace is damp. Go beg some mugwort and smoke the room a bit. And wrap your knees. If your body gives out, you've got nothing.

The sun shines bright, and pear blossoms drift down once more. Afternoon light filters through the bamboo leaves, scattering like flecks of gold. A warm breeze, soft as a cat's paw, gently teases your cheek. You have seldom returned since leaving home at sixteen. Cobwebs beneath the eaves have woven into intricate paintings, while the master of the house has wandered to the ends of the earth. Sitting on the long bench where he once sat, you recall your childish prattle from long ago and slowly drift off to sleep.
In a daze, you open your eyes, only to see Uncle Jiang leading a horse toward you. In your memory, Uncle Jiang's back is forever straight, his broad shoulders like a sturdy mountain sheltering you from the wind and rain. Yet now, you notice his hem is slightly soiled, and a barely perceptible weariness lingers on his face.
Thousands of words rush to your lips, but before you can even speak, he raises a hand to stop you. As if guessing your thoughts, he gives a slight nod and asks:
"Even so, do you still wish to wander in the jianghu?"

Meeting his gaze, you blurt out...
#YNo. A sudden, bone-deep weariness washes over you. If you stayed here forever, chasing cats, teasing dogs, and retreating to a peach-blossom haven with everyone, would you have lived a different kind of life?#E
Hearing your answer, Uncle Jiang nods. His gaze remains steady, as if your response is exactly as he expected. Before him, you can always speak your mind. For you know that no matter your choice, he will always stand behind you. Once, you were a sleeping infant in his arms, his tether to this world. In the future, will you become his pride, or his lingering worry?
You rise and run toward Uncle Jiang, curious about where he has been and whether he has been well. Suddenly, your leg twitches, striking the corner of the table. The pain jolts your eyes open.
The sun remains bright, and the pear blossoms keep drifting down. The daylight scatters like flecks of gold. The wind carries no news of old friends, yet traces of him, and of them all, can be found everywhere.

My patar once asked me, "Marga, do you know why we must wander all our lives?"
I shook my head. He stroked my hair and said,
"To survive. We Sogdians are born to chase profit—where the gold is, that's where we go. From the moment you're born, you are destined for a life of ceaseless travel."
"Then can't we ever stop?" I asked.
He gazed into the distance and, after a long silence, sighed. "A place where we could stop... such places are gone for us."
"Marga, remember this: in a caravan, to keep your belly full, your feet must be swift and your heart must be hard. Business is business. Sentiment will be your ruin. It won't let you get far."
I never forgot his words.

Years later, I came across a troop of Tang soldiers.
Their armor was in tatters, their blades chipped and dull. With my years of trade in the great desert, I knew at a glance: any dealings with them would be utterly profitless.
This troop had been stranded in Hexi for a long time, and the Bodchens watched them like wolves circling a prize. Where there is no profit, a merchant does not go. A trade must have equal weight on both sides of the scale.
I could not fathom any reason for them to hold their ground. To defend a lost cause was, to them, a bargain with no return. Is anything in this world worth more than survival itself?
Looking at the young general, I couldn't hold back my question:
"Why don't you leave? If you leave, you survive."
He pointed to the desert poplars nearby, his gaze unwavering and bright.
"As long as the roots run deep enough, we will live."
"And if the poplars live, more people will get to live because of them."

"Easy now. Don't hurt yourself," came a soft voice beside him. A cool palm covered his, threading a rare warmth into the rain-soaked night.

Jiang Wei paused, then turned.

The woman beside him was someone he had rescued not long ago from a ghost marriage. For years, he had disguised himself as a bride to infiltrate such dark rites, saving women from the clutches of the Ghost Matchmakers, searching always for the one behind his sister's death. This woman... her brows and eyes bore a faint resemblance to his sister's. So when she offered to come with him, Jiang Wei did not refuse. Turns out, it was much-needed company for him.

Along the way, she had held the umbrella for him against the rain, halted his reckless strides through blizzards, listened quietly as he recounted his past, and calmed him down when rage threatened to consume him. Without her, his fraying mind might have already shattered.

"Thank you... for everything you've done for me along the way." Jiang Wei scooped another handful of earth. "Once I bring my sister to the sea, I'll see you safely home."

As he dug, pale bones came into view. Jiang Wei froze, a half-smile tugging at his lips, half joy, half grief.

"The freedom my sister longed for... This time, I'll give it to her."

But no answer came. The oil-paper umbrella slipped from his shoulder and fell to the ground. Jiang Wei turned around, there was nothing but silence behind him.

Pain ripped through him. Memories flashed before his eyes, then shattered into dust. There had never been anyone. On this long, twisted, bloodstained road, he had always walked alone.

Jiang Wei curled up beside his sister's bones, staring up at the rain pouring from the heavens. 

If all the warmth, all the companionship he believed in was but a lie. Then what in this world was ever real?

The people he had saved. The ones he had killed. Everything he had seen, everything he had endured, was it all just a dream spun out of his own madness?

阿姐说，村子最重要的事就是及时帮助过路人，让大家都能找到回家的路。额已经帮了好些: My sis says the most important thing is helping travelers in time, so they can find their way home. I've helped lots of people already. That's amazing, isn't it?
阿姐还让他保证了——他之后再也不许欺负人了，才能让他和我们一起当大侠！保护承恩镇: My sis made him promise to never bully anybody again. Now he's going to aim to be a great hero, like us! Hero of Gracetown!
阿姐这是要上哪去？: Where are you off to, sister?

阿姐！你，你怎么来了——: Sis! What are you... how did you...
阿姐，爹娘什么时候来接我们呀？: Big Sis, when will Mom and Dad come for us?

阿娇妹妹，阿胶妹妹，两位都是我的好妹妹。: A'jiao, Ah Jiao, both are my beloved sisters.
阿娘——阿娘，孩儿不孝，回来迟了——: Mother—I'm sorry. I came back too late...
阿娘……好像也见到你阿爷了呢。: Your Dad... I think I see him too.
阿娘……阿娘……痛……想阿娘……: Mom... Mom... it hurts... I miss you so much...
阿娘也喜欢。可惜，我太笨了……只记住一半。: Mama loves it too. I'm just not very clever... I can only remember half.
阿娘住在淮水畔，阿爹住在沂水尾……小沂儿，小沂儿，哪去了？莫叫河水冲跑了……: Mother lives by the Huai, Father by the tail of the Yi... Yi, Yi, where did you go? Don't let the river wash you away...
阿娘和我说过，这是谷子烤热了的香气！: Mama told me once, that's the smell of grain toasted over a fire!
阿娘夜夜在缝补那件五弟的旧袍，哼的是我五弟年幼时最爱的小曲。: And Mom... she's still patching up that old robe he used to wear, humming the tune he loved as a boy.
阿娘撒手时候说了，花灯是天上的星星。: When Mother passed, she said that the lanterns were the stars in the sky.
阿娘要去赶坏人，要去做很厉害很厉害的事情，也是……很危险很危险的事情。: Mama's going to chase the bad men away. Do something brave. Something really, really big. And... really, really dangerous.
阿娘说了，不是所有人都有机会当一个大侠，但我可以保护好我心里的小小侠。对吧，阿娘: Mama says not everyone gets to be a big hero. But I can keep the little one inside me safe. Right, Mama?
阿娘说了，外头有坏人！在外头，困了、冷了、饿了，危险。出去之前，要吃饱。: Mama said there are bad people out there! You'll get tired and cold and hungry. It's dangerous! You have to eat first.
阿娘说，小十八总跑出去，可能是因为在外面有家了。: Mom thinks maybe Eighteen keeps running off because it has a family out there.
阿娘说，挖不了井就搬土，搬不动土就学编筐子，年轻时你能仗着好看哄她，现在你年纪大: Ma said if you can't dig a well, then cart soil. If you can't cart soil, then learn to weave baskets. When you were young, you could rely on your good looks to fool her, but now they've faded, you really can't afford not to work hard!
阿娘说，最亮的星星就是我的阿爷，让我来找找……: My mom says the brightest star is my grandpa. Let me see if I can find it...
阿娘，好烫，好烫啊……阿娘救我……: Mama... It's so hot... Save me, Mama...
阿娘，我们明年还要再来看！: Mom, I want to see the dragon lantern dance again next year!
阿娘，灯笼都挂好了，爹爹该回来了吧？我们去佛堂找爹爹吗？: Mother, the lanterns are all hung. Should father be home by now? Shall we go to the temple to find him?
阿娜，阿娜——你就不想知道传了什么消息？: Ana… don't you want to know what message I delivered?
阿娜，额今天又帮秋草姐、张石哥传了信哩！: Ana, I helped deliver messages for Qiucao and Zhang Shi again today!
阿娴……你找到不死树的叶子了……: A'xian... did you really find leaves from the Immortal Tree?
阿娴……怪我……怪我……: A'xian... it's my fault... all of it...
阿娴平日喜欢什么都不爱说，只是路过的时候会看上几眼……: A'xian usually never says when she likes something. She just sneaks a glance every time she passes by...
阿娴，我想也给我娘接个风……: A'xian, I also want to welcome my mother home.
阿婆可宝贝它咧！没有歌本子，阿婆会伤心的，宝儿睡觉也听不到歌了，呜呜……: It's Granny's treasure! Without it, she'll be so sad… and I won't hear her lullabies anymore. Boohoo…
阿婆生前做的馍最香了。虽然现在吃不到，不过，河西的月亮馍也不错。给你捞个尝尝？: Her bread was the best. I can't have it anymore, but the moon bread is close. You want me to get you one?
阿婆的娘家在这，我们从北边过来，原本就是想来投靠亲戚的。可到了才发现，这里的人也: Grandma's family is from here. We came from the north, originally hoping to settle with relatives. But when we got here, we found they'd all left months ago.
阿婆若是还在，我一定要把所有的好东西都给她。: If Grandma were still here, I would give her all the finest things.
阿婆说了，过去凉州的孩子都会唱这首歌，都会跳这支舞！: Granny said that children of Liangzhou all knew this song and dance in the past!
阿婆请讲。: Please tell me your request, Granny.
阿婆，你说的，要跟我一起回长安……可你怎么说话不算话……: Grandma, you promised... you'd come to Chang'an with me. Why'd you lie?
阿婆，娘，我们为什么不出去？: Grandma... Mama... why can't we go outside?
阿婶别怕，我真没坏心，就是路过躲个风。谁欺负你们了？: Auntie, don't be afraid. I really didn't mean any harm. Just taking shelter on my way through. Who bullied you?
阿嫂，你别怪爹爹，土粑粑已经是爹爹能找来最好的了。: Auntie, don't be cross with Papa. Dirt cakes... the best he could find.
阿嫂，思思还小，还需要你……你们抓紧跟着下一队走，剩下的交给我们。: Ma'am, Sisi is little and she needs you. Go with the next group. We'll take care of the rest.
阿宗，别吹牛了，你那师父我们连影儿都没见过。快回去吧，再溜出来，被你爹抓到了打屁: A'zong, nobody's ever seen this master of yours. Go home before your father catches you out here again!
阿宝！阿宝?你在哪儿?有没有人看到我的阿宝?: Bao! Bao? Where are you? Has anyone seen my Bao?
阿实也回来了？嗯，人呢？……呀，怎么跑隔壁去了？这不浪费么！: A'shi's back? Where... oh, he went next door?! What a waste of time!
阿寿不在这边啦！真的！福福才、才不骗人呢！: I swear! I'm not lying—she's not here!
阿寿啊，你那是想看雪山吗？你是还想着那姑娘呢！: A'Shou, you want to see the snow-capped mountains? You're still thinking about that girl!
阿巧？怎么是你，老纪没在？: A-Qiao? Why is it you? Where’s Old Ji?
阿弟传来的消息……嗯，先这样回复门主吧。: I just got a message from my little brother... Hmm, for now, just reply to the Clan Master this way.
阿弟：\n 待你见信，想必已经得知此处消息，心中疑惑，但此事我思虑良久，决意:
To my young brother, 
   If you're reading this, then you know what has happened, and you likely have doubts in your heart. I thought about this for a long time and made up my mind. For many years, I blamed the death of Father Li on my adoptive father. Recently, through the master, I discovered that I had been harboring my hatred for the wrong person. Father Li was killed by a single phrase from the government: "When there are no more birds, the bow becomes useless." I had been in the wrong for many years and assisted the culprit. The kindness of my adoptive father and the revenge for Father Li... I bear both on my shoulders. 
   Only by destroying the ship can I put an end to this. Now I can go see Father Li. 
   Please fulfill my wish by stopping the hatred and not coming with me. Take care of yourself, and put on more clothes when the weather gets cold.
阿张来玩啦: A Zhang is Here to Play
阿弥陀佛……也罢，看来时机未至啊……: Amitabha... the time is not yet right, it seems.
阿弥陀佛……施主且往前方看去，可不正是茫茫苦海？: Amitabha... Look ahead. Isn't that the endless sea of suffering?
阿弥陀佛……能在此处与施主相逢，或许便是有缘吧？: Amitabha... Perhaps our meeting here was fate.
阿弥陀佛……阿弥陀佛……: Buddha help me... Buddha help me...
阿弥陀佛…此番进益，还多谢小友解惑。: Amitabha. I have gained much from this exchange. Thank you for the illumination, young friend.
阿弥陀佛。“灯者，明也。燃灯者，何也？”小友可有答案？: Amitabha. "A lamp is light. But what is it to light one?" Do you have an answer, young friend?
阿弥陀佛。出家人以慈悲为怀，若我将他逐出山门，任由其自生自灭，与刺人之刀何异？: Amitabha. We believe in mercy. If I had cast him out to fend for himself, would I not have been no different from the assassins?
阿弥陀佛。听闻天水集有看八卦的，看水晶球的，还有把戏团！: Amitabha. I heard there are fortune tellers, crystal ball readers, and circus troupes in the Skybrim Market!
阿弥陀佛。好孩子……愿你来世投个好胎，生在那太平年间、温柔富贵之所……以慰今世夭: Amitabha. Good child… may you be reborn in a land of peace and plenty, to make up for the sorrow of leaving this life so soon.
阿弥陀佛。施主来此，可是遇到了难处？: Amitabha. Did you run into any trouble, traveler?
阿弥陀佛。施主，白雀经阁如今可去不得。: Amitabha. Benefactor, you can no longer visit the Sparrow Sutra Hall.
阿弥陀佛。真金百千担，持用行布施，不如一团泥，敬心治佛塔。: Amitabha. To offer is not equal to offering a lump of clay, if it is given with a sincere heart to restore a pagoda.
阿弥陀佛。贫僧路过此地，碰见这人横尸于此，心有不忍，要为他超度埋葬。: Amitabha... I was passing through here and found this soul lying unburied. I couldn't bear it, so I stayed to chant and lay him to rest.
阿弥陀佛。这位方施主搅风搅云，只怕心中所图匪浅。: Amitabha. Master Fang Bai stirs up trouble, and I fear his intentions run deep.
阿弥陀佛，《大般若经》非我寺独有，且此经书仍在校勘中，节度使为何……: Amitabha, the Wisdom Sutra is not unique to our temple, and this scripture is still being amended. Why would the Governor…
阿弥陀佛，上次多亏施主助我与裴施主师徒解除误会，贫僧每每念及此事，心中都万分感激: Amitabha, thank you for clearing the misunderstanding between me and Mister Pei. Whenever I think of it, my heart is filled with gratitude.
阿弥陀佛，下山化斋果然不容易，脚底板磨破也没遇上好心人……: Amitabha, begging for alms down the mountain is really tough. My feet are all blistered, and I didn't come across a single kind soul...
阿弥陀佛，下山化缘一无所获……: Went down the mountain seeking alms, but got nothing...
阿弥陀佛，不管您是佛家弟子还是圣主信徒，都愿您获得喜乐……: Amitabha. Whether you believe in the Buddha or in Ahura Mazda, may you be blessed.
阿弥陀佛，众生之苦，苦于生，亦苦于死……南无阿弥多婆业……: Amitabha... we suffer in life, we suffer in death... Buddha's mercy...
阿弥陀佛，众生欢享今宵，天下承平，此乃大造化也。: Amitabha. The people celebrate, the world is at peace. What greater blessing could there be?
阿弥陀佛，佛祖保佑哪。: Amitabha, may the Buddha bless us.

阿弥陀佛，可是铁心将军？: Amitabha. Are you General Ironheart, by any chance?
阿弥陀佛，多谢施主出手相救。: Amitabha, thank you so much for your help.
阿弥陀佛，小僧敢问施主，何人为善？何人为恶？: Amitabha, this humble monk presents a question to you. Who is good? Who is evil?
阿弥陀佛，小摩诃还没有剃度，不能算作小和尚。: Amitabha. I am not yet tonsured and hence am not a monk.
阿弥陀佛，小摩诃还没有剃度，不能算作小和尚。不过施主猜得很对，今天早上，小摩诃才: Amitabha. I am not yet tonsured and hence am not a monk. But you're right—This morning, I did make offerings in the mountains. How did you know that?
阿弥陀佛，师姐前段时日刚下山，怕是不能……: Amitabha... My senior sister just left for the village. She isn't here.
阿弥陀佛，幸未伤及无辜。: Thank the heavens no one was hurt.
阿弥陀佛，徒儿莫哭，为师无碍……: Amitabha, don't cry, my disciple. I'm safe...
阿弥陀佛，我佛不渡该死的鬼。: Amitabha. The Buddha does not intervene when fate has been sealed.

阿弥陀佛，施主可是来山顶祭拜？还是请回吧，自世宗灭佛以来，舍利塔便已封存，再不接: Amitabha! Sir, have you come to worship at the peak? Please turn back. Since Emperor Shizong's persecution, the reliquary pagoda is sealed to visitors.

阿弥陀佛，施主说笑了。救人一命胜造七级浮屠，施主善行必有福报，我佛曾经曰过，善行: Amitabha, you're too kind. Saving a life is the greatest blessing of all. Your kindness will surely be rewarded. The Buddha said good deeds are the root, and blessings the fruit.
阿弥陀佛，施主这是做什么？此乃妙善禅师修行的佛光塔，佛缘之地，还请莫要造次……: Amitabha! What are you doing? This is Buddha's Light Pagoda, where Master Miaoshan practiced Buddhism. You mustn't disturb this sacred place.
阿弥陀佛，施主，可曾听闻过西天极乐妙音鸟，迦陵频伽的伟业?: Amitabha. Have you ever heard tell of the divine music brought forth by the celestial bird of the Western Pure Land, the wondrous Kalaviṅka?

阿弥陀佛，燃灯只懂救人，不会举刀。: Amitabha... This monk only knows how to save lives, not to harm.

阿弥陀佛，贫僧口中的未竟之事，正是游侠面前所见的骸骨……: Amitabha… the unfinished business I spoke of… is the remains before you…

阿景与阿达拖着步子挪回营地。阿达瘫在草垛上彻底歇了心思，阿景却咽不下这口气，偏要:
Jing and Da dragged their feet back to camp. Da collapsed on a haystack, completely giving up the idea. But Jing couldn't swallow his frustration; he was determined to uncover Uncle Zhang's origins. After all they'd been through, he no longer acted recklessly. Instead, he hid behind a woodpile, watching for a glimpse of that familiar tattered robe. 
Later, as the ancient scroll was gradually restored, inch by inch, Uncle Zhang's madness seemed to recede. He would often crouch in the moonlight, stroking the yellowed paper, his knuckles rasping against the worn edges. Finally, when a wanderer filled in the last stroke of missing ink, Uncle Zhang suddenly smiled, deep creases forming at the corners of his eyes. 
That night, Jing hid as usual in the reeds. He saw Uncle Zhang standing on the riverbank, throwing back his head and laughing loudly, the sound startling roosting birds. The previously blurred characters on the Heng Blade now glimmered with golden light, clearly discernible as the characters "Guiyi." 
"Thus, we can go home now." 
No sooner had the words left his mouth than his broken armor seemed to ripple. Uncle Zhang's body began to blur, dissolving into fireflies that vanished into the night wind, flying westward, disappearing into the darkness. All that remained was half a scroll of the "Hexi Map" lying among the pebbles. 
Jing rubbed his eyes, unable to believe what he had seen. He rushed over and snatched up the map. 
Unfurling it slowly, he saw the territories of the eleven prefectures of Hexi meticulously outlined, with military fortresses like Jade Gate Pass and Yangguan Pass clearly marked. At the end of the map, a letter slipped out. 
Uncle Zhang's message was kind, his tone calm.
"Young man, following me these past few days must have disappointed you." 
"...I remember it... I remember my home, I remember the Great Tang, and I remember my soldiers. They were just like you. Their eyes bright, looking at me as they waited for me to lead them home..."
"We, too, risked our lives escorting, crossing over, standing on the bodies of comrades to look ahead... Only, what we escorted was a map. What we crossed were the icy crevasses of the Qilian Mountains' passes. And what we stood shoulder-to-shoulder, straining to see... were the beacon fires in the desert, and beyond those fires, Chang'an city." 
"Sorry... these past few days... I mistook you for my boys..."
The morning light was piercing. Jing rushed back to camp, wanting to tell everyone. To his surprise, everyone's memory of Uncle Zhang had dissipated like smoke. 
"No, I still have the letter!" He hurriedly unfolded the letter, only to find the writing had vanished without a trace. 
"You must have been dreaming, right?" The crowd laughed and dispersed. Jing rubbed his head, his heart full of confusion. 
Could it have been... just a dream? But these past few days... they felt so vivid...

Chen Tu had spent his entire life crossing one hurdle after another.

In the past, to join the Mohists, he had endured countless nights studying until his oil lamp burned dry. After entering the sect, he buried himself in the study of mechanics day and night. Later, when he decided to return home, the hurdles he had already crossed became entirely new challenges.
But he had crossed them all in the end. All those past hardships had faded away like smoke, leaving behind only his worn Mohist disciple's robe as a quiet testament to his journey.

At first, Chen Tu had planned to simply take the robe with him to the grave.
But on second thought, he remembered his apprentice, that quiet, silly lad.
Aside from this robe, he really had nothing else of value to leave behind for the boy.
So, Chen Tu folded the robe carefully and set it aside.

That kid hadn't even been to Mohist City yet. Since this robe was a relic of the city, it could serve as a keepsake.
And if the boy decided he didn't want to go in the future, that was fine too.
Everyone has their own hurdles to cross in life. Chen Tu was merely a guide for one short stretch of the boy's journey.

Keep moving forward, kid!
Perhaps one day, that silly lad would cross his own hurdles and see even more beautiful sights.
Chen Tu only hoped that when that time came, this tattered disciple's robe could keep the boy company in his stead.

Hidden in the southern woods of Moonveil Mountain is Tiger Fort, supposedly founded by the three legendary outlaw brothers—Zhang Long, Zhang Hu, and Zhang Bao. Xue was the pride and joy of the schoolmaster. In every lesson, she sat in the very front row, her back straight as an arrow. She always took her coursework seriously, keeping her handwriting perfectly neat and orderly.
But Xue had no friends. The other children didn't like playing with her, calling her a stickler and a bore. She didn't care. She just needed to read more books, solve more equations, and memorize more blueprints. Only then could she pass into the Inner Sect and become a Grand Artisan.
Yet... whenever she stole a quiet moment away from her books, she couldn't help but wonder what the outside of Mohist City looked like.

"The world outside is dangerous," her mother always warned.
The farthest Xue had ever traveled was to the Old City, where they went to pay respects to her father. The stone tablets were weathered and mottled. When the wind blew, they sounded like someone whispering. Her mother would point to the row of small boxes, reciting the names one by one.
"This is your grandfather, this is your uncle, this is your father... He passed away when he left the mountains to build a bridge for people."
Xue only felt a heavy weight on her young shoulders.

So when the schoolmaster asked her to look after two kids from Jadestream Valley, Xue was thrilled. She had it all planned out. If they were girls, they would build wooden kites together. If they were boys, she would give them the latest editions from the Shangxian Bookstore.
But Su and Mi from Jadestream Valley were completely different. One took three whole days just to assemble a single wooden eagle. The other folded his textbook into a paper crane, sending it soaring out the window with a whoosh while laughing out loud.

Xue grew anxious, her words tumbling out. "If you keep this up, you'll never get into the Inner Sect! What will you do if you can't become Grand Artisans?"
Mi didn't even look up from folding his paper bird. "Then we just won't be Grand Artisans. We'll be the Three Junior Paragons!"
"The Three Junior Paragons?" Xue froze. "What's that?"
"That's the three of us!" Mi tossed his hand up, letting the paper crane catch the breeze and fly out the window. "A title we'll make for ourselves without relying on anyone else!"

"So... what does it take to be these Three Paragons?" Xue asked hesitantly.
Mi was stumped. He scratched his head. "Hey Su, what does it take to be the Three Junior Paragons?"
Su slowly looked up at the question. "Probably... being as amazing as Master Raven."
Xue smiled. "Who is Master Raven? How amazing is he? Is he even greater than the Grandmaster?"
"The Grandmasters of today are all Master Raven's disciples. Of course he's the greatest." Mi blinked at her.

"You're just bragging again. I don't believe a word of it... If you're really his disciples, why are your quiz scores worse than mine?" Xue shook her head.
"It's just a silly little quiz. We don't bother studying that stuff!" Mi stood up proudly. "Dare to challenge me in mechanics?"
"You're on!" she blurted out, only to lose spectacularly.
"Master Raven always said reading alone makes you rigid. Tell you what, I'll teach you mechanics, and you teach me how to read," Mi said, rubbing his nose.

...

Sitting atop the mechanical ox, Xue watched the silhouette of Mohist City fade into the distance. From afar, it looked like a wooden kite waiting to take flight.
She thought it wouldn't be too late to decide her path after visiting Jadestream Valley. Whether she became one of the Three Junior Paragons or a great Mohist artisan, there was still plenty of time.

Again and again, Han Wei traced that man's visage in his mind.
A dragon robe drenched in blood. City gates thrown wide. The man came riding through on horseback, each hoofbeat pressing a crescent moon of blood into the earth, one after another, trampling over loyalty and treachery, love and hatred, all the way to the Golden Throne Hall. And those blood-red crescents would begin to curve into a smile, a grin about to split open and swallow the world whole: the heads of grown men, the flatbreads clutched in the hands of women and children. Every time, it ended this way.
Try as he might, he could not picture that face unsullied by blood. Yes, blood. His father's blood. His mother's blood. The blood of the entire Han clan.
And as he lingered on the thought, blood began to trickle from the corner of that face's eye in the vision before him, winding down in a long red thread. That man was crying? How could he cry? He was emperor now. His name would be written into the chronicles for ages to come. What did he have to weep for?

Then pain jolted him back. Ah, the blood was flowing from his own palm.
He released the guqin string. It was already slick with red. He had gripped it so hard that it had cut into his palm. The most beautiful woman in Velvet Shade had once told him he ought to cherish these hands, hands made for the guqin, for the flute. How had they ended up sullied by work like this? "Drink this cup of poison yourself, and you'll have repaid Velvet Shade for all its kindness over the years..." It seemed like a lifetime ago, and yet he still remembered every word.
But the moment he lifted his head, that blood-streaked face was about to fade away again. No. He could not allow that. He must not forget. If even he forgot how to hate, then who in this world would remember?

"You're really going to kill him? By yourself? Are you mad?" asked the woman, another soul as solitary as he was, her eyes wide with a rare flash of shock.
He did not answer. He only took the blood from his palm and drew it lightly across his throat, tracing a crimson line like a noose.

Han Tong sat alone in his study, writing a petition as his thoughts drifted. The late Emperor had passed, the young heir had ascended, and the winds in Bianliang were turning dark. In the streets and alleys, rumors about the Palace Guard Commander were spreading. Han Tong didn't want to dwell on the gossip, but his intuition, honed by half a lifetime of leading troops, told him the sky was too quiet: so quiet that one had to be on guard.

The wooden chest beside him was half open, and an old battle helmet lay quietly at the bottom.

His illegitimate son Han Shouliang had returned to the capital. Having sneaked back to Bianliang from Jiangnan, he had become the faction master of Grace Pavilion at Revelry Hall. Despite being in the same city, Han Tong had never visited Revelry Hall. First, he didn't want to expose his son's status as a hidden agent; second, the Han family were archers and warriors, unaccustomed to the entertainment and music of such places.

Rumors said Master Han was a master of both flute and zither, a musical genius. Han Tong would only snort coldly whenever he heard this. But in the deep of night, his hand would pause while polishing his armor.

Perhaps once this ill wind in the city subsided, if the boy knew his place and returned home in one piece... perhaps he would allow him to play some trifling tune. Just one.

"General! An urgent letter!"
The servant's cry came suddenly. Han Tong took the note, and his expression changed as if struck by lightning. He kicked over the table, grabbed his blade, and rushed out...

He left in such a hurry that he forgot to don his armor and forgot the half-open chest by his feet. The battle helmet that had accompanied him through years of bloodshed missed his final battle.

I have so much fresh gossip bottled up here that I am nearly fit to burst. In the daytime, there is at least Xiao Lian to listen to me for a few words, but all she ever does is nod, shake her head, nod, shake her head. But this time is different. There is nothing in this letter about the Northern Vow's serious affairs, so surely you will not have the heart to burn it. You will just have to find a little box and hide it away instead, which suits me perfectly.
No doubt you find that strange. With war at hand, and Khitans along the Hutuo swarming like cockroaches, step on one and a whole nest comes scuttling out, how could there be nothing worth writing about?
Ah, but that is because I have lately come upon a secret so great it nearly rattled me apart. Truly, it is something astonishing.
But I am not telling you.

Heaven is high and the world is wide. You have no way of knowing beneath which eave I am prattling away at this very moment. Even if you stamp your foot in frustration, you still will not catch me. I have always admired you. You can look after the Qi family estate, handle trade and the affairs of cultivation, and win the trust of so many besides. Even along the borderlands, the common folk often speak of you. Hearing it makes me proud, sweet as honey on the tongue.
But before long, my own name will be known throughout the realm as well. Once this business is done, the tales sung on the opera stage, the stories told in the teahouses, and the storybooks sold in every street and lane will all resound with Ding Xiang's great name.

On a snowy night, a group of soldiers arrived at a farmer's thatched shed. 
The farmer's hands trembled. If he didn't open the door, he would die immediately; if he did, he would still die. He stuffed his wife and daughter, huddled in the corner of the bed, into a tattered wardrobe and unlocked the door with shaking hands. 
The leader was Zhang Yichao, and his soldiers the Guiyi Army. The farmer didn't know those names, but he felt that this group of soldiers in blue robes was different from the usual jackals. 
They only borrowed forage to feed their war horses and dry firewood to build a campfire. The farmer invited them into the house to escape the cold, but the blue-robed soldiers declined. This was the farmer's house, and the Guiyi Army would not disturb the people. 
When dawn arrived, no one in the thatched shed had slept a wink. Zhang Yichao asked for the farmer's name and said he would definitely return what he had borrowed. The farmer thought it was just polite talk. The soldiers were merciful enough to leave him and his family alive. How could he dare to hope for anything else? 
That was until the blue-robed soldiers appeared again. With them came a new land system, a new household registration list, and that name, Zhang Yichao. A soldier called the farmer's name from the roster and exempted him from a year's firewood tax. 
The farmer looked at the blue-robed soldiers. Surprised that the powerful would keep their promises. At least this Zhang Yichao did, for now.

Forgotten bundles were no rare sight along the post roads. A young scholar bound for Chang'an to sit the examinations came upon a faded cloth sack propped against the gnarled roots of an old locust tree by the road. The sack was full and round, but its owner was nowhere to be seen. A pack of wolves stood circled around it, yet not one would go near. The scholar, not wishing the owner to return and find it gone, reached down and picked it up. It was warm to the touch, and from somewhere within came what sounded like quiet, low weeping.
The sack was not heavy, but it clung to his palm as if it had taken root there. That night, when he stopped at an inn and tried to open it, the drawstring cinched itself tight on its own, like a living thing refusing to give. Under the lamp, the cloth looked old and worn, and a stubborn smell of rust and damp earth clung to it that would not leave.
He dreamed of an armored figure, broken and bloodied, crawling across a field of corpses, murmuring without cease: "Home. Let me go home." He woke with a start to find the sack burning hot in his hand. A sticky, dark liquid was seeping through the weave and dripping between his fingers. Half his body had gone numb. When he looked into the mirror, his left arm had grown faint, fading toward nothing.
Three days later, the sack lay open on the bed at the inn, empty of everything but the thick smell of old blood and rust. The scholar was gone, leaving no trace. Only the faded cloth sack remained, still round and full, the drawstring now slack and loose. Outside, the wind moaned low, and beneath it came the distant sound of armor, fading down the road.

The girls of Ghost Revelry Hall often whispered about the "devouring room" hidden within its walls, a place where the living walked in, and only bones came out.
So they obeyed the overseers with trembling diligence, never daring to wonder, speak of, or question what lay inside.
Only a young pageboy knows the truth: the dark chamber holds a girl.

She is tattered, half-scarred, and deranged. Anyone who meets her gaze falls to her blade.
Yet in rare moments, the girl would lapse into silence, then begin humming a fractured lullaby. The melody came in gasps and whispers, a wounded sound that hung in the air like blood in water.
Like a flower trembling in the dead of night, battered by wind, broken by rain, its roots rotted and veins severed... yet deep within its crumbling petals, a stubborn crimson still clings.
It made listeners ache with pity.

But pity changed nothing.
To survive here, one learned to turn away. To forget the devoured.

Among the Fourteen Fiends of Ghost Street, none inspire more fear than the Seventh—Ghost Master Jiang Kui. 
Man or ghost? Virtue or vice? No one knows for sure. At times, he is the gentlest of princes, reciting sutras and bidding farewell to innocent women crushed by a cruel world. Other times, he becomes a nightmare cloaked in flesh, spinning his paper umbrella as he cuts down all who stand before him. 

They respect him. They fear him. But none understand him. 

And Jiang Kui doesn't care. For years, he has wandered in a faded wedding robe, waiting for one who will never return. Day and night blur into a haze of remorse that gnaws through the soul. And when he heard rumors of a remedy hidden deep in the Mistveil Forest, a drug that could raise the dead, restore flesh to bone. For the first time in years, he felt truly awake. 

Sis... even if it's a fool's errand, A'kui must take this path.

The carp is king among fish, and its patterns come in red, white, and yellow. 

Carp is delicious, and the practice of raising carp flourished during the Han dynasty. The ancients believed that a carp could leap the Dragon Gate and transform into a dragon, making it the most revered species among fish. China's earliest fish farming manual, Fan Li's Fish Farming Classic, also records methods for raising carp.

Crucian carp were domesticated in China over a thousand years ago. Later, a golden variant emerged, becoming the ancestor of today's goldfish and eventually forming a distinct breed. It wasn't until the Ming and Qing dynasties that breeding techniques became more advanced and standardized.

She had broken countless promises in her life, but upon hearing that the remnants of the Khitan Flying Dragon were still searching for Hidden Mountain,
she immediately set aside all mundane affairs and left the mountain to intercept and kill.
She had intended to assist him, but unexpectedly, she lost an arm in the process.
While her wound was not yet healed, during a brief return to the mountain to recuperate, she tried to recreate Halcyon Brew.
But with only one arm, weak as she was, she could only produce a jar of blood wine...

Another year passed. One day, a jar of wine brewed from red fruits was placed at her door without anyone knowing who.
She asked Ying Ning and Ying An, but both mumbled evasively.
The taste of this wine was completely different from Halcyon Brew or Monkey Brew.
Subtle and smooth, gentle on the throat. It's a pity the brewer said nothing, and the drinker remained silent.
Though the paths they walked were different, even the finest wine now has two distinct flavors.

Peng had once been young, young enough to ride the gale into the heavens.
From the depths of the abyss, the great peng soared, ascending to the very sun to pluck filaments of light like gold leaves, pressing them into withered, skeletal hands.
She was not like the "geniuses" commonly found within the Mohist.
Most "geniuses," however brilliant, display their mastery only within the pages of books or the intricacies of their inventions.
But set them to deal with the world, to force a smile for greedy officials while yielding not an inch, to slip half a string of copper coins to a cunning sergeant for a crippled youth, or to confront a derelict peasant who drank away the seed grain lent by the Mohist...
These geniuses would likely stammer a few clumsy excuses before fleeing back to their mountains in tears, retreating to the safety of their scrolls and mechanisms.
But Peng was different.
Peng was no mere bird suspended in the heavens; when called for, she could be the fish lurking in the lightless depths.
Managing wealth, vying for power, playing all sides, trimming her sails to the wind, sizing up her mark...
So long as she could wrench grain from the mouths of the rich to feed the famished, she cared not if she walked alongside greed, folly, and the absurd.
In her youth, she accomplished a feat of great renown. Back during the Changxing era, the official farm tools were shoddy and dear. Loath to see the season squandered, she exploited a loophole to procure modular planks and wheels, fashioning them into mechanisms for the villages.
Should the officials come to inspect, they would find nothing but a heap of inscrutable timber.
The ruse was so masterfully executed that even the minor clerk, having pocketed her silver, could only click his tongue in awe during his rounds.
Peng did not let the moment slip. She brewed a pot of coarse tea-stalks and invited him to rest.
Gazing at the wheat, the minor clerk drained three cups of that base brew. Upon leaving, he "forgot" the silver on the table.
She encountered the minor clerk a second time upon the streets of the county.
He was gnawing on a cold, hard bun while pasting up notices of a new levy.
At the sight of her, he straightened his back, feigning nonchalance as he spoke of a recent petition he'd submitted, mentioning, in passing, matters of the harvest, iron-smelting, and inspections.
He clumsily adopted an official air, boasting that his words now held a measure of weight.
She smiled and offered a few claps of her hands.

All under heaven is the Emperor's land.

She refilled the second.

In her lifetime, Heron had seen too many people who lived by the creed of striving beyond their limits.
