In truth, she was somewhat like them herself. Yet more often than not, she had to embody the laws of Gasping Cliff. She was the Gatekeeper. Much like the hidden ratchets turning unseen in the darkness, she guarded the throat of Mohist Hill, keeping those who dared to trespass at bay.
The irony was that it had been Feng who allowed that person inside.

Heron, of course, did not believe a single word of his story. As for the man himself, she had already reached her own conclusion. After all, she was the one who had opened the gate for him.
Had she not done so, that foolish disciple of the Inkbound Order would have long since become another nameless ghost haunting these peaks. Some careless master had given him a Disciple Token and taught him the path to the precipice, yet failed to reveal the secret mechanism to open the mountain's maw.

The timing had been unfortunate as well. He arrived during the quietest period when no one entered or left. Had even a single disciple passed through on their return, he would not have been reduced to surviving on tree bark and wild roots, looking more like a forest savage than a scholar.
Heron dragged the half-dead wild man into the depths of the cliff. The moment he awoke, his gaze was captured by the towering, grim mechanisms hidden within. He completely forgot his strange surroundings.
Only after a long while did he notice Heron standing in the shadows.

Before she could speak, he mistook her for a fellow lost traveler. He began fumbling through the gears on his own, and to her surprise, he actually found a path upward.
"Miss, follow me! There might be a way up." The wild man did not rush ahead, but instead turned and offered her his hand.
Exactly as she wished. The corner of Heron's mouth twitched into an unreadable curve. Very well. She would see for herself if this Disciple Token was truly earned.

Back then, he was just a desperate wanderer struggling to find the gate. Now, he was guiding others, leading them toward the heights they held in their hearts.

Heron recalled the Everlink Form. When iron chains interlocked, they could repel thousands of troops. Yet when hearts interlocked, they formed a mountain range that stretched endlessly. Though the peaks were high and the road long, a united front could withstand all storms.
She was the one who opened the gate. Like the sunrise breaking over the peaks, she waited for the next unyielding soul, ready to personally guide them up the mountain path.

What trouble have they run into lately? What books are making the rounds? What's the latest gossip? And, most importantly, what new nicknames have they cooked up for the old "Rotten Stork"?
Watching them, he sees echoes of himself when he was young. And echoes of the ones who never came back.
This old soul, with his relentless inquiries and occasional bouts of eccentricity, never forgets what he really is: an elder of the Mohist Hill. He watches over every disciple like they're his own. He keeps his finger on the pulse of everything that happens within the mountain.
Truth be told, among his peers, there were many who eclipsed him in brilliance. In his youth, the thought of ascending to Elderhood had never crossed his mind. The reason was simple: so many of those radiant souls left the mountain, and they never returned.
Generation upon generation, his eyes have clouded with age, while his heart, once raw and unversed, has been chiseled open, valve by valve. He is like a weathered foundation stone, quietly wedged at the very base of this great edifice, unassuming, unyielding, watching the tides of change wash over Mohist Hill for decades. A new Grandmaster has arrived, another youth. To be young... it is a wondrous thing.
The only constant within the walls of Mohist City is the spirit of these young souls. There is always someone young, generation after generation...

The rain by the Yellow River was unlike the rain anywhere else in Kaifeng.
Some said the rain was the tears of the River Master, trapped in the Yellow River for millennia, crying endlessly.
Que from the Bujian Hill, hearing this tale, found it amusing: how could the mighty River Master, who could summon wind and rain, be like a child, wailing at the slightest grievance?
Otherwise, how else would there be such relentless storms along the Yellow River?

But Que had never been one to cry. Crying couldn't defeat mountain bandits, fill an empty stomach, or cure a lingering illness. To the sparrow, crying was the most useless thing in the world. The most useful? Her own two hands. When pain was unbearable, she gathered herbs to heal herself. When hunger gnawed at her, she foraged wild plants and hunted animals. When her family was homeless, she apprenticed to a craftsman in Hidden Mountain, learning to build the best houses in the land for her crippled father and blind mother. She believed, up until the day their home was completed, that there was nothing her hands couldn't accomplish. But then, the young doctor from the clinic came running: "A'que, your parents... they didn't make it."

Some things, she realized, were beyond human effort. It all seemed to depend on fate. That day, she buried her parents by the new house and walked southward. Behind her, flames engulfed everything. Men were so small in the grand scheme of things, powerless to move the heavens or earth, no matter how hard they tried. So, where should one go? What was the point of all her skills? "Even the River Master, who can summon storms in the tales, can't stop the Yellow River from weeping," she thought bitterly, drenched in rain.

But at that moment, the storm ceased.
Before her stood a figure in red. "Hey, you're soaked. Come home with me."

The flying squirrel eats mist and dwells in the forest. It flies and nurses, appearing as both beast and bird.

The flying squirrel is mentioned in the Xunzi from the Warring States period. The "Encouraging Learning" chapter mentions its five limited skills: it can fly but not onto a roof, climb but not to the top, swim but not across a valley, burrow but not hide its body, and run but not outpace a man. This led to the idiom "The flying squirrel's skills are exhausted," meaning someone has reached the limit of their meager talents. However, Guo Pu of the Wei and Jin periods took a different view, praising it as a little immortal that lives on mist and dwells in the forest, untainted by the world.

I
This fleeting life, a waking dream,
I sing to my qin by the blossoms' gleam.
Let not the east wind wait in vain.
I long for your letters, again and again,
And pray the years are kind and bright.
Though frost now settles in my hair like light,
It is to you I give my spring.

II
I play an old and somber strain,
While crows sit silent in the chilling rain.
My tears have stained the letter red,
I watch the empty skies for words unsaid.
My youth before a shattered mirror wanes,
And every day of yearning adds new pains.
Cursed is this long life, let it be brief instead.
